Uniform title: Piṅgalāmata Secondary title: Jayadrathādhikāra Manuscript: NGMCP 3-376/vi, Śaivatantra 113

Description: The *Piṅgalāmata* is a *Pratiṣṭhātantra*. In this context, the term *pratiṣṭhā* denotes the rites of consecration and installation of a representation of a deity, a temple, or a shrine, as well as related matters.
By means of this [knowledge], one [attains mastery] over such subjects as iconometry, iconography, and the structural design and layout of temples,
monasteries, royal palaces, and towns. Practically all the early surviving *Pratiṣṭhātantras* belong to the *Siddhānta* tradition.

The *Piṅgalāmata* is an exception, as it affiliates itself with the predominantly Śākta *Brahmayāmala* (*Picumata*). Furthermore, as its alternative title— *Jayadrathādhikāra*— indicates, it is also associated with...

The *Jayadrathayāmala* is centered on Kālī. The *Piṅgalāmata* itself also confirms this. Thus, although the procedures it teaches are for the most part Saiddhāntika, in addition to those, it also teaches ritual procedures.
and provides details of the iconography of the Vāma, Yāmala, and Trika traditions.

Piṅgalā said:
"O Lord, one understands the characteristics of all things through scripture; yet scripture itself is endowed with characteristics. O Master, explain this to me in its true manner."
O Lord of Gods, how is the connection of this scripture described? For the sake of the individual practitioner, please explain its purpose and the method of its exposition and study.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Your inquiry and deliberation are appropriate.
I shall explain it without doubt, as well as its foremost characteristic.

Because it is understood everywhere as the object of knowledge, because it has arrived at renunciation, and because it instructs and causes one to wander [from ignorance], it is therefore called a "śāstra."
That by which one knows and leads is not called "knowledge";
it is merely thought to be so constantly, yet the wise know it to be false.
The meaning of the words, whether established by the wise through scripture or even inferred,
has come down through the lineage of succession from the lotus-mouth of Śiva.
That which is established through the characteristics of intention is called "scripture" (āgama);
it should be understood by the wise according to the principle of the relationship between speaker and listener.

The oral teacher (vaktrācārya), however, may be a primary practitioner (sādhaka) or someone else; the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka) are certainly not those who have mastered even half of the Śiva-scripture.
Even though these two are knowers of the meaning, those who seek results should not listen [to them];
rather, it is the initiate, the son, and the adept who are the listeners of the Āgama itself.
All the preceptors and lords were firm-vowed devotees of Śiva;
they were consecrated by means of mantras and non-mantras, and were devoted to the rules of Tantric conduct.
Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, the scripture should be heard and explained;
this is the rule proclaimed specifically for the scripture known as Bhairava.
In a well-pleased, level, and pure pavilion prepared for the sacrifice,
one should then cause the exposition to take place upon a portion of ground smeared with lime.
Facing either east or north, pure and with his mind fixed upon that [deity],
he should utter three claps of the hands and protect the directions with the weapon-mantra.
Having established the nature of one's own practice both externally and internally,
and having meditated upon the state of omniscience, one becomes Śiva himself.
Compassionate toward all, steadfast, and sympathetic to all sentient beings,
he is preeminent in wisdom and exerts himself for the sake of benefiting everyone.
1b) Or, he should first inform his guru, or his paternal elder brother, or one of equal learning— if he is approved— out of affection regarding the knowledge [he intends to impart].
Listen now to how it should be heard by the listeners according to the prescribed rule:
a ceremonial cloth (paṭṭa) must be prepared for the purpose of the Yoga-pīṭha.
And that [seat], auspiciously marked, is made of śrīparṇika wood and other materials;
it is two cubits long including the fingers, and one and a half cubits wide.
And when, O Goddess of the Gods, both the preceptor and the disciple are present in their primary form, the Yoga-pīṭha extends to a length of forty finger-breadths at its end.
In length and breadth, it shall be nine finger-breadths; O Dear One, the two feet extend for one cubit and are as broad as before.
The two feet of Gajapāda, with their curved nails in the middle, should be joined together;
one should fashion that pair of conchs facing each other.
One should decorate the center of the pedestal with various leafy creepers;
above that, one should draw a central lotus and some slightly blossoming vines.
In the same manner, two lotuses with auspicious characteristics should be fashioned as wings;
at their ends, they are suspended by a garland of leaf-fragments.
Indeed, the Guru who desires to hear [the teaching] must act in this manner:
[the seat] should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length and likewise in width.
The practitioner should prepare the yoga-seat as before,
O lady of excellent complexion, whenever there is a principal listener who is indeed a spiritual son (putraka).
Then, the yoga-pīṭha is said to be thirty fingers in length and four fingers in width.
The remaining form, characterized by auspicious marks, should be made as before;
that which was previously mentioned is primary, whether it be the *liṅgin* or even the one with the Lord (*seśvara*).
The *yogapīṭha* (seat of yoga) shall be twenty-four finger-breadths in length as before;
it is two finger-breadths in width and distinguished by its specific characteristics.
The feet, with a span of twenty finger-breadths, move gradually like the sun;
by this sequential yoga, they are well-restrained.
Seated upon a lotus throne, he is indeed wisdom itself, perfectly worshipped.
Having placed a waist-belt joined with a girdle and provided with a female elephant’s tusk and chalk before the yoga-seat, one should propitiate the Guru.
"By your grace...
[omitted] "...thereupon the illustrious Guru, being delighted, set his mind upon the task of exposition."
When the middle term is omitted, that which is written— whether it be the root-mantra or what is presented—
is where the Śaiva preceptor should worship Bhairava or the Śaktis.
One should worship the lineage of gurus in the lotus previously prepared on the left; one should worship the chalk and the thread of knowledge in the lotus on the right.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth— and with special unguents if they are available— having praised Śiva, Vāgīśvarī, and likewise Vighnarāja;
One should reveal the Guru and the Knowledge-Guru through their relationship and so forth;
for one is indeed common to all, while the other is unique.
All that is well-known is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*);
they know that which is established for this [subject] to be common at that time.
Now I shall fully explain the connection that exists therein,
as well as the designation, the cause, the agent, and the measure.

Having first stated the purpose, one should subsequently describe it according to the speaker. "Of this" refers to that [purpose], and "of him" refers to the name; thus, it is known by the name of the *Piṅgalāmata*. It is the foundation and the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for worship according to one's qualification, and it is said to be within the *Brahmayāmala*. Piṅgalā is the venerable mistress (*bhaṭṭārikā*), who is the causal sign (*nimitta*).
Who is the agent? The Blessed Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha is the agent. What is its extent? It is said to be eight thousand [verses]. And that [text] is of two kinds: the Kāmarūpi and the Oḍayoni.
This one is the Kāmarūpi. What is its purpose? Its characteristic is the establishment of the manifest and unmanifest liṅgas.

The purpose of thorough knowledge is as follows: although both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) exist, that which consists merely of the subtle elements (*mātra*) is the unmanifest.
That which is joined with all the characteristics of the constituent parts (*avayava*) is the manifest.
Thus, the manifest and the unmanifest possess the characteristics of both forms. And that which possesses both forms [is characterized] by the heart, the throat, the palate, and so forth.
One should describe the subsequent sections after having established the connection; for it is said, "one should relate [them] subsequently.
Alternatively, the connection must be stated beforehand, and that is of three kinds.
The relationship characterized by the introduced and the introducer; the relationship characterized by the suggested and the suggester;

and the relationship characterized by the manifested and the manifester. Among these, the relationship characterized by the introduced and the introducer is stated as follows: the Teacher is the introducer (*avatāraka*) and the treatise is the introduced (*avatārya*). Thus, the treatise is what is introduced, and the Teacher is the introducer.

The relationship characterized by the indicated (*vyaṅgya*) and the indicator (*vyañjaka*) is now stated: for the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the defined (*lakṣya*) is the indicated; for the defined, the definition is the indicator. The relationship characterized by the illuminated (*prakāśya*) and the illuminator (*prakāśa*) is now stated: for the word (*śabda*), the meaning (*artha*) is the illuminated; for the meaning, the word is the illuminator. Now, [the end] of the *Brahmayāmala*—
The Prātītyātāśaṅkādaurvāsya, the Paicika, the Sārasvata-mata,
as well as the Jayadratha and the Phetkāra, which is proclaimed as the fifth.
The *Brahmayāmala* is sevenfold, beginning with the *Rakta* and beginning with the *Laṃpaṭa*.
Among these seven types of *Brahmayāmala*, what is this? This is the *Jayadratha*; the *Jayadratha* is also a sevenfold scripture (*sūtra*).
The Sūtra, the Uttarasūtra, and the Śaktisūtra are called Kriyā.
And the *Vimalajñānasaṃjñā* is the seventh among all the compendiums.
Among these seven types of sūtras, which one is this? This is the *Kriyāsūtra*. The *Kriyāsūtra* is also fivefold.
Free from pride, protect him; he is indeed endowed with meditative concentration.

And that which is joined with the purpose of the ritual (*kalpa*) is considered the "action of the five bowls" (*pañcapātrakriyā*). Among these five types of action-sūtras, what is this? This is the sūtra joined with the purpose of the ritual. What is meant by "the purpose of the ritual"? The essence of the ritual is the "purpose of the ritual"; it is that which is correctly joined with the essence of the ritual.

Appointed for the purpose of the ritual (*kalpa*). Alternatively: "Or else, one who is purified by initiation from me and endowed with his own office should perform [the rite] based on the *liṅga*, having understood the mantra and the *liṅga* with its characteristics. For even through mantras, divinity is attained by relying upon the *liṅga*, even by those who are destitute."
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment, one should take refuge in that very linga.
3a) Once the connection [between the words] has been established, one should then provide the explanation by means of word-by-word analysis and so forth;
or rather, one should begin the explanation in such a way that the listener understands it.
By means of chalk and other such materials, by lines, or by verbal description;
The disciple, having come forward to face him, knelt upon the ground and bowed again and again to the Guru, who was like a venerable deity descended from heaven.
Afterwards, with one's mind fixed solely on Śiva, one should listen in due order;
when doubt arises, one should inquire, and wherever one gains understanding, one should recite it.
One should not create an obstacle, whether it be primary or conceived by the intellect;
rather, O Goddess of the gods, one should act whenever it is approved by the Ācārya.
A great fault arises if [the ritual] is interrupted, even for those of superior intelligence;
therefore, upon its completion, one should again worship as before, in the proper sequence.
Having dismissed the sacrificial altar and [removed] the remains of the offering, the flowers, the wealth, and so forth,
one should cause the preceptor to rest well, from the head down to the feet.
Having performed prostration and worship, one should ask the Guru for forgiveness;
then, with the nectar known as Bhairava and other substances, one should perform both the commencement and the dismissal.
If he has prepared that [offering], it should be offered with sacrificial porridge (caru) and other such items;
at that time, whatever food has arrived—whether cooked or even raw—should be used.
The listeners should offer betel, camphor, and all such items,
as well as garments, gold, jewels, and the like, whenever they arrive during the time of the exposition.
All of that is obtained from the Guru, or whatever else is approved;
having risen and reflected upon the supreme, at midday, one should perform the daily rite with the *Hnikā* mantra.
Listen: whether it be for two days, or even for a single day of the Guru, one should reflect according to one's own capacity, or those of dull intellect should recite it.
Having recognized his own wisdom, he should undertake one of these [stages],
beginning with what is to be heard and the scriptures, until indeed their completion.
If one should be negligent regarding the meaning [of the texts], one must perform an expiation;
one must observe a suspension of study—listen to that, O fair-faced one.
In general and in particular, regarding hearing, study, reflection,
and the [four] attainments, as well as on the fourth, eighth, and ninth [lunar days], [one should practice].
3b) On the auspicious day of the full moon, there is indeed no white commentary or the like;
likewise, O Dear One, on the dark fortnight, one should perform [the rites] for six days ending with the *riktā* tithis.
The remaining study and other practices for the two fortnights are new every day;
this has been declared as the general rule, so now understand the specific details.
The two equinoxes, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the southern and northern solstices,
as well as Viṣṇupada and the six Aṣṭakās, should be known as the "mouths" (entrances) of the year.
O noble lady, this period is known as the *tridaśāha* (thirteen days), yet it consists of twelve years;
during the periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*), one should perform [the rites] for each day in due order.
During the Aṣṭaka festivals, there should be three days, and for those [other occasions], the number shall be three;
during lunar and solar eclipses, one should perform it for five days.
There are five days of impurity on the occasion of Indra’s festival (Śakrotsava), three days when [an eclipse] has occurred,
five days during the Pavitrārohaṇa ceremony, and likewise on the full moon day of Kārttika.
The three days known as Mahānavamī and Vedhamajñā,
as well as those designated as Pavitrārohaṇa, should be observed as days on which study is prohibited.
When a sage has died, when a perfected being (siddha) has passed away, or when one is in the presence of something invisible;
having seen or heard [such things], one should suspend study and perform meditation, recitation, and so forth.
The husband’s companions should perform the act accompanied by kissing;
listen now as I describe that momentary rite exactly as it is.
When there is a thunderclap without a preceding cloud, when the Great King has died,
when Tāraka has risen, and when there is a conflagration spreading through the quarters of the sky;
In the case of mist, a great wind, the appearance of a comet,
and unseasonable rain, it is declared that [the impurity] lasts for that duration.
O Goddess, I shall now tell you something else concerning the timely events involving ascetics,
brahmins, and the circle of kings during the planetary conjunction.
Upon hearing of the consumption of dead flesh, when a nearby woman is weeping,
when a guest has arrived, and during the festivals of cow-calving;

When the *vandinī* has arrived, during song, during the purification by vomiting, and likewise in the subsequent [stages], these indeed are the *khanikā*s in the *vāha*; they last for that duration of time according to their sequence.
When Tvaṣṭṛ has arrived from afar, and likewise his paternal group of brothers,
one should perform an equal distribution for them and then begin the explanation of their designations.
One who is not composed and lacks self-control should not perform the recitation there;
nor should one meditate on "A Ā Na Na," nor speak according to what is within [the mind].
4a) It may be a cat, a mongoose, a monitor lizard, a frog, a water-snake, or a *kālasa*.
The mongoose, the lizard, and the iguana are species belonging to the lineage of dogs and humans.
One should recite one hundred and eight times with the ear at the end [of the mantra], three times from within the presence of the Guru, and with the ear at the end of the Vidyā-mantra.
O beloved, that which was previously deficient in the interval between the kisses,
one should then recite it three thousand times within the ear-cavity for three days.
Whether situated within the *cumvaka* [cavity], in the center, or on a *yogapīṭha*,
there should be a five-night vigil, gifts and so forth, and a recitation (*japa*) of ten thousand [times].

All those [periods] designated as unfit for study (anadhyāya) must be avoided for listening to, reciting, or reflecting upon [the scriptures]; during them, one must certainly not perform great acts such as japa or pūjā.
Or, at the command of the Guru, they should be led [there] by means of acquiring wealth for one's own sake and so forth;
or one should write them down or cause them to be written, excluding those that are full or empty.
Then this noble Śāntyārya should recite the ancient Dharmaśāstras;
or he should daily practice his craft, whether it be drawing auspicious lines or carving.
Thus ends the section on exposition in the chapter concerning Jayadratha within the Piṅgalāmata.
He stood within the womb of Mahāmāyā, encompassed by the Great Yoga;
he was the state of great delight, joined with the Great Mothers.
Vāmana was accompanied by Vetālas, Tālajaṅghas, and Tāḍijaṅghas,
as well as by Nāyakas, Siddhayogins, and others such as Bhṛṅgis and Dārakas.
With dances, songs, and various musical instruments, and with many prose and verse hymns,
Bhairava— the Lord of Gods, the Master of me— was thus praised.
Seeing the Lord thus delighted, all those assembled there spoke these words to Piṅgalā, even though the rite had already been performed according to the prescribed rules.
And for those who rely on the signs of accomplishment, O Lord of Sādhakas, that which was previously described—
endowed with the characteristics of the object to be perceived and its defining marks, and consisting of the forms of valid cognition and measurement— is [to be applied].

"O Lord, that which was not known—what is its characteristic, by whom was it remembered, who is the teacher, and who is the artisan; and what is the friend of the creator for the sake of the ritual action?"
The characteristics of substances are clearly manifested by means of substances;
in what place, however, are they to be grasped, as well as the mountains and lions?
How is it that one departs from the forest in this manner?
At that time, there occurs a divine and non-divine power, both auspicious and inauspicious.
The lunar days, asterisms, and yogas, as well as the strength of the stars and the moon,
the *karana* conjoined with the day of the week— whom do these auspicious factors not bring prosperity?
O Leader of the Gods, tell us everything regarding whatever is to be performed,
for the sake of the welfare of the world— the supreme ritual manual for consecration.
Bhairava said:
O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall provide the detailed exposition for this ritual manual, which includes the fivefold installation,
exactly as it was indicated.
The object to be characterized (lakṣya) is indeed established by its cause; the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is considered to be the mode of being (bhāva).
Furthermore, the characteristic as taught in the scriptures is accepted as the long-term means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It measures out the foot, the division, and the form of the *liṅga*;
it dissolves at the end of the dissolution and creates again in the course of the Ganges.
Because it possesses the constituent parts of dissolution (*layana*), it is called a *liṅga*;
or they say that a *liṅga* is a sign (*cihna*), and a sign is indeed a seal (*mudrā*).
In this world, the mudrā is indeed the means of conviction; for this reason, it serves as the cause of grace.
This is the indicator and the signifier, whereas otherwise, the vow would lack a basis.

The talliṅga is said to be of two kinds, bestowing liberation through both the mobile and the immobile; listen to what Śiva has declared in the Āgama regarding that which grants worldly enjoyment in this world.
The teacher Cala, however, was a follower of Śiva who maintained his own dharma;
he was a benefactor of others for the sake of achieving his own goal, whether by means of mantras or otherwise.
I shall now describe the characteristics of those two in terms of their dimensions and forms,
as well as how they bestow enjoyment and liberation according to the colors from which they arise.
Now listen as the particular is being explained by way of the general;
it is not thus when one has reached the *cintyottara*, nor by another who follows the path.
To the south of the Himālaya mountains and to the east of Pañcāla, the region known as Āryāvarta is situated; its inhabitants are the foremost among practitioners.
Since he is born into a family of the first-born and is common to all,
I shall now state his specific qualification, which denotes the power of leadership.
That which is produced up to the limit of power (śakti) is called "birth at the beginning of birth" (janmāgra);
it is free from the eight defects beginning with *ka*, even if it arises in another land.
One should avoid those born in Kāmarūpa, Kāśmīra, Kaliṅga, Koṅkaṇa, Kāñcī, Kośala, Kāverī, and Rāṣṭraja.

6a) For what purpose is that? It is for the sake of accomplishment and for the sake of liberation; both are auspicious when produced by the All-Knowing One. The preceptors who maintain the Śiva-vow should be neither too tall nor too short.
He was neither deficient in limb through any measure, nor did he possess any extra parts;
with all his divine limbs complete, he was never at any time deceitful.
The mind is indeed not deluded, and consciousness is indeed the supreme fair form;
it is joined with the characterized and the characteristics, the knower of the path and its destination.
One who knows the rules for the construction of Vidyāvāstu, who understands the rules for the installation of Liṅgas and the measurement lines,
who has practiced astrology, and who is always devoted to the practice of Yoga.
Or the practitioner may be a householder; listen to how that is:
a householder who, through union with his wife, is devoted to yoga and knows the ritual procedure.
One who is industrious, endowed with courage, skilled in the arts, and possessed of intellectual dexterity is the best in all undertakings, and especially in this matter.
Devoted to the devotees of Śiva, esteemed by his guru, and a sovereign among artisans—
he must not be one-eyed, deaf, blind, or have ears like those of a cow, nor should he suffer from elephantiasis.
One whose nose, fingers, or feet have been severed, one who is cruel, or one with missing or extra limbs, is not [qualified];
nor is one with a deficient or redundant body, one who eats white food, or one whose senses are unrestrained.
He too should be knowledgeable regarding the characteristics [of the site], starting from the measurement and dimensions;
he should be wise in the rules for laying the foundation lines, steady-handed, upright, and clear-sighted.
Brave men who possess human prowess, acting as assistants, accomplish the intended task even at the cost of their lives when they are at their throats.
All were devoted to Rudra, possessed of daring, and intent on dharma; with their whole being, they were dedicated to the Self once their goal was attained.
Therefore, I shall explain the duties of the performer, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa,
who is disciplined, endowed with power, and whose mind is solely intent upon Śiva.
One whose life is sought for the sake of Dharma should undertake purposeful action;
for such action must always be performed so as to follow the path to the state of liberation.
One may construct a shrine (caitya) out of stone, wood, clay, gold, copper, silver, bell-metal, tin, lead, or even iron and other such materials.

That which is born from eggs, that which is born from wombs, that which is born from jewels, and that which arises from gems—I shall describe their causes and locations; listen to how they truly exist.
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Gandhamādana, Vipula, Nīla,
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Supārśva.
These mountains are indeed white; they are known as the lords of the great field (mahākṣetra), as well as the sages, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, and the Apsarases perfected in yoga.
All those devoted to the worship of Śiva are empowered by omniscience;
I shall now describe for you how these fires are kindled and from what materials they arise.
The Himalaya, Malaya, Vindhya, the one called Sahya,
Pāripātraka, Mahendra, the one named Nandi, Śrīśaila, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
Urjayanta, Hariścandra, Śuktimat, and the Kulaparvatas;
the rivers that have issued forth from them, as well as the forests and mountains.
On both banks of the river, there are indeed nine delightful secondary sites;
the location for these is ten yojanas outside of them.
I shall now fully explain the entry for the purpose of the mountain; listen to how it should be, as well as the departure, both favorable to oneself and for others.
Among the lunar days, the second, the third, as well as the fifth,
the seventh, the tenth, the eleventh, and the thirteenth [are auspicious].
In the bright fortnight, these [days] are indeed auspicious; now hear also which are inauspicious for auspicious purposes:
the fourth, the sixth, the eighth, and the ninth.

On the twelfth, the full moon, or especially on the fourteenth day— whether it be for inauspicious purposes or even for auspicious ones— the rites beginning with Nandā should be performed, even during the dark fortnight.
Venus, the Sun, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Moon—these are indeed auspicious when full or devoid of their ends; however, Venus and Mars are inauspicious.
Śanaiścara, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, Aśvinī,
Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, and Jyeṣṭhā are the asterisms that bring auspicious results.
Since these [asterisms]—
Kṛttikā, Maghā, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, and Mūla— are oriented with their faces turned downward, they serve as the cause for coming and going.
The first three are for inauspicious purposes, as they are declared to be downward-facing;
while Āyuṣmān, Prītisaubhāgya, Śobhana, and Śukla are auspicious.
Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Harṣaṇa, Śiva, Siddha,
Siddhi, Sukarmendra, Śubha, Brahmā, and Vaidhṛti belong to you.
7a) Due to the unfavorable conjunction of auspicious causes, there are the Śūla and Vajra [yogas] in the inauspicious;
likewise Gaṇḍa, Atigaṇḍa, Viṣkambha, Vyāghāta, and Parigha.
Sādhyā, vyatīpāta, and bhadra are the karaṇas in inauspicious [matters];
for auspicious purposes, those excluding them are stable, with the exception of the fourth.
Tārāsampat, as well as Kṣema, Mitra, and Paramamitraka;
these are the auspicious [periods], while Enaidhana is birth, and Vipat is the means for the Pratyara.
I shall speak because of the attainment of success through the general rule and its specific exceptions:
the Sun is in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, and Mercury in Kṛttikā.
Bhūsutā (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Uttarabhadrapadā, Śukra (Śukra-vāra), Pūrvaphalgunī, and Guru (Jupiter) in Punarvasu are praised for the purpose of setting out on a journey.
Now, understand the divine and non-divine foods for those eating during the time of the journey:
non-divine food is that which leads to the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), while that which is auspicious in speech is fit for the journey.
The playful troop of maidens, the assembly of the Śrī-saṅgha, the jar of clay,
the complete Pāśupata, the auspicious Śaiva who upholds the Great Vow.
He should honor the Brahmin with words of auspiciousness accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,
as well as the resonance of conchs, kettledrums, drums, flutes, and cymbals.

salutations to the Left-handed One, whose form is the universe, who possesses the form of Bhairava.
O Śambhu, Lord of the Gods, tell me my dream regarding every undertaking.
The Śrāvaṇa-vidyā: Oṃ hūṃ hili 2, to the Lord of the Quarters, the Trident-bearer, destroy 2 the bad dream, shatter 2 the auspicious [obstacles], svāhā!
Having first recited the *māṇavaka* mantra, or else having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra upon oneself,

"O Lord of the gods, O gentle one, I have sought refuge at your feet;

Having seen an auspicious sign in the presence of Śiva or in the Guru’s book, the Siddhācārya should announce it;
having requested permission, he may then speak of it elsewhere at some point.

however, a bad dream should be disclosed, and one should relate it to their own teacher for the purpose of performing a fire offering (homa).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with that [mantra], one should perform the ritual acts;

Whatever auspiciousness has been declared for the lord of the year, or whatever else may be obtained, let the wise man bring it about;

Having dug [the pit] as previously described, starting from the north in the northern direction,
or in an intermediate direction between the northwest and the north— that is called the "quarter of the direction" (diśāpāda).
O daughter of the Mountain, having marked it with general signs by means of the *praṇava* (OM),

One should well-thread Śiva there according to the procedure of the Śivatantra;
for the supreme power known as Tattva is established as the thread.
She is infinite, boundless, and all-pervasive, facing every direction;
because she is omnipresent, there is nowhere she has not reached, for she abides in the act of bestowing grace.

Just as in the world, the inseparable connection is established through the example of the black woolen blanket, so too is the establishment [of the relationship] here through non-separation from the Śiva-sūtras.
Having meditated upon that which possesses the attributes of those deities and having marked it with a thread other than the ordinary one,
one should perform the rite for the stone-thread using ordinary threads.
O Goddess, the first liṅga is desired by Tārā through the rays of fire; it is prescribed as being of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior.
9a) The sages say that the thread [of the lineage] is threefold due to further conceptualization;
that which is joined with those who have counted the number of stars is called the "eldest of the eldest."
The wise know that there is another [set] of eight, consisting of the eldest and the middling;
the sages declare that the eldest and the youngest among these are the middling ones.
The season (*ṛtu*) is from the bottom up to the fourth; the middle is the eldest, and the wise one is the season.
The past is the middle-middle, and the fourth is the middle-youngest.
The fire [element] is the youngest and the eldest of the wings; the moon is the youngest and the middle. At the end of the nine, there are again three [units].
The wise one should arrange each one separately; they should be separated by their respective junctions (saṃdhi).
Indeed, the number [of these] is four, and beneath the hands of the four liṅgas, there should be three.
By decreasing it by four finger-breadths at a time until it reaches twelve finger-breadths, one should then perform the *utpāta* [elevation]; it must not be understood, nor indeed, nor indeed.
That Raudra-piṇḍa, characterized by three signs, consists of thirty-six units;
one should first fashion the Prāsāda and then the Liṅga.
Beginning from the smallest and ending with the largest according to the measurement of the womb,
the smallest and the largest are each divided into five types within half the womb, resulting in nine varieties in total.
The middle and the highest [levels] have been declared; the fire of the elements (bhūtāgni) is the eldest of the eldest.

One should assign two [units] below the maiden by measuring them as equal to that portion;
one should then arrange each of those three intervals in the same manner as before.
In this case as well, by way of number, the gender shall be thirty-six;

Having made the width equal to half the height, the projection should be the number of seasons;

Having divided it into two parts like a base, according to the number of Vedas, elements, and beings,
that which is beginningless is designated as the universal characteristic of all.
I shall now fully describe the third [Veda], which is honored by the hosts of Asuras;
it is not divided into parts during the Kali age, as the fourth Veda is.
O Goddess, everything else bestows wealth, grain, and happiness equally;

Below that, one should again divide the sixth part into three;

This measurement has been specified; now I shall describe the proportions.
Having divided the diameter of the area designated as *brahman* into three equal parts, [the following is established].
The eight-sided portion is called the Viṣṇu-portion; when the sage-portion is established, there is a reduction by the number of Aśvins (two) situated in the middle of the three portions.

then another [portion] is divided eightfold by drawing lines through the middle of the fourth.
Having reduced [the measurement] by four, one should likewise fashion an eight-cornered [pedestal] above;
furthermore, I shall describe another method for the turning of the head, according to the number of parasols.
First, having divided the head into eight parts, one should set aside the two ends and the one called the fourth;

When the rising [measure] is divided, one should exclude two and a half [units] twice;

Having divided [the circle] into four parts, one should set aside two and avoid the other two;

If a circular mark is seen during cutting or carving, it is the sign that the image contains an embryo (sagarbha); hear now its designations as they are.
If [the color] is madder-red, it is said to be a frog; if tawny, one should indicate a *khuṃ*; O Goddess, if it is red, it is a lizard, and one should indicate a black snake.
They say that in the Khaḍga-bheka [omens], one should know a stone the color of molasses;
in the Kāpota [omens], one should indicate a stone from the womb of a lizard, like ashes or sand.
One should know that in a variegated appearance there is a scorpion; in yellow, a lizard or a snake;
and in a bee-like appearance, O Goddess, there is poison; in a dark-blue appearance, one should indicate it is of human origin.
In a dark blue [dream], one should predict a water-snake; in a dark green [dream], a human-snake;
in a dream with the hue of a blue jay, a bird; in a dark blue womb [or interior], a human-bird;
and in a color resembling a yellow bee, one should indicate a lizard or a serpent.
And when the color is pigeon-grey and variegated, one should predict a lizard.
When the mandala is seen covered in ash, the wise know it to be as if sprinkled with water;

In the case of two colors, one should indicate two types of embryos; in the case of a single color, one should designate it as one.
One should observe the mandalas beginning with the vowels and consonants, and the [syllables] such as *ghṛṣā*.
If something has been seen by us, what delusion could be applied there? Or, if it is a delusion, why should we abandon it, or why would there be an examination of it with medicines?
The preceptor should perform the rites for the prosperity and growth of the Brahmin;

Having smeared the linga there, one should place it in a windless spot at night;

One should observe each of the rules concerning the *ucchistika* and so forth as they have been fully prescribed;

Bhītikā, Svapnā, Pathyā, Vajrī, Vakrā, and Aṅkalāñchitā—

and his mass of matted hair takes the form of a flame, radiant and bound upward by serpents.
The western face has a full wheel [forehead], with a slightly smiling countenance;
it possesses a nose, is very serene, has a beautiful brow, and three eyes.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
he stands with hands in the form of a bud, absorbed in meditative concentration.
I shall further describe another [form], possessing a gentle, lovely,
and beautiful body, adorned with two earrings that resemble curved bees.
Adorned with ornaments of gold, with a mind unattached to mirrors, and endowed with the beauty of fine attire,
let there be a tilaka upon the forehead.
The wise one should cause [the deity] to have three faces, excluding either the eastern or the western;

One should conceptualize either the eastern or the western face as the single [primary] form;

For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment or liberation, the general characteristics of all [the deities] are [to be worshipped];

I shall describe each of the lingas worshipped by the world-protectors (lokapālas):

O Queen of the Gods, listen now to the characteristics of the Vāyavya, Saumya, Aiśānya, Vaiṣṇava, and Brahma [mudrās] exactly as they are defined.
Having made the long half equal to a season (six months), the width is produced from a fourth part;

The conception of the seven-pointed [mandala] is above; in the cardinal and intermediate directions there are three, excluding the southeast, which is endowed with the general characteristics of the southeast.

By making half of the *nāha* (circumference) as the *graha*, one becomes a *tripakṣī* here;

And when there are three signs in the fifth house, make nine by dividing it into six parts;

One should avoid a southern [altar] that is either provided with sixteen corners or is perfectly level;

The beating with a staff is established as that [punishment] for enemies;

When Tārā and Viṣṇu are divided, three remain due to the decrease of the seasons;

Endowed with the characteristics of the Dhvaja (Banner), that which is called Dhvaja is known to be watery and gentle; it bestows stability, nourishment, and wealth.
That which is endowed with the characteristics of a mace is called "asat" (non-existent/unreal);

Having divided [the year] into two halves like Rudra, one becomes the Self-born (Brahmā) at the end of the seasons;

it rests upon the gate of Pātāla and the very gateway of the chasm.
For the purpose of establishing the doctrine of subterranean treasures (khanyavāda), one should certainly accomplish that which is called the "Wheel" (cakra).
When divided by half a lunar mansion (tārā), it consists of four, zero, and five parts.
In the same way, one should fashion the middle and upper portions as circular;
endowed with the characteristics of a lotus, it is called the *padma-liṅga*.
Having established the practice for the Yakṣa maidens and others at the tip of the nose,
one should fashion a *trapuṣa* (cucumber) shaped like an umbrella, belonging to Viṣṇu, in the southwest wind-quarter.
The head of the Brahma [direction] is gentle and has the luster of a parasol; that of the Yama [direction] is like the moon.
O Goddess, the head of the Agni [direction] is proclaimed to be like a hen's egg.
In the general [classification], that which consists of those [elements] is said to bestow the attainment of enjoyment and liberation;
here, the specific [classification] regarding the vajra and other [substances] for the purpose of fulfilling particular desires is now described.

12b) When the seasonal transition occurs between two [months] after the emergence of the directional quarters has been made,
one should designate that as the "Staff" (daṇḍa) of the one known as the Staff, and it is to be understood as the umbrella.

Having divided [the circumference] into eight parts, when three [parts] are diminished from the two upper [sides], it is called the *pāśa-chatra*; the one called *dhvaja* is described hereafter.
Having performed the *vasubhāgodaya* (the emergence of the eight parts), there occurs the abandonment of two qualities.
The banner has been described; now hear that which is called the mace (*gadā*).
Having performed the *bhūtabhāga-udaya* and when the abandonment of the *pakva* occurs in both [the *nāḍīs*], it is called the *gadacchatra*; now hear about that which is called *śūla*.

When, after the rising of the Tārā portion, [the Moon] is diminished by three [degrees] while two [portions] remain, it is called the "umbrella" (chatra) of Śūla; in this state, there would be an elevation in three places.

Having established an eight-part rising [of the signs], when there is an omission of two [houses] from the eyes (the second), it is called the *cakrāṅka* for that which is known as the *cakra*; next, the one named *padma* is described.

O Goddess of the gods, when one performs the calculation of the nine-part rising (*navabhāgodaya*) and discards the pair [of signs] when two are present, that becomes the head of the lotus-liṅga; it cannot be otherwise.
The head of the Liṅga known as Sahasra would be equal to Indra;
among these Liṅgas, whichever one is desired is accepted therein.
One should fashion the Rudra portion like Rudra himself, making it long;
the wise man should make the *pṛthu* part consist of eighty-nine divisions.
In each division, one should fashion the linga-mālā with odd-numbered parts;
it should be made according to the measurement of the parts, characterized by marks shaped like barley grains.
For one seeking liberation, even without that [knowledge], devotion alone is the cause here;
that which is called Brahman is as described before, and that which is called Keśava is likewise of that same nature.
Likewise, the ground [measuring] one hundred and eight [units] should be divided into four triangles and then by Rudra (eleven);
the wise man should then construct the body with twenty-seven divisions.
I shall describe the characteristics of the *raudra* [mudrās] according to the determination of the scriptures:
they should be made in the portion of Rudra, excluding four, eight, and twelve [units].
Therefore, this is declared to be the "Fierce" (raudra) method even for a mandala of one hundred thousand squares;
for it consists of hanging lines, being devoid of the side-lines.
Likewise, the Bāṇaliṅga is most excellent, possessing the characteristics common to all;
it should be installed merely by sight, or else according to the injunctions of the scriptures.
13a) It should be fashioned from metals according to one's own preference, either as the manifest (vyakta) or unmanifest (avyakta) form with limbs;
or it may be made unmanifest, measuring up to three cubits in height, but not exceeding that.
It should be made of wood and clearly possess three tiers;
it may begin at one cubit and extend up to six cubits.
And one must certainly not perform the *ūrdhva* rite for a linga made of clay without the *mahāpratiṣṭhā*;
for a linga made of clay, one should follow the procedure as prescribed for stone.
White, red, yellow, and black indeed belong to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively;
that [color] is declared to be of three kinds, as well as ripened, unripened, and blended.
Having kneaded the clay thoroughly and mixed it with fine sand,
one should fashion the linga by dividing it into three parts.
One should likewise prepare the pedestal and have it baked with the fire of cow-dung;
O Goddess, this cooked [image] is proclaimed as the "stable liṅga" (sthiraliṅga).
Whether it be made of unbaked clay or pure [stone], that marriage rite is of three kinds;
however, in the case of an image made of wood or the like, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) alone should be performed without the fire-oblation (homa).
Every day, at the conclusion of the worship, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) must be performed;
whether accompanied by a specific number [of recitations] or not, it grants the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall now fully describe the consecrated linga made of clay:
[it should be fashioned from] the bark of the banyan, the holy fig, the palāśa, the plakṣa, and the udumbara.
One should prepare a paste from the ingredients and blend it with clay;
furthermore, a powder consisting of black gram, green gram, barley, and lentils should be added there as well.
One should likewise employ *masūrāṅga*, incense, resin (*vālā*), and *sarjarasa*;
one should also add linseed oil (*atasī-taila*), cow’s milk, and ghee to it.
O lady of excellent vows, having soaked the *madana* and *sandhana* seeds for five, seven, or ten days, or for a fortnight of black gram (*māṣa*), one should proceed according to this ritual method.
Clearly, the Caṇḍikā and other [deities] should be fashioned in their respective fields as is beneficial;
likewise, a face-liṅga or especially a [standard] liṅga should be fashioned.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be fashioned according to the various types, such as the square and so forth;
it may be made of coral, pearl, lapis lazuli, or topaz.
This excellent linga composed of all kinds of jewels, made of pearls among gems and pearls,
has indeed been described by me as the general characteristic of accomplishment.
Or, in the case of a rite for desired results, [the image] should have a long face, be scarred, and have its belly lacerated;
its back should be low in front and high behind, and likewise, its head should be heavy toward one side.
One with a distorted mind, short in stature, and lacking wings, situated in the middle—
this is indeed auspicious by its very nature, yet it is praised for the sake of inauspicious ends.
The characteristic of the *liṅga* has thus been described; now I shall proclaim the characteristics of those situated above it.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Signs of Accomplishment," in the Piṅgalāmata, within the Jayadrathādhikāra of the Brahmayāmala.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, you have indicated that forests are for the purpose of providing wood;
therefore, please explain the procedure for this, as well as the characteristics of trees.
The characteristics of manifest beings, as well as the means of measurement through weight and dimension, have not been stated;
O Lord, how should one apply devotion in rites performed for desired ends and in those pertaining to Soma?
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, one should enter the forests and groves according to the previously prescribed rules;
there, the wise man should observe the trees to determine which are suitable for collection and which are not.
Candana, and indeed candana, sāla, nimba, and arjuna are considered [suitable];
likewise panasa, śrīphala, raktacandana, and siṃśapā.
The *tinduka*, *kāma*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, and likewise the *sāla*, as well as the *sarala* and *devadāru*, and whatever other trees possess a hard inner core.
They should be flawless, free from internal knots, devoid of hollows, and not produced in saline soil, anthills, or funeral mounds; nor should they have been struck by a potter's wheel.
For these, as well as others endowed with various defects, must be avoided;
having carefully examined [the site], one should first select a location that is firm and free from disease.
Having leveled the ground beneath it, one should carefully smear it;
there, those seeking boons should perform recitation according to what is appropriate.
Having covered the tree with a cloth, one should perform a fire sacrifice according to one's ability;
then one should offer the bali-oblation to the quarters and cause those residing in the vicinity to be gratified.
Oṃ! Homage to you, O Lord of the Forest, who are the abode of glory and are cherished by the gods;
transfer [this] from its place to another location that is endowed with qualities and beautiful to the mind.
With this vidyā for summoning, one should offer an oblation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and food; thus he becomes transferred [into the disciple].
Having eaten the sacrificial porridge (caru) and being properly prepared, one should indeed sleep according to the previously prescribed ritual.

Oṃ śrī hrīṃ hūṃ vauṣaṭ. O beloved, at dawn, the Dream-Māṇavaka should relate the dreams according to the previously mentioned ritual; [the practitioner], having taken a sharp axe consecrated with the weapon-mantra, should observe the pledge (samaya).
One should consecrate his face with the *mṛtyujit* mantra while it is smeared with ghee;
first, one should mark well the limbs of the face, the head, and the feet.
Since its head is below and its feet are above, it is called a "pādapa" (a tree).
One should fashion the wheel just like the door of the palace;
it should be cast toward the east, the northeast, or the north by those who desire the fruits of auspicious deeds.
Marked by the procedure for his own task, the preceptor should cause [the vessel] to fall in another direction;
having first performed the ritual of lying down while it falls, he should do so with the mantra.
Oṃ, salutation to Śiva; salutation again and again.

Svāhā to the one who has a support! This mantra is for [the purpose of] falling and lying down. Once the cutting of the branch has been performed, there follows the distribution of the portions with the weapons-mantras.
When he has been brought to the workshop, the marking out of his form should take place;
it may be performed unmanifestly, or manifestly, or likewise both manifest and unmanifest.
This is proclaimed to be stable according to the previously mentioned procedure;
or else, the characteristic beginning with Rudra should be clearly performed.
That [entrance] is declared to be of two kinds by the one who has mastered the hand-measures:
the door is to be constructed with specific proportions, and therein the characteristic is threefold.
The lowest door of the palace should have a height divided into eight parts;
having set aside one part, divide the remainder again into three parts.

Having established one part as the pedestal (pīṭha), the image should occupy two parts; this is declared to be the smallest (kanyasa) [proportion]. Now listen to the description of the medium (madhyama) [proportion].
The door is divided by the left [side] and so forth; having discarded one part, it is again divided into three.
By one part there shall be the pedestal, and by two parts the image is designated.
One should divide the excellent door of the palace equally according to its proportions;
having established one part as the pedestal, the image shall occupy two parts.
Jyeṣṭhā has thus been fully described; now the measurement of the karas is stated:
those particles of dust (sareṇu) which are seen when the sun has reached the end of its [daily] course.
In a lotus that has been divided eightfold by dust, an atom (aṇu) is established;
a hair-tip (keśāgra) consists of eight such atoms, and a louse-egg (likṣā) consists of those [eight] hair-tips.
Eight *likṣās* make one *pūka*, and eight *pūkas* are known as a *yava*.
Eight *yavas* make one *aṅgula*, O Goddess; twice that [is a *vitasti*], and so on through the sequence of measurements.
One vitasti indeed consists of six kalās; from that, one should know the characteristics of a kara. The numerical measurement derived by that standard is called the measurement of a kara.
14b) That is taught as the general [measure]; otherwise, it is measured differently. O Goddess, one's own *jyeṣṭhāṅgula* [is used], and twenty-four of these constitute a *hasta*.
Starting from one cubit up to nine as the limit of the scope, the measurement of the images is like that of the lingas; likewise, their number has been proclaimed.
And hear, O Goddess, how the Mahāpratisarā is threefold:
it is reckoned as fifteen [syllables] in the Mahāpratisarā-kanyasa.
O Goddess, with thirty-two fingers it is called the Mahāpratisarā-madhyama;
with nine or five [fingers] in a compact form, it is declared to be the Mahājyeṣṭha.
O auspicious one, beginning from one finger-breadth up to twelve finger-breadths, one should worship that [liṅga] in the domestic rite; it shall be situated within an upper temple.
Whatever the measurement of the door may be, whether it be the measurement of the hand or another unit, one should divide their length into nine parts.
Having made that one [digit] like the sun, it is designated as its own *kāmlalam*;
from the two parts of that, the eye is taken, and its synonyms are called *kalā*.
A *tārā* consists of six parts; light (*jyotis*) consists of one-sixteenth of that. A *tāla* consists of six and two [parts], and its synonyms are now being stated.
The tāla, the face, the span (vitasti), the prādeśa, the half-prādeśa, and the cubit (kara)—
the measurement beginning with the finger-breadth (aṅgula) and ending with the span is here described as the primary standard of measure.
O auspicious lady, this [face] is called Netraprakṣāla-mukuṭa and Kirīṭin;
it measures half a cubit, has two eyes, and is said to be at the throat.
The heart, the navel, and the testicles [are measured] from the navel;
together with the *kalās*, the two thighs and the two shanks constitute two *tālas* each.
When the [image] is deficient by one unit, the two knees should be made with two *netra*s;
the two ankles should be made with two *kalā*s, and the two feet should be seven *gola*s.
An excess of two *yavas* is prescribed; this is proclaimed as the measurement for length.
That [measurement] is for the *jūṭa* (tuft of hair), excluding that [length]; by that [standard], it is nine *tālas*, excluding the feet.
One should determine the forehead and the space between the nose and the mouth by dividing the face into three parts;
O beautiful one, each of these two sections should be equal in width according to the measurement of a *golaka* and in length as well.
The forehead should be three times [the width of the face] and four finger-breadths in measure;
the two ears are situated at the ends of the outer corners of the eyes, with the eyebrows being two *golaka*s in length and shaped like the curve of a knee.
Its length should be half of that, and one should determine the transverse measurement accordingly;
likewise, one should prepare the wick for one born of a lineage of twice-born brahmins.
The two *yava* measures make a *caturdraka*; half of that becomes a *kakubhī*.
The two loops (*pāśa*) should be shaped like two spheres; thus they are described as being in their natural state.
The two nooses should be adorned according to one's whim or in a symmetrical manner;
their measurement on the forehead, between the eyebrows, is three finger-breadths in both width and length.
Immediately after that, there should be half a *kalā* at the base; for the thick part, two *yavas*;
and one and a half *yavas* plus half a *yava* for the tip, which should be shaped like a bow.

The tip of the nose should have a height of two finger-breadths; there should be two barley-corns on the sides of the chest. The outer eyelids should be like flattened grains of rice, and the sockets should be as wide as the pupils.
It is slightly curved at the tip, twice as long as it is wide, auspicious, resembling the half-moon,
and gradually tapering from the root to the end of the nostrils.
At the base, the pupil should be half the size of the iris and slightly depressed;
the two eyes should be made oblique and long, with a width equal to half that of the eyes themselves.
O Goddess Tārakandevī, like Tārā, light is said to be light;
the line that goes to half, half, and half again of a barley grain, should go to even half of that.
The work should have a belly like that of a fish, with a point at its tip like the end of a barley grain;
its base should be like the root of a barley grain, and its pupils should be separated by a distance of one hundred thousand units.
The mandala on both cheeks should be four finger-breadths all around;
the cheek should be made elevated, along with a barley-corn-sized mark for the star.
The *hanu* (jaw) should be six finger-breadths in length, and the *golaka* (orb) at its tip should be one finger-breadth;
the cavity (*gartā*) is traditionally said to be one finger-breadth, and the *gojī* there is half a finger-breadth.
O beautiful one, they know its lower part to be the lower lip, which is half the size of the eye;
a line should be drawn for it with a measure of half a barley-corn.
The upper lip should be half a finger-breadth higher than the lower, marked by a line like a barley-corn;
the distance between them should be two barley-corns, O auspicious lady, and likewise one barley-corn at the ear.
The width across the mouth is proclaimed to be four finger-breadths;
extending upward from the tip of the nose, it should be two barley-corns long and half that in width.
By means of the fourth thread being laid diagonally, the face is formed;
the first [thread] is called the hairline, and the second is called the backbone.
The third [line] is the nose-thread, and the fourth is said to be the chin;
likewise, one should fashion the ears above those two, as well as the two shoulders.
The fifth is the Brahma-sūtra, located at the junction of the eyebrows, the chin, and the tip of the nose;
it extends to the hairline, measuring eight kalās from the ear.
From the hairline down to the chin, the face is thus prescribed with nine parts;
such is the gentle countenance—now hear of the other bodily limbs.
Having made a thread from the chin to the heart, the navel, and the root of the penis,
one should arrange two threads from the armpit to the breast and the knee.
The two armpits, the two hips, and five others situated above;
one should extend the peaks (the shoulders), the breasts, the center of the heart, the navel, and the hips.
The horizontal thread (tiryaksūtra) is likewise positioned there; the two elbows are at the increment of one-sixteenth (kalā);
the knees, the ankles, the tips of the feet, and the base are similarly situated.
This is stated with equal proportions for each individual limb:
half a *kara* for the neck, and half of that for the exterior of the shoulders.
The girth at the shoulder and between the armpits is eight *golakas*;
the two arms are said to be twelve *golakas*, and from the base of the limbs, they are six *golakas*.
In the middle, it should be Rudra-folders (eleven) wide, arranged in rows;
the two upper arms are remembered as being long, but not according to the measurement of the eyes.
The joint should be a hemisphere; at its end, the width is proclaimed to be five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) together with seven barley-corns (yavas).
The elbow is on the outer side; three finger-breadths from that is the base of the arm, or else the mouth [of the joint] is there, and the wrapping around it consists of eight *golaka*s.
The joint there is half a finger-breadth wide and devoid of horizontal measurement; from that, the upward projection (upavāhu) should be five finger-breadths wide horizontally.
At the base, the interval between the eyes is one *muni* (seven) *yavas*, and the fourth part is four *aṅgulas*;
the distance between the pupils (*golaka*) is one [unit], and one should lead it gradually by decreasing it by one *yava*.
The upper arm should likewise be four finger-breadths wide and slanting;
the joint is one *kalā* (one finger-breadth), and its circumference is three times that on all sides.
Hayavāhu has been fully described; now listen correctly to the description of the hands:
from the wrist, the length of the hand is seven finger-breadths, equal to the span of a palm.
One should determine the width as five *aṅgulas* across the middle, with five *yavas* added at the base,
and likewise extending upwards by six *aṅgulas*.
The length of the middle finger is proclaimed to be five finger-breadths;
the ring finger and the index finger are each three and a half finger-breadths.
The little finger and the thumb, being equal at three and a half fingers' breadth,
with the thumb positioned below the index finger, is known by the measurement of the interval between the spheres (golaka).
One should fashion the knotted section (*parvaga*) of the *deśinī* [finger] as high as it is elevated;
the base of the middle finger (*madhyamā*), measuring two barleycorns (*yava*), is called the knot (*granthi*).
The middle joint should be three *yavas* less than the *kalā* joint; the knot should be two *yavas*.
In the auspicious *kalā* joint, one should fashion the middle joint as four *yavas* less.

The knot at the base of the ring finger should be one barley-corn (yava) in height; the knot at the base of the index and middle fingers should likewise be equal to a barley-corn. The knot on the shoulder [of the hand] should be slightly less than a barley-corn in height, and the Rudra-knot should extend upwards.
One should fashion twelve joints at the base;
O lady of excellent complexion, the knot should be at half a barley-corn above that.
One should designate eleven and a half barley-corns as the middle joint;
the knot is situated at half a barley-corn above, and the end of the thread is situated at the new moon (the tip) above that.
The knot of the two smaller [fingers] is like a barley grain at the middle of the base;
the upward-extending knot is half a barley grain, and the root of the joint is determined by the measurement of barley grains.
The middle joint of the thumb is the Vasu (eight) [finger-breadths], and its upper portion shall be one and a half;
the knot at the base of the thumb is four barley-corns.
The first knot that is proclaimed should be made equal to a barley grain;
the second knot, moving upwards, should likewise be made equal to a barley grain.
The uppermost joint of that [reed] should be twelve barley-corns long;
the middle joint, however, should have a circumference three times its width at the base.
In the middle, the circumference should be three *yavus*;
having made it like fire (three) minus two (*yavus*), it is proclaimed as the upward-pointing *gonāhaka*.
At the base of the ring finger and the index finger, the circumference is threefold as before;
in the middle it should be the same, but it should be devoid of the letter *pū*.
The circumference would be two cubits; when multiplied by three, it extends to the upper joint. In the case of Kanyā and Mūla, however, the circumference would be as before, being threefold.
The circumference of the middle joint should be two barley-corns;
the upper joint should be three barley-corns in height and have a circumference three times that [of its height].
At the base of the thumb, there should be an encirclement of three kalās;
at the middle, two kalās; and above that, one kalā for each finger.
16b) Furthermore,
there should be an upper enclosure for the wheel of two yab-yum deities;
O Goddess, one should arrange the nails at every point, reaching halfway up the vertical joints.
All the nails are depressed at the base, elevated in the middle with a reddish luster, and sharp and black at the tips; indeed, every characteristic is as beautiful as it ought to be.
By means of one established at the beginning, the second arm is established;
below the well, however, are the two spheres, Cūdraka and Kauri.
Those two [shoulders] are also slightly inclined sideways toward the left and right;
above them, the two armpits are equal and slightly inclined sideways.
O Goddess, one *tāla* above the middle line is the *golaka*;
the two circles (*maṇḍala*) on either side are each the measure of a barley grain (*yava*), with their central nipples likewise measuring a barley grain.
From the heart-line, upwards to the nipple, it should be two finger-breadths; and from there, it should be half of two finger-breadths (one finger-breadth).
One finger-breadth below the breasts, the semen is located transversely within the region of the base of the heart;
extending as far as the armpit-line on both sides, it constitutes the three kalās.
Having fixed a thread from the heart to the interior of the navel, one should determine the measurement;
one should know that there are three units above it and make three units below it.
From the middle, extending five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) transversely within the range of the breast-line,
one should likewise measure the distance between the armpits on both sides.
O Dear One, at the navel, the line known as the middle is said to be one and a half *bhūtāṅgulas* in width;
likewise, the two flanks from the armpit lines to the edge of the garment should be the same.
Above that, the measurement of two kalās should extend as far as the middle line;
likewise, one should arrange it on both sides below the heart-line.

The belly of the four-faced one should have its center depressed according to the mark, and not otherwise; having fixed a thread at the navel and the two sides of the depression, one should lay it out crosswise.
The measurement for each of the three periods is two *pakṣas* in width at the hips;
the navel should be a right-turning spiral, measuring one and a half *yavas*.
The two testicles, situated on the buttocks, are desired to be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;
the circumference at their base is two kalās, and the length of the penis is twice that of the balls.
Its wrapping should be threefold, with two globes at the middle and the front;
the width at the base of the thigh should be one tāla in measure.
Dividing that [measurement] from the bottom up as far as the range of the knees,
one should set aside half a finger-breadth at each division starting from the base.
This continues until there are exactly three *golaka*s at the front;
everywhere the circumference is tripled, while the transverse [measurement] is two *golaka*s, forming the line of power (*śaktyālī*).
The joint there is one finger-breadth wide, with Rudra-sized globules for its wrapping;
below that, the series of digits is proclaimed as the *nāhajaṅghā*.
In the middle is the circumference of the solar digits; below that, divided by ten, one should omit one finger-breadth each, and here the circumferences are mutually [proportioned].
It should be brought to its maximum extent until it measures seven golakas;
furthermore, across the middle of the foot, it should be one angula and two kalās.
The wise one should perform three *kalās* on the forefoot, two *kalās* on the heel,
and likewise two *kalās* between the heel and the ankle.
The ring finger (seya) is five yavas long; without that [ring finger], the middle finger (deśinī) is four yavas;
the middle finger (madhyā) is six yavas; and the nameless finger (nirnāma) is twenty yavas.
The length of a maiden is declared to be eighteen *yava*s;
the day-measure (*nāha*) is five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), starting from the root of the thumb and extending upwards.
Furthermore, six finger-breadths [is the length], with five [finger-breadths] as the target, like a noose at the head;
the width of the ring finger is three finger-breadths, and its base and middle are according to the digit.
Furthermore, the *arha* [measure] is three finger-breadths less than the upward [measurement]; now hear concerning the remaining [parts]:
the circumference of the middle finger is said to be reduced by one-eighth of the index finger.
When the midday [shadow] is diminished by one-eighth, it is called *nirnāsa*;
when diminished by one-eighth of the ring finger's length, one should designate it as *kanyā*.
All [the nails] should have their roots depressed, their middles elevated, and a reddish luster;
they should be raised at the tips and white at the edges, so that the beauty of the marks is fully manifest.
Its headband should consist of eighteen eyes,
and the encircling of the chest should consist of twenty-five eyes.
The encircling band below that has twenty-one eyes;
the navel consists of twenty-three kalās, and below that is the twenty-fourth.
The waist should be made beautiful with a girth of five finger-breadths;
having aligned it with threads, they should be positioned according to their respective places.
The two nipples should be equal and shaped like a bud, with a stream of light [emerging from them];
likewise, the two armpits and the nipples are said to lie on the same horizontal line.
The characteristics of a pleasing image have been thus described;
for one that is uneven, O Lord, the proportions and the arrangement of the lines are likewise uneven.
Indicated by their respective postures and equipped with weapons beginning with the bow,
there are seven [deities] starting from Padmā and ending with Daṇḍā, seated and extending three times across.
Deformed, cruel, and like a vetāla, with the staggering gait of a hunchback,
another woman stood at the beginning of the path like a serpent due to some cause.
These and other such [lines] are designated as long, short, thin,
distressed, uneven, and those others which are neither equal nor unequal.

I shall now describe the form of a woman according to both her defining characteristics (*lakṣya*) and her marks (*lakṣaṇa*); having grasped the proportions of her height and likewise the proportions of her limbs, one should examine them.
One should fashion the waist-band at the hips because it is broad;
taking one part from the long middle section, it should extend sideways by one finger-breadth.
One should fashion two breasts as stalks, four finger-breadths in circumference;
the measurement from below the pit of the throat to their base is one finger-breadth each.
The two nipples are one *iṣu* (five *yava*s) in diameter and three *yava*s in height at their centers;
from the base of the jaws, the width is to be taken as nine *aṅgulas*.

One of that kind should be placed as an offering on the forehead; the mouth should have length, and the nose should not be elevated; one should place a single barley-corn-like mark at the junction of the two eyebrows.
At the root, there is the bulb (kanda) which is thick; beyond that, as before, one should take a sixteenth part from the height of the cheek and place it at the two eyes.
Its length is twice its width; the two ears are spheres of one-sixteenth part [of the width].
Having grasped its breadth from that, it has been described by me as existing in its natural state.
The measurement of that [forehead] is the ornament of knowledge; its support is either new or appropriate.
The forehead is the fourth part, extending horizontally to the range of the ears.
It should be made as long as the hair-line (kaca-sūtra), with no doubt regarding that measurement;
the two shoulders should be made lower by half a *golaka*, and not otherwise.
Taking one-sixteenth of the length for the back, one should form the two buttocks as circular;
having subtracted half a neck-measure from the sphere, one should place it above according to its width.
Having likewise taken the length from the *pravāhuka* joint according to the measurement of a sphere,
one should place half a finger-breadth above [the navel] and the knees in the same manner.
Having placed this width and the *pauḍīla* at half a finger-breadth,
O beautiful one, the two feet should be made elevated by half a finger-breadth.
The soles of the feet should be made level, as should the heels and the ankles;
O beautiful one, one should grasp the natural span of the fingers and the eight parts.
The wise one should likewise place [the syllables] in the two hands according to their length;
the remaining characteristics should be as previously specified and enjoined.
And I shall fully describe the characteristics of a woman as they truly are:
her shoulders should be slightly sloping, her waist well-proportioned, and her belly slender.
She has beautiful cheeks and a fine nose, she is very serene and pure;
adorned with locks of hair as ornaments, her lovely lower lip is like the bimba fruit.
With large eyes slightly reddened at the corners,
she was languid with desire, her hips adorned by the weight of tinkling girdles.
The form of the Lord Bhairava is described exactly as it is:
his topknot consists of nine digits (kalās), and all things are bound within its center.
In the upper portion, it is joined with the moon; its length is measured at two *kalās*, and its width in the middle is like half a finger at the tip.
The second [mark] is the source of Indra; the ears are long with three globes; the face measures eight and a half digits;
and the forehead is said to be three digits.
The nose should be as long as a finger, one and a half *golaka*s in height,
the facial portion six fingers wide, and the nostril opening two fingers.
The two fangs should be shaped like balls, with sharp tips and the luster of the moon;
the neck-encircling [portion] should be five finger-breadths long, measured as a digit (kalā) of the moon.
The two shoulders are seven finger-breadths long; the two upper arms are seventeen finger-breadths;
the forearms are as long as the directions and digits (ten); and the two hands are eight finger-breadths each, being equal.
The middle finger is one and a half finger-breadths [in width], while the other two are equal at five finger-breadths;
the little finger is less by half a finger-breadth, and one should arrange the thumb accordingly.

Having repeatedly examined the nails, the long fingers, the upward curvature, and the successive encircling of the arms, one should fashion them with a circumference three times that [of the forearm].
The chest has an increase of two units, and the length of the heart should be one *aṅgula*;
likewise the navel, and the thigh should be four *kalās* in height.
The lower legs are considered to be thirteen finger-breadths in length, with the ankles measuring five finger-breadths;
here too, the circumference is three times that, and the feet are fifteen finger-breadths long.
The toes are one finger-breadth wide; this is proclaimed as the seventh [measurement].
The feet are arched like the back of a tortoise, and their soles possess the luster of red lac.
18b) One should fashion the toes such that they are one-eighth of the length of the forepart;
the circumference should be proportionate so that it may be as beautiful as possible.
O beautiful one, the girth at the chest region is twenty-nine kalās;
the girth below that is twenty-seven, and the girth at the navel is said to be twenty-eight.
The circumference of this [pedestal] is declared to be thirty *golikās*;
its height above the *liṅga* is three *kalās*, and its circumference is four *kalās*.
The two testicles are two digits long and hanging; the circumference is two equal digits.
This characteristic has been declared by me; it is called the primary *lakṣa*.
The two eyes should be shaped like circles, and it is said that the eyebrows should resemble the letter *ci*.
On the forehead is the third eye, which is devoid of eyebrows and perfectly circular.
A garland of skulls hangs from his head like a floral wreath;
he has twelve arms reaching down to his knees, or perhaps sixteen or eighteen.
Having extracted two arms pierced by spears, one should fashion them [as follows]:
a sword and shield, a cow-horn (dhenu) and an arrow, as well as a bell and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
His two hands hold a skull and a severed head, as well as a noose and a goad;
he is two-armed, bearing a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and wears an elephant hide.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, with a tiger skin draped around the waist,
and with a sacred thread made of serpents— or alternatively, it is proclaimed that this [deity] is adorned with sheaths.
Endowed with the five mudrās and surrounded by the Bhūtas and Mātṛs, he has one face or five faces; or else, there should be two on the left.
Two [faces] should be made on the right, while the middle face is the fifth;
indeed, everything should be of that same form, with mouths wide open and faces possessing fangs.
Radiant, with the *lelihā* [tongue] and filled with the protective vessel of liquor—
this Bhairava should be fashioned separately, or he may be situated in the midst of the Mothers.
I shall describe their forms as they stand in their proper sequence:
Vighneśa is the western face, having the face of an elephant and a large belly.
The height is known to be five tālas; the belly is auspicious like that of a serpent;
the neck is adorned with a garland; and the arms hold a bow and a measuring cord.
Joined with the juice of the axe-fruit, wearing the sacred thread of all [the gods],
holding a morsel of food for the teeth in his hand, he has three eyes and a dwarf-like form.
Seated there in either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the heroic posture (vīrāsana),
one should draw Kṛṣṇa in the form of a mouse, situated beneath the lotus.
19a) Beginning with Brahmāṇī, those situated in the row face north;
[they are located] in the city, village, hamlet, capital, and indeed in palaces and the like.
Since auspicious results are to be produced in the southern direction,
she has four faces, large eyes, a tawny complexion, and a high crown.
She should be depicted with four arms, holding a rosary and a water-pot, being gentle-faced and auspicious, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
She has a deer-skin as an upper garment, her two eyes are smeared with collyrium,
and her face and belly are [measured] by five and a half tālas respectively.
One should visualize the Goddess as assuming the form of Brahmā, seated upon a swan,
possessing three eyes, four arms, a gentle countenance, and a beautiful form.
The Goddess has her hand raised with a trident, while her other hands grant boons and protection;
one should likewise imagine a bell, a ḍamaru drum, and a lotus.
Clad in a tiger skin and having a tiger skin as her upper garment,
she may stand upon a durmukha or a lotus, manifesting herself in the form of Rudra.
The Goddess, assuming the form of a maiden, should be depicted with six faces, a peacock as her vehicle, and twelve arms;
alternatively, she may have two arms and one face.
One should fashion [the deity] with the left index finger extended in the gesture of grace, or else as seated upon a lotus;
in the month of Kārttika, one should have it made in whatever form corresponds to that specific deity.
The form of Vaiṣṇavī shall be sixteen years of age, rich in beauty,
four-armed, with a gentle countenance, and adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in her hands, beautiful with a plough in her hand,
she may be seated upon the king of birds or else upon a lotus seat.
She who crushes all the asuras should be fashioned in the form of Viṣṇu;
Vārāhī has the appearance of a snout-faced countenance, or she may have the face of a jackal and a forest of food.
To the south is the terrifying Daśabhujā, with a face distorted by protruding fangs,
wielding a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a noose, a goad, and a formidable staff.
Holding an axe, a saw, and likewise a pestle,
she may have the form of Yama, or be slender-limbed Vārāhī, or possess a large belly.
She should likewise be depicted with two arms, equipped with a sword and a staff;
however, she is cloud-colored and has a form like that of Yama, elongated in two ways.
