Vārāhī should be depicted standing upon a buffalo; she who belongs to Yama should have a seat of a rhinoceros, or she may be made seated upon a lotus, dark in color.
19b) She who has subtle eyelashes— whether she be beautiful or endowed with youth— one should cause her to perform the marking.
Marked with a mole and a dark spot, holding a vajra in her hand and bestowing boons, the goddess has two arms and one face; she bears the form of Indra and is auspicious.
Or she may be fashioned as standing upon a lotus, and likewise, one should depict her as being supported by an elephant;
I shall now describe in its entirety the form of Cāmuṇḍā.
In the Lord of Gods, there is no defining characteristic by way of a mere mark;
for some, a characteristic is proclaimed, while for others, it is merely a mark.
O Goddess, for some, both [forms] arise from the expansion of the eye-sockets;
while Cāmuṇḍā is of fierce form, she has arisen from the *jaṭharoṣṭha*.
The third [mark] is a circular, elevated area on the forehead, devoid of hair, resembling a flame, and possessing deep-set eyes. This should be fashioned there.
The matted locks rising upward have the form of a flame, with the brilliance of a forest fire;
upon the forehead are fierce serpents, and above that is a garland of severed heads.
With a broken nose, jaw, and thighs, and with two pits (kūpa) in the form of hollows on the cheeks;
having a long neck and being mute, such a person is struck by the *trikalā* and *tāla*.
Her mouth is wide open like a spreading lotus, from which flows a crimson torrent from her fangs;
her tongue, resembling blood in color, licks the exterior for two finger-breadths.
The two long arms, joined by skin, bone, and sinews, have fingers and nails that are long and sharp at the tips;
his chest is broad, and his belly hangs down ten finger-breadths.
The chest is like a skeleton, with veins showing and devoid of flesh; the river of the belly is sunken and fleshless, broken by the wandering of the current.
The hips are withered and devoid of flesh, naked and accompanied by a rattling sound;
likewise, the thighs and knees are fleshless, and the shanks are covered with long veins.
Her body was bound together by skin and bone; her feet had long toes, and she wore anklets on her calves, while her girdle was fastened with snakes.
Clad in tiger skins or with elephant hides as upper garments,
wearing a long garland of severed heads, she is beautiful, possessing great limbs, and upholding the Great Vow.
Seated upon a great corpse-throne and joined with a great wheel, she drinks blood to fullness; auspicious, she has made the khaṭvāṅga her very limb.
One should fashion auspicious earrings from the skulls of children, using the terrifying hands of those who shave heads as the tools for carving them.
Alternatively, one may also fashion beautiful earrings from the skulls of infants.
20a) One should likewise adorn the neck, hands, arms, knees, hips, head, and belly, as well as every limb, with snakes or scorpions.
Just as one should conceive of [the deity] in the form of Bhairava, so too should one conceive of Cāmuṇḍā;
however, she is specifically a female form devoid of flesh.
Bhairava should be depicted facing east; Bhṛṅgī is without a left shoulder, his hair and skin fallen away, possessing the luster of a dry skeleton.
The three-eyed Lord of Dance (Nāṭeśvara) should be fashioned, endowed with yoga and seated comfortably in a yogic posture, constructed in the northeast.
However, the commencement of the *sautāṇḍava* dance, crowded with many arms,
extends from the lower regions to the upper regions, reaching as far as the ten directions at its beginning.
Moving with steps like those of Viśākha, he performs a dance characterized by the contraction of his limbs;
his bright face quivers, and his head is held high, having cast aside all pride.
With the binding of matted locks, two hands should be formed; two others should hold an upward-turned shield;
another two should be joined in the *tālikā* gesture; and two more should hold a trident and a sword.
With a khaṭvāṅga raised in one hand and a skull held in the other,
he moved through the various directions with graceful *cārīs* and rhythmic movements, employing tempos such as the rapid (*druta*) and others.
Having understood this, one should act accordingly according to the number of arms;
likewise, Nandin, intent on the music of the *suraṅga* drum, should do the same on the right.
To the left were Kālasaṃkhyā with his bamboo flute and dancers;
and there were the leaders of the Gaṇas, accompanied by lute players, singers, celestial musicians, and dancers.
Therefore, all [the deities], beginning with Bhṛṅgī, should be worshipped accompanied by dance and song; one should cause them to assume a dancing form adorned with every ornament.
Seated upon a peacock, six-faced, Kārttikeya is like a youth;
he resembles the javā flower and is adorned with twelve arms.
The arrangement consists of two [emblems] on each side, a face, and likewise one at the back;
[the emblems are] a bow, an arrow, a spear, a banner, and another cock.
One should likewise fashion twelve [deities] with a bell, a hand-drum, a lotus, a sword, and a shield, as well as hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
And when one should have [the deity] made with one face and two arms, then rags are bound upon the forehead, and the hands display the gestures of grace, fearlessness, and the threatening pose.
The ears should be fashioned from palm leaves, and the neck should be adorned with a necklace;
there should be a girdle of tinkling bells on the feet and a waist-belt around the hips.
One should break the garland with both arms, while the hands remain adorned with bracelets;
one may also adopt the *utkaṭāsana* or the *vīrāsana* posture.
Seated upon a lotus, with a crest-lock, a broad chest, and a slender waist—
now hear the form of the god Sadāśiva.
Surmounted by four elephants and situated upon a seat of fourfold dimensions,
it consists of four petals and is established upon a pericarp shaped like half a lotus.
Four-faced and eight-armed, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
three-eyed, perfected in meditation, and firmly seated upon a lotus throne.
Two faces are on the sides, and three are proclaimed to be in the middle;
the fourth is to be considered at the back, for that which is visible is indeed the face.
This procedure has been fully described for those with four faces;
for those with six, eight, or ten faces, the ritual arrangement is the same as that for the one-faced.
One should form the two hands into the *mukula* (bud) gesture placed at the heart;
the two hands raised upward at the hips likewise represent the trident and the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*).
With a rosary of rudrākṣa beads joined in his hand, and a book likewise in his hand, he should fix his gaze solely upon the Name; thus engaged in yoga, his intellect shall become serene.
Śrī should be depicted on the right, holding a chowrie and other items in her hands;
on the left, Sarasvatī should be depicted, adorned with a chowrie and a peacock.
Having drawn the image of the Creator with his legs bent in a posture of prostration,
he made obeisance with flowers in full baskets and incense in hand.
This procedure is prescribed for a manifest [deity]; the donor should perform an imitation [of the ritual].
That which is established as the state of Sadāśiva is declared to be the auspicious Śiva.
The tranquil one who bestows Sadāśiva is likewise called Sadāśiva;
Umā and Maheśvara are to be fashioned as twins of divine form.
Or Umā, standing upon the beautiful thighs [of Śiva], her eyes wide and gazing intently at one another,
her gaze fixed on the face of her beloved, was as radiant as a pair of lotuses placed together.
The goddess stands with her trunk-like arms, while Maheśvara has his hand at his chin;
Rudra looks downward, and the goddess looks upward.
In a single image there are two forms, either as the Lord who is Half-Woman (Ardhanārīśvara),
or else the form of a woman in the left half and Hara himself in the right.
Two women with eyes like those of a doe, endowed with the fullness of breasts and slender waists,
wearing fine garments, with half their chests raised and uncovered.
Lakṣa is remembered as being in the form of a male, adorned with a crown of matted locks;
likewise, Hari and Rudra become so through the conceptualization of the left and right [sides].
The two arms of Hari are lowered and adorned with the conch and discus;
Rudra’s are raised, and likewise Bhūta holds a trident and a rosary in his hands.
Half of his head was matted, while the other half was radiant with a crown;
half [of his body] had a serpent as a sacred thread, and he was adorned by half of a garland.
Likewise, the form of Hari and Śaṅkara as Ardhanārīśvara should be fashioned; it may be depicted either seated or even not seated.
I shall describe the form of Durgā according to the definitive conclusion of the scriptures:
she has one face, three eyes, and is endowed with twenty arms.
Equipped with weapons, both gentle and enraged, she was slender-waisted and beautiful;
likewise, she held a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, and a staff.
A noose, a goad, a mace, a banner, a bell, and a mirror;
likewise a saw, a spear, a trident, an axe, and a mallet.
She who crushes the demon Mahiṣāsura holds a ḍamaru drum and the gesture of fearlessness;
from the severing of his head, he takes on a human form, sword in hand, both joyful and fierce.
Having risen, one should seize that head and show it with the hand of the Goddess;
blood flows like a river from the head of the enemy of the Bhogins.
Her back, which should not be struck by fire at the junction of the three channels (trikaṭu), must be pierced with spikes;
she should be placed upon a lion-throne or a lotus, seated on a cloud.
Endowed with the form of Ambikā, she should be like Kaumārī;
one should fashion fragrant substances above and below her.
She has two arms and three eyes, with the radiance of a single moon-like face;
she is seated upon a lotus throne there, her hand extended like the scorching sun.
Since she whose slender waist is the thread of liberation is conjoined with the five fires,
I shall explain those five fires according to the determination found in the scriptures.
The first fire is said to be the renunciation of mother, father, and so forth;
the second is the summer season, and the third is remembered as the sun.
The fourth, however, should be without food, or she may eat at every sixth mealtime;
the fifth should be constantly devoted to the fire-oblation in the sacrificial pit.
The five-fire rite is declared to consist of the five fires of the thread and the sacrificial pit;
I shall now describe the form of Śrī and how she acts for the sake of prosperity.
Seated in the lotus posture, she stands upon a lotus, adorned with a lotus in her hand;
her two hips are raised upward while her two [other] faces are bent downward, and she is auspicious.

On both sides, one should draw two elephants with trunks raised holding water-pots, together with Śrī, who holds a lotus and is engaged in the act of consecration; thus one should depict her as the bestower of prosperity.
At the top of a door, or in a house, or at a solitary tree, or at a crossroads—
I shall describe Mahādeva, surrounded by the one hundred and eight Rudras.
According to one's own doctrine, the height and width [of the structure] should be divided by twenty;
it should be made one part wide and as many parts long, whether square or rectangular.
O auspicious lady, two hundred and sixty squares are established there as the foundation;
the external perimeter, consisting of fifty-four [squares], is for the sake of beauty.
Alternatively, it may be variegated with lotus garlands or a series of jars made of fine wood;
leaving three finger-breadths from both the bottom and the top, [the design] is also applied on both sides of those two.
One should have the principal form fashioned in the center using forty squares;
the lotus or likewise the lion-throne should consist of six squares.
O Lord, there should be three five-padas for the deity; the remaining beauty should be distributed elsewhere.
For the Lord of Devas, there should be six padas on both sides from the center of the lower row.
The incense holder and the food offering (naivedya) should each consist of two full squares;
as for the other two squares, they are indeed equal to the maker.
When those two have bowed with palms joined and fallen upon the earth at their feet,
one should there assign the Rudras to the remaining one hundred and eight steps.
All have three eyes and two arms; they have blue throats and a single face.
Their hands are occupied with tridents, their hands are [the bestowers] of knowledge, and their gaze is fixed upon that [one object].
All [the deities] are situated in the vīrāsana posture, or else in yogic postures;
the three-eyed god Nīlakaṇṭha, however, should be in the padmāsana posture.
One should fashion his two hands with eyes fixed intently upon him as he prepares to explain;
he is endowed with all ornaments and his arms are adorned with serpents.
He is adorned with a garland, radiant in appearance, and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament;
he is gentle in form, serene, and clearly resembles a blooming lotus.
One should cause each of the four parts above to be reduced by one;
listen now to how that which is divided by twenty becomes the additive.
One should fashion the *śobhā* with a transverse part equal to one-fourth of the *ku* (kūṭa),
and likewise, one should fashion the four *koṇas* (corners) with four parts each.
O Goddess, one should likewise fashion the stalk as three parts high, the lotus bud from two parts,
and the peg at the bottom from three parts.
O Goddess, one should not draw my head in the center with various paintings, goddesses, jewel garlands, and so forth, nor with words.
O lady of excellent hips, in that form I am four-armed;
I shall describe the twelve feet [of the mantra], while you are the first leader of the Gaṇas, Bhṛṅgin.
O Prince, [one should depict] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as those who dwell in the six realms;
Śeṣa, and the Vidyādharas should be made with garlands in their hands, positioned horizontally.
From the chest down to the head and feet, situated like steps in the midst of the clouds—
I shall now proclaim the names of those Rudras individually.
Vāmadeva of great splendor and likewise Halāhala—these indeed stand behind you; listen now to those who are beyond Kumāra.
I shall describe individually each of the eight-and-a-half [deities], namely Paṭarudra, Jyeṣṭha, and likewise Gahanīśa, as well as those below.
Situated in the northeast and the other directions, they are, in their respective order:
Gomutrī, Amareśa, Mahākāla, Gokarṇa, and Aṣṭahāsaka.
Saṃkukarṇa, Prājeśa, Krodheśa, and likewise Bhairava;
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and he who is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Sambāha, Vivāha, Nata, Lipsa, Vicakṣaṇa,
Vidyeśa, Jñānavān, Mitrajñānajña, and Vedapāraga.
The wise Lord of Vidyās, King Mātṛpiṅgala,
who wears a garland of jewels fashioned from suffering and bears a crown of matted locks.
The lord of treasures, handsome, fortunate, one who bestows grace with a gentle body,
manifest, O Lakṣmī, desire, subtle, sharp, and the ender of the night.
Swift as the force of a light wind, wearing a loincloth and riding upon clouds,
he is the ender of the five elements, possesses five tufts of hair, holds a noose in his hand, and is of great strength.
Valo, Hṛti, Bala, Dīrghabāhu, Jalāntaka, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Vaḍavāsya, and Subhīmaka.
Nirṛti is the slayer, the killer, with a cruel gaze and terrifying;
in the upper chamber he is Virūpākṣa, possessing smoke-colored and blood-red fangs.
He is the Lord of the South (Yāmya), the remover of death, the supporter, the ordainer, and indeed the agent; he is called Kāla, the Lord of Dharma, the disjoiner, and the beloved of Yama.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala,
Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Vakra, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka.
Kapālīśa, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha,
Pramadaka, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa.
Sudhairyā, Grāsana, Śarva, Pātālīśa, Vṛṣa, Vṛṣa, Pālaka, Vīryānanta, Śubhra, Lohitaka, and Para.
These Rudras are fully enumerated as one hundred and twenty-two;
this is declared to be the Saila-khaṇḍa, and one should have it made without the Citra.
In a bow made of wood, the variegated three-sectioned joint should be even;
however, the connection between the arrow-shaft and the interior must be performed using materials of its own kind.
Having removed the parchment from the sounding board by means of iron pincers,
one should not cause the wooden pins to enter the water.
The principle regarding those made of wood is that their root is the *mūsthāsandhana*;
I shall now explain in due order the nature of Anantīśa.
In this case, the width should be one-third less than the length;
having made the length like the moon, the width should be like the sun.
The wood should be divided into forty parts according to its quality;
one part [of the width] is for the base-plate, and from the length, two parts at both ends are likewise [for the joints].
One should determine the middle Ananta with thirty-six parts;
the lotus should consist of eight parts, and its stalk above should be one and a half parts.
Make eighteen parts infinite; then make it twice the number of the earth (two).
Having made it like a cloth-strip below and above, there shall likewise be two placements.
Through the union of the left and the right, he is indeed subtle and the supreme Śiva;
he is Ekanetra, Ekarudra, the one of great splendor, and the three-fold form.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Śikhaṇḍin, Vāma, and likewise Āvindhya—
these two donors should be written below, O beautiful one, in the place of ornamentation.
The lower portion of the stalk should be like a lotus, and the remaining beauty should be like a silk band (*paṭṭa*);
having fashioned the upper part of the head as before, one should fashion the Lord in the center.
The wise one, devoted to the practice of yoga, [should perform] the yogāsana and the lord of yogins;
as for the remainder, the beauty should be arranged such that the swan is surrounded by the speech of the Aghmaras.
All the Rudras have three eyes, hold tridents and books in their hands,
are adorned with crowns of matted hair, and are marked by the crescent moon.
The Blessed One is seated in the lotus posture, his hand raised in the gesture of exposition;
he is endowed with a trident and a rosary, possesses three eyes, and has a serene countenance.
I shall now describe the sequence for the images of Bhairava:
having made the length like that of the wings, the width should be ten [parts].
The width should be divided into fifteen parts, and likewise the height;
having set aside three parts from the top, there should be fifty-two *sadvāru* units.
Having made one cloth-strip at its end, and likewise another yoke-interval,
one should have Bhairava fashioned there in the middle with fifty squares.
One should fashion the halo above with two parts;
its shape is said to be either circular or like the outline of a lotus.
One should fashion the form there with twenty-five wooden pieces;
with ten, however, there should be a lotus and a base slab for the fourth layer.
One part should be made like a stalk; in the middle, that should be circular. As for those two wings consisting of forty squares each, double them.
In that case, one should make a six-unit interval for the stepmothers, but with a double division;
having made the lower and upper parts like a band (paṭṭa), the same applies to all the intermediate spaces.
Through the union of the left and the right are Cāmuṇḍā and Vināyaka;
likewise Aindrāṇī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Kumārikā.
The Māheśvarī and Brahmāṇī [lines] are considered the givers;
one should destroy two horizontal parts and the upper portion as well.
As before, one should fashion a kīla measuring one-quarter [of the height] for the head;
it should be one part wide, and the head itself should be two parts. May there be auspiciousness!
Seated in the peaceful lotus posture, joined in yoga and having the form of knowledge,
when Cāmuṇḍā is in the center, place Bhṛṅgin in those positions.
One should fashion Śivabhairava as before; the arrangement of the remaining [deities] is as follows:
Gaṇa and Bhṛṅgin should be placed at the entrance in either the northeast or the southeast.
I shall describe the true form of the Lord of Meru as it is:
the area is said to be the width reduced by one-third of its length.
When divided into equal parts, the wooden molding should be outside;
with fifty-four squares, the form shall be "Guṇaśiras."
A wooden beam shall not be made by a single [artisan], just as it is at the end of a Yuga;
likewise, at the end of sixty [years], one should fashion the Lord, dividing the lotus into twelve parts.
O Lord, having likewise formed two [faces] consisting of thirty-six [units] as the nature of Śiva,
and having made two heads as before, one should place Sadāśiva in their midst.
One should arrange those two parts, each consisting of eleven units, so that they are doubled;
having made them like a band below and above, the *pālī* there shall consist of eight parts.
Brahmā as well as Īśāna, Kuvera, Vāyu,
Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Yama, and likewise Agni.
Likewise, Indra and Viṣṇu should be placed through the union of the left and right [sides],
and one should place Īśvara, the three-eyed wielder of the trident, in the center.
Wearing a sacred thread made of serpents, his arms adorned with snakes,
he was endowed with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
He has a blue throat and an upward-pointing linga, is clothed in a tiger skin,
possesses four arms and one face, and likewise displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding a rosary and well-seated upon a lotus throne,
Brahmā shall have four faces, with long moustaches and wearing a fine girdle.
He should be depicted wearing a deer-skin as an upper garment, with his hair tied in a matted topknot;
he must not be made the color of fire, but rather with a large belly and four arms.
O Pārvatī, he is remembered as being five tālas in height, with a wooden staff, a rosary, and a water-pot raised in his hands; his belly is likewise [five tālas] in circumference.
Seated upon a swan-throne, with a gentle countenance and auspicious eyes,
he possessed the form of Īśvara as before, yet remained in a state of humble prostration.
Soma, having ascended his celestial chariot, possesses a large abdominal region;
one should fashion its circumference with a measurement of seven and a half *tālas*.
With mace in hand, possessing a massive body, and adorned with all ornaments,
one should likewise draw a treasure-trove beneath him at the third, fifth, or seventh [position].
The Mṛgāsana-vāyu has curved eyebrows and a thin abdomen;
he holds a banner in his hand, possesses slender limbs, is coarse in appearance, and has a pendulous belly.
Varuṇa, standing upon a crocodile, should be depicted adorned with celestial ornaments;
he has a gentle countenance, is perfectly full-bodied, holds a noose in his hand, and is most beautiful.
24a) Mounted upon a corpse-shoulder, he is proclaimed as the King of Rākṣasas;
his form has the appearance of a Rākṣasa, and he is terrible, with a sword in his hand.
But Mahiṣa was of fierce form, radiant with a staff in his hand;
his brow was knit and furrowed, and his face was exceedingly harsh.
Mounted upon a goat-seat, holding a spear in his hand, he is like the sacrificial fire;
with a radiance rising upward in the form of flames, he is sharp in appearance and exceedingly terrible.
Mounted upon Airāvata, with a thunderbolt in hand,
the lord of the gods is marked on all his limbs with a thousand eyes.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with a crown upon his head,
he is shaded by a divine parasol above, provided with a golden handle.
Viṣṇu, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
four-armed and handsome in form, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, was stationed upon the king of birds.
With arms raised like ploughs and possessing a luster like the trunk of an elephant, they were slender-limbed yet broad-chested; likewise, Dāruka was a giver of gifts.
Just as there is beauty above, filled with hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas,
so too is that field of transformation, elevated together with the Bhagas.
He should be depicted in such a form, or else with both [hands] in the *garuḍāsana* posture;
the sequence of the names for his ten incarnations (*daśāvatāra*) situated at his sides is now described.
O Goddess, now hear concerning the ten [aspects] of the characterized and the characteristic,
according to the sequence of upward and downward, as well as of the left and the right.
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Paraśurāma, Balarāma, Buddha, and Kalki— these are the ten.
One's own field should be divided into seven parts; the wise practitioner should cause the emergence of the mouth in one part and the emergence of the tail in two parts.
Having made two parts the end-maker, one should rotate it by five parts;
by the procedure for the half-moon, one wing is accomplished.
And the second [part] is likewise situated, resembling the tip of a tail-banner;
therefore, having set aside two parts from that, the foot shall be equal to it.
At the base, place the letter *kṛ* in front; make it faceless and then endowed with a face.
Having thus formed its facial shape, the two eyes are [marked] by a circle of two finger-breadths (*yava*).
The arrangement of its own limbs is formed by compartments shaped like half-moons;
it is clearly proclaimed that the skin is the element and the fish has the form of a Śāla tree.
Because its head is marked with circles, it is not eaten by Brahmins;
in the same way, I shall describe the form of the tortoise here.
Having made one's own field like a Veda-square, one should lead the ear-line outward;
having divided that [line] according to its qualities, one should discard one part and rotate [the cord] evenly.
Having divided it into two parts like the moon, one should make an entry in the form of a curve;
then, having rotated from one-third of that, one forms a svastika with the end shaped like a wheel.
Therefore, one should mentally draw the emergence of the wheels at the joints of the hands and feet;
the neck should be one part, and outside the field, it should be two parts.
The head is circular with two parts from the eyes; the two eyes are three *yavas* each. At the end of the eyes, the ears should be fashioned as two *yavas*, having the form of the moon.
Having made the facial shape even, with a beautiful heart and a raised back,
the form and the measurement of the face of Varāha are now described.
O beautiful one, the face is said to have eight eyes and its length is seven aṅgulas;
the distance between the corners of the mouth (sṛkvaṇī) is two aṅgulas.
The face should be seven finger-breadths [in height]; the two tusks should be two white finger-breadths [in length];
and the circumference at the base of the trunk should be four finger-breadths in measure.
Those two faces [should be placed] in front with sharp [edges], while the nasal cavity is in the globes;
it should be circular at the front and in the middle, beautiful with each half being half [the size of the other].
The tip of the nose, shining like a golden flower, should be slightly quivering;
the two eyes should be one and a half finger-breadths [apart], and the mouth should be somewhat prominent.
One should imagine the two ears as two spheres, extending for two *yāmas* and rising high; the distance between them at the crown of the head should be four *golakas* in width.
The head should be elevated by two *golaka*s, and the neck should be eight *aṅgula*s long;
the form of Śrī should be hidden in either the right or the left hand.
The chest should be held steady and the face turned upward with the mind;
the feet are fixed upon the earth, while the conch and discus are held in both hands.
The remaining limbs of that [image] are indeed Vaiṣṇava, but its body is somewhat short;
the face of the Nārasiṃha, however, should be slanted and consist of eight kalās.
The face is said to be six kalās in length and three kalās in width;
its opening is two kalās wide, and from it two tusks protrude.
The remainder of the vessel's [measurement] is like the Kali age; likewise, the ear is half of the filament.
The face is white and fully blossomed, and the eyes are circular with a measurement of one finger-breadth due to their curvature.
The eyebrows should be curved with a frown; the shoulders should be four *kalās* wide on the outside;
the neck should be diminished by one *aṅgula*, while the circumference is increased by one *kalā*.
One should visualize the entire body in the form of Bhairava as being full;
however, the two hands should be roundish and likewise holding a mace and a discus.
On the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu, two streams of blood flowed downward from the wounds torn by his claws, as his long arms hung down like a cage.
With a dagger hanging from his hand, his head reaching down to his feet, and his knees touching the ground like a corpse, O Daityas, he is then called Nārasiṃha.
With one foot slightly raised and the other thumb touching the ground,
the face of Vāmana should be seven kalās in length.
The distance between his two ears is proclaimed to be ten *netras*;
from the line of the eyebrows downwards, it should be two *kalās* greater.
The head is twenty-four digits in circumference and shaped like a jar;
the neck is three digits in length, and its circumference is twenty-five digits.
Know that the two shoulder-balls (golaka) together with the collarbone (aṃsa) constitute the arm-machine;
for the seven-eyed [deity], the arm consists of three balls (golaka).
All the fingers are deficient by one joint at the fourth;
here, the measurement of width is derived from the length, with the calculation applied to each successive joint.
The arm-span (vāhu) is the same as the nāha, according to the enumeration of qualities as before;
having subtracted the length of the heart, the stalk, and the trunk, one should determine the width there.
Likewise, taking the heart and the navel as one unit, one should fashion the navel transversely;
the eye should be taken between the navel and the end of the creation-line, and that should be the width of the hips.
Having taken the two thighs and the two eyes, one should determine their breadth there; likewise, having taken the two shanks according to their length, one should determine them by their thickness.
Having reduced the two feet by one-sixteenth in length, one should arrange them transversely;
one should determine the thickness of the toes as one-sixth of a finger-breadth.
The buttocks are round and well-fleshed, while the belly is exceedingly circular;
the ears are shaped like the hoods of serpents, and the two testicles are long and pendulous.
Her face was exceedingly restless from the recollection of Kaparda;
she held a water-pot in one hand and likewise a wooden staff in the other.
One should draw the form of a twice-born man wearing an upper garment and intent on binding the folds [of his skin], with King Bali positioned in front within the six-part division.
One should give a gift to Vāmana accompanied by a water-pot and rice;
I shall also declare the specific targets for both Bali and Vāmana.
Vāmana, who was skilled in deceptive speech and charming, though small in stature,
possessed a voice as sweet as that of Soma and Aṅgiras.
Entering into the midst of the assembly, seeking a place at the feet [of the king],
Viṣṇu, disguised as a Brahmin, causes the sacrifice of Bali to be shattered.
Then Trivikrama-Rāma became possessed of a beautiful form;
he likewise became four-armed, as well as equipped with his weapons.
Standing on the earth with one foot while the second was not supported by the sky,
he was intent on binding Bali for the purpose of measuring the earth.
The heroic wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow shall have matted hair and a tuft of hair;
he will have two arms, a most excellent form, and will likewise hold a bow and arrows in his hands.
And Rāma, holding an axe in his other hand, should be depicted with a plough in his hand;
both should be seated on a seat and fashioned with beautiful forms.
The Buddha should be depicted seated on a lotus throne with his hands in the gesture of meditative equipoise (samādhi);
he is gentle, with long ears, and wears the religious robe tucked into his armpits.
His heart is adorned with jewels, his eyes are fixed upon the nose,
his hands and feet are marked with lotuses, and his face is slightly smiling.
His essential nature is consciousness, his innate disposition is a mind directed solely toward compassion,
and his face is exceedingly beautiful, resembling a fresh lotus.
And Kalki is a harsh disposition, appearing in a body like that of a barbarian;
with a quiver fastened to his back, he holds a bow with an arrow in his hand.
Born from a family of Brahmins and appearing in the form of a brahmin, Mādhava,
as the supreme Viṣṇu who is half the head, should manifest a peaceful form.
Below, one should arrange the wood for the giver as before.
Piṅgalā said:
For what purpose is Viṣṇu, the supreme and the inferior, tenfold? Tell me how.
Bhairava said:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— these three lords of the gods—
reside having taken refuge on Mount Meru, even as they extend throughout the entire universe.
Brahmā is indeed the Lord and the creator of both, the sovereign of the world;
Viṣṇu is the protector of the world for the sake of establishing the cosmic age.
In that terrible ocean where water overflowed everywhere,
he assumed the form of a fish and approached for the sake of sport.
In that [ocean], the supreme sage Mārkaṇḍeya, who had lived for a very long time, sported like a playful wave; there was no other refuge for him there.
Then, between those two, there occurred a mutual encounter of their teeth and their knowledge;
thereafter, O Mārkaṇḍeya, the great Asura [attacked] the host for the sake of the earth.
Then Viṣṇu also, having understood this,
assumed the form of a tortoise and quickly went down to where that Earth herself was located.
Having abandoned their true form and assumed the forms of women along with Śrī,
they abide there as the presiding deities of the kūṣmāṇḍas through the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
Having seen him, the Tortoise then stood assuming the form of a Boar;
with his face alone he was the Lord of Gods, while in all his limbs he was the form of Viṣṇu.
And seeing him, Queen Śrī was delighted and settled upon his chest;
then Pṛthivī bowed at his feet and sought refuge in him.
Having placed the earth upon his foot and supporting Śrī with both hands,
Janārdana was seen rising up swiftly in the form of Ghoṇa.
But as long as he was not revealed in the presence of Mārkaṇḍeya,
that earth remained manifest in its true form.
The seven continents and the oceans, together with their mountains, forests, and groves,
as well as the worlds, are established with Meru and Dhruva as their fixed center.
The gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rishis, obstacles, vetālas, and likewise humans and others.
At the beginning of the Kṛta age, when the destruction of the Yugas was near on this earth with its leaders,
there was a king named Hiraṇyakaśipu, a great asura in the Kṛta age itself.
Seeing that [the deer] was invulnerable, he created a lion-form;
his grandson was named Valin, who was generous and proficient in dharma.
For the purpose of binding him, Viṣṇu assumed a female form;
at the end of time, he brought about the arrival of Sandhyā in order to bind Bali.
Then Viṣṇu, in the form of Rāma,
established himself as the Vikrama [incarnation] at the end of the Sandhyā period of the Tretā Yuga, which was crowded with many Asuras.
Seeing the Lord unbound and the destruction of Rāvaṇa,
the hero Gāṇḍīvasaṃjāta was born, for Hari had assumed a form through his illusory power (māyā).
And at the end of the Tretā age, during the twilight period, Kārtavīryārjuna appeared once more;
endowed with a thousand arms, there was no one equal to him in the entire universe.
In order to sever the arms [of Śiśupāla], he became the wielder of Rāma’s axe;
and when the Dvāpara age arrived thereafter, he became the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace.
Viṣṇu himself, the four-armed one, was exceedingly dear to the Pāṇḍavas;
after them came the age named Kali, which is devoid of righteousness.
Having seen the destruction of the Daityas and others, the gods became free from thorns;
therefore, he is considered the Buddha of Compassion for the sake of establishing them in their own duties and observances.

At the end of that as well, O Great Goddess, there will be a Yuga known as the Cāṇḍāla; there, the conduct of the twice-born and so forth will cease, and no distinction between caste and non-caste will exist.
Therein, there is no distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten, nor likewise between dharma and adharma;
it is the dissolution of the ages and their re-establishment.
The Brahmās shall be named Kalkis, who have themselves assumed the form of Viṣṇu;
and by this method, [this shall continue] until the fourteenth Indra.
For the sake of sport, Keśava remains in the world in ten forms,
O Pārvatī, until Brahmā is dissolved along with the cosmic eggs.
Then, having become the cessation (virama) and possessing a tranquil form,
it is thereafter called the supreme upper body of Śiva.
When Brahmā is of a separate form and the field becomes solar in nature,
one should likewise imagine him with a head of black hair, as before.
Just as there are two wings within the intermediate divisions, or alternatively, various conceptual constructions;
Brahmā consists of four parts, while the lotus consists of one and a half parts.
One should fashion it like the lower band; in the upper portion there should be a halo.
And that which consists of seven parts should be like the upper band.
Furthermore, one should place two more lines between those two; there, one should place two Brahmas—the Gāyatrī and the Sāvitrī—in the middle, as before.
Seated upon a lotus, or likewise standing upon a swan-throne,
the Supreme Brahmā above should manifest his form as possessing the quality of tranquility (sa).
Or Indra may be the king, standing in the middle as before;
and Rambhā, Tilottamā, Śrī, and Sarasvatī [are positioned] likewise.
Or if these two are brought to the sides, O Gandharva, it would be a dvaya;
or when Agni is in the middle, the form is conceived as before.
Then two wings should be fashioned, known by those forms as Tejinī and Jvālinī,
as well as Dahanī and Śoṣaṇī.
27a) O fair-faced one, Yama should be placed as before in the center, while Kālapāśa should be made on the two sides, and likewise Dīna and Udanta should be positioned as the two Bhūtas.
One should likewise arrange the Pitṛs in the east, the west, and the middle;
the Rākṣasa, however, has wings of ghee, and that form consists of four parts.
He is cruel, terrible, fierce, and likewise difficult to look upon;
or when Varuṇa is in the center, one should cause him to be fashioned in his former form.
One should visualize him as being situated within the four oceans;
when the wind is in the center, his two wings are his attendants.
One should draw two spears for him: one that arrays the troops and another that causes them to tremble;
likewise, there are two others of the same form, and one that carries [the army] across.
Likewise, in the center, between the two yakṣiṇīs, there are two yakṣas; such is the reality of the beings—now listen to their names.
Jaṃbhala, Udghṛtarāṣṭra, Dhaninī, and likewise Sominī;
when Īśāna is in the center, Skanda and Vināyaka are on the two wings.
O fair-faced one, Gaṅgā and likewise Durgā should be fashioned;
thus, by all those established in these forms, there is in some cases a single characteristic of form.
Just as the form of the sun is established in the circle of planets, so too,
when the field is divided into its respective portions, one should make that which is measured by the cord double.
One [square] below for destruction, two above that in the same manner, and likewise two between them; there one should place the eight planets.
Through the conjunction of the left and right [channels], beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu,
I shall describe their forms as they pertain to the Sun and the other planets.
The moon should be on the head, the sun at the feet; he should have a body adorned with armor and earrings.
His two hands should be depicted holding lotuses, and he should be auspicious with three eyes.
Alternatively, one should be seated in the ubhrasana posture with a beautiful form; likewise, O Soma, one should be of peaceful aspect, situated in the ardhacandrāsana.
Mars is harsh and yellow in appearance;
Mercury likewise has the form of a young child and a broad chest while seated.
Vṛhaspati is seated in the lotus posture with a peaceful form,
and Śukra likewise remains established in his seat with one eye.
With his gaze directed downward and being cruel, Saturn is situated in the girdle;
Rāhu is remembered as having half a body, with fangs and a gaping mouth.
27b) The Yoginīs should have their gaze directed downwards; likewise, they should have four faces.
These goddesses possess complete and auspicious limbs, appearing as sixteen-year-old maidens, just as described in their own Āgamas.

The *kinnaras* were of various forms, appearing like tigers, lions, and so forth; some had faces like cows, horses, or dogs, while others had the faces of crows, owls, or deer, and some took the form of monkeys.
With thick eyebrows, a prominent chin, and a large nose, his eyes and lips likewise [were formidable];
he possessed a fierce form with all his limbs fully developed.
With palms joined in *añjali*, that hair-like Rāhu held a discus and a mallet.
Mounted upon all their celestial chariots and adorned with every ornament,
those beginning with Soma and ending with Aśanīcara likewise held water-pots in their hands.
Likewise, another [form] has instruction [imprinted on it], while another is adorned with a rosary;
when the Sun is situated in a chariot, the sage [Garga] should be depicted below him.
They should be fashioned in sequential form, corresponding to the charioteer;
having placed them upon the head with their branches, they are to be bound in front of the chariot.
Revanta, the nectar of horses, was joined by his own doorkeeper;
he had long arms and feet, and his hands and thighs were very coarse.
I shall describe the forms of the Nāgas; above them are those of divine form.
The Nāgas beginning with Ananta are remembered as bearing the eight families and the [eight] jewels.
One, three, five, and seven [days] ending with the seventh are situated in the pair;
likewise, two, four, and six—the sixth and the pair itself—one should not cause [the rite] to be performed.
The serpent's tail, extending below the waist, is remembered as being adorned with jewels;
and the beautiful-faced female serpents (nāginīs) are likewise endowed with gems and ornaments.
Their tails are below the hips; they have slender waists, prominent breasts, and long faces; the two Yakṣiṇīs and the Apsarases possess the luster of the moon.
The Vidyādharas should be fashioned holding garlands, stationed upon the clouds;
likewise, the Kheṭīs [should be placed] on the chest, feet, head, and also on the feet.
The Gandharvas stood with swords in hand, arranged in successive order;
the Kinnaras held lutes in their hands, and the Gaṇas were likewise of beautiful form.
Those who bear human form are to be known as yakṣīs; likewise, those with curly hair and resembling the appearance of barbarians are to be known as kiṃpuruṣas and kiṃkaras.

The Kṣetrapālas, possessing large fangs, with massive bellies and long pendulous limbs, were joined with skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅga) and the like; they were accompanied by Bhūtas and other spirits, as well as Rākṣasas.
The Bhūtas have dejected faces and lack memory; the Piśācas have long faces;
while the Rākṣasas are of terrible form, possessing long claws and always having fangs.
I shall describe the form of the hunchbacked and likewise the form of the lame:
seizing the eye within the dried navel, and likewise making the heart defective.
Having fashioned them with elevated chests and backs bent from that point upward,
they are flat-nosed, broad-chested, and have feet turned sideways, making them lame.
With knees broken and arms severed, these Kaulas were exceedingly radiant;
yet, having realized the fruit of their store of karma, they became faceless and remained suspended in mid-air.

Those with heads tilted sideways, those who are cruel, those with severed noses, limbs, or feet; those lacking fingers on their hands, those with cavities in their bellies, and those with emaciated stomachs.
Forms such as these should be fashioned by those seeking their own welfare or misfortune.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Images," in the Piṅgalāmata within the Jayadrathādhikāra of the Brahmajāmalatantra.
Piṅgala said:
O King, the characteristics of the cloth, as well as those of the wooden panel,
and the distribution of colors for the painting of an image are likewise described.
"Speak a description of the deities who possess forms such as Śiva and Vyoman.
Bhairava said:
For the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should prepare an excellent cloth made of cotton.
O Goddess, in the case of the Kośaja and other [types of cloth], or when performing rites such as those for the reversal of misfortune,
one should take fine cotton cloth from a corpse, wash it three times, and then determine its status as pure or impure.
O beautiful one, having taken the seeds of *tintaṭī*, which are crushed, pounded, and softened with conch-shell powder and other substances, the wise man should grind them well.
Having ground the upper shell of that [skull] and made it into a single mass, one should knead it;
having stirred it with clear water, one should smear it upon a cloth.
This is indeed known as the adamantine paste (vajralepa); one should apply it again and again.
Listen now to how it is otherwise for the image on the panel of the banner.
Having taken clay from Vālmīka, one should drink it mixed with an equal amount of grain and boiled rice;
then, having stirred it again with water, one should smear it with a small spoon.
When each layer has dried, one should apply the plaster again on the wooden board or the image;
in the center of the board, there should be a seed of the *rāla* tree produced from a *vilva* fruit.
One should rub the pigment with that for five or seven days;
thus, the white color of the *kaṭikā* becomes red when combined with *darada* and *gerika*.
Likewise, vermilion and yellow orpiment;
and [the features] with thick eyebrows, a prominent chin, and a nose, as well as the eyes and the lower lip.
And Ketu, indeed, was of fierce form, with all his limbs fully formed.
With palms joined in reverence, that Rāhu, possessing hair and holding a discus and a mallet,
was mounted upon a celestial chariot along with all others, adorned with every ornament.
Soma and others emerged from the thunderbolt, holding water-pots in their hands;
likewise, another appeared with instruction, adorned with a rosary of beads.
When the sun is situated in a chariot, the sage should be positioned below;
the steps should be fashioned in form, and the charioteer should be in the form of a bow.
Having bound him with his hair tied up on the crown of his head, he was placed at the front of the chariot;
accompanied by a dog and a doorkeeper, he was led forth.
With long arms and feet, and hands and thighs that are very rough, he has the form of a nāga; his upper body, however, possesses a divine form.
The serpent-kings, beginning with Ananta, are remembered as the bearers of the eight families;
they reside in pairs, numbering one, three, five, seven, and nine.
One should not cause [the tail] to be made with two, four, six, or an even number [of beads];
it is traditionally taught that enjoyment consists of a jewel-encrusted [tail], shaped like a tail and positioned below the waist.
Adorned with jewel ornaments, the Naga women have beautiful faces;
from the waist downwards their tails are present, and they possess slender waists and elevated breasts.
The yakṣiṇīs should have long faces, and the apsarases should have the radiance of the moon;
the vidyādharas should be depicted holding garlands and standing upon clouds.
The Gandharvas, with chests, feet, and heads [as their lower halves], and likewise with shields and feet, stand in successive order with swords in hand.
The Gaṇas, beautiful in form, hold vīṇās in their hands like Kinnaras;
likewise, the Yakṣīs and Kimpuruṣas should be known as assuming human forms.
The *kiṅkaras* have crooked hair and resemble those of barbarian appearance;
the *yoginīs* have a sidelong gaze, and their vision should likewise be directed downward.
Likewise, the goddesses have four faces, their limbs are complete and auspicious,
and they possess the appearance of sixteen years of age, just as described in their own scriptures.
The kinnaras were of various forms, with faces like lions and tigers,
as well as those with the faces of oxen, dogs, crows, owls, and deer.
There were those in the form of monkeys and wolves, with gaping mouths and massive bellies;
these Kṣetrapālas had prominent fangs, enormous stomachs, and pendulous limbs.
29a) The Bhūtas and others, together with the Rākṣasas, are joined with staffs and skull-topped poles (khaṭvāṅgas);
the Piśācas have dejected faces, are mindless, and have long, gaping mouths.
The Rākṣasas are indeed of terrible form, with long claws and prominent tusks;
now I shall describe the hunchbacked form as well as the lame form.
Having grasped the eye within the space between the navel and the breast, and likewise [grasped] the heart-region,
one should fashion the chest elevated and the back bent, with the upper half [of the body] thus disposed.
They have flattened noses and broad chests; their feet are turned sideways and they are lame;
their knees are broken, their arms are like those of apes, and their faces are exceedingly radiant.
Having realized the fruit of their store of karma, those devoid of wheels and situated between the two [wheels]—
with heads upturned or turned sideways, cruel, with severed noses, limbs, and feet— [suffer].
Those who lack fingers on their hands, those with holes in their bellies, and those with emaciated stomachs—
such forms as these should be depicted by those seeking benefit or harm.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on the Counter-Practitioner," in the Piṅgalāmata within the Jayadrathādhikāra of the Brahmajāmalatantra.
Piṅgala said:
O King, the characteristics of the cloth, as well as those of the wooden board,
and likewise the distribution of colors for the painting of an image, [are now described].
"Speak of the description of the deities, such as Śiva and others, who possess forms of various colors.
Bhairava said:
For the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should wear excellent garments made of silk or cotton.
O Goddess, in the case of the Kośaja and other such [mantras], when performing rites such as those for averting misfortune,
one should use soft cloth from a corpse or similar materials, which has been washed three times, whether it be pure or impure.
O beautiful one, the wise man should grind the seeds of *tintaṭī* grown in his own house, which have been crushed, pounded, and softened with conch-shell powder and other such substances.
Having ground half of that with *khapara* (black salt), one should mix it together and knead it;
having stirred it in clear water, one should smear it upon a cloth.
Vajralepa is said to be hatred; one should practice it again and again.
Listen now to how it is otherwise regarding the image on the banner's board.
Taking black earth from the bank of the Vālmīka [ant-hill] and equal parts of cooked grain, one should grind them together;
then, having moistened them again with water, one should apply the paste with a small spoon.
Having repeatedly applied [the paste] to a dry wooden board or a statue,
one should then use the middle portion of a bilva fruit and seeds produced from the *rāla* tree.
One should rub the pigment with that for five or seven days;
thus, the white color of the *kaṭikā* becomes red with *darada* and *gerika*.
Sindūra, yellow orpiment, realgar,
*kaṅkuṣṭha*, and black [substance] rubbed with the flame of a lamp.
That which is born from indigo is blue in color; the pair of palms (tālayug) should be green;
the pair of white [palms] is red; the smoky-colored is yellowish-red, and the variegated is mottled.
Having understood that the colors white, blue, and lotus-colored (red) may be mixed, one should employ them;
one should draw with lac-juice using lines skillfully fashioned.
A skillful artisan, with a straight gaze, should fashion [the image] using hairs from the ears of a cow, prepared by anointing them, which are neither too thick nor too thin.
The wise should draw lines with numerical marks according to the principles seen in the scriptures;
the designation of the scent of the *ketakī* flower is produced by the keys arising from its feet.
A water-pot made of gold, silver, copper, brass, bell-metal, or iron, as well as one made of coconut shell or clay— vacā is prescribed for each of these.
The support for the colors must indeed be made very beautiful;
it should be Sadāśiva, ending with the heart and accompanied by the Cakravartin.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Mahādeva, Īśvara, and Rudra; Bhṛṅgin, Gaṇādhipa, Śambhu, Bhairava, and Śrīsarasvatī.
Gaṅgā, Soma, and likewise Śubhrā; Raudrāṇī, Caṇḍikā, and likewise Ṣarāraktā; Jayā, Svadhūti, and Sarahasundarī.
All those others who arise from auspiciousness are declared to be white;
likewise are the six-faced one, Hutāśa, and Agnirudra, the tenth.
Āditya, Bhūsuta, Kaumārī, and Nandikeśvara—
these are indeed remembered as being red in color, as are Karālī and Vijayā.
And Aparājitā with her female messengers, as well as those others who are her attendants;
and Dhaneśvara and Brahmā, as well as Aindrī and Brāhmī.
Indra, Rudra, and Kubera; likewise Brahmā and Rudra;
Vācaspati, as well as Buddha, and the three Rāmas along with Vāmana.
Ajitā, Caṇḍākṣī, Dūtī, Asahā, and Varānanā—
all these are declared to be yellow in color and endowed with excellent retinues.
The virtuous ones, Hari, Rudra, Yama, and the Yama-Rudras;
likewise Mahākāla, Durgā, Vaiṣṇavī, and the Boar-faced goddess.
Mādhava is of that same form, as are Rāhu and Ketu;
likewise [are] Parāparā, Mahocchuṣmā, Ajitā, and Kiṅkarī joined together.
Indeed, these are known to be black in color, as are those others born from them;
likewise, the ten Rudras of the southwest, the Rākṣasas, and the Piśācas.
They are described as being blue in color and accompanied by their retinues;
these include the Tiryagāvāyu Rudras, the Kṣetrapālas, and their servants (kiṃkaras).
They are declared to be smoke-colored and joined with their respective retinues;
they are Varuṇa, Jalarudra, and Īśarudra.
Those who are declared to be of white complexion, as well as others who are their followers,
the wise man should correctly depict them exactly as established by the statements of his own Tantra.
The hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases are of various colors;
the Bhūtas are known to be smoke-colored, while the serpents (Uragas) are blackish-blue.
The Yoginīs and Śākinīs are of various forms, like the night and its divisions;
they are indeed Śyāmā, Mīna, Kūrma, Kṛṣṇa, Śyāma, and Kālikika.
Ārakta is Nārasiṃha, while Hiraṇyaka is tawny-dark;
likewise here are Valirāja and the daughters of the Nāgas.
One should likewise conceive of the form of Hari and Rudra as half-and-half, with the conceptualization of black and white;
and one should likewise fashion that very form as Ardhanārīśvara.
According to the procedure of Mahāyoga, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus; having inscribed the [mantra] beginning with "rakta" upon the diagram, one should place Bhairava above the pericarp.
Having made Bhairava the center, those deities are situated in rows;
likewise, there are the fourfold, the sixth, the twelvefold, and the sixteenfold [mandalas].
O lady of excellent vows, one should thus draw the twenty-four [deities] according to this rule;
likewise, one should write Jayā and the others, either positioned within the circles or arranged in rows in due order.
Or, they may be depicted as having ascended a boat; Tumburu is to be drawn holding a staff, while Parā and the others hold tridents in their hands, and Tripada is upon a three-petalled lotus.
Having written the six [syllables] as stated in one's own scripture, they are then arranged in rows within the wheel;
the [deities] such as Vimba and the others are likewise situated in the wheel, specifically formed into rows.
Either by joining the left and right or by making them equal in the middle,
one should draw four quadrants in the morning, as previously described, arranged according to the squares.
Furthermore, having carved out human heads and likewise the back of a tortoise,
one should not make a variegated design there, because it would result in instability and so forth.
Likewise here, [the image] may be made of gold and so forth, or even of stone of that same kind;
having fashioned one made of clay as a coating, one should perform the painting upon the field.
Ekavīrā, Mahālakṣmī, Bhairavī, and then Caṇḍikā;
Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, as well as Kṣetrajā and Pīṭhajā.
One should not cause them to be made by those born of mixed unions;
rather, they should be adorned with various wonderful paintings, beautiful and of many colors.
There, a wise person, with an undisturbed and unagitated mind, should skillfully draw [the image] together with garlands and the like, endowed with various kinds of flowers.
He is an expert in painting and mantra-lore, established in his authoritative position;
endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, he is a knower of the scriptures and affectionate toward his devotees.
Furthermore, one should draw two [images], one made of clay and one made of wood;
likewise, one may draw them on the walls of a house or within a dwelling enclosed by an earthen wall.
One should always diligently cover all painted images with cloths;
however, at the time of worship, meditation, and recitation, one should perform the ritual after uncovering them.
Thus the wise one should conduct himself; he should never reveal his own [inner] state. He should always manifest the common [outer] form, awakening his devotees.

The wise one should worship that which is unmanifest, that which has a manifest form, and likewise that which is both manifest and unmanifest; for action is rooted in that which resides in the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Section on Variegated [Cognition]."
Piṅgalā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, you have stated that the *pīṭha* is to be worshipped as the triple-liṅga (*tridhāliṅga*).
But the *pīṭha* itself is not known by me; what is it, to whom does it belong, and of what nature is it, O Lord?"
"Tell me of the universal or the particular, characterized by name and definition.
Bhairava said:
I shall now describe the installation of the *liṅga* for images that possess two forms.
Listen now correctly to the characteristics of the pedestal, including the ritual marks for those honored by the world-protectors, as well as the characteristics of the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
If the portion is divided by eight, the planet Mercury is indicated by one-fourth;
if divided by nine, the king [Jupiter] is indicated; and with five [parts], it becomes middling.
The Jyeṣṭha seat is declared to be situated at the end of the Sarabhāgas;
two [units] each should be made at the ends, and there should be a pair below the Kanyā.
For those [structures] consisting of palaces, garlands, and liṅgas, the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of thirty-six [units], with an interval of twenty-seven [units] between each set of three.
For those made according to the *hasta* measurement, the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be equal to that;
it should be joined with the pedestal-base (*piṇḍikā*), reaching up to two parts in height.
31a) The height and the width of the facial emblem (mukhaliṅga) should be equal [to its length];
for images that are double the size, they are determined by the measurement of the door-hands (dvārahasta).
The length should be equal to one's own measurement, and the width should be half of that;
the height of the pedestal should be half of its width for the sake of well-being.
The conduit for that [type of linga] should be situated on the pedestal outside the piṇḍikā;
this is declared to be the rule for one made of stone, while for one made of wood, the conduit is indeed different.
Likewise, the pedestal for one made of clay should be without a drainage channel;
now hear how their pedestals are to be arranged for the installation of great images.
The length should be ten cubits, and the width half of that;
O lady of virtuous vows, one should not make the height half of that, but rather one-third or one-fifth.
One should likewise fashion the length as twelve cubits;
the pedestal for the thirty deities should have its width and height as previously described.
For the supreme [image], it should likewise be fourteen cubits in length,
as well as in width and height.
O fair-faced one, for the images up to eleven cubits in height,
the pedestal should be nine cubits in both width and height, as previously described.
O Goddess of the Gods, the thirty [fingers] are the end; the first is sixteen; the pīṭha is ten and one;
and above the thirty are the two sages of the pratimāṇas.
In the thirteenth [chapter], one should not construct the pedestal as before;
one should make it according to the stated measurement, neither more nor less.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the rites for determining the directions, according to the distinctions of cruel rites and so forth, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be made either smaller or larger.
This is indeed the general characteristic; now understand the specific types:
the Vaidika, the Padmaka, and likewise the Payodhārāmṛta.
The *pūrṇamaṇḍalasaṃvarta* and likewise the *nandikāvartaka*—
these are the seventy-two types of lingas fashioned by those whose own [inner] self has been established within the womb [of the altar].
For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, these have been proclaimed in general;
however, when classified by gender, those pedestal-bases (piṇḍikās) are said to be seven in number.
One should recognize by their characteristics the Vedī, Padmā, Payodharī, Amṛtā, Pūrṇamaṇḍalā, Saṃvartā, and Ānandikāvartā.
Having made it as wide as the *liṅga*, its height should be two parts;
and the upper portion should be fashioned like a modification (*vikāra*), likewise for the two wings.
Starting from the foot up to the end of the throat, one should decrease it by one unit at each stage;
having established two parts for the throat, the exit should likewise be formed.
In each and every division, one should fashion it together with a thousand *piṇḍikās*;
it is called by the name *vedikā*, and it is marked with the *nandikāvarta* motif.
That very Nandikāvarta design accomplishes all desires and purposes;
it constantly bestows wealth and grain, and like a sacrificial altar, it grants happiness.
The upper portion, divided by three and five, should likewise be so for both wings;
having made one part equal to the ground, it shall take the form of petals through the three [divisions].
In the same way, one should fashion two [panels] for that [side], and likewise one [panel] with three [sections] for the raised architrave (*unnatikaṇṭhaka*);
one should arrange one [panel] for the exit-awning (*nirgamacchada*) and likewise two [panels].
Likewise, in each and every part, there is further a water-soaked cloth;
this is declared to be the Dharma-seat (dharmapīṭha), honored by hosts of gods.
The gift of a kingdom, the attainment of wealth and enjoyments, and even divinity—
each of these was previously fashioned as sixteen parts, while one part was equal to the entire earth.

The shank should be four parts; the *kumbha* (vase) should likewise be three parts. Having made the *karṇikā* (pericarp/base) like the foot, the height of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be like that of the *kumbha*.
The exit likewise occurs through one [opening] at the pericarp and not otherwise;
and there is the northern, the further northern, and the successively higher band.
For this is proclaimed by its characteristic to be like a reservoir of water;
it is known by the name *payodhara*, possessing the common characteristics of all [such forms].
O Goddess, it always bestows happiness and brings about both seen and unseen fruits;
having fashioned [the image] with the luster of Tārā, it should likewise be made on both sides.
Having fashioned one part for the base, the shank is said to be two parts from there;
above that, it is one and a half parts, and the pericarp is indeed half a part.
Furthermore, the neck should be one and a half [units];
the outer projection on the pericarp and the projection [on the other side] should likewise be made, with two bands according to the division.
It is known as Amṛta; one should perceive it as being surrounded by arrows. It constantly bestows all accomplishments, and [the woman] has a good husband and many offspring.
If, in each of the two fortnights, there should likewise be twelve parts,
then one part would constitute a quarter-verse through three or two revolutions.
Furthermore, one [part] has two necks with a circular section protruding by one unit;
likewise, at every unit there is a protrusion, forming circular bands.
The full mandala is described as having a radiance equal to the full moon;
it bestows divine knowledge and yoga, and is conjoined with the thousandfold Khecarīs.
And likewise, above, it is divided according to the seasons; in both fortnights,
by means of entering successive divisions, it revolves in a circular form.
The neck should indeed be equal to that portion of the circumference of the throat;
one should likewise fashion its projection as being two parts in circumference.
This is indeed remembered as the Vṛttasūtra, known by the name Saṃvarta;
the distinct classification of [the deities] beginning with Vedyā and ending with Nandikā has been proclaimed therein.
Their forms were distinct from one another, and they were likewise numbered as eight:
Vaidika, Padmaka, Pāyodhārā, and Amṛta.
That which is known as the *nandikāvarta* is described as being square;
the *pūrṇamaṇḍala-saṃvarta* consists of two circular pedestals.
The five types of pedestals (piṇḍikā) are known as Vedī, Padmā, Payodharī, Nandyāvarta, and Amṛtā; they are square in shape and provided with a raised rim.
Saṃvartā, Pūrṇavṛttā, and Devavṛttakā are like a pedestal;
I shall now describe their forms, as well as those of the Vedikā and others, according to tradition.
The circumference of the water-receptacle should be equal to the width of the pedestal;
one-third of that should be the inner [diameter], and the hole itself should be one part.
Having set aside half of the field, the girdle (mekhalā) should be formed in one part;
its threefold depth is known to be equal to the girdle itself.
The lower part [of the base] is three parts less than the end, and it is equal in width;
the upper girdle is three [parts], while the height of the pit is equal to its own circumference.
The wise one should cause the life-breath (prāṇa) ornament to extend out in the portion of Rudra;
its width at the base should be one part of the measurement in finger-breadths (kṣetrāṅgula) of that field.
One should determine the width to be half of that, extending forward;
first, one should dig a pit in the middle of the *bhūtāṃsa* with two parts, just as it is within.
Having made that half the outer [measurement], the girdle (mekhalā) should be fashioned with a height double the width of the knowledge-base (jñānamra), and its circumference four times that measure.
And thus the altar (vedi) is described as being provided with three girdles;
when it is adorned with garlands of *nandikāvarta* patterns, it is then called an *alāñchita* altar.
At that very time, the Nandikāvarta and the Mekhalā should likewise be formed;
the Vedic altar (vedī) rests upon the Vedic platform (vedikā), and the Nandikā rests upon the Nandikā-platform.
A single, very beautiful girdle of lotuses should be fashioned;
there shall be eight lotus petals in the middle, as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The cavity is prescribed for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the remainder is as before;
the altar (vedikā) possesses water-channels, and the girdle (mekhalā) is four [units] from that.
The fifth [line] is joined with the girdle (mekhalā) and is known to be like nectar as before;
having drawn out half of the diagonal of the square by means of the ear-line, perform it like fire.
By abandoning one part after careful deliberation, the full mandala is accomplished;
its girdle is likewise remembered as being like the seasons or like Samvarta.
The girdle (mekhalā) and the water-channel (praṇāla) should be as described previously and likewise bright white;
whatever fruit is proclaimed for being situated on the pedestal (pīṭha), that same fruit belongs to the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
In the lotus, one should place Padmā; in the ocean-bearing receptacle, Dharā;
in the full earth, one should join Pūrṇā; and likewise, in the nectar, Amṛtā.
The term *saṃvarta* should be diligently applied [to both];
the distinction between the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the base (*piṇḍikā*) has not been stated by the Venerable One, as they are essentially identical in their function.
And it should be very long; its characteristic is said to be that the upper part is divided like a deity's [image], and likewise both ends are elongated.
One part [of the height] is formed by two [units], the triple-jointed shank by two, and the pericarp by one;
the neck should be made by the *ḍimbhas*, and the exit of the flame by the *varṇikas*.
Likewise, one should perform it with two [verses] for those with two divisions; indeed, this brings about auspicious results.
For these images, there may also be very beautiful pedestals or altars.
I shall describe the seats, each individually, which are worshipped by the world-protectors:
those of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa.
O Goddess of the Suras,
the ten seats (pīṭhas) are declared to be those of Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
The vajra, the śakti, as well as the staff, the sword, the noose, and the goad;
the mace, the discus, the trident, and the lotus—these are declared to be the ten [weapons].
Now the pedestal (pīṭha) and the base (piṇḍikā) for the liṅgas are described:
[the directions] are Pṛthvī, Āgneyī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, and likewise Vāruṇī.
Airāyākṣī, Raudrī, Vaiṣṇavī, and likewise Brāhmikā;
their dual form is to be perceived in both the obligatory and occasional rites.
They are always described by their shapes according to the distinctions of the square and so forth;
however, they receive a specific designation when they are marked with oil for occasional purposes.
Vajriṇī, she who is named Śaktidaṇḍā, Khaḍginī, Pāśinī,
as well as Dhvajinī, Gadinī, Śūlinī, and likewise Cakriṇī.
33a) And she is proclaimed as Padminī, the fulfiller of diverse desires;
and that seat named Aindra is celebrated as being square.
Just as the wall has equal compartments, so too is its upper part equal to that;
yet, what is your single girdle, while the second one is together with the roots?
The water-channel and the natural or excavated pit should possess the same characteristics as previously described;
that which pertains to the Aindra-liṅga is thus declared, and one should establish it in the eastern direction.
One attains sovereignty in heaven and the status of a god as the lord of the deities;
by performing what [deed] are the gods and others known to be his obedient servants?
One attains temporary enjoyments through you, but thereafter reaches the partless state;
the square field of the city [of the body] has Brahma’s station at its center and extends to the two sides.
Having made half of the *karṇa* equal to a *veda* (four units), one should discard one [unit] and rotate [the cord] between the two;
having placed a *bhūta* (one unit) outside the field, its width should be equal to that.
From the circumference, one should first draw a line; likewise, there shall be another part.
Having made the height six parts, that which is fashioned in the shape of a vulva is completed.
That form [should be made] with the lower leg portion, and likewise on the pitcher;
having made it equal to that by reducing [the measurements], so too should the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and the stalk (*thiva*).
The neck is prescribed for the *karṇikā*, and one should not cause it to diminish there;
having made a projection of one part, it should likewise be so above again.
This has been declared as pertaining to the fire-altar (Āgneya); now hear about its upper pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Having fashioned the pedestal like a throne (pīṭha), the water-channel (praṇāla) should likewise extend outward.
Having placed half of the portion of the elements (bhūtāṃśa) in front, the girdle (mekhalā) is outside above it;
this is the prescribed rule for the conduit (praṇāla), while the remaining characteristics are as previously described.
The yoni is said to be at the end of the girdle; its width is above and below.
The two girdles are known as belonging to Agni, and they are proclaimed for the fire-altar of the Liṅga.
Having established that in the portion of Viśākhā, one who is intent upon it bestows the enjoyment of sovereignty;
having experienced the fruit of that moment, he shall thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
When divided by half the diameter, one should discard two units from the east and west;
by rotating [the cord] toward the east, south, and north, it is accomplished like a crescent moon.
Having made the height like the star [the distance between the eyebrows], one should know the throat by three parts of the *ghaṭakarṇikā*; again, the exit is likewise.
This is indeed known as the southern [part], and the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is said to be made of honey;
having fashioned the pedestal like a throne, the spout should be like a vessel with a stream.
Likewise, it should be shaped like a bow, with a protruding rim and a girdle;
it should be naturally hollowed out, yet it too must have three tiers.
That [attainment] is declared to belong to the Liṅga of Yama, situated in the portion of that direction;
having enjoyed various pleasures and sovereignty throughout his entire kingdom in that city, [he attains it].
One should give [the gift] until the time of the Yamaka festival,
and thereafter, for six months from the Vedāstra [festival], one should give it outside the two fortnights.
Having led out the fifth line externally, equal in extent to the previous one,
and having drawn three lines from that point, a triangle is accomplished.
Having established the height like that of the Vasus (eight), one should decrease three units for each [subsequent part];
then, two parts constitute the neck, and there is a gradual projection of three [units].
This is indeed the Nairṛta pedestal; now hear concerning the piṇḍikā.
Having fashioned the piṇḍikā like the pedestal, one should provide a channel at the tip of the enclosure.
As before, one should conceive of one's own brother as being devoid of the girdle;
however, when joined with three girdles, he is remembered as "elevated" (unnata), just as previously described.
The Mekhalā of the channel should extend outward by half its width;
it is called Nairṛtī, and it belongs to Nairṛta in that direction.
The enjoyment of one who has established [the image] is remembered as being equal to that of the kingdom in former times;
having enjoyed it for that duration of time, he shall thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
Having made half the ear like a Veda (four units), one should discard one and rotate [the other] evenly;
thus it becomes a complete circle, possessing a luster equal to the full moon on the fifteenth day.
Having made the height like that of Rudra, the arrangement of the base (pāda) is in one part;
the shank (jaṅghā) is declared to be in two parts, and the pericarp (karṇikā) should be like the base.
The neck should be known as three parts; from the pericarp (karṇikā) there is an outward projection.
From that, it is again like the shank, and its upper part is like the foot.
The measurement from the bottom to the top of the neck is equal to its own parts;
this is known as the circular line, and the pedestal is designated as Vāruṇa.
That same *samāpiṇḍikā* is circular in shape at the top and very beautiful;
its *praṇāla*, *mekhalā*, and the hollowed-out pit (*svabhrakhāta*) are as described before.
At the edge of the pit, one should construct three tiers of the girdle (mekhalā);
and for the Vāruṇa-liṅga, one should install it in that direction.
Having enjoyed various pleasures in that city, which possessed qualities equal to his own,
and having ruled the kingdom for that time, he thereafter attained the state free from affliction.
The field, divided according to the seasons, should be led [extended] by one part toward the east;
likewise, one should lead that part back, and from that, there shall be the taking of half.
There should be two "crow's feet" marks to the south;
by means of the north-south alignment, one should drop two lines.
A pair [of lines] going from the water-quarter (west) to Īśa (north-east) and likewise from the east to the wind-quarter (north-west)—
by laying down six such lines, the hexagon is indeed accomplished.
Having divided the upper portion into thirteen parts,
one should understand that the foot, the pitcher-base, and the pericarp are formed by three, two, and one part respectively.
In these two parts, one should fashion the *kaṇṭha* (neck) and the *karṇikā* (fillet), with an outward projection;
the *ūrdhvapaṭṭa* (upper band) is like a water-pot, while the *ūrdhvapaṭṭikā* (upper strip) is like a foot.
The Vāyavya [mandala] is endowed with a water-receptacle and possesses auspicious characteristics;
I shall now describe that water-receptacle situated above the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Having fashioned a pedestal like a throne by omitting the six corners,
there should be a water-channel in the intermediate corner, possessing characteristics identical to those previously described.
The girdle-thread and the trench should be as they were before;
the girdle should be on top, and the trench at the bottom—this is the arrangement.
The emblem of Vāyu is known as Irā, consisting of two digits;
in his city, he is equal to the wind, possessing the vigor and prowess of the wind.
Having enjoyed various pleasures endowed with the sovereignty of kingship until the end of time, liberation will thereafter come to pass.
Having performed the Vāruṇa [section] exactly as it occurred, one should then perform the Saumyaka;
having made it six parts in height from that, one should execute the drawing of the leaf-designs.
