Having thus correctly rotated sixteen and twelve [spokes], when this has been done, the twelfth and the sixteenth [are placed] above; likewise, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is above that.
As before, it is joined with three girdles of equal measure;
there, the center is marked with eight [petals], and the pericarp contains a circular depression.
The Yakṣī named Yākṣī is celebrated as belonging to the Kauverya Liṅga;
in that city, the enjoyments of the maker are equal to those of Vaneśvara himself.
This very faction is served by innumerable yakṣiṇīs;
having enjoyed the end of the period of the faction, one shall thereafter attain the state of liberation.
One should divide the distance from the center of Brahma’s site to the ear-line equally like the sun;
by discarding one part on all sides, the well-known four-cornered [altar] is established.
Having taken the cord from the Brahma-position and marked out the directions, one should likewise lay down four cords; thus the eight-sided figure is accomplished.
Having made the height like that of Rudra, the arrangement of the pedestal (pāda) shall be one part;
the shank (jaṅghā) shall be two parts, and the pericarp (karṇikā) shall be just one part.
One should know the neck by three [parts], with the emergence of the pericarp;
then above that it is like the shank, and the fillet above that is like the foot.
This is indeed remembered as the Āiśāna [mandala]; the piṇḍikā (pedestal) is equal to that height.
Having turned out the eight corners, there is a water-channel (praṇālaka) at each intermediate corner.
The girdle and the moat should be as previously described and possess the same characteristics;
it should have three girdles and is renowned by the name Raudrī.
And one should duly install the emblem of Aiśānya to the northeast;
endowed with the yoga of knowledge, one shall dwell for a long time in the world of Īśa.
Possessing three eyes and a trident in hand, with prowess equal to Rudra,
he shall enjoy various pleasures in that city and then proceed to the city of Śiva.
Having divided the field into eighteen parts on all sides, one should discard the square [in the center]; thus the other [remaining area] is perfected by the wise.
O virtuous lady, the projection should be only three units in width and one-third of that in extension; having first removed the corner from the field, O lady of excellent vows.
One attains a form equal to that of Vainateya through the auspicious scripture;
the upper portion is made with ten parts, and one part is level with the earth.
From two parts, the lower jaw is formed; from one part, the pericarp (karṇikā) arises.
One should know that the neck consists of two parts, and the emergence of the flame occurs at the pericarp.
The upper band for the shanks is called the *jaṅghāvarddha-paṭṭa*, while the upper strip for the feet is the *pādavarddha-paṭṭikā*;
this pedestal, worshipped by the gods, is renowned by the name of Vaiṣṇava.
Having fashioned a very beautiful pedestal above the base,
one should place the water-channel in the center of the Garuḍa as previously described.
35a) One should mark the excavation for the girdles according to the previous measurement;
indeed, two girdles are to be fashioned for those called Vaiṣṇavīs.
One should install the Vaiṣṇava liṅga in the southwest,
either in the center of the city itself, or in a village, or even in a small settlement.
In the world of Viṣṇu, possessing great majesty and valor equal to that of Viṣṇu,
he likewise became four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having enjoyed its various portions, O beloved, until one reaches the presence of Viṣṇu, one shall ultimately attain the divine state of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
The Brāhma [liṅga] is prescribed for Kauverī, and its pedestal (piṇḍikā) is of the same kind;
it is declared that the Brāhma-liṅga should be installed in the northeast.
Or if it is established in the center, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
having enjoyed temporal pleasures there, one subsequently goes to the Niṣkala state at the end.
I have described in brief those who are honored by the world-protectors;
through their grace, they attained renown as gods and achieved divinity in heaven.
Piṅgalā said:

O God, if a seat (pīṭha) is said to possess the characteristics of a vajra and so forth, it is for the purpose of accomplishing the directions; whatever is its means of action is for the sake of accomplishing that specific rite.
"Please tell me all of this in brief out of your grace.
Bhairava said:
The field, which is square on all sides, is divided like a row of seats.
Having discarded three parts each from outside the middle sūtra,
one should draw [the lines] like a crescent moon from both sides.
This is declared to be the *grāha*; it is twice the length of the *bhasa* at its end.
At the root, it is equal to the end of the *grāha*, and one should omit two parts at its tip.
The four horns are likewise [formed] by a fourth part of the length;
the central horn is four parts in width, and its length is equal to that.
Leaving an interval of one unit between each, one should fashion it in the shape of a vajra;
the vajra should have five prongs, and one should distinguish it by its characteristic marks.
The seat named Aindra is joined with that which is designated as Vajra;
likewise, there are four vajras in the four directions and also upon the pedestal.
And she is proclaimed as Vajriṇī in the direction of the Vajra-liṅga;
whatever accomplishment (siddhi) may arise when it is installed, I shall declare that in its entirety.
One should paralyze the enemy army, obstruct it, and pin it down; likewise,
one should secure one's own stability, as well as sovereignty, fortitude, and victory.
For as long as life lasts, his existence shall be well-accomplished and free from thorns.
Having enjoyed various pleasures existing in the mortal world,
he is accompanied by thousands of women, possesses a vajra-body, and is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
At the end of the body, his departure to the world of Śiva is certain,
provided he is endowed with that substance and state, and his mind is fixed upon that mantra.
Success is achieved here without doubt, according to the certainty of the scripture:
one should divide the field into four parts and discard two parts on each side.
That which is the total length should again be made equal to the height;
the width, moreover, is declared to be exactly twice the length.
Having divided the fourth part into two, divide the width into three;
at the tip of the staff, one should fashion the end of the *gaṇḍikā* with one part.
The *gaṇḍika* is proclaimed to have two parts, the seventh;
there, the two wings are like half-moons, and the fixed point (*dhruva*) will certainly have the form of a planet.
Therefore, O beloved, one should cause the junction of the two [lines] from the Brahma-line and the Agra-sūtra;
one should eliminate two parts on both sides of the staff (daṇḍa).
Having grasped the base of the staff at both ends where the portions curve,
and having placed the hand upon the Brahma-thread, the *gaṇḍikā* should be positioned below that.
This external weapon known as Śakti is said to have the form of a *śruva* ladle;
joined with that, the seat of Śakti is proclaimed to be in the southeast.
And the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is likewise declared to be renowned by the name Śakti;
one should install it in that direction for the Śakti-liṅga, O Lord of Gods.
It certainly brings about the burning and drying up of the enemy's army, as well as their utter defeat,
and the torment of a great fever-fire for the foes.
There shall be radiance for the performer, success from me, and the destruction of enemies;
moreover, there is victory, possession of power, and the destruction of disease by the Tejogra [mantra].
Having enjoyed a vast kingdom on earth and all pleasures without exception,
his departure from the body occurred at the place where the god Maheśvara resides.
One should divide the field into four parts as before and eliminate two;
from the center of the field, one should lead a line equally toward the eastern direction.
Having divided the width into three parts, divide the fourth part into two.
Having made it bow-shaped beneath that part, there shall be a *gaṇḍikā* at the base of the staff.
38a) Above that, as before, one should grasp [the material] by fashioning it in the shape of moonlight;
and the portion above that belongs to the two sides of the rounded *gaṇḍikā*.
O fair-faced one, one should destroy two parts of the staff's wings;
taking the upper portion as a part, there is a circumambulation from the Brahma-position.
This [staff] is indeed remembered as being at the top of the staff, and the staff itself consists of three threads;
O Dear One, the seat marked with the sign of the staff is said to be joined to the south of the staff.
And likewise here, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is celebrated by the name Daṇḍin;
one should install it upon that region of the liṅga known as Daṇḍa.
That rite is intended to be performed with substances, mantras of existence, and instruments;
it involves striking with a staff or a club, as well as piercing the vital organs of the enemy.
There shall be the increase of the destruction of enemies, the defeat of foreign kingdoms,
the elimination of one's own loss of time, and the enhancement of manly prowess and splendor.
For by Yama one slays the enemy, which cannot be achieved even by oneself;
having enjoyed various pleasures on earth and a kingdom free from thorns.
The extent of his movement at the end of the *piṇḍa* is where the Lord of the Mother (Ambikāpati) resides;
that field is divided like the Vedas by excluding two [units], as previously described.
One should lead two fields together with the eastern end as before;
the length divided into nine parts shall likewise be fourfold in width.
One should arrange the loss of time and the two lower parts such that they are doubled;
and one part of the circle should be placed below according to the method for the crescent moon.
One should fashion a barley-corn shape beneath the wheel according to its beauty;
above that, O auspicious one, the supporting element should be shaped like a barley-corn in two parts.
Above that, one part is for the circular *gaṇḍikā* of the two *paṇḍas*;
one should remove two parts for the wings, taking half a part from the middle.
O virtuous one, one should whirl [the hand] from the tip to the crown of the head with the "half-moon" gesture;
by making the tip of the trident slightly curved, the sword [mudrā] is perfected.
The seat belonging to Nairṛtya is joined with that which is known as the sword;
it should be seen as having a pedestal, and it is renowned by the name "Sword."
One should install that [liṅga] upon the site of the liṅga known as Khaḍga;
by means of those mantras, meditations, and ritual materials, one shall partake in the fruit of that rite.
It causes the destruction of armies, madness, the piercing of stakes, and delusion; it brings about the ruin of enemies, mutual hatred, and the incitement of Māras and Rākṣasas.
There is the onset of urinary disorders and other ailments, as well as suffering from leprosy caused by enemies;
yet there is personal valor, prosperity, and through one's splendor, extreme invincibility.
One endowed with human effort and the quality of passion (rajas) shall become a sovereign lord of the earth;
and having enjoyed various pleasures under a king of the Rakshasas, he shall eventually attain the state of Shiva.
One should likewise abandon the field portion created by the sun in the four directions;
for that which is established other than the field, treat that field according to the seasons.
One should conceive of the sky as the portion of Brahmā, O Goddess, by dividing it into two parts;
that measurement is both above and below, on the two sides of the Brahma-sūtra.
In that regard, O fair-faced one, one should take two cords extending upward from the measurement of the field;
the downward cord should be double that length, and the tail should be according to the measurement of the face.
The thread, having been made to mark the divisions, should be rotated from the Brahma-position;
one should rotate it again for the secondary divisions (upasaṃdhi) and likewise for the junctions (saṃdhi).
They should rotate further upward in that very same sequence;
drawing the thread made at the Brahma-position like a half-moon at the junction.
This indeed should be rotated clockwise; having rotated it once, one should rotate it again.
The measurement of the two wings should be equal to that of the exit.
By means of the method of the sword and the moon, there shall be two pitchers for those two;
having established the measurement of the pitcher at the bottom, O future one, along the Brahma-thread.
Like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree, [the shape] should be formed at the end of the pitcher by drawing lines;
the two eyes should be made situated upon the two side-lines.
Auspiciously circular on all sides with a measurement of half a finger-width less than half [the total],
it is formed by the union of the two ends of the pitchers at the boundary-line of the field.
But at the bottom of the question, the wise one should cause a short *sudanta* to be made;
the conjunction of limbs occurs in due order, as it is correctly inscribed at the tip.
Having placed the face downward with its own limb, and having likewise made the *nalāṅgula* [measurement],
one should perform the *āgamayoga* and thus destroy the remaining line.
Having abandoned the Brahma-sūtra and established two [points], the serpent [line] proceeds by a measurement of half of a quarter-eye; the lines of the face are indeed transverse.

The pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of the two nooses and the base (piṇḍikā) must likewise be fashioned for the sake of the accomplishment of one's own purpose, for the liṅga whose nature consists of the noose.
Rites such as those for peace and nourishment (śānti-puṣṭi) should be performed with [mantras] established in the Vāruṇī [mudrā];
having enjoyed worldly pleasures, he indeed goes to the world of Śiva.
The field, divided into four parts, is square on all sides;
its projection [the *nirgama*] is equal in width to the measurement of the northernmost portion.
O beautiful one, that field is twice as long on the other side;
thus, having made a hand-mark at the corner, there is a rotation through two squares in the middle.
By means of the method for drawing a crescent moon, one should fashion three lines;
then, having erased the remainder, one should place a thread at the end of the staff.
Having gone by the measure of the portion, one should place [the mark] and rotate the thread around the center;
one should likewise do so at the base, and thus a circle will certainly be formed both below and above.
The staff should have three threads and likewise be smeared with ashes;
the seat should be named after Vāyu, and it should be joined with a goad.
The goad, known by its name, should be regarded as being like a small ball;
now I shall explain the banner correctly—listen to that accordingly.
The field, divided into four parts, should discard two parts from the wings;
one should determine the measurement of the field externally and its length in the east.

Having made the width equal to that of the Veda (the altar), the wise man should construct a pedestal with a single elevation; he should then omit those two long wings by means of their inward contraction.
Two parts are declared to be the pillar due to the arrangement of three threads;
having established the pillar above, one should rotate from the station of Brahmā.
At the top of the pillar there should be a circle; from that measurement, one should lead [the line] toward the south.
Slightly inclined, the cord should extend so as to have a width equal to that of the pillar.
At the tail of the *gaccha*, two bundles of feathers (*picchikā*) should be attached;
it may consist of three or five sections, with the transverse lines being in pairs.
Having made it with a space of one finger-breadth [between], it is proclaimed as the "flag" (dhvaja);
that which was previously described as the pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be joined with that flag.
Piṇḍikā is to be seen as Vahni; she is renowned by the name Dhvajinī.
She who is called Dhvaja belongs to the Liṅga named Dhvaja, and she who is called Aṅkuśā belongs to the one named Aṅkuśa.
One should establish that measure with the substances of the bhāvas in that same direction;
it effects the eradication of enemy armies, as well as confusion, agitation, and trembling.
In that circle of enemies, mutual strife will certainly arise;
the victor quickly attains triumph over both factions of the enemy.
Having become equal to the power of the wind and enjoying royal pleasures upon the earth,
when his body has dissolved, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
39b) Having made it four-cornered like the Vedas, one should discard two parts as before. Having brought that measurement from the east, divide the width into four parts.
Having divided the field into two parts, the *gaṇḍikā* should be formed by one part;
it should be shaped like a bow, and above that, the *grāhavartanā* should be one part.
Of that [upper part] as well, one portion should be below like the cheek;
then, one should eliminate two equal portions from both upper wings.
After the destruction of the two parts, one should rotate upward from the station of Brahmā;
by means of the method of the crescent moon, the head itself is accomplished.
Having fixed the two ends and the two ends of the *gaṇḍikā* onto the cord, one should shorten it;
this, O auspicious lady, is called the *gadā* (mace) due to the removal of the middle cord.
The neck should be the pedestal (pīṭha), and that which is joined with it is the gentle pedestal (saumyapīṭhaka);
the one called the mace (gadā) is joined with the axe (pākṣī), and there is no doubt regarding the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
And one should install the liṅga known as Gadā in the northern direction,
endowed with all kinds of jewels and accompanied by elephants, horses, and other such [attendants].
A most beautiful maiden may come from a foreign army to choose her own husband;
she will always obtain peace, affection, and extreme excellence.
He has no enemy, and his kingdom is free from all thorns;
he possesses wealth of unfathomable extent, accompanied by thousands of women.
Endowed with an excellent maiden, he becomes equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera);
having enjoyed the entire surface of the earth, he finally attains the state beyond all form (niṣkala).
Having made it four-cornered like a square, one should discard two parts from the two wings;
that [remaining] field, divided threefold and extending downward, shall become equal to the eight [squares].
Having made half the field equal to that, one should rotate it according to the portion of the *kauṇa*;
having made it terminate at two parts, this is done by the method of the crescent moon (*khaṇḍacandra*).
Having formed the hand externally, one should again rotate it upwards;
having divided the hand into two parts according to the procedure for the crescent moon (khaṇḍacandra).
Having placed the hand on the exterior, one should again rotate it upwards;
having placed the hand at the upper half, that which constitutes the Brahma-thread [is formed].
One should then rotate it within the mouth [of the triangle] so that it extends two parts upward;
in this way, the two horns are indeed accomplished. Now, the middle horn is described.
Having taken two parts from the middle of the meaning of the Brahma-sūtra for the wise one—
yoga situated in the Brahma-sūtra and wisdom occupying half a part.
The remaining lines are to be erased; having made the staff as wide as a Veda (four units) and equal in height and width to the prongs, one should mark it with the characteristic of a half-moon.
Due to that connection, like a girdle, from a measurement of four finger-breadths below, the lower staff should consist of two parts; one should eliminate two equal parts below.
The waistband (kañcī) should be three finger-breadths [in width], and the wooden peg (kīlaka) should be eight finger-breadths;
the staff (daṇḍa) is traditionally said to have three lines, while the trident (triśūla) is fully described.
The seat named Śūla is situated in the northeast;
it is joined with Rudrī, who is celebrated as Śūlinī.
One should install the emblem known as Śūla in the northeast;
this results in the completion of undertakings already begun, a stable kingdom, and freedom from thorns.
What must the kings who rule over islands and continents do to be submissive? And what, then, need be said of those who dwell within their own respective domains?
Having enjoyed various pleasures born of mortal birth, O lady of beautiful hips, those established in the yoga of knowledge shall return once more to the abode of Śiva.
Having drawn a line from the corner of the Vedas (fourth part) to the middle of the ear, fashion it like fire;
then, setting aside one part, rotate twice from two parts.
Having made it equal at the end of three parts, one should rotate from the middle part;
having made it equal at the tip of the horse's nose, one should rotate again at the end.
Within the *siddhāntara*, the number of *kalās* is traditionally recorded as twenty-four;
at the navel, it is half of that, and the navel-maṇḍala consists of two parts.
The discus is proclaimed as being wide-spreading, and by name it is indeed the Sudarśana;
that Vaiṣṇava seat is joined with what is designated as the Cakra.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should likewise be known as the one renowned by the name Cakriṇī;
the characteristic of the pedestal for the five-liṅga [image] is said to be half a wheel (cakrārddha).
One should duly install [the deity] in the southwest or in the central region as before,
for the sake of alchemy, elixirs, and the mastery of the underworld and other realms.
The daughters of the Daityas for the sake of accomplishment, the daughters of the Nāgas as the means of attainment, the dwellings of the Vidyādharas, the mantras, and the Āgamas.
The illusions, nets, and secret spells are indeed accomplished through non-investigation;
likewise, for one who is constantly established in ritual action, they are achieved by means of those states, substances, and mantras.
Having enjoyed various pleasures upon the earth and ruled the entire kingdom,
at the end of his body, he goes to where the god Maheśvara dwells.
With a cord whose length is one-third of the diagonal of the square and equal to its vertical side,
one should draw a circular mandala after setting aside one part.
Having made half a circle like a Veda (square), one should rotate it twice at the end;
having fashioned the pericarp, one should draw the filaments in the second [circle].
With twenty-four *āvakra* lines, three of which are curved,
one should fashion eight petals at the end, each separated by two parts.
Having formed a grid of sixty-four squares marked out in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
one should arrange pairs of lines between each cardinal and intermediate direction.
With a sharp point and a split tip, adorned with eight beautiful petals—one should fashion a lotus; this is the procedure for a variegated stalk.
O wise one, there should be nine dots situated in the pericarp;
that which is called the seat of Brahmā is joined with that which is known as the lotus.

One should fashion the protective [deities] ending with Padmānta, distributed according to their respective divisions in the four directions, specifically upon the shanks, the silken cloth, and the neck.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) is known as Brahman; when it is joined with that, it becomes the Padminī.
One should install the Śaiva [liṅga] in the center of a liṅga marked with a lotus.
For the purpose of accomplishing the earth, [he gave] the seven continents in their entirety,
as well as the nine regions surrounding Jambūdvīpa.
Possessing Kumārī and joined with the eight islands,
he becomes a most righteous king, ruling the earth under a single umbrella.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the rite of rising, there is the wooden staff and the water-pot;
and for the sake of accomplishing the lotus and other [symbols], there is the practice of the lotus-linga.
Having enjoyed various pleasures throughout the mortal world,
at the end of his body, he goes to where the Lord Maheśvara dwells.
The characteristics of the *pīṭha* and *piṇḍika* have been briefly explained;
having seen both the visible and invisible fruits, they are proclaimed as being common [to all].
It is taught that the pedestal and the base should be equal to the liṅga;
and on all sides of the image, there should be two bases corresponding to its own depth.
But when the measurement of the pedestal or the linga exceeds [the prescribed standard] in any respect,
all the inhabitants of that region are constantly afflicted by diseases.
The supervisor, the artisan, and the sculptor, together with the image-protectors,
are all afflicted by diseases such as consumption, leprosy, fever, and the like.
And when the liṅga exceeds the measurement of the pedestal (piṇḍikā),
then it incurs all the faults previously mentioned.
Just as the *liṅga* should be joined according to one's karma— otherwise in the case of auspicious [deeds]—
so too silence results from one who lacks pride, while expulsion and the like result from one who is overly arrogant.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) shall always belong to the lingas and their bases;
it should always be present when there is disease or when a deficiency occurs.
There is no doubt that one who installs a *liṅga* or other objects without knowing the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) will suffer the destruction of prosperity;
this is especially true if one fails to understand the characteristics and other qualities of the *liṅga* and so forth.
I shall declare its defect, just as there is affliction for the kingdom when a *liṅga* or a pedestal is installed devoid of luster.

In the *saṃpuṭa* yoga, there is difficulty with the bowels and excrement; in the *sodara*, eight types of abdominal diseases; in the *sakṣata*, consumption (*kṣaya*); and in the *kukṣicchidra*, purgation.
Indeed, epilepsy occurs when the *pṛṣṭha* is deficient; fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*) in the vaginal opening;
and the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) in the penis or the seat of vital energy (*tejas*) when it is devoid of luster.

If the *sūtra* (the thread) is deficient, there will be lameness; if it is excessive at the head, there will be headache; if it is deficient at the eighth knot (*aṣṭhaphala*), there will be enlargement of the intestines; and if it is deficient at the wings, there will be a severe fever.
In the case of a subtle birth-channel (sūkṣmayoni), there is misfortune; in a large birth-channel (vṛhadyoni), urinary disorders (prameha);
likewise, cough, consumption, and hiccups occur when it is torn (vilupita).
If the *lambasūtra* is omitted, ear disease arises;
and if the *pakṣasūtra* is omitted, one is born with a deficient chest.
Whether in a linga, or on a pedestal (piṇḍikā), or on a throne, or in a manifest form; or in the mouth born from the limbs of the linga, or in a painting, or even on a wooden panel.
If there is a movement of the mobile liṅga, or of earth, clay, stone, and so forth,
then that deficiency will certainly result in disease for the subjects at the time of its manifestation.
Therefore, having consulted with his wives and kingdom regarding what is beneficial,
the king should install a Liṅga endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Having perceived an adverse sign, one may perform an obstacle-rite at that very time;
for one who knows the Dharma and protects the Dharma, no fault arises from this.
O Pṛthvīpāla, you are remembered as a king who proclaims the conduct of the virtuous,
renowned for the restraint of the wicked, and established like the very King of Dharma (Yama).
41b) Since there is a loss of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, the king should consume one-fourth [of the merit].
And he should make the *piṇḍī* at the mouth and the *liṅga* into two segments.
Otherwise, a fault arises from piercing the mouth, nose, and other parts; even in the case of arranging a large image, there too it should be done in two sections.
The joining [of the bow] should be done with firm metals, avoiding iron and the like;
one should avoid iron, brass, bronze, and so forth, because they lead to inauspicious results.
One should likewise employ gold, silver, copper, pegs, and so forth;
if it is soft, there is no extraction of it, [but rather] auspiciousness through gold and iron.
O fair-faced one, for the Liṅgas and the Raudra types, the pedestal (piṇḍī) should be three parts; however, for the two [other] types, it should be equal on all sides.
In the case of a mobile liṅga, the worship for those two [the pedestal and the liṅga] should be performed proportionate to their respective portions;
however, for those made of jewels, that measurement need not be observed, and the portion for worship may be as one desires.
Since it consists of barley, wheat, mung beans, creepers, and various jewels, their pedestal should be only a finger-breadth in height; the jewel should never be placed below that.
The pedestal of the Liṅga known as Sahasra should indeed be square,
and the piṇḍikā should be made in the same manner, avoiding the placement of the yoni and other such features.
For a linga made of stone, a pedestal made of stone is prescribed;
from the lower portion of its base, the piṇḍī-pīṭha (the plinth-base) should gradually descend.
The stone representing Brahmā should certainly be situated beneath the pedestal;
it may consist of sections below the portion of Brahmā, or its width shall be one-sixth [of the total].
And there, at the girdle (mekhalā), the excavation is said to be measured according to that [same standard];
its thickness is proclaimed to be three parts less than the Brahma-portion.
Or, O lady of excellent vows, the large liṅga may be fashioned with a fourth part;
something of its own [proportion] should be made according to the middle division.
In this case, however, [the pedestal] may be made of gold and so forth, or even of stone, according to what is available;
but for a linga made of wood, a wooden pedestal is best.
In the case of a metal element, the work produced from that element is conceived according to its own kind;
in the case of a gem, the construction of a pedestal is performed using gold, silver, iron, or copper.
One should not make noise and the like; rather, it should be done with a different intention.
O fair-faced one, this applies to the pedestal of a movable liṅga made of metal.
One should determine the height by dividing the length of the *liṅga* into two parts;
that which is of its own material and made of crystal is the best, as it always brings happiness.
The arrangement of the pedestal (pīṭha) made of gold such as Jambūnada and other materials is as before;
likewise, the channel (praṇāla), the girdle (mekhalā), and the arrangement of the cavity (svabhra) are also as before.
For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should be intent upon the means and the goal;
[the linga may be] mobile, made of wood, water, metal, earth, or produced from gemstones.
Whether it be produced from fragrant substances, from molasses, or even from sesame and rice;
or likewise produced from tortoise-shell or conch-shell—specifically that which is produced from human bone and conch-shell.
Whether superior, inferior, or middling, that which bestows accomplishment is beyond doubt;
yet, it is always without garlands or boats, for the conceptualization of existence arises only from non-existence.
Then, another [liṅga] born of other materials should be fashioned according to what is prescribed for independent [liṅgas];
however, one who seeks spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) should never have a mobile liṅga made of stone.
One who desires liberation should indeed cause a single *piṇḍa* to be made for the mind alone;
it is not [required] for the *samayin*, the *putraka*, the *sādhaka*, or the *ācārya*.
Since he is indeed the mere *liṅga*, devoid of action and consisting of pure consciousness,
one should install a *vāṇa-liṅga* for the sake of accomplishing all spiritual attainments.
That which rests upon all seats and is contained within all palaces is likewise proclaimed here as "rolling," like an arrow.
Having seen that which arises from all rivers and that which originates from all mountains,
one should install the form of the Liṅga with mantras so that it becomes present.
And the pedestal (pīṭha) and the temple (prāsāda) should indeed be according to one's intention;
thus has all this been told to you regarding the characteristics of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and the base (pīṭha).
Whether it be the general or the specific, that [knowledge] is contained within the palace.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Section on the Pīṭhas," in the Piṅgalāmata within the Jayadrathādhikāra of the Brahmayāmala.
Piṅgalā said:
And that, O King, which pertains to the Prasāda, has been indicated but not fully revealed;
likewise, the characteristics of temples on the earth, preceded by the planetary positions, have been shown.
"Speak out of your grace, O destroyer of Kāla, Kāma, and Andhaka.
Bhairava said:
And the measurement by weight, measure, and capacity, preceded by the formal acquisition of land.
I shall describe the characteristics of palaces; listen with a one-pointed mind. First, one should properly examine the division of the ground therein.
Whether it be a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), a secondary field (*upakṣetra*), a gathering place (*saṃdoha*), or even a seat (*pīṭha*),
as well as a secondary seat (*upapīṭha*) or a secondary gathering place (*upasaṃdoha*), or on both banks of a river; || 42b ||
On a mountain peak, on your head, in a city, a village, or a market town;
under a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, or at the confluence of rivers.
One should examine the ground at a place where three, four, or five channels meet, or in a hollow, a deep pit, or a cave, or in the direction of one's own quarter.
White, red, yellow, and blackish are the colors [of the rays] belonging to the Brāhmaṇa and the other castes respectively;
their tastes are sweet, sour, pungent, and bitter.
Those ending with *ghṛta*, *asṛk*, *sūtra*, and *viṣṭā* are each marked by their respective scents;
*brahmāṇī* is marked by the growth of *kuśa* grass, and the three [others] by the growth of *sarasa* grass.
From a Vaiśya [father], she bears a child with the growth of *ūrvā* grass; from a Śūdra [father], she bears a child with the growth of *kāsa* grass.
One should avoid ground that is saline, infested with anthills, or flooded with water.
It was strewn with my own biting insects, a heap of bones from cruel creatures,
black with charcoal dust, and devoid of stakes or shards.
For a virtuous purpose, one should perceive it as virtuous; for a non-virtuous purpose, one should consider it as non-virtuous.
Having dug a hole only a cubit deep, one should then fill it back up with earth.
By a superior [sign] the highest stage is indicated; by one equal to it, the middling;
and by an inferior one, the lowest is declared. Thus should one discern the threefold stage.
O Umā, in the highest [practice] there is the highest accomplishment; in the middling, the middling;
and in the lowest, the lowest accomplishment, such as killing, driving away, and so forth.
O beloved Sulāṅgalī, one should place three, four, or five fruits on top; or else, one may offer other grains such as sesame, rice, barley, and so forth.
Chickpeas, chickling vetches, mung beans, black gram, and peas,
as well as wheat, wild rice, or any one of the various grains used for external offerings.
That which sprouts in three days is proclaimed as the best;
the middling in five days, and the inferior in seven days.
Therefore, it should be known that from there upwards [the tree] is inauspicious, because it does not sprout;
having encircled that spot with a wooden wedge at the onset of night.
Above the water-pot, however, there should be a vessel filled with ghee;
in the four directions, the four lamps should be prepared by members of the twice-born castes and others.
To the east is the Brāhmaṇī wick; one should consecrate it with the mantra of Abhimatrita. To the south is to be known the Kṣatriṇī, consecrated with the Ghora mantra.
43a) In the west, the Śūdrī is proclaimed, consecrated with the Sadyojāta mantra;
in the north, the Vaiśyā is to be known, consecrated with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Or with the mantras of Svatantra, Vaktra, or Praṇātha, O beloved, [one should practice] in a well-concealed and perfectly secluded place protected by the Astra-mantras.
Having performed the survey of the directions, one should veil [the site] with the armor-mantra;
if all [fires] blaze up, they bring benefit to everyone.
One whose mindfulness is unconfused shall abide for the accomplishment of all desires;
for one who has pacified the inauspicious, auspicious things arise, and the opposite for one who does not.
Furthermore, although all things are inherently extinguished and pure, they are set ablaze again;
yet, until the fuel is exhausted, they incur no fault in its absence.
Having thus concluded the night, one should perform the measurement of the ground;
at that time, one should observe divine omens and the extraordinary characteristics of the hour.
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and Anurādhā, Śatabhiṣaj and the three Uttarās,
as well as Śravaṇā and Anurādhā joined with Maitra (Jyeṣṭhā)— these are remembered as the upward-facing constellations.

Those who undertake steadfast efforts are praised when the previously mentioned lunar days and weekdays coincide; furthermore, O wise one, the yoga, the karaṇa, and the lunar asterism must also be favorable.
However, I shall now declare the power of the Moon, for the strength of the Moon is indeed essential:
the Moon [is favorable] at birth, as well as in the third, sixth, and seventh houses.
The tenth and eleventh houses grant success in all undertakings;
the ascendant, Virgo, Libra, and Aquarius are especially auspicious for this purpose.
And Vṛṣa is indeed declared to possess the perfection of all auspiciousness;
success shall be attained under the hand of the Sun (Sūryahasta) and likewise under Mṛga and the Moon (Candra).
Mars conjoined with Kṛttikā, Mercury with Abhijit, Jupiter conjoined with Revatī, and Punarvasu on Friday; [these are the auspicious conjunctions].
Success-yogas (siddhiyoga) are proclaimed to occur during the conjunction of Saturn and Śravaṇa,
as well as during the conjunction of the Sun and the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī), and the conjunction of the tenth lunar day (daśamī) and the Moon.
The eleventh lunar day conjoined with Venus, and the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with Mercury—
these are proclaimed as yogas that bring success for undertakings requiring stability.
In the center of Mount Meru, one should establish and draw the essence of the sun and moon;
likewise, lines should run from east to west and from south to north.
The right half belongs to the wheel of day, while the left half belongs to the wheel of night;
this division of day and night applies to both the external and the internal.
43b) I shall explain the two wheels correctly; listen to them accordingly.
Smoke, embers, and flame occupy the first half-hour.
Wherever the sun moves having abandoned the auspicious quarter and is considered to be in the "charcoal" (aṅgāriṇī) state,
and wherever it is remembered as being in the "flame" (jvālāmā) state, one should predict the arising of inauspiciousness.
One should draw two lines for the "rising" and the "inauspicious," marked with smoke and embers respectively;
then, between the east and south, one should drop three lines.
Likewise, for those who follow Dakṣa, there is this arrangement of lines,
beginning from sunrise until the sun has set.
O Dear One, one should perceive the internal by means of the division of the external wheel;
likewise, one should perceive both the external and the internal by means of the division of the two flames.
O Goddess, one should know that through the omens arising from those [beings], characterized by their respective directions and parts—
as previously described— whether they are situated outside or belong to the sky and the earth.
Thus, according to the division of the day, that which is auspicious regarding the acceptance [of gifts] has been stated;
now I shall fully explain how it stands within the wheel of peace (śāntācakra) during the night.
One should observe the floral offerings, whether in full bloom or as buds,
beginning from the onset of night until the range of the morning twilight.

Having made it equal to the eastern line, together with the six [digits] and endowed with three and a half watches (praharas), this is indeed known as the Moon-wheel (śaśicakra); when these are abandoned, it is called the "garland-free" (nairmālya).
The flower is said to be "moon-fallen" when it is about to fall as a bud;
even at that stage, one should perceive it as being capable [of its function] just as before.
Through the yoga of the external and internal, one should grasp what is auspicious and abandon what is inauspicious;
O Dear One, [this occurs] from the position of the letters in the sentence of the *horā*, or else from the arrival of the *āya*.
Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel, the wise one should arrange the [emblems] beginning with the banner;
one should know the banner is in the east, and the lion is said to be in the south.

The bull is to be known as being in the west, and likewise the elephant in the north; these are designated as the fixed [signs], and the [sign] beginning with Aries is beneficial for those directions.
One should recognize smoke when [the breath] is situated in the fire; when it is in the head, it is called a dog.
When it is directed crosswise, it is said to be a donkey; when it is situated at the crown of the head, they know it as a crow.
That which is desirous of it, capable, and not yet arisen causes the diminution of strength;
it is considered inauspicious when it is inauspicious and ungraspable, and auspicious when it is for the sake of the auspicious.
Having correctly understood this, the knower of mantras should perform the measurement of the ground;
he should dig a pit one-quarter deeper than the intended measurement.
The extent of the excavation all around has been declared to be as deep as the water's edge;
a wise man should dig this pit for the sake of pure consciousness or for the attainment of human goals.
Alternatively, it may be half of that half, or even half a cubit; wherever it is firm within its range, the wise man should subsequently fill in the excavation on both sides to match that level.
Filling with leather is not desired; rather, it should be done with bricks.
Furthermore, a foundation made of stone is considered heavy in weight.
O Goddess, both [the earth and the chariot] tremble due to the recoiling of the lord of serpents,
as well as by earthquakes, the movement of chariots, and the wandering of elephants and horses.
Therefore, one should not make this [image] out of lac, nor from a heap of stones; it should not be said that it may be made of clay alone, for it would not be firm and would break.
Having filled the hands with handfuls of earth and spread them out to a height of eight finger-breadths,
one should perform the sprinkling and the smoothing for each individual [section].
With *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and other such materials, and having fashioned it with the foot of an elephant,
one should make its base broad and its height equal to the measure of a navel.
One should grasp the morsel and form it into a ball; the planet [the head] should have its upper part rounded.
Having struck it according to one's ability, there is again a single expansion for each [verse].

One should fill the excavation with this [mixture] until it reaches a level one-quarter lower than the height of the temple; thus is the arrangement of the Vāstu site determined from the measurement of the palace.
Whether the site is pierced by a stake or free from stakes, or whether it has been altered or rendered incapable,
one should determine the presence of stakes after having mentally visualized them within the site.
I shall now describe the extraction of the site as it stands in the Vāstu-sūtra;
having extracted that and made it level, one should stretch the Vāstu-sūtras.
O lady of excellent vows, the procedure for the one called Pāda, as well as the characteristics of its consecration, will be explained according to the method that is about to be described.
Having brought eight stones from that place which measures one square eye (four cubits),
the skillful Guru [should prepare] eight jars, eight fire-pits, or even just one.
One should worship Vāstunara there with divine offerings such as perfumes and flowers, and with oblations that fulfill all desires, in the manner that will be described.
Above that, one should worship Śakti, who sustains all the paths;
upon half of Śakti, one should place the altar (vedī) consisting of eight parts, beginning with the number eight.
In the ninth [section], in the middle region, one should indeed place the *hyahuka*;
above that, one should place the Brahma-stone and the Śakti of Sāmbhava.
Upon that [pedestal], one should install the entire group of the eight Rudras, together with their forms (mūrtis) and so forth,
containing within them minerals, gems, medicinal herbs, metals, seeds, and mercury.
One should place the infinite lords of the gods and others— arising from gold, stars, and the dawn—
along with the digits of the moon, within the Śakti, arranging them with their respective mantras starting from the center.
Above that, one should place what is called the altar (vedi), which has the vowels as its essence;
it should be one cubit in measure, four-cornered, and three parts high.

Having recited the incomparable Śiva-mantra situated in its respective color, one should place the ninth [syllable] upon those [petals] which bear the weapons of the world-protectors and are adorned with eight-petaled lotuses.
O lady of virtuous vows, this lower world belongs to the one named Kāla;
it is proclaimed to extend through six enclosures, beginning with that which is called Kāla.
The principle of time (kāla-tattva) is the self-nature of the upper [evolutes]; one should know that the subtle elements (tanmātra) are the thread [of its manifestation].
The pervasion of the sense organs of cognition and action is taught as being contained within that.
One should thus conceive of the path called Śiva as being characterized by the display of the three qualities (guṇas) and endowed with the intellect of pride, during the practice of the feet.
One should conceive the three principles (tattvas) in three ways at the base, as well as above;
having thus conceived them, one should then [conceive] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara in sequence upon the intellect (dhī).
Knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth—
these exist in sequence starting from the southeast (Agni) and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna.
For these are remembered as having the form of the feet, or rather, the form of Hari himself:
unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of mastery (anaiśvarya).
For these four limbs extend from the east to the north;
this path is always stable, reaching as far as the worlds of Brahmā.
There, having first fashioned [the forms] with flowers and having restrained [the breath],
one should again place the eight Rudras according to the rule, accompanied by the eight forms (mūrtis).
O auspicious lady, one should worship the eight stones with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
having placed Kṣamā in the east and Agni in the southeast.
The wise one should place the sacrificer in the southern direction, and place Eka in the southwest;
having placed Indra in the north, he should place Vyāsaka in the northeast.
One should place the form of Śiva in the center and the one moving in the sky at the edge of the temple.
After the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) has been performed, these other presiding deities follow:
Sarva, Paśupati, Ugra, and likewise Rudra.
Īśāna and Mahādeva, Bhīma— the presiding deities of the forms—
and likewise Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, and Varuṇa.

Vāyu, Soma, and likewise Īśāna are to be placed in the eight pitchers located in the directions starting from the east and ending with the north, together with their respective supports, the world-protectors (lokapālas).

Indeed, their own names, beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namaḥ," should be employed at the time of worship; they should end with "svāhā" during the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
Having performed the purification through the sequence of emanation, expansion, and so forth, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and reabsorption (saṃhṛti),
one should worship according to these injunctions with offerings of bali, incense, and divine liquor.

Having worshipped one's own limbs within the sacrificial pits, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in one's own fire using fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth, after ascertaining the strength or weakness of the ritual materials.
For the forms and the lords of the forms, as well as for the world-protectors,
one may offer a hundred, a thousand, or even half of that.
One should purify [the path] according to the divisions of the paths of the principles (tattva) as they correspond to one's own consciousness;
having gone near the stone, one should sprinkle it with the water from the jar.
Having touched the stone with darbha grass, the Guru should worship the lords of the directions;
then, having performed the placement of the three principles (tattvas), he should recite the mantra and offer oblations according to his capacity.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform [the ritual] for each portion of beings according to the sequence of the two realities,
by means of the short and long vowels and the *kusamvara* syllables, [distinguishing] between those of pure and impure nature.
Having thus completed [the construction], one should then settle the site, avoiding the vital points (*marmas*),
under a fixed conjunction (*dhruvayoga*), with an auspicious asterism (*sanakṣatra*), and joined with a favorable *karaṇa* and planetary motion (*cāra*).
Or, at a time favorable for the donor’s merit, one should begin the installation of the stone;
this should be done by one who has commenced the construction of the temple with meditative absorption on the auspicious time.
Afterwards, one should offer seven oblations while meditating on those qualities ten thousand times;
by this application of the ritual, [the disciple] is established by the Guru.
Success occurs exactly as intended and not otherwise;
having visualized above that the path which is about to be described, [one should proceed].

One should likewise conceptualize the temple as being of the nature of the self, beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) and ending with Śiva; and one should also fashion the presiding deity through the unification of the principles (tattva).
Then, having assumed a physical form through his own mantra, he should offer a bali-oblation that fulfills all desires and consists of all kinds of food to the hosts of spirits.
Then the Praṇava, the word "diśām," and "vāsibhyaḥ" following that;
then "aghorebhyaḥ," "ghorebhyaḥ," and "ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ."

Having uttered "Sarvataḥ Śarvaḥ," "Namaḥ Sarvebhyaḥ," and "Sarvātmane," and having added the three words ending in "bhyaḥ" [to each], [one should worship] the elements, the Mothers, and the lords of the directions.
A wise person should employ "namaḥ" at the end [of the mantra] during the time of worship;
"svāhā" should be employed for incense, and the utterance "svadhā" when offering food.

One should offer the drink with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and the rite of the *bali* offering with the mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*. Then, having dismissed [the deity] with *hūṃ*, one should depart while uttering the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*.

In this manner, one should offer [the oblation] everywhere; however, in that specific location, one should perform the line of offerings (diśāvali) or carry out the ritual of offering (balikarma) and so forth as prescribed in one's own scripture.
Having identified [the planets] by means of mantras containing their own names, one should cause the protection from the planets to be bestowed;
having offered the bali-oblation, there shall be the attainment of auspiciousness and the planning of the temple.
Otherwise, however, the Vināyakas create great obstacles;
therefore, an offering that fulfills all desires should indeed be given everywhere.
In this sutra, the connection with the fruits [of action] pertains to rites both completed and commenced;
having performed that, and having sipped water, one should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Śiva.
Having been granted permission with the words "May it be auspicious," one should begin the temple. Now I shall fully describe the characteristics of temples.
Having made it square and even, marked out in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and divided equally into eight parts both horizontally and vertically in due order.

The pedestal (pīṭha) should occupy one-fourth [of the width], and there should be a circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa) of two seasons (six parts). Furthermore, the arrangement of the walls consists of forty-eight [parts].
The height of the *kṣetra* (base) and the *samordhajaṅghā* (middle leg) should be equal, while the *gaṇḍordha* (upper leg) should be double that;
and the *śikhara* (spire), O beautiful lady, should be measured from half the *śuka-nāsa* (beak) and the *garbha* (inner sanctum).
One should fashion its front protrusion to be equal to one-third [of the width];
its breadth according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha), and its height up to half the height of the spire (śikhara).
Having expanded it like Vasu, the inner sanctum (garbha) is said to be one-sixth;
one should fashion the neck of the Śukāghrā temple with two parts.
The eastern neck is known as the wall, and the *śukāghrāsa* is the projection;
this is indeed remembered as the measurement of the site (*vāstu*), characterized by the absence of pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).
Therefore, I shall describe the measurement of the *liṅga*: it should be equal to the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
O lady of excellent vows, the inner sanctum (*garbha*) should be half the size of the pedestal, and there should indeed be symmetry.
The *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be of that same proportion, and its width should be equal to that;
the *śikhara* (spire) above the *jaṅghā*, O fair-faced one, is said to be twice [the width of] the *jaṅghā*.
The inner core of the pedestal is the ear; by that same measurement, the parrot-nose (śukāghraka) is declared as the projection, and the remaining parts should be as previously described.
This measurement of the liṅga has indeed been declared; now the measurement of the door is being stated. Having divided [the base] into four parts like a Veda, the door should be equal to one part.
It has been explained in detail that the height should be double [the width];
the pedestal in the middle should be like the door, and the remainder should be hollow.
The wall consists of eleven parts (pādas), with its width determined by half of half the door-width;
the plinth (jaṅghā) is equal in extent to that, and the spire (śikhara) should be twice as high.
The *śukāghrā* (parrot-beak) should be understood as before, as well as its projection and height;
it is designed for a temple that lacks a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
O Lord, O Beloved, I shall describe to you the practice regarding the *śukāghrā* as it is performed in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*):
the womb (*garbha*) is neither in the two parts nor in the five parts.

At the front of the exit, it should be constructed provided with a pavilion for the parrot-feeding (śukāghra); the remaining measurements, as well as the width and height of the parrot-feeding area, are to be as previously described.
This installation of the supports (āśrayas) without a physical base has been proclaimed for lingas measuring from one cubit up to five cubits.
They are proclaimed as being either with a pavilion (maṇḍapa) or without one, and likewise as having no supporting pillars (nirāndhārā).
The most excellent pavilion is situated to the side of the pillar-base (śraka), starting from the central axis (garbhasūtra).
Therefore, it should be like a field outside; moreover, it should be superior on both sides.
This has been explained in detail, or it may be equal in front.
O beautiful goddess, the pavilion is declared to be of medium size when its wings and frontage are measured by the same unit as the inner sanctum.
The merit of the two half-garbhās (inner sanctums) is equal to that [of the full garbha] combined;
the kanya is declared to be half of that, and the ardhamaṇḍapa is half of that again.
The *śukāghrā* is equal to that [central hall], square on all sides;
the *pādamaṇḍapa* should be understood as being equal in size to the *garbha-sūtra*.
And directly in front of the maṇḍapa, there should be a mukhamaṇḍapa measuring half the size of the sanctum (garbha).
In front of half the mukhamaṇḍapa, there should be a porch (tuṣkikā) for the bull.
It should be square on all sides, with an interval equal to one-fourth [of its side];
now hear how the height of the victory-pole (jayaṣṭi) should be half the total measurement of the pavilion.
From the three pavilions, the arrangement of the teeth [pedestals] occurs along the threads;
it is four-cornered, eight-cornered, and circular, and above that is its own weapon.
The bull should be fashioned from black iron, or it may be made of bright, pure stone;
it should be robust, sharp-horned, and facing forward.

Below that, at half the height, there should be a pedestal (bandha) or a pot-shaped base (ghaṭa), and then the lotus-seat (kajāsana); below that is the Valipīṭha, which should be four cubits in extent.
It should be made square, or circular, or like a lotus;
there, O beloved, one should always place offerings of garlands and food, which are dear to the Beloved.
The circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇā) should be understood as one-fourth of the height of the spire (śikhara);
it should be level with the front of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and there the base-platform (jagatī) should be constructed.
The enclosure wall of the two equal [mandalas] should be known as being like the walls of a palace;
its height should be a mere measure of consciousness, or else it may consist of silk-cloth and be one and a half [times that].
O beloved, this has been described as the *samaṇḍapa*, which is without a supporting pillar;
now listen duly as I explain the *sāndhārika* according to its true nature.
Starting from the Sadṛṣṭa and others up to the Kaliṅgas, it should be nine cubits in length;
for those made of gold, silver, and so forth, it should be of great proportions.
O lady of excellent hips, one should construct palaces with water-channels;
otherwise, they must not be made, for if they were, it would result in misfortune.
Just as the accomplishment should be performed because they are superior to you in measure,
one should divide one's own field and property equally, like a material object.
In the first part there is the outer wall; in the second, the *andhārikā* (blind wall) should be;
and in the third, again a wall, while the inner chambers are like those of the Vedas.
The *śukāgra* should be constructed at the front, according to the measurement of its internal core;
its wall should be equal to the wall [of the main structure], and its projection and height are as previously described.
Alternatively, in another manner, make it four-cornered like a star;
[consisting of] the pedestal, the inner sanctum, the wall, and again the supporting walls.
By dividing [the space] into middle, beginning, and end, the characteristics of the single *pada* are established;
the placement (*nyāsa*) is first like that of a parrot, and it is joined with the wall within the womb.
47a) O fair-faced one, this measurement of the site is indeed known as sāndhārika;
now I shall describe the measurement of the liṅga correctly— listen to it accordingly.
Having made the pedestal equal to the liṅga, the womb-chamber (garbha) should likewise be so;
the walls should be half the size of the womb-chamber, and the enclosure wall (andhakārikā) should be equal to those walls.
O fair-faced one, the outer wall should be like a pedestal; its width, height, and projection should be as previously described, such as in the case of the *śukāghrā*.
The measurement of the linga has been fully described; now the measurement of the door is likewise stated.
The door should be half of half the inner sanctum (garbha), and the central pedestal (pīṭhaka) should be like the door.
One should know that the opening is half the width of the door, and the walls are of equal measure;
the wall is to be known as the *randhārikā*, which is beautiful on all sides.
The outer wall of the gateway should be like the *śukāghrā* as described before;
its width, height, and projection, O fair-faced one, should also be as previously stated.
However, its exit should be proclaimed as half the size of the door; for this is remembered as the measurement of the doors. Now, the measurement of the pavilions (maṇḍapas) is being described.
From the *śukanāsa* on both sides, one should lead the measurement of the site outward;
its width at the front should be equal to that, forming a square on all sides.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) described as excellent possesses auspicious characteristics;
it is square on all sides and is proclaimed as the middling type.
From the center line to the wall of the inner sanctum, there should be a *śukāghrā* (eaves) on both sides.

That [measurement] would be the full extent for the extensive [mandala], while one who knows it should understand the smallest as that [same measurement]. The womb-thread (garbhasūtra) would be the full extent, and there should be a portico (mukhamaṇḍapaka).
The maṇḍapa should be understood as being like the wall of a temple; of this there is no doubt.
The circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇā) should be known to measure one-third of the temple.
In this case, however, the jagatī and the blind wall (bandhakotra) shall occupy one-third of the pavilion;
the arrangement for the bull's face-pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) is to be understood as previously described.
One should construct the Arthaja shrine according to the measurement of two pavilions; the abodes for the deities are prescribed on the side, occupying one-fourth of the temple's area.
Those [walls] joined with rampart-battlements should not be stepped over during the circumambulation;
others, shaped like spires, are located in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneya).
The pinnacle that was previously described should be placed in the middle, provided with a door-projection.
The entrance pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) outside is provided with four supports;
at half the height of the door is a divine platform, which is called the "House of the Jar" (ghaṭīgṛha).
One should establish Nandin and Mahākāla at the gateway;
one should install Rudra as Arddhanārīśvara in the region of the southeast.
The wise man should place the form of Bhṛṅgin in the south-west, belonging to the deity Mātariśvan;
and he should place the divine abode of Yogeśvara in the west.
Then the doorkeepers [should place] Āpya in the east, Yogeśvara in the northwest, the two Aśvin gods in the west, and that Goddess likewise in the north.
Likewise, one should designate Caṇḍeśa in the northeast, and the world-protectors (lokeśas):
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Soma.

These deities, beginning with Īśāna, are remembered as having the eastern direction and so forth as their domain; one should place the Lord Īśvara in the northeast for the sake of the portion belonging to that deity.
Having established Dhūpa, one should place it in the southeast;
the divine Yogin in the south, and the two Aśvins are said to be in the southwest.
One should place the seat of the digit of the moon (Candrakalāsana) in the direction of the eastern quarter; one should place Viśvakarman in the north-west and Kāmadeva in the north-east.
O God, having thus surrounded [the site] with these, one should install the central deity;
then, one should station these deities within the moat of the enclosure wall.
Likewise, O blessed lady, due to the lack of material wealth, one should have [the images] made as if they were situated in a temple;
listen now to the method for that, which consists of both prosperity and devotion.
A temple with one hundred and eight liṅgas is called the *varāyatana*;
one surrounded by eight liṅgas in the center is the middling *navāyatana*.
I shall describe the characteristics of those [temples] with four, five, or six liṅgas, as well as the arrangement of their sanctuaries (āyatana).
The field, divided like the sun, is square on all sides;
joined with a water-clock support, it should be provided with walls and a pedestal.
Thereafter, O beautiful one, one should proceed with a single portion;
from that point, extending to the end of the square, it should go toward the east and the north as before.
Having established the inner liṅga and that which conforms to the root-liṅga, one should make it nine parts from that;
by means of these parts, the pedestal (jagatikā) shall be formed.
That which consists of four parts in the center and follows the liṅga—
having made another division from that, the jagatī should be formed by means of those parts.
In the center, the conception of the main temple consists of four parts;
this is declared to be the five-shrine (pañcāyatana) form, with four equal [shrines] at the intermediate directions.
Having properly installed the *liṅga* in the eight directions, there shall be a place of worship.
O beloved, I shall now describe the installation of one hundred and eight *liṅgas*.
Having divided the field on all sides into twenty-four parts,
the enclosure wall, formed by the outer sections, is to be made perfectly square.
Therefore, one additional part and two parts in the middle of the entrance should be laid out;
thus, one should construct four doors in the four directions at the edge of the enclosure wall.
There are two doors, it is provided with turrets and stories,
and in the corners there are four lingas and boundary-marking stones.
The remainder for the walls of the enclosure should consist of one *pādika* layer of *kośīra*;
its height should be five cubits, or four, three, or two.
One should fashion rows of liṅgas from the interior by means of the rows of bhagas,
leaving a space of one square between them, starting from the four corners in sequence.
In the center, there should be two parts, and there should be an interval in the four directions; therefore, one should conceive that interval as consisting of the *bhaga*.
The series of liṅgas should be aligned with the inner portion as before;
however, the middle [portion] should be within that, either at half a part from both ends.
In the center, a liṅga should be fashioned by taking half of a half-part;
and again within that, likewise, a series of liṅgas should be made in the same manner.
Now listen further regarding the *prāṇa*, the *liṅga*, and the *mālā*:
in the middle, there is a space of two parts, and therein the *liṅga* consists of twelve parts.
Furthermore, having again discarded the intermediate [factors] and retaining only the roots,
all these combined thus become one hundred and nine.
O Great Goddess, the number of lingas together with their bases is proclaimed;
there, one hundred and eight lingas are recorded, each measuring one cubit in height.
The middle [size] is recorded as being from three cubits up to nine cubits;
the side-liṅgas are recorded according to the proportions of the central [liṅga].
One may construct a dance pavilion with four doors or even one facing upward;
it should be of the Sarvabhadraka type in the east and of the Tripiṣṭapa type in the west.
The one on the south shall be elongated, and the one on the north shall be square;
I shall describe their characteristics and their respective applications exactly as they are.
The field, which is square on all sides, is divided into sixteen parts;
by entering one part [into each side] and omitting four [parts] at the corners.
By joining that [line] with the intermediate directions (vidiś) and extending it outward, one obtains the Sarvabhadraka;
from its extension toward the four cardinal directions, the auspicious Mattacāraṇaka is formed.
The outer wall is on one part, and this is the arrangement all around;
on the second [part] is the residence for the [principal] deity, and on the third is the residence for the gaṇikās.
And during the fourth intermediate aeon, there was the ritual for the altar’s qualities;
it was the four-footed dwelling of the dancer of the north wind.
Likewise, singers were positioned to the east, and similarly, flute-players to the west;
on the south, drums were played, while the spectators took their seats around the perimeter.
In the center, there should be a dance-platform (nṛtyapīṭha) with a height of eight finger-breadths;
O Goddess, one should fashion a space of thirty-six squares at the end of the dance.
Thus, in brief, the former dance-hall is described;
when the dance occurs in the west, they know this to be the dance of Tripiṣṭapa.
O lady of virtuous vows, its length should be equal to that of Vāruṇī;
and that field, extending toward the east, should be like the Mukhamaṇḍapa.
In that case as well, the placement (nyāsa) of the singers, the followers, and the lineage-holders is as before;
one should perform the remaining placement as before, beginning with the "bhinna" [scale] and ending with the "nṛtyakānta."
The triple-heaven (tripiṣṭapa) is so called because it has exits at three places;
I shall now describe its length as it is situated to the south.
When a square field has been made level and its sides have been aligned,
one should set aside each successive portion from east to west.
Having practiced for a long time in the east, one should arrange the Nartāvaka residence in the west, where the muraja drums and other instruments are played at the conclusion of the performance.
The wall that can be traversed by a single footstep is the level ground (gatā), while the depressions following it are the hollows (agartā).
That which is known as Guṇanīśāna is very long in the southern direction.
To the north, a square area is called the *ghaṭīgṛha* (water-clock house);
O Goddess of the Gods, this is declared to be the general measurement for palaces.
I shall describe the specific characteristics according to the designations of the forms, positions, and suns:
Meru, Mandara, and likewise Kailāsa.
Sarvabhadraka, and others, as well as Vimānonnata;
likewise Nandivṛddhi, Garuḍamāla, Siṃha, Kumbha, and Gaja.
The bull, the one named Padma, and likewise the square and the eightfold.
Then there are the sixteen-angled and the eight-angled [mandalas], as well as the Vṛkṣa and the Vardhamāna;
likewise the Pūrṇa, the one named Śrīvatsa, and the Khaṇḍa-Śrīvatsaka.
Likewise, Khaṇḍārddhaka, Bhadra, Haṃsa,
Nalina, Śrīnaga, and another, Gṛharāja.
Half of the house is called *valabhī*, and another is known by the name *miśra*.
Whatever the measurement of the width may be, one-eighth of that constitutes the minimum.
Having made the exit to the exterior, one should fashion the base-level design;
for the superior type, the middle section should be increased by twelve parts, according to the prescribed modification.
For the Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and Sarvabhadra types, the Creator himself [prescribes] the measurement for the palaces and so forth; their characteristics are determined by that specific time.
Now, its characteristic is stated by the name of the twenty-seven lunar mansions:
having made the field square, divide it into one hundred and twelve parts.
By entering with a division of the qualities, that pair has a middle width;
the division, the sub-division, and the further division should be such that the projection is equal.
In terms of width, there are two, one, and three [units] for the arrangement of the chariot;
likewise, one should effect the entry, and the corner-piṇḍikās should be like arrows.
Again, in the same manner, one should proceed in the four directions until the *nārta* is completed;
there, one should fashion the *śṛṅgāghrā*, which occupies one part in the middle.
And that [structure] has four pinnacles joined together according to measurement;
it has four doors in the four directions, and likewise, there are śukāgras.
The first enclosure (āghāṭaka) is known to consist of twenty-six *gamas*, being square and provided with four gates, located at Kumbhakoṇa.
O lady of excellent hips, there are five tiers above the shank;
the second tier is at the ankle-joint, consisting of twenty-four steps.
The four levels situated there should be made very beautiful;
likewise, the third level at the *ghāṭaka* consists of twenty-two *gamās*.
In that regard, O lady of auspicious marks, one should prepare three levels;
and within the fourth enclosure, one should arrange it with twenty gateways.
And therein, two [stages] belong to the [same] level, while those above the *vedya* belong to two levels;
by means of the four, eight, divine, and twice-eight levels.
O Goddess of the gods, the height above the shanks is known to extend to the edge of the altar;
the altar is said to consist of eight eggs, supported by sixteen teeth of the parrot-eater (the lion).
The mountain Erū is said to have one hundred and twenty-four peaks,
adorned with various wonderful paintings and beautified by leaves and other ornaments.
Meru is proclaimed to be four-faced and richly endowed with beauty;
one should divide it equally into eighty-four parts, forming a square.
One should fashion the chariot-frame in the middle, situated across six parts;
by entering one part [into the side], one should designate a jar in that part.
The path is traditionally taught as four parts during the retention (kumbhaka), with four [parts] for exhalation;
having made the exhalation one part, it should become like the wheel of a chariot.
Furthermore, the entry is likewise, and the exit is exactly the same;
one should perform the entry in that manner, while the exit is by means of a single division.
One should likewise perform the corner-piṇḍīs with three parts;
the pedestal (pīṭha) consists of chariots (rathaka), pitchers (kumbhaka), paths (mārga), and corners (koṇa) situated in the center.
In this very manner it should be constructed until the end is reached;
this is described as the "equal-thread" rotation situated below Mount Mandara.
One should fashion the *śukāghrā* (peacock-beak) projections on the middle sections in the four directions,
using four peaks with *śukāghrā* shapes, measured according to the proportions as previously described.
O Dear One, above the shanks there too is the four-ghāṭaka;
with twenty-three gamas, the first ghāṭaka is recorded.
With twenty-one [syllables] in the second, nineteen in the third,
and seventeen in the fourth [pāda], this is the excellent Ghāṭaka meter.
One should conceive of that object of knowledge according to the divisions of the stages (bhūmikās), like the portions of Indra;
it is further endowed with peaks resembling parrots and possesses a hundred summits.
The one known as Mandara alone is proclaimed to have eighty-four [peaks];
it should be understood as having four faces, beautifully adorned in the four directions.
But the temple at Kumbhakoṇa, provided with supports for its exit,
has Śeṣa bound to its walls and is crowded with various types of spires.
It should be constructed according to its beauty, with the cause of the *lakṣa* clearly discerned;
joined with various paintings, it is celebrated by the name Mandara.
When a square field has been made equal and divided into thirty-six parts,
one should fashion the chariot-base (*rathaka*) in the middle region by means of eight divisions.
By the entry of one part, there would be three above;
the *praveśaka*, however, is situated in the middle with four, followed by the *athaka*.
One should compose the *rathavyakta* with a single foot, while the *luptapiṇḍī* consists of four feet;
this best of *padārtha* compositions is known by the name Kailāsa.
Adorned with corner-pavilions, chariots, and likewise upper-terraces,
it was beautified by four gates in the four directions, each bearing one of the four names.
Standing tall with four peaks, white as parrots, and possessing lofty summits,
it is also surrounded by four enclosures measuring twenty, eighteen, and sixteen [yojanas].
Established with fourteen *gamas* and twelve *bhūmikas*,
and joined by the peaks of Śukāghra, it is declared to have eighty-four [divisions].
Devoid of the *śukāghrā* pinnacle, it is proclaimed to have sixty-eight [parts];
it is beautifully adorned on all four sides and provided with a supporting base (*sāpāśraya*).
With its various peaks marked by the number one, Kailāsa is renowned as the abode of the gods and Vidyādharas; it is exceedingly dear to Rudra.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should divide the Veda equally into twenty-eight parts; with the parts representing the seasons, Bhadra shall be situated in the middle.
By the entry of one additional part, there would be three *upabhadrakas*;
again, by a reduction of one part, there would be two *bhadrakānugas*.
And in its manifestation, one should make a single square with a corner divided into three parts;
it is adorned with doors equal to the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) and decorated with white eaves.
One should conceive of it as having a foundation on all four sides through its rotation;
when it is merely a floor-plan, it is beautiful when level and facing downwards.
Above, the components of the celestial palaces may be Meru,
Mandara, Kailāsa, Nandana, Śrīvatsa, or Bhadra.
Since it is auspicious everywhere and endowed with peaks that constitute its entire self,
one should cause it to be drawn out on all sides externally, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths.
The second [mandala] shall indeed be square; of this there is no doubt.
One should divide the original field equally on all sides into ten parts.
Then, with four [parts], it is the middle; from that, it becomes composed of divisions.
With two divisions, however, there is a corner-binding, which is square on all sides.
That [mandala] consists of four *āghāṭakas* at the beginning with seventeen [units],
and one should arrange the second [section] with exactly fifteen *gamās*.
In the third enclosure (āghāṭaka), there are ten [deities] with three groups of three;
it is endowed with ten levels (bhūmikās), including the fourth and the eleventh.
One should construct the vimāna joined with eight gavākṣas;
the windows of the spire (śikhara) should be fashioned from twenty māṃsas.
By that alone,
it was filled with divine peaks rising high and long, crowded at the summit, and with moon-chambers situated in the middle.
One should fashion the half-body of the Goddess with turrets situated at the top of the spire, provided with moon-chambers (candraśālā), along with door-panels, latticed windows, and high turrets.
It should be made with four doors and likewise with śukāgras;
