thus, the vimāna has been described by me as having forty pinnacles.
That which is to be known as the form of Sarvabhadra, accompanied by the word *tan*, one should recognize as Nandana; it consists of two seasons (*ṛtu*) and is composed of eight squares (*bhūmika*).
It has four enclosures and is adorned with four gates;
it has four prominent turrets, beautiful peaks, and is provided with sixty-four small pavilions.
Endowed with four bases consisting of half-moons and full moons,
and joined with various wonderful paintings, this is declared to possess auspicious characteristics.
Nandana rejoices in enjoyments through his grace;
that field is sixteen parts, and it extends outward by one part.
The second field is established; between those two, it becomes threefold horizontally.
With the middle chariot [measured] by four parts, it is indeed modified at the edge of the field.
The upper part should consist of one and a half parts, and the interior should be equal to that;
one should arrange the corner-binding on all three sides in an auspicious manner.
At the end of the path, it should be marked with the Nandaka-avarta design or simply a lotus;
it possesses four names, four gates, and is endowed with four bases.
The Nandivartana palace has four enclosures, is provided with ten levels,
and is endowed with forty pavilions.
When the field has been made square, there is an extension of one quarter at the back;
the width of the wings is likewise according to the measurement of the inner sanctum.
At the tip of the beak, one should first fashion the human-like form;
within it is a hexagon, and on the two wings there are two houses.
One should fashion the outer door in accordance with the type of house;
Brahmā and Rudra are situated there, positioned on the left and the right respectively.
Having installed Viṣṇu in the center, the temple is known as Garuḍa;
it is adorned with brick-made Garuḍas situated on the wings and at the śukanāsa (front porch).
On stone [images], they should be fashioned with stones; likewise on those made of wood, with wood.
They should have necks bound with serpent-girdles and adorned with snakes.
O virtuous lady, the temple in the form of Garuḍa has long projections extending from its mouth; its measurement and its projection are equal to that of the śukanāsa (the frontal pediment).
Having taken that measurement behind [the center], one should rotate it to form a circular mandala;
there, having omitted two corners, it is provided with two corners at the front.
One should fashion it in the form of a lion, with the face of a lion smelling a parrot;
or, when one makes a pinnacle (śikhara), then there should be a lion situated at the tip of the snout.
One should raise the height of the shanks; this is considered the "Lion" (siṃha) style, which is pleasing. Having set aside one-eighth part of the four sides, one should rotate it into a circle.
When the thighs and shanks are well-developed and rounded like those of a potter’s wheel,
and the belly is likewise circular, one becomes free from the affliction of *śūkadoṣa*.
Above, by means of four squares that decrease in size, one should lead [the lines] as far as the edge of the altar; this is proclaimed to be the *kumbha*.
Having set aside one-fifth part from the Veda (the eastern side), it should be curved like a half-moon;
however, there is no corner at the back, just as previously described for the tip of the parrot's beak.
If the back is elevated and endowed with a high [forehead],
and it is strewn with various peaks, it is called "Gaja" (Elephant) and bestows happiness.
The interior chamber, however, is square like a water-pot (kumbha) with its exterior curvature;
it is situated above the lap of Kailāsa, or else marked by the Vimāla.
At the outset, indeed, the bull named Vāghra was proclaimed;
having made the field circular in shape and divided it into three parts.
O fair-faced one, each [segment] should be made sixteen parts;
O lady of virtuous vows, having circled the portion all around with fire.
Having made a single part an interval, where there is a conceptualization from two parts,
and by the reduction of one-third of the three lines, the shank is likewise obtained.
O Vasuvrata, where the portion above the shank is designated as the *mañjarī*,
and at the front there is one part, the arrangement consists of four parts with corners.
The lotus is remembered as having sixteen sides and is situated in the shape of a lotus;
the thunderbolt has four sides, with its characteristics being equal from the base to the end of the prongs.
O observer of good vows, having made the pinnacle (śikhara) twelve [parts] and reaching the edge of the altar,
one should make the excellent asrivaraṇḍaka by leaving an interval of one part.
A single Śukāgra should be fashioned; it is proclaimed to be square.
One should make the eastern [side] eight-pointed by the turning of the diagonal thread (karṇasūtra).
It is extremely square, with a triangular seat and a face like a parrot;
likewise here, it possesses sixteen sides and is endowed with a face joined to those sides.
O lady of excellent vows, the circular portion at the end of the shank should be like a water-pot (kumbha);
above the shank, the twenty-finger-width section should be a circular molding (varaṇḍa).
Even that [plot] devoid of śuka- and āghra-[lines] is known as the *gava-vṛkṣa*.
When the field has been divided into ten parts, an equal portion on the outside is [the measure].

The other Veda-sūtra, however, should be a chariot-like structure situated in the middle; it should have a chariot-like upper part measuring one and a half parts, and the interval should likewise be so.
The *koṇapiṇḍī* (corner-pile) consists of two parts, and it is declared that the *vardhamāna* (increasing part) is likewise;
one should make half a part for each of those two as the excellent *jalāntara* (water-interval).
Furthermore, one should construct it with peaks adorned with moon-garlands;
this is known as the Pūrṇaśrīvaccha, which accomplishes all desires and goals.
The field is divided like Rudra; the exit is as before.
It has two parts like a corner, and it is designated as having one and a half parts.
The path of knowledge is as before, and the chariot consists of three parts;
with half a deer [shape] above the chariot, the Śrīvatsa design is considered to be formed by the segments.
The *jaṅghāntavardhamāna* has its upper section of the leg (*jaṅghordhvakhaṇḍa*) as its *śālaka*;
alternatively, when it extends to the edge of the altar (*vedyanta*) with well-placed internal sections, the wise know it as the *khaṇḍārdhaka*.
The Śrīvatsa is said to be threefold; its divisions are Nandivardhana.
It should be seen as having become threefold: namely, the full, the half, and the fragment.
Nandana is divided by the Bhadrabheda; thus it becomes threefold. It is proclaimed to range from the Pūrṇaśālā division down to Khaṇḍārddha.
When the field is divided into seven parts, one part is likewise outside;
in the middle, there is a width of three parts, while two parts each are situated at the corners.
52a) O Bhadrā, having made the previously mentioned field equal to the auspicious characteristics (of the mandala),
and having divided it into four parts like a square, there shall be one part for each of the two wings.
The exit is described in detail just like the womb;
at the front, it is joined with the *śukāgra* and the *garbha*, which is perfectly circular.
Above the shanks are Nandana, Nandi, Vṛddhi, and Śrīvatsavardhanī; then another marked with a celestial chariot (vimāna), and behind it, nothing at all.
On the two sides, it should be provided with two houses, and the outer door as before;
Hari and Rudra should be stationed there, while Brahmā should be installed in the center.
With side-entrances and a śukāgra pinnacle, and marked with the emblem of a swan's eye,
this temple is known by the name Haṃsa, dedicated to Pitāmaha (Brahmā).
When it is either Sarvabhadra or Bhadra, marked with lotuses (nalina), then one should know that as Nalina; it brings about auspicious results everywhere.

The celestial chariot (vimāna) reaching as high as the shanks, with Mount Mandara rising above the shanks, is renowned by the name Śrīśaila; it bestows all prosperity and grants all spiritual perfections.
It is quadrangular with great gates, auspicious due to its exits in every direction; here, Rudra and Bhūmi are present in the form of the pillars, most beautiful to behold.
O King of Houses, that alone is considered here to be common to all;
however, one devoid of the characteristics of Rudra is merely a structure of wood, as was previously stated.
The Gṛhārddhaka is declared to be joined in front of the Paṭṭaśālā;
the site should be divided into eight parts, and one should exclude two parts at the east and west.
One should place a long horizontal line extending across the entire width;
one should provide four parts at the front, while the door in the middle shall consist of one part.
The wall should be one and a half parts, and the arrangement of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be half a part;
the Mothers are to be installed there, and the remainder shall be the excellent hollow space.
And the beauty should be fashioned through the application of *bhairī* and *īṣa* patterns,
made very beautiful by being strewn with *nandikāvarta*, *haṃsa*, and *padma* designs.
The divine pitchers are half the height [of the base], arranged in four rows;
it is covered with peaks at the back and front, and may be three stories high.
On the sides, however, like a *bhairiva*, the palace should have *avalambhīs*;
the interior of the *avalambhī* consists of the *meru* and other structures, each with its own distinct name according to its form.
All this has been explained; one should now divide this primary thread. These [threads] should be divided according to their mutual proximity.
There, a mixture of palaces arises in that same number;
whichever form is the lowest, for that one the mixture must be uttered.
In that [region], temples are to be understood as being made of stone for their walls and likewise of wood for their spokes (structural supports),
according to the application of their defining characteristics and marks.
A hut constructed for the purpose of using clay and grass is traditionally known as a *kuṭī*;
now I shall describe its dimensions according to the measurement of cubits (*hasta*).
Regarding the peaks such as Meru and others, that which has been proclaimed for the altar and so forth is as follows:
Meru is fifty cubits in size and square on all sides.
Mandara, being likewise, is forty-five cubits [in height], excluding five cubits;
Kailāsa and Gaja are each forty cubits.
The Sarvatobhadra is said to be thirty-five cubits [in extent],
while the auspicious Vimānacchandaka should be made thirty cubits.
Nanda, Ananda, and Vṛddhi—these two are twenty-five *karas* each;
these are to be known as the great enclosures (*mahāndhāra*), adorned with four gates.
The [number] for the Kaliṅgas, beginning with Ṣaḍṛṣṭi, shall be twenty-five and so forth;
starting from Khageśvara, it continues until Valabhī is reached.
But those [deities] who are without support or foundation have five fingers at the end of their *liṅgas*;
Garuḍa and Pañcaka are both proclaimed to have twenty hands.
Both the sixteen-sided and the eight-sided [mandalas] measure sixteen cubits;
the third is the Śrīvatsa, and the next is the Vardhamāna.
In the case of twelve cubits, one should not perform it by way of the number four;
rather, there are the pitcher (kumbha), the bull (vṛṣa), the swan (haṃsa), and likewise the *valabhi* style.
Temples ten cubits in height should be constructed with four stories;
they are [named] Siṃha, Nalina, Śrīśaila, and Gvavṛkṣa, and are square in shape.
It should be made eight cubits [in height], as well as others possessing auspicious characteristics;
the Gṛharāja and Ardha-gṛharāja, however, are both fifteen cubits.
O Dear One, the measurement of the linga may be according to the standard of the body, or up to four cubits at the maximum,
or even three or two cubits, for purposes such as planetary protection and the like.
I shall now describe their characteristics, beginning with the *pīṭha*, as they should be:
the field is divided into nine parts, and the *pīṭha* in the center occupies one part.
It is said that the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of two parts, and the walls should likewise be so;
alternatively, one may divide the square equally into five parts.
53a) The division, the sub-division, and the further division; the pedestal, the womb, and the walls;
these are known as being devoid of walls, yet they are extended according to the dimensions of the walls and the womb.
Those [temples] beginning with eight cubits that are joined together are considered to be superior to walls;
however, in the case of Meru and other mixed types of structures, even those very large ones are proclaimed [as such].
And those [images] which are of that same size, or even those with the form of a *cāṇḍāla* or a dwarf,
should be made merely according to their outward appearance, depending on the intention of the patron.
Therefore, I shall describe the measurement of the lingas for temples without doubt:
for a linga measuring one cubit, the temple should be four cubits.
The temple for a Pādakara-liṅga is five cubits [in height];
for a liṅga of one and a half cubits, it is proclaimed to be six cubits.
For a linga measuring one and three-quarter cubits, a temple of seven cubits is auspicious; for a linga of two cubits, the temple should be eight cubits.

O you of excellent vows, the construction of the temple for that [deity] is performed with hands numbering twelve (the directions) and eleven (the Rudras), within the three genders and the intermediate points.
A temple measuring twelve cubits is not suitable for an image of three cubits;
nor is it suitable for a liṅga that is three cubits or more in height.
The number of modifications for a four-cubit linga ranges from one additional cubit up to fifteen cubits, corresponding to the measurement of the palace.
O observer of good vows, above that, within the three liṅgas and the intermediate spaces,
there are seventeen, eighteen, and nineteen [liṅgas] respectively.
The temple for a five-cubit *liṅga* should be one cubit in height;
above that, it is likewise for the three-fold *liṅga* and the *antakara* [liṅga].
O auspicious lady, the temples consisting of twenty-one, twenty-two, and likewise twenty-three [modules] are proclaimed to be most beautiful when they are without internal pillars.
O beautiful lady, the temples based on the twenty-five cubit measurement for that same type of linga are proclaimed as sāndhāra.
O lady of virtuous vows, above that, within the interval of the triad itself,
there are those measuring twenty-six, twenty-seven, and likewise twenty-eight finger-breadths.
O lady of excellent hips, the palaces with their supporting galleries should be very beautiful;
for a linga measuring seven cubits, the palace should be thirty cubits in height.
Above that, for the triad itself and for the intermediate *liṅga*,
there are thirty-one and likewise thirty-three.
O lady of excellent vows, for a liṅga of eight cubits, the support is thirty-five cubits; and for the three [liṅgas] above that, it is the same for the inner liṅga.
I shall now describe the temple for a nine-cubit linga, which has a base of thirty-six, seven, and thirty-eight cubits respectively.
It should be made very beautiful with exactly forty spokes;
when joined with the syllables *anvā* and *ri*, it is declared as the "Exceeding Name" (*nāmādhikya*).
O auspicious lady, for those who bear the marks [of initiation], such as gold and silver, even when there is no realization due to delusion,
that which is above them has been described, up to a hand-span of fifty [units].
Above this, however, a *prāsāda* (temple spire) should not be constructed, as it is considered to cause defects;
instead, among the various types of lingas, either the Drāviḍa or the Nāgara style should be used.
Regarding the ritual procedure prescribed for the installation of gods, dānavas, and siddhas,
the measurement of the temple there has not been stated as being equal to that arising from mortals.
Even for a small liṅga, a large and auspicious temple should be constructed;
even for a large liṅga, the temple may be small according to one's financial means.
When one has personally visited a sacred site (tīrtha) endowed with a pilgrimage,
one should there construct a Meru mountain consisting of fifty karas.
In the hundred-thousand-fold [calculation], when nine cubits are prescribed,
that which was previously conceived by the Mānasas is remembered there as the Mandara [measure].
In the case of the *vāṇaliṅga* and the manifest (*pratyakṣa*) forms, as well as among the excellent *mukhaliṅgas*,
a temple should be constructed there, either in the form of Meru or Mandara.
Let it proceed; I shall indeed tell you about the Śikhara.
Now, regarding the Sāndhārikās, those which were proclaimed at the beginning as being like Meru and so forth—

Having first determined the height according to the original measurement, one should fashion the crest (śikhā) at half that height; where the height above the shank is double [the width], there one should make it like a broad row (pṛthupakti).
Divide the upper half of that [height] into four parts;
the height of the neck (kaṇṭha) is one part, and the malasāraka is two parts.
At the foot, a pitcher (kumbha) is prescribed;
above that, the height is proclaimed to be one and a half parts, while its width is one-tenth of the total measurement.
O lady of good vows, by the expansion of the fivefold essence of the filth,
the neck should be three parts and the very beautiful altar six parts.
Whatever measurement is for the interior two parts, one should extend that same amount outward;
it is divided by parts consisting of equal width and height.
One should lead [the line] toward the end of the Vedyanta by reducing it in successive portions;
the altar (vedi) consists of five sections and is square on all sides.
One should then lead a cord from the middle of the *jaṅghā* above the altar-base down to below it;
by means of the southern and northern junctions, one should likewise perform the circular tracing.
Furthermore, regarding those [deities] such as Nandi, Vṛddhi, and Antaka who are proclaimed to reside on Meru and other mountains,
their respective territories and the divisions of the ground are described in sequence.
But it should be seen, O lady of excellent hips, as previously conceived by humans;
extending half the height of the peak, it is measured by the same standard as the Śukāghrā.
The contraction of its cheek should be performed through the union of the *bherī* and *saṃvarta* [mudrās],
to be executed upon the *haṃseṣṭaka* [brick] up to the limit of the counting fingers.
For those [temples] that are without pillars or foundations, the characteristic is that they are provided with pavilions;
their height is measured by the extent of the site, and the plinth (jaṅghā) is considered to be three times that.
Having made the upper part of the shank like a Veda (fourfold), the upper part of the foot is a fourth turn;
O lady of good vows, having divided the width as for a Rishi, the upper third part is [the measurement].
One should measure the altar (vedī) as being one part in length and one part in width;
the broad neck (kaṇṭha) is one and a half parts, and the amalasaraka is two parts.
The pitcher (kalaśa), however, is very beautiful and occupies one-quarter of the total area;
the remainder below is known as previously described, characterized by the form and its placement.
In this case as well, O fair-faced one, the śukanāsas are endowed with the same characteristics as before; however, those temples that lack pavilions (maṇḍapas) are said to be inferior.
Their height is declared to be one and a half parts, while their shank is said to be half of that;
their proportions at the end of the curvature are to be divided into seven parts as before.
For that [temple] as well, the *śukaghrā* should extend half [the length], just as before;
and those others which are without walls should have a height double that of the *jaṅghā*.
Divide the thread made into eight parts into seven ways with the seventh;
having placed it above like sweat, the rolling should be as before.
The base should be three parts, while the curvature above should be three-quarters of a part;
one should fashion the altar as consisting of five sections using one part.
One should fashion the Śukāghrā [shape] above the portion of the elements;
this pavilion is endowed with a proper door for the location of the banner.
In order to achieve worldly excellence, one must effect the destruction of desires through the ninefold self;
just as it is measured, so shall its fragmentation and reintegration come to pass.
Likewise, the lion [ornament] should be fashioned according to the method of the *bherī-saṃvarta*;
the windows of the celestial palace (*vimāna*) should be made with a length of twenty *mātrās*.
For others as well, four months combined should be performed;
[the rites] for Vātaka are with sprouts, and those for Gaja are with the movements of chariots and the earth.
Because of the bursting [of the structure] without windows, windows should therefore be made;
above the neck [of the spire], there should be an opening in the four directions for the hoisting of the banner.
Below the neck, with the fourth [part] and the fifth [part] of the extended body,
the installation of the flagstaff (dhvajayaṣṭi) should be made as the nature of the altar (vedyātmaka).
When one establishes the positions of the deities in the chariots according to the directions,
one should arrange the hollow space by means of the eightfold division of the walls.
The height above should be twice the width, and the entrance should by no means be otherwise;
thus has the complete characteristic of the temple been correctly described.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Section on the Prāsāda," in the Piṅgalāmata, within the Jayadrathādhikāra of the Brahmayāmala.
Piṅgalā said:
The door has been indicated by you according to its characteristics as spoken by the gods;
likewise, here is the division of the pavilions according to the number of their pillars.
"Speak out of grace, O trident-wielder, O bull-bannered one.
Bhairava said:
And the measurement of the door should be made as half the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha), extending upwards.
O fair-faced one, the width should be made half of that;
from the ear-line arising from the center, it should be two out of six parts.
One should determine the height and the width as before;
likewise, by means of another measurement, one should exclude a sixteenth part.
For the best [type of liṅga], the height is proclaimed to be twice the width;
for the medium-sized liṅga, the height is twice the width.
O fair-faced one, the measurement for the smallest [size] should have a width exceeding its own [proportion],
and the height should be made as before.
Likewise, listen now to the measurement of the door in finger-breadths (aṅgula):
its height shall be exactly one hundred and forty finger-breadths.
The width is proclaimed as half of that;
O fair-faced one, the Ṛṣidvāra should be made with a reduction of ten [units].
Furthermore, for sixty-five [other types of images],
whatever may be the smallest of the small, it is not intended for other images made with finger-breadths as the unit of measurement.
The width of the branch should be one-fourth of the total width;
one should likewise determine the thickness of the branches to be half of that.
Half of the width shall be the height; below that, there should be a *udumbaraka* (pedestal). One should likewise fashion the *puṣpī* (flower-base) at half of that [height].
The Ūrdhvādumbaraka is likewise formed by excluding one-eighth of that;
the various parts of the image there are mutually reduced by one-third.
O Dear One, the branches are remembered as being either half of the moon (one), the Rāma (three), or the directions (ten) plus half; or they may be the portions of the sages (seven).
They are known to be odd in number, ending with nine, and never exceeding that upward.
At one-fourth the height of the branches, two door-keepers (pratīhārau) are traditionally prescribed;
likewise, two rivers, a couple, and bearers of burdens.
Furthermore, the Vidyādharas, as well as the Kinnaras,
the cows, the mountains, and the Nāgas were likewise fashioned, along with the nine branches.

One should know [the lineage] ending with the Nāgas as having nine branches; that ending with the Garvas has seven branches; that ending with the Vidyādharas, the Bhūtas, and the Triśākhas ends with the Mithunas.
But when, O beloved, the gateway has a single branch, it is called Ekalapratihāra;
it is adorned with the figures of Śeṣa, a bird, the Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, and garlands of lotuses.
With conch shells, elephant-enclosures, and likewise with *śriyāvarta* designs,
and with serpent-nooses richly adorned, let there be beauty like that of the branches of a tree.
At the beginning is the *ūrdhvodumbara*, and likewise Śrīgajāsya, Hari, Yakṣiṇī, and Śaṅkara; these eight planets are situated within the bird.
Vyākhyāda is Śrīkaṇṭha, and likewise Nāṭeśvara is remembered;
those situated in the row of Mothers are declared in sequence, ending with the ninth.
The *saṃjūṣā* should be known as occupying half the portion of the beam (*śākhā*) in the assembly of beams;
and within that, the door-panels (*kapāṭa*) situated therein are to be seen.
It may consist of two sections or a single section, and it is said to be made from hard wood;
it should be provided with pegs at the bottom and top, but one should never make it from a single piece of wood.
The lower peg should be four finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths high;
for the middle of the door-panel made of *kanasa* wood, it should be fifteen finger-breadths.
The peg (kīlaka) is above and below; in the highest [type], it is twelve and a half [units].
The support for the peg is made of stone, and the support for the [peg] above and below is made of wood.
It is well-fastened with bolts made of iron, joined by leaf-patterned bands and cloth-straps,
secured by pairs of horizontal crossbars, or even by vertical bars.
In this way, the door is well-joined, and the panel is provided with a bolt;
there is also a chain or a key for the purpose of opening it with a key.
The *ardhacandraka* is [formed] by reducing the width by one-fourth or more;
alternatively, two [such parts] from the lower end toward the tip are proclaimed as the *paripaṭṭa*.
From that, by one-sixth, there should be two wings shaped like a wood-apple and an elephant;
and below that, the root and branches [are formed] by the nine [deities] beginning with Kumbha and ending with Aina.
One should proceed by fashioning the branches according to the sequence of the rules;
likewise, the well-constructed door should be made from the heartwood of trees belonging to its own species.
If a new door is constructed using old wood,
then at that time it will always be both a friend and an enemy.
When the two branches are completely occupied and joined by a door,
then the builder will be impoverished and will belong to the same lineage [as the owner].
If the lower part of the door is wide, one should predict restlessness for women;
if the upper part of the door is wide, there will be authority and beautiful women.
If the ants are at the door and the wealth, grain, and good stars are in the middle, it is auspicious;
likewise, if they are in the middle like barley-grains and at the door, an increase in disease occurs.
O observer of excellent vows, if there should be a deficiency in the Sūtras and likewise at the gateway,
then a royal punishment arises there year after year.
If the door is crooked, there will be the loss of cows, buffaloes, and servants; but when it is at the end of the direction, there is confusion, and when it is at the edge, it cuts away one's vigor.
When the door is reversed, there is the destruction of all prosperity;
through branches with broken minds and harsh sounds, there is then the ruin of the family from birth.
Having thus examined with effort, O Dear One, one should observe the piercing and other signs,
using rotating chariot-poles as the means for attaining the great goal of a single tree.
[One should avoid] door-frames, side-chambers, pavilions, corners, pillars, and banners; likewise [places with] four, three, or five crossroads, roads, wells, or houses.
The wise should know that the door is inauspicious when it is constructed by Śilothara, Vālmīka, Rathyā, Kumbhāraka, or others such as these.
The middle thread among them should be properly aligned,
whether it serves as the thread for the thread or the thread for the meaning, extending according to the northern direction.
The installation is performed toward the door facing the middle direction of the site to be established;
having made a cord for the portion, one should then fashion a śaṅkulā.
One should begin the construction of the door from the center of the palace;
and the thread that runs through the middle of the interior should be drawn level from the middle of the door.
In that case as well, one should abandon the middle of the middle, which is the cause of piercing;
now I shall describe to you the installation that consists of the door.

On an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion and weekday, endowed with a favorable conjunction of stars, during the *karaṇa* conjoined with the moon, and likewise at the rising of the *kālavēlā*.
The preceptor, having first bathed and being adorned with garments and other ornaments, should perform the mounting of the door in accordance with the wishes of the patron.
The wise artisan, having likewise become pure, bathed and adorned himself;
he then bathed the divine tree with auspicious Vedic chants and sacrificial blessings.
O Dear One, the wise one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of the great weapon (mahāstra) for the purpose of purifying that direction,
as well as for the installation of the door and its facing.

One should offer oblations to the deity of that direction and beautify the door; having gratified the deities of the forms (mūrtis), one should touch them with the root-mantra starting from the base up to the power (śakti).
Below and behind the location of the door, one should likewise worship the Vāstu-puruṣa;
then, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should place the Dhāraṇī, the Śakti, and the deposition of the jewels (ratnanyāsa) below.
Ironwood (*yāyasa*), *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, *yava*, *siddhārthaka*,
as well as *lakṣmaṇā*, *viṣṇukrā*, *amṛtā*, and *mohanā*.
A hundred each of mūlī, tālamūlī, pāṭhā, go-vandanā, sahadevā,
aruṇā, caru, raudra, rocanā, and sesame seeds.
Gorocanā, realgar, and haritāla, together with curd and dūrvā grass, [should be used] on a variegated cloth; likewise, one should perform protection above at the udumbara tree.
Having first performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma) accompanied by auspicious benedictions and joined with the sound of the Vedas, one should subsequently open the door.
The door, wrapped in fine cloth, should be encircled with three threads,
and adorned with *kutapa* grass, flower garlands, and mango sprouts.
One should place a jar containing jewels together with a full *vardhanī* vessel;
having set aside a small portion from the center, one should place it slightly to the north.
But by means of the yoga of the equinox, together with consciousness,
when that which consists of the self is below, the sacrificial ground of the worlds is within the two branches.
O Goddess of the Suras, having again placed the principle of Māyā at the top of the Udumbara,
one should then place the five principles beginning with Vidyā.
Vidyā and Tatveśvara, and Sadāśiva is the third;
Kriyāśakti is the fourth, while Jñānaśakti is the fifth.
One should place the Śiva-tattva in the center, situated at the end of that path;
this is said to be the sequence of purification, and the placement [of the tattvas] should be performed according to the yoga of emanation.
One should offer seven oblations endowed with those qualities:
"The firm one, the immeasurable, the mark of awakening, the eternal, the all-pervading, the soundless."
Ending with *tṛpti* and ending with *svāhā*, well-illuminated by the *praṇava* at the beginning;
having thus offered seven oblations, one should then sprinkle water and offer the *diśā-bali*.
Having given [the offerings] and sipped water, he installed the two doorkeepers, Nandi and Kāla, by their very names;
having worshipped them, he was encompassed by the self-nature of pervasion.
When the gate has been thus established, one shall obtain whatever is desired;
likewise, the installation and the initial raising of the archway (toraṇa) should be performed here in this same manner.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability to the twice-born, artisans, and teachers;
for if [the rite] is performed by Citra, Svāti, or Antura, it will be accomplished even during travel.
Then, having performed the oblation to the deities of the directions, one should bring [the ritual] to completion;
furthermore, one should give gifts one hundred and eight times, as is appropriate for each direction.

From that time forward, those learned in the scriptures should understand that the term *caitya* refers to a temple (*prāsāda*), a sanctuary (*āśraya*), or a lineage (*kula*), as these are synonyms for a shrine of Śiva (*śivāyatana*).
O lady of excellent hips, one should not apply a thick coating over what has already been designated as a stone-like [firm] surface; rather, a moderate application of ointment is praised.
One should not perform an equal joint, nor likewise one with a deficient foot;
one should certainly not perform one with an excess of head, for in such a reversal, it would become cracked.
A wise man should not join corner to corner with the corner of a brick;
rather, the head [of the structure] should be laid crosswise, well-jointed with well-formed corners measuring half a cubit.
I shall describe the joints according to their characteristics, how they may be with or without wings,
and whether the joint consists of a number of *bhūta*s (five) or *ṛtu*s (six) finger-breadths multiplied by their respective factors.

O lady of excellent hips, it may also be measured by the fingers according to the *ṛṣi* system, or by the fingers starting from the star [the *tārā*] up to the *rudra*; however, when joined with the joints, it will become firm over time.
Therefore, one must certainly not perform [the ritual] above, nor indeed below the *bhūta*s;
in this manner, one should fix the *chandas* upon Meru and so forth, ending with the *valabhī*.
A rest for the beam (bhāraviśrāmaṇa) should be made in the middle with very firm wood from heartwood trees;
it should be constructed at the midpoint of the leg (jaṅghā) both externally and internally.
One should lead [the breath] in such a way that the decrease previously enjoined in the sūtra does not occur;
once it has reached the end of the nose, however, it should be placed within another layer of ground beneath the altar.
O virtuous one, in the center of that, one should construct a small pit within the womb of the altar;
for the purpose of the causal principle, there should be a beautiful cavity protected by the heart-mantra.
Having purified the Vāstoṣpatis situated there according to the prescribed rite,
one should prepare a jar made either of copper or of clay, beautiful in appearance.
Having mixed medicinal herbs and grains with the five jewels of the seeds,
one should place mercury therein and wrap it with a pair of cloths.
A jar adorned with garlands, auspicious threads, and smeared with sandalwood paste,
filled with milk, honey, and clarified butter, or covered with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having meditated on a lotus within the jar, and the heart-lotus as it is in the heart,
one should meditate on the jar in its primordial form and then perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
The channels, the winds, the senses, the guardians, the moon and the sun, fire, and the Self-born;
Rudra, Mahendra, Mitra, Vāgīśī, the Aśvins, and the directions.
Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the [five] elements; sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities. Hearing, sight, taste, and smell are likewise [the sense organs].
Speech, hands, anus, genitals, and likewise the organ of locomotion;
mind, ego, and intellect—these are the modified elements, belonging to the Taijasa (fiery) state.
Those [powers] are to be seen in the palace, within the lower level beneath the altar;
O beloved, they are the primordial nature (prakṛti) which was previously conceptualized in the form of a jar.
Having invoked the Self-principle (ātmatattva), one should cause it to enter into the center of that lotus—
the pervasive Lord of the quarters (vidīśvara), who abides as the activity of the self of all beings.
Through the favor of that karma, the individual soul (satva), endowed with its office and impurities,
[is joined by] passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), time (kāla), and likewise limited agency (kalā).
Having thus placed [the mind] which is attached from the very beginning to Māyā, one should restrain it;
remaining in the steady center of the ego (ahaṃkāra), one should suppress that which is inflated by the three qualities (guṇas).
Having covered that [altar] with darkness, one should fix it at the edge of the temple;
the purification of conceptual constructions is according to the sequence of their manifestation.
That ocean which is square is called the Vidyātattva;
the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, reside there together with their attendants.
Therefore, O Lord, I shall describe the characteristics of the *sārikā* within that vast and pure essence, exactly as it is established therein.
One-fourth of the temple, divided into twelve parts,
should have one such part used for the construction of the Śārikā chamber.
On an even [ground], it should be made even; on an uneven [ground], however, it should be made uneven.
Alternatively, it may be made in the Drāviḍa style; that is the conceptualization for its head.
The pinnacle (cūlaka) shall be one-thirty-second part of the width of the central shaft;
it may be square, octagonal, or perfectly circular, conceived in these three ways.
When the pitcher (kumbha) is situated above the trident and has ascended upwards,
or alternatively, when the pitcher is in the circular portion (vṛttabhāga), the wise one should show two [pitchers].
Then that is proclaimed by the name Īśānakīlaka;
likewise, its form as a *kalaśa* arises from its being encircled, thus it has the shape of a *kalaśa*.
One should then install that form of Sadāśiva as the sacrificial altar with the Praṇava;
O auspicious lady, when the trident is upright, there is the conceptualization of the three powers.
If it is on the lower horn, it is like the power of action (kriyā-śakti); on the middle horn, however, it is awakening;
and above the Śiva-tattva, at half that level, it is dissolved into the self through the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).

O Dear One, the entire collection of principles beginning with Earth and ending with the place of dissolution is declared to be that which is to be purified; one should perform the fire-oblation with the Praṇava.
Having first smelled [the substance], one should subsequently place the crest-jewel of the planets above it;
thus, one should install the principle (tattva) through the yoga of emanation, beginning with Śiva, as in the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The power known as Granthinī is beneficial throughout the entire path;
she is endowed with the three powers and accompanied by the eight forms.
Having first meditated upon and conceptualized everything as it is supported by its foundation,
the reality residing therein is worshipped within that mass presided over by the person.
And in this context, how can reality be void through conceptualization?
Earth is cited as a reality by virtue of its being the sustainer of water and the other elements.
A jar filled with eight [handfuls] and so forth, or one that stands full by itself;
or else, in this collection, a *gaḍḍuka* (small water-pot) and the like.
Whether it be the fire of ripe age, or incense and lamps,
or speech and food, or even the fly-whisk and other such items—
In the cavity (suṣira), however, there is the principle of space (khatattva); sound arises from the name "palace" (prāsāda).
Touch, moreover, is impelled right here by its own nature as hardness and so forth.
Each individual form is proclaimed to be experienced with delight;
that which is conjoined with the perception of form is called the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra).
In incense, flowers, and the like, there is fragrance, as well as the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra).
The window is known as the sense of hearing, and hunger is proclaimed to be the sense of touch.
O beloved, let the cluster of sacrificial offerings go toward the eyes;
the turning of the pedestal is the tongue, and the repeated smelling by the parrot is said to be the nose.
The tongue is known as the leaf, speech is the tip of the neck, and the arm is said to be the stalk; the generative organ is the conduit, and the anus is proclaimed to be the gate.
O fair-faced one, that which begins with "pāda" has been fully explained as pertaining to dharma and so forth;
furthermore, the establishment of the *maṃbhava* is fixed by means of the differentiation of the *sūtra*.
Consciousness is the faculty of volition, the intellect is the faculty of determination, and the ego is the faculty of action;
resolve is involved in the production of sound, while the qualities pertain to the manifestation of color.
Prakṛti is the enclosure, while the palace is the essential nature itself;
the cause is known as Puruṣa, and the heart is considered the inner covering.
Just as a young boy is [compared] to a lion part by part,
so too is another [type of comparison] known as the "common" (sādhāraṇa), which pertains to both the agent and the palace.
Passion is known as the penetration of the Dharma; knowledge is the cultivation of permanence.
But for the purpose of undertaking the observances (niyama), destiny (niyati) is established therein.
The dissolution of substances is proclaimed there as *kāla* (time);
that which is declared as the value of dharma and artha is proclaimed as *kalā*.

The state of oneness consisting of the principle of *māyā*, free from the processes of inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), is the consciousness of the abode of Śiva; it is proclaimed as *śuddhavidyā*.
In the presiding deity of the foundation, the reality is designated as Īśvara;
from the feet up to the kalaśa, at the conclusion, however, it is Sadāśiva.
The excellence of a creator, consisting in the possession of all powers, is to be seen as power itself; indeed, it is manifest even in external sound, just as it is in the internal.
Because he is all-pervasive, this Śiva is indeed declared to be the form of the Prāsāda;
in that state of equality lies the knowledge of reality—the forms, the deities presiding over those forms, and the Supreme Deity.
Having established the deities of the path to be purified as previously conceptualized,
one should again conceive the three principles (tritatva) conjoined with the three deities.
The reality of the self (ātmatattva) extends as far as the knees; Brahmā is the presiding deity there.
The reality of knowledge (vidyātattva), however, is that which is to be known; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.
Above the Śivatattva, Śiva himself is present there in person;
having established the three deities and brought about the unity of the conscious body.
Then, having become firm through the initial oblations,
one should establish [the deity] with seven offerings as before, joined with the word *svāhā* and ending with *tṛpti*.
One should conceive of the vertical axis extending upwards and downwards; know that the remainder is distinguished by its specific characteristics.
Within the intermediate space of the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), one should establish the creation beneath the feet through the power of sustenance (pratiṣṭhā).
The residence of Śiva within the entire body, beginning with the heart,
has been established by means of the Prāsāda-mantra, together with its neck, its base, and its crest.

At the conclusion of that, having fed the preceptors, the Brahmins, and the artisans according to the prescribed rite, sacrificial fees and other gifts should be bestowed upon them according to one's capacity.
From this [basic] division according to the number of pillars,
various pavilions arise, established through diverse numerical configurations.
They will speak just as they were previously conceived by the Mānavas:
Puṣpaka, Puṣpabhadra, Puṣpānanda, and Kuśalyaka.
The one named Buddhisaṃkīrṇaka brings victory and prosperity;
may Śrīvatsa and Vijaya be present, for the Saṃkīrṇa preserves the sacred tradition.
Yajñabhadra, Viśāla, Suśīla, Śatrumardana, Bhāṣaṃca,
Nandana, Vṛddhi, and likewise Māṇibhadraka.
Śugrīva, Harṣa, Karṇikāra, Padardhika, Siṃha, Vaiśyāma, Bhadra, and Susūtra—
these are the twenty-seven names; now their division is described.
That which is proclaimed as the Puṣpaka, consisting of sixty-four pillars and accessible via the Meru palace, is called its *cchanda*.
And that which is named Puṣpabhadraka consists of sixty-two pillar-pairs;
it is proclaimed as Mandara, a meter beneficial for cattle.
O Goddess, Puṣpānanda is proclaimed to be endowed with sixty pillars;
behold him gone to Kailāsa, for he is an image [of Śiva] in that very form.
It is proclaimed that it should have fifty-eight pillars and be constructed by a skilled artisan;
its specific characteristic is that it should be quadrangular and lead to the Gajaprasāda.
With six hundred and two pillars, it is considered the *Buddhisaṃkīrṇaka*;
and that *Sarvatobhadra-ga* stands in the same manner as the *Sarvatobhadra*.
It is proclaimed as the Japabhadraka with fifty-four pillars.
That [palace] was followed by celestial chariots, and situated within a chariot,
it was renowned by the name Śrīvatsa and possessed fifty pillars.
He was followed by Nandivṛddhyānuga and established as Nandivṛddha;
there were eight more, making forty-eight in all, known by the name Vijaya.
Following the king of birds (Garuḍa) and residing like the king of birds (Indra),
these are proclaimed to be the forty-six names of Vāstu.
The fourth, known as Saṃkīrṇa, consists of forty-four [villages] and is situated in the form of a lotus, located within the Padmaprāsāda region.
May he who follows the sixteen spokes and possesses sixteen spokes protect us;
may Paśupati, the best among those who have heard the Vedas, [protect us] with forty-two [spokes].
And following the eight-angled [shape], it should be of that same form as Aṣṭāmraka;
the sacrifice is proclaimed by Rudra as consisting of forty pillars.
And in front of the king of houses, situated as if within the king of houses itself,
was one named Viśāla, supported by thirty-eight pillars.
And that which follows half the house is established with its corresponding form;
it is remembered by the gods as having pillars and is celebrated by the name Nadana.
And in front of Vardhamāna, he is established as Vardhamāna;
O lady of virtuous vows, he is also known as Vṛddhimān, being supported by twenty-eight pillars.
That [deity] is to be known as Kumbhāsṛta, established in the form of a water-jar (kumbha);
Māṇibhadra is proclaimed to be formed by twenty-six pillars.
It is said that in front of the Valabhī [style], it should have four equal sides;
however, the Sugrīva is proclaimed to be constructed with twenty-four pillars.
In front of the bull, there was one in the form of a bull according to his true nature;
known by the name Harṣa, he stood upon twenty-two pillars.
And having followed Siṃha, he remains established in that very form;
Karṇikāra is remembered as the twentieth, and he shall follow Haṃsa.
The most beautiful pavilion should be visualized in the form of a swan;
when it has eighteen pillars, the pavilion is half the size of a *pada*.
One should see [the deity] as situated within a lotus, following the lotus;
O Goddess, with sixteen pillars, there shall be a pavilion known as the Lion Pavilion.
58b) Śrīnagānugata and Śrīnageva-vyavasthita;
Syāmabhadra is proclaimed to have pillars numbering [six] times ten.
O Goddess, he stands before the Khā tree just like the Khā tree itself;
with twelve single pillars, it is proclaimed as the Susūtra.
The fierce [aspect] of Vedaśiras is said to be like that [of Vedaśiras] itself by its own forms;
it should be known as fourfold, consisting of ten, eight, six, and four.
O Goddess, pillars are established as supports for light palaces;
they consist of sages, seasons, and elements, arranged in sequence with the Vedas held in their hands.
Two pillars should be placed in front, below the tip of the *śukanāsa*;
they should be made very beautiful according to the division of the three pillars.
I shall describe the forms of the pillars individually by their respective names:
Ruvaka, Vajraka, and likewise Supralīna.
The two-vajra is the essence of the digits (kalāsāra), while the maṇḍala is the hīramaṇḍala;
the four-cornered is named rucaka, and the six-cornered is the vajraka.
The Supralīna, the Smṛta, the eight-spoked, the twelve-spoked,
the double-wheeled, the sixteen-spoked, the Kalāsāra, the Supravṛtta, and the Hīramaṇḍala.
Variegated with shimmering diamonds, it is indeed named Hīramaṇḍala;
my seven bones are the pillars known by the designation of their beautiful characteristics.
The pillar is of four types: Kumbha, Upakumbha, Viṣkambha, and Sthira;
this is known as the Dvaha. Now its characteristics are being described.
O lady of excellent hips, for the smallest [pillars], the height should be eight parts and the width slightly more than four parts;
for the middle-sized ones, it is twelve parts.
The height and the width are said to be [calculated] by a sixth part;
in the best [type], it should be by a sixteenth part, and the width should be eight parts.
The height is declared to be from one height to the next, and the width is said to be from one width to the next;
however, that which is proclaimed as the height is divided into three equal parts.
Square at the base, circular in the middle with the shape of a jar,
and likewise lotus-faced at the top— this is known as the first type of water-pot (kumbha).
Below that, O lady of virtuous vows, within the square with its four corners,
he [should be placed] by means of four porters stationed at the corners, lifting up the jar.
And that should be known as the Upakumbhaka, distinguished by its characteristics;
its upper portion is divided into nine parts, and likewise its width.
By three [units] there is the *kṣurikāvarta*; it is produced by one part.
The *loṭa* consists of three parts; this sequence is called the neck (*kaṇṭha*).
A circle with one part protruding, followed again by one part protruding—this is declared to be the *viṣkambha* (crossbar);
it should be like a *veda* (altar) above and below.
The pillar-form and the gait arising from these are proclaimed as the one named Sthira;
it is declared to have an even measure, and the head is said to be at the top of the pillar.
The measurement of the pillar's base (aṃsaka) should be equal to its side;
one should likewise cause the Yakṣa’s emergence to be half the size of the ornament.
As long as the cloth remains, it should be of that same measurement;
and that is said to be the *nandikāvarta* and likewise the *dvirāvarta*.
O lady of virtuous vows, it should be performed with three revolutions and well-established;
and the holder of the four [streams] should emerge in the four directions.
That which is known as the Grāha-vakra (the crooked-grasper) is the Nandikāvartaka;
it is joined with two coils and is shaped like the trunk of an elephant.
It should be understood as having two revolutions, distinguished by its characteristic marks;
however, the three folds at the tip arise from the whirling of the three revolutions.
At its base, it has the form of a pillar upon a fourfold support;
it is free from circular carvings, well-settled, and possesses auspicious characteristics.
If the upper portion is to be fashioned with lotus-designs,
then one should provide a lotus-petal of that same measurement above the nose-ornament.
It is declared that its width should be eight parts, and its length should be more than that;
likewise, its height should be made [the same], and not greater.
Above that, there should be a band whose width is equal to the width of the leaf;
its length should be according to the measurement of the interval, and above that, there should be a pedestal.
Fitted with iron pegs, its openings are carved with lotuses and are inauspicious;
above that is a great slab, sixteen units in width.
It should be auspicious when fashioned with great cloth-like bands over the sections;
furthermore, at each section, the wooden joints should be made without visible seams.
Having covered it with bricks, one should smear the top with mud;
likewise, one should apply powder made from Gaṅgā-bricks as well as powdered black gram (māṣa).
One should add oil-cake, clay, and lentils there;
then one should rub it with the bark and leaves of milk-exuding trees and with water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
59b) It was eight finger-breadths in height, and it was filled up with that;
having been struck with a mallet, O beautiful one, it was done gradually, step by step.
One should have the palace made smooth and plastered, resembling the surface of a mirror,
and likewise purified and smeared with plaster.
Again, after a year, one should smear it with conch-shell powder;
this is said to be "Kṣīrakuñcaka," namely conch-shell powder mixed with milk.
Adorned with various peaks and provided with banners and arches,
these beautiful palaces are described as being complete with pavilions.
"O lady of excellent limbs, the palaces have been thus proclaimed according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Doors," in the *Piṅgalāmata*, within the *Jayadrathādhikāra* of the *Brahmayāmala*.
Bhairava said:
I shall now proclaim the rules for the ritual cord (vāstu-sūtra) as it is established upon the field:
it may be made of cotton thread, or of linen, or of hemp, or from the bark of trees.
These [threads] are indeed auspicious, for they are auspicious when measured equally and wound three times;
they are free from knots and clumps, unentangled, and straight as a reed.
In the case of an inauspicious [thread], it may be made of silk, hemp, flax,
sinew, bark, or even a six-stranded thread of grass.
Just as the conjunction of tumors and knots occurs according to one's karma,
so too does the movement in reverse order and likewise the double revolution.
Therefore, at the outset, for the sake of understanding the vital points (marmas), one should prepare the site;
having made that field level, it should be filled with water at the beginning of the night.
Within Citrasvāti, the star Tārā should be somewhat elevated;
having established the Ādāya, it should be in front of that, and having made the Śaśakta, it should be in front of that.
One should distinguish east from west by means of the division of the shadow;
having first distinguished the station of Brahmā, one should cast the line for the object to be established.
Another pair of fish, either by means of a fixed star or otherwise, should be drawn south and north;
from that, the line of the cardinal directions is established, and the corners of the intermediate directions are grasped.
Therein, the fish-quadrant is accomplished without doubt;
from one fish to another, by means of a thread, the square is established.
Having divided [the area] into nine channels, one should lay down the thread:
Śrī, Apas, Avatī, Kāntā, Sa-priya, Vimalā, and Śivā.
The channels (nāḍīs) that have emerged from the mouth of the face are Suśobhā, Bhānunī, Cetā, Procī,
Mukhī, Udgatā, Dhanyā, Dhanā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Gadā, and Niśā.
And having become free from passion and non-existent, they have reached the northern station.
From the combination of eighteen channels, there are sixty-four squares;
the two [squares] known as Pārśvavaṃśa and Ardha-vaṃśa are difficult to conquer and are elevated.
Agni, when situated in Vāyu, is proclaimed to be invincible; O auspicious lady, when situated in Īśa and Rakṣas, he is indeed difficult to restrain, without a doubt.
The *raktacoṣṭas* and the *abhyātānas* are known by their names; listen as they are described.
Pressing the two ears and the two ankles with the feet—these are proclaimed [as the *raktacoṣṭas*].
O Dear One, Kīlanī and Bandhanī are located at the ears and the ankles;
likewise, Sṛjanī and Pakṣī are located on the right or on the left sides.
From these two [points] located in the fifth square, lines extend toward the heart and the corners;
likewise, two lines go toward the hips or the sides. By the union of those lines, the *prekṣārajju* (the viewing-string) is formed.
The *saṃvartī*, the *vivartī*, the *hṛdyāṃśā*, and the *kaṭijānugā* are located on the right side; the *pakṣī* and the *sadbhāvā* are situated on the left.
The lotus, the thunderbolt, the joint, the foot, the ploughshare-union,
the trident, the wrist-bind, the triple-fold, and likewise the swastika.
The cord made of *vaśa* grass is not to be used; it is taught that there are thirteen vital points (*marman*).
It is taught that there are eight threads, and the lotus is proclaimed to be fivefold in number.
Starting from the position of Brahmā, extending east, south, west, and north,
the vajra situated along six lines is said to be the twenty-eighth.
Where the channels meet, that is remembered as a joint-marmman;
O fair-faced one, the number of joints is said to be sixteen.
The pure square is declared to be the "pada," and it is remembered as being twenty-four [units] in size;
the cord, the thread, and the measuring line are known to be above that, resulting in the fruit.
O lady of excellent hips, its number is declared to be sixteen;
the thread extending from corner to corner is undoubtedly the *saṃpuṭa*.
That very [mandala] is said to be the thirty-second; there is no need for deliberation here.
And as for the trident reaching the three lines in the corner, there is no doubt about that either.
O Dear One, that which is said to be the fourth is called Mīśa and Agni; situated on the shore, it is called Maṇibandha due to its connection with the five threads.
That very [line] is said to be eightfold, arranged in pairs starting from the east;
following that is the triple-thread and the triple-fold, of this there is no doubt.
The number five has been illustrated previously in that direction;
however, there is no doubt that a svastika should be placed in the middle of the sixth square.
That which is possible has not been stated [by us] in this context; it would have been stated where it was applicable.

O lady of excellent vows, two lineages were previously mentioned, as well as the eight cords (rajjus) and the eight lips (voṣṭas); therein, the eighteen channels (nāḍīs) are declared to be the vital points (marmas).
Furthermore, from our union, there shall be the piercing of vital points and other matters;
likewise, the ritual sites for deities and the rites of the Rākṣasas.
One should never press upon the vital points (marmaka) where there is a junction between a deity and a rākṣasa;
for if the lotus is pressed, total destruction occurs.
When the *vajra* is pressed too hard, the destruction of the master occurs;
and when the joint is pressed too hard, affliction by disease arises.
If the foot is injured, there will be the destruction of one's dwelling or the loss of a vehicle;
if the plow is injured, one should predict the depletion of grain.
When the *saṃpuṭa* is pressed, one should predict the three types of suffering for the performer;
likewise, when the *triśūla* is pressed, there is the destruction of wife, brother, and son.
If the wrist-joint (maṇibandha) is pressed, servants meet their death;
if the trikaṭa is pressed, there is suffering for friends, Brahmins, cattle, and the king.
Likewise, when the Svastika is pierced, there is defeat for that kingdom;
and when it is crushed by the bamboo-staffs, the paternal lineage suffers decay.
Likewise, in the Vaṃśa and Mātṛka [lineages], suffering from cords is declared;
when the Nāḍī is pierced, however, the entire body constantly falls apart.
When [the recitation] is marred by errors regarding the vital points (*marmas*) or the secondary rules (*upadharmas*), it brings forth all manner of fruit here [in this world].
O Goddess of excellent vows, one must not cause pain to the deities or the *rākṣasas*.
At that time, one should worship the deities and likewise cause an offering (bali) to be presented;
for when they are worshipped or oppressed, they are known to be the bringers of happiness and suffering.
The piercing [of the vital points] always causes great fear for the king, the kingdom, the creator, and the establisher; therefore, one should not afflict it.
Knowing this, one should touch [the object] without piercing its vital points (*marman*), such as walls, pillars, and so forth.
Piṅgalā said:
Who is declared to be the Ātman, and what is the nature of his body? For what reason, O gods, have you taken refuge within that body?
The constituent parts of his body were indeed fashioned from primordial matter (prakṛti). Who are those deities there, and what are their respective numbers and designations?
61a) "And likewise, O Śaṅkara, tell me about the field and its form. Bhairava said:
When the earth was uplifted by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar,
all the mountains were produced, possessing massive bodies and great strength.
O Dear One, those joined with the lunar fortnights— Durjaya and Durddhara—
are all sky-farers and non-mountains who cause the delusion of living beings.
Having arisen from there, they fell upon the surface of the earth and struck down living beings,
driven by the wind from their own wings.
The sages, perfected beings, celestial nymphs, goddesses, as well as men, nāgas, and others, were likewise there;
then the ṛṣis, being struck by the great serpents, became filled with joy.
Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śākalya, Parāśara, Bhṛgu,
as well as Nārada, Tumburu, Sālaṅkāyana, and Kauśika.
The Vālakhilyas and all the others went to where Indra was stationed;
having reached heaven, O Lord, they stood before the king of the gods.
Having heard their words, Yavipāṇika became violently enraged;
mounting the shoulder of an elephant, he raised a radiant spear.
Bhima, in the form of Hari, struck the army of the mountain-like [demons];
and they indeed entered into a most terrible battle with the best of the gods.
Together with the unassailable Nagas who agitate the hosts of gods,
they fly up and strike swiftly, struck by the wind from the flapping of their wings.
The gods watched that battle between Hari, the wielder of the thunderbolt,
and the swift Śakti, who had severed the heads and wings [of the mountains] in the sky.
O beautiful one, when they fall and strike the earth, let them not cause a thunderous crash;
for then Śeṣa and the others would be oppressed, as they are already burdened by the weight of the world.
They vomited forth poison mixed with blood, as well as the contents of their stomachs;
and the earth, overcome by the stench of that poison, fell into a swoon.
Having remained in a state of swoon for a single moment, he emitted the great wind Arṣṇa; and from the union of that poison with the wind, O lady of virtuous vows, [the being] was born.
O lady of excellent vows, there is a great asura named Kāya, whose massive gates are overflowing with poison; he knows that this material body is indeed impermanent in its end.
Therefore, the planets, the stars, the moon, fire, and the various kinds of gems;
the directions, wind, earth, and space—this entire host of Gargas has its origin therein.
61b) Both the gods in heaven and the birds, as well as the sages on earth and the hosts of Apsarases perfected in sacrifice, speak to those who are hidden.
There is no twilight, no day or night, no specific time, nor the ritual of libation;
there is no meditation, worship, or recitation, nor is there the offering of oblations to the directions.
Then all the leaders of the clans went to where the presence of Ambikā was;
having arrived, they began to offer praise with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.
Having praised Bhava and Bhavānī many times with prose and verse, employing the utterances *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ*, they prostrated themselves and sought refuge.
Having heard the hymn beginning with Brahmā, and being blinded by fear at the manifestation of the Lord,
they beheld the Blessed One directly and approached the King of the Asuras.
"O Indra, O Lord of the Earth, protect us! These gods have been defeated by Śrī.
This was said by Brahmā, and likewise by Viṣṇu to the lords of the gods.
The Protector who removes all affliction, the remover of all suffering—O Lord Sūta, why is this? The moon has vanished; shall I dwell in the water?
Having heard the words of Brahmā and the others, and having himself understood their great purpose,
the Goddess said, "O Lord, restrain this great asura."
Having heard the words of the goddess and perceiving that the gods were indeed distressed, she said:
"O Mahendras, exert yourselves with firm resolve and great speed!"
"O steady-minded one, by means of this bowing of strength, I shall restrain this [world].
Hearing the words of their master, all were delighted and their minds were filled with joy.
Then, having reflected through meditation, the great-souled Bhairava brought forth Rudra, known as Atibala, who possesses great illusion.
Having requested permission, Mahāmāyā departed;
she then adopted the superior mode of life belonging to that great Daitya, O lady of virtuous vows.
Having been dragged by the hair and thrown down before Bhairava upon his knees,
he then remains lying on his back with his hands drawn in toward his knees.
Having given the bamboo and likewise the cord, it is made equal to the cross-bar;
this body is indeed a transformation, and in the field, it becomes like the field itself.
All the gods, their minds freed from fear, are stationed there:
Parjanya is in the northeast corner (īśakoṇa), while Vahni and Pūṣan are located in the southeast (vahnigau).
The Pitṛs and [the others] are situated in the corner;
likewise, Vāyana and Aśa are situated in the half-and-half portion of the wind [quarter].
Jaya, Mahendraka, Āditya, and likewise Satyaka;
Bhṛśa, Antarīkṣa, and Padika— these are stationed in the east.
In the south is Vitatha, and likewise Gṛhakṣata;
Gāndharva, Bhṛṅga, and Hariṇa—these are the lords of the single padas in the Tretā age for me.
Sugrīva, Śrāviṇaja, Pracetasāsu,
as well as Śoṣaroga and Paṅktipadika are situated in the west.
At the mouth [of the diagram] are Bhalvāṭaka, Soma, Rigi, Aditi, and Diti;
in the north is the Paṅkti consisting of five steps; listen now as they are situated.
The body consists of four squares; in the center and in its northeast corner, there is a bow-shaped figure.
Its two sides are said to be the two feet.
And Sāvitrī is situated in the fire of Brahmā; one should delineate her as having two feet.
And Savitṛ is situated in the fire of that [Brahmā], and he too stands upon two feet.
From the *kaja* [position], the "elephant-moon" (*dvipacandra*) is situated in the cardinal direction;
and when that too has passed, Indrajit is situated in the position of the elephant.
In the *karaṇa* Gajapakṣman, it is established as two units for bipeds;
and when that [period] has passed, Rudradāsa consists of two units.
In the eastern quarter of Brahmā’s city, Marīcaka is situated;
among them, Vivasvat is in the south, while Dhara is in the north, near Soma.
Carakī is in the outer corner of the northeast; likewise, Vidārī in the southeast;
Pūtanā in the direction of the south; and Pāparākṣasī in the northwest.
Outside in the eastern direction is Skanda, and likewise Aryaman in the south; Jambha is likewise situated in the west, and Pilapiñchaka in the north.

The state of being established is for the purpose of maintenance; there is no such establishment otherwise than through the ground of flour. "Establishment" (sthiti) means that which is to be performed or that which is to be accomplished, as it is desired.

By five synonyms, the state of being a real entity is designated as "substantiality" (*vāstu*). That which is non-substantial is called "natural" (*prākṛta*); it is a state that does not perform any purposeful function.
In the alternative sense of "that which is not to be done," the entity and so forth are said to be "created";
or it may remain pervading the earth, pervading the field as desired.
And likewise upon the palace, the rampart, the city walls, the watchtowers, the archways, the pillars,
the Brahma-stone, and the door-sill of the house.
Whether in a monastery or a royal palace, or in a city joined with suburbs;
whether in a town, a village, a hamlet, or a district comprising many regions; 62b) |||
Wherever there is the presence of what is desired, there one should designate the site.
A square temple is said to have sixty-four parts; it is free from unevenness in form and is likewise provided with balconies and eaves shaped like parrots' beaks.
On a pillar, on the Brahma-stone, and on the pedestal of the bull,
as well as in other such even surfaces, it should be like a Veda (four-sided), having four corners.
On Mount Meru, the form of the *chanda* meters is proclaimed;
one should employ the planetary protections after understanding them according to the division of their respective positions.
Within, one should fashion a four-cornered [diagram] as before;
Meru is like Mount Meru, and the fire-chamber is on Mandara.
Kailāsavāyunāsā is proclaimed as Vahni on Kailāsa;
it should be understood as being like Sarvatobhadra by the name Sarvatobhadra.
The one called Vimāna is proclaimed as Vahni in the Vimāna;
Nandin is like Nandivardhana, and he is Nandana in the Nandana grove.
In the form of a lion, he is indeed a lion; in the form of an elephant, he is likewise of elephantine shape;
in the form of a lotus, he is a lotus; and so too in the eight-sided and sixteen-sided forms.
That which is *vardhamāna* is proclaimed as being in the *vardhamāna* [diagram];
likewise, the *śrīvatsa* [diagram] and the *śrīvatsa* site-plan each become threefold.
The wind known as Bhadra is like a noble elephant (bhadra), and that very same one is like a swan (haṃsa);
the wind named Nalina is proclaimed to be within the lotus (nalina).
Bhadravat, Gṛharāja, Śrīnara, Vahi, and Śrīnaga—
among these meters, one should arrange the planetary protection.
The remaining others should be placed as before in the cardinal and intermediate directions; having understood the proportion, it should be executed extensively where there is abundance.
To an equal [longitude], an equal [result] should be applied; to a lesser [longitude], one should calculate a lesser [result].
Now hear concerning the water-jar, the bull, and the tree, and their respective [applications].
One should cause one's own field to revolve like a water-pot;
having fixed the pivot in the center, one should rotate it evenly with three rims.
One should first cast the Brahma-sūtra facing east and then the one from south to north;
outside, one should fashion twenty-eight parts for the rim and the pedestal.
In the second [section] there are twenty steps, likewise twelve in the third;
in the fourth, the number is four, and thus there are sixty-four steps.
One should place water and fire, Pūṣan and the two Pitṛs, as well as the two belonging to water, and Vāyu and Nāga, in order starting from Īśāna, according to the sequence as before.
The placement of the remaining [deities] is as before, from Brahmā at the beginning to the end, just as previously described.
Īśa is above and below, Go and Vaṃśa are on the sides, and Agni and Raga are likewise;
Īśa and others are situated between Yama and Madhya, and Ityā is in the east.
To the north of Agni is Vāyu, and to the east of Dakṣa is Īraṇā;
these eight cords are traditionally taught, starting from the east, just as described before.
One may place the planets and other deities as before in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
for this is known as the circular site-plan (vṛttavāstu), O Dear One, and it is auspicious for those who favor a circular form.
The temple of the Aindra-liṅga, which is the Vajra, is quadrangular;
its sacred site (vāstu) is likewise declared to be as previously described.
O Agni, O you of virtuous vows, for whichever phallus it may be, whether it be a Śakti-liṅga,
its temple shall have the form of the Bhaga, and its site (vāstu) shall likewise be so.
Having made one's own [central] line like a womb, make it equal at the end of the three wombs;
likewise, one should make a crossroads so that the Brahma-thread remains as before.
As before, one should arrange the squares and perform the placement (kanyāsa) as previously described;
likewise, one must identify the cords (rajju), the beams (vaṃśa), the vital points (marman), and the non-vital points (amarman).
The Blessed One is said to reside in the womb of those who take refuge in magical spells (kṛtyā);
the temple of the staff of Yama’s emblem is like a crescent moon.
And likewise, O auspicious lady, the Vāstu [diagram] should have the characteristics of a half-moon;
make its own measurement according to your own system, like the full moon.
At the end of the three moons, one should perform [the rite] characterized by the equal and similar;
likewise, the twenty-eighth, the twentieth, the twelfth, and the fourth.
One should assign the deities as before upon the equally divided squares;
one should likewise fashion the bamboo-string, and the vital points (marmas) and so forth shall be as previously described.
O lady of excellent vows, the site for those shaped like a half-moon is indeed like a half-moon; so too is the site for the Linga of the King of Rakshasas and for that known as the Sword.
The palace should indeed be triangular, and the site-plan (vāstu) should likewise be so;
according to one's own preference, make the field and the boundary as before, forming a triangle.
The three-cornered [mandala] possessing qualities is equal in the center and conceived with equanimity;
having laid out the squares as before, one should install the deities as before.
The bamboo-string is likewise declared to be like the vital points (marmas) and so forth as previously described; however,
for those residing in the corners of the qualities, it is said that there are three corners.
One should fashion a single corner situated on the circumference, shaped like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O lady of excellent vows, the temple of the Varuṇa-liṅga and the Pāśa-liṅga is known as being shaped like a water-pot (kumbha); its site-plan (vāstu) has already been described previously.
For the banner of the wind-linga, a hexagon is the recommended support;
O beautiful one, having first fashioned the hexagon, one should likewise prepare the field.
At the end, one should likewise perform it with three [lines], characterized by equal and uniform intervals;
O fair-faced one, the sixth line is equal, while the corner situated on the perimeter is likewise.
Likewise, there are twenty-eight, twenty, twelve, and four;
here too, one should assign the deities to the sixty-four squares as before.
Likewise, O auspicious lady, the bamboo-string, as well as the vital points (marmas) and so forth, should be [drawn] as before;
similarly, the planets and other elements should be placed on the exterior in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
O lady of excellent vows, for those whose bases are hexagonal, a hexagonal site is prescribed;
this applies to the Kauvera-liṅga as well as the Gadā-liṅga.
The temple known as Padmaprāsāda, as well as its site (vāstu), should be likewise;
having fashioned the sacred field (kṣetra) like the Padmaprāsāda, just as was done in ancient times.
One should arrange two lotuses for each Śrī and Adīnavā outside;
the ground plan from the center should be circular, as previously described.
For those whose bases are shaped like a lotus, the site (vāstu) should be lotus-shaped;
this applies to the Īśāna-liṅga and the trident-liṅga (śūlaliṅga), O lady of excellent vows.
The basis is said to be eight-cornered, and the site (vāstu) should likewise be so;
having made it eight-cornered as before, it becomes the eighth situated within the enclosure.
The field on the exterior should be square and its width should be of that same measure;
likewise, one should fashion the three corners at the end to form the conception of an octagon.
As before, one should divide the squares and perform the placement [of the seed-syllables] in that same manner;
likewise, one should fashion the bamboo-string and mark the vital points (marmas) and so forth.
The corners of the drinking vessels should be octagonal, and the sacrificial site (vāstu) is likewise declared to be octagonal;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be of the nature of Brahman, and it should be hollow at its center.
O lady of excellent vows, for the Vaiṣṇava Liṅga marked with the discus, the wall should be two parts, and the base (bhaga) and so forth should likewise be of that same measure.
The palace named Garuḍa and its site should likewise be so;
for the lotus-liṅga of Brahmā, the refuge known as Haṃsa is prescribed.
64a) Furthermore, O auspicious one, the site (vāstu) has the characteristic of the form of a palace; it consists of the proportions of the palace,
the liṅga, and the pedestal, each according to its respective part.
Their functional portion should be taken up in that manner;
or else, one should have it made equal in measure down to the end of the shanks.
Whatever form is proclaimed for whomsoever, by that form is the Varaṇṭhaka [to be understood];
likewise, the Maṇḍapa is so described; these indeed have been declared in the context of the ritual practice (sādhana).
Temples characterized by square and other shapes are distributed according to their respective directions; they are beneficial for the performance of their intended functions.
One should likewise establish the facial expressions and the internal states;
understand that the fields are divided by the channels, just as in the case of the lakes.
The Aindrī is declared to be in the east; the Yāmyā is situated in the south;
Jayā is said to be in the west; and the Saumyā is in the north, as the wise know.
But when divided by the eastern channels (prāgnāḍis), there are four external ears;
likewise, there are two bamboo-sticks (vaṃśa) and also a fourth rope (rajju).
The three-footed [mantras] are to be understood, as well as those consisting of four, five, and seven feet;
likewise, the vital points (marmans) and so forth should be known, and the placement of deities (devatānyāsa) is now described.
Carakī is in the chamber of the western quarter, while Skanda and his follower are likewise there;
Vidārī is in the chamber of the southeast, and Aryaman is situated there as well.
Jambha was his follower in the southwest,
and likewise Pilipiccha was in the northwest against the evil rākṣasī.
