In the second square, which belongs to Īśa, the wise man should place Īśa;
likewise, he should place Agni, the other [Yama], Pitṛ, and Vāyu.
O lady of excellent vows, from Paryanya at the beginning up to Diti at the end,
there are twenty-four deities who are proclaimed to be bipeds.
The eight deities are to be known as occupying eight paces; at the end of the remainder, however, it is as before.
O lady of excellent vows, the site known as "Nagara" (the city) is prescribed for the commencement of a city.
Its eastern face bestows the attainment of enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, the wise know that one should fashion the western face, as well as those facing north and east.
When the linga is facing east in a city that faces east, it should likewise be considered as facing east;
so too, it is taught that one should arrange it to face east in other directions.
Whether facing east or west, or even south or north,
the conceptualization of the form of the repetition (*vīpsā*) is said to be performed in the center. 64b)
I shall describe to you the Prāsāda placement for the general sādhana.
One should first design the palace named Vṛṣabha in the east;
Kumbhaka by name should be in the southeast, and Balabhī should be in the southern direction.
In the southwest, one should arrange the king of birds upon a banyan tree;
in the northwest, it is sixteen-cornered, and in the north, it is shaped like an elephant.

In the northeast, however, the Sarvabhadra [mandala] is the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; the remaining ones may be established according to one's desire, with Mount Meru situated at the center of the city.
Now listen duly to that other site consisting of different regions:
it is remembered as being thirty-four *nāḍīs* in extent and square on all sides.
O lady of excellent vows, it should be known that there are thirty-three locations where one is born;
therein, the channels (nāḍīs) following the eastern channel are situated under various designations.
One thousand one hundred and nine padas,
arranged in two lines of two quarters each, he should place outside [the diagram] starting with the planets and so forth.
In the single corner of the thirty-five squares,
there are thirty-four [squares] less one-quarter, starting from the eastern direction, for the planets.
O Dear One, within the four lines at the end of the feet, one should assign the deities beginning with Īśa;
likewise, one should assign Īśa, Agni, Vāyu, and Īśa in the directions starting from the northeast.
The division [of the first group] consists of fourteen quarters;
one should arrange an excess of one quarter for the others, which consist of eleven quarters each, with the excess of a quarter being assigned to water and the rest.
For this [mantra] is remembered as having its sūtras divided among the gods together with the rākṣasas;
one should place the eighteen words beginning with Ā and ending with Mā.
From Marīci down to Ādharā, consisting of fifty-four [deities],
at the end of the eighty-one words, Brahmā is established there.
Now listen to the two lineages as they truly are, and also to the rope:
the ninth is remembered as the Fourth (Turya), while the others extend through the twenty-four.
One should correctly observe the vital points (*marmans*) and so forth as previously described;
for at the commencement of the site, this calculation of *yojanas* is prescribed by means of *padas*.
O lady of excellent vows, O Queen of the Gods, he who is the very self of the mandala should, at the commencement of its construction, perform ten thousand recitations over the site.
And as it has been stated: "Within the tenfold compartments known as *paktyākhya*,
there is Carakīśa, Sata, and likewise Skanda and his follower."
Having torn it open, one should give a hundred [oblations] to Agni, and likewise the attendant to Arpaṇa.
One should offer a hundred oblations to Pūtanā, and likewise to her follower Jambha;
and to the sinful Rākṣasī in the northwest, there should be a hundred offerings with the feet [of the mantra].
The wise know that its accompanying [text] is likewise the Pilapiccha;
and one should practice the Caraka, the Śata, and the Īśāna according to the prescribed rules.
Likewise, they are split apart by the hundred chambers of fire;
and at the end of the Pūtanās, there shall be a hundred steps for the ancestors.
One should offer one hundred oblations to Vāyu; by that, at the end, the sinful Rākṣasī is destroyed.
One should offer two hundred oblations during the Paryañjana rite, and likewise it shall be so in the Jaya rite.
The wise know that there are two hundred [verses] in the Māhendra and likewise in the Bhadra and Āditya;
one should give two hundred for Satya, and there should be two hundred for Mṛśa.
One should assign one hundred [oblations] for Antariksha and Vahni in the outer [layer];
one should give two hundred to Pushan and likewise to Vitatha.
Two hundred [should be given] for Gṛhakṣetra and Yama;
likewise, O auspicious lady, two hundred again for Gandharva and Bhṛṅga.
Thus, for the outer [circle], there are two hundred for Śataiṇa;
beyond that, one should arrange two hundred for Cārika, and Sugrīva should likewise consist of two hundred.
Likewise, O auspicious lady, there are Puṣpadanta and Pracetas;
and the asura known as Śoṣa—each of these occurs two hundred times.
Two hundred for the Naga, O blessed lady, and again two hundred for Sukhya.
In the same manner, two hundred [stalks] should be prepared for Bhalvāṭa;
there should be two hundred for Soma, two hundred for the god Ṛgī, and likewise for Aditi.
In the Īśānta [diagram], one should give a hundred; there is no doubt regarding these two. O auspicious lady, from the Āpavacchādi onwards, it shall extend up to the king for two hundred.
From Marīci down to Earth, accompanied by the hundred [units] of the Veda-count,
one should properly fashion a single [unit] of four hundred [units] within the center of the self.
Likewise, the two lineages became such that from the rope there were one hundred Rāmas;
similarly, another number fourfold would have reached one hundred Munis.

Furthermore, having understood the vital points (*marmādi*) and so forth, there is the conceptualization of the mandala; for that purpose, one should arrange whatever object corresponds to whatever name it bears.
The wise know that there are one hundred and eighty-four [squares];
from the meeting of the three lines, it is formed by twelve compartments.
65b) Carakī is stationed at the corner of the house on a base of six squares; Skanda is in the eastern quarter on six squares,
and Vidārī is in the southeast on six squares.
In the southeast is Ṛtvāvasthā, in the south is Yāmyā accompanied by Pūtanā;
in the southwest is Jambhāyī, and in the west is Turasāvasthā along with the sinful Rākṣasī.
In the gentle [direction] beginning with Earth, Pilipiccha is endowed with the flavor of water;
again, near the inner Lord, Nakta occupies one square.
Parjanya, Jaya, and Māhendra are proclaimed as your two-footed [verses].
The fourth state is declared to be the Āra; in the two-footed [verse], Satyaka is exceedingly [powerful].
Antarīkṣa, Padāvastha, Vahni, and likewise Āgni; Pūṣan, the one named Avitatha, Dvipada, and Gṛhakṣata.
O Bhṛṅgin, the Ādhyātmika, the Gāndharva, and the one with wings (the Vaiṣṇava) are likewise;
Hari takes but a single step, and the Pitṛs do the same.
The two Varikas, then Sugriva, Śraṅga, and the twice-born; these are the bipeds.
Yamavat, Varuṇavat, Āsthā, Ṛtīya, and Aśoṣa are like the pairs.
Rāgaika, Vāyu, and Nāga are the primary ones;
beyond these are the Bhalvāṭas and Dvipadas, while Soma is endowed with four feet.
Likewise, Rig and Yajus are further proclaimed as the two-footed;
Diti is to be understood in the position [of the second foot], while the remaining [syllables] at the end are as before in the fourth.
The two lineages are likewise established; now hear about the eight cords (*rajjus*):
the third is reckoned as having three feet, while the fourth is considered to proceed through the *tāras*.
Having identified the vital points (*marmas*) and so forth as before, one should begin the effort;
O Goddess of the Gods, there is another [type of site] called *vāstu*, which consists of the planets.
From the junction of the twelve channels, the throat-region (kaṇṭhikā) consists of ten;
when all are added together, there are one hundred and twenty-one.
Outside, it is joined in the four directions with the grahas such as Carakī and the rest;
the number of bhūtas occupies the positions in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
I shall describe to you the second row of enjoyers, beginning with Īśa:
having well-placed Īśa in the northeast, Parjanya follows immediately after that.
Having placed Jaṣomāhendraka and likewise Ravi and Satya,
and having assigned Bṛhat and Antarikṣa, the wise know that one should place Agni in Yāvaka.
One should assign Pūṣan (named Avitatha), Gṛhakṣata, Yama, the Gandharvas, Bhṛṅga, and Hariṇa, as well as Rakṣas and others, to the eastern direction.
Know that the two Vārikas, Sugrīva, Śraṅgadvija, Pracetas,
the Asuras, and the Śoṣarogas belong to the wind element. Know them as belonging to the wind.
Likewise, having placed Nāgamukhya, Bhalvāṭa, and Soma upon another [seat],
one should place Ṛg, Āditya, and Aditi, and then place Vatsa and the others as before.
At the end of the *padya* [section], Marīci and the others [are mentioned]; at the end of the *brahmānava* [section], the two lineages as before; [then] three *padas*, and four *rajjus*.
The other eight squares of the *turyā* should be known as being like the vital points (*marman*) and so forth, as previously described;
having understood this correctly, O lady of excellent hips, one should proceed with the commencement of the planetary diagram.

O lady of excellent vows, I shall now describe the site-planning for a village; at the commencement of a village, one should construct a field in the form of a *bhadra* and eliminate one [portion] from the east.
O blessed lady, exactly one hundred [demons] are born there, and not otherwise;
namely Carakī, Pilipicchā, Jambhā, and the wicked Rākṣasī.
Those planets situated in the northern course (saumya-pakti) are assigned two and a half divisions each;
likewise, those in the southern course (yāmya-pakti) are so constituted, and one should arrange [the positions] starting with Vidāri.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Īśa and the others as before, and likewise that of Vatsa and the others,
and having similarly placed Marīci and the others, [he places] Brahmā in the center in the same manner.
In the beginning, after having brought down two bamboo poles, there are three-footed [sections] with the fourth as the cord;
however, because of the omission in the middle, the other eight should be known as four-footed.
Having likewise understood the vital points (*marmas*) and so forth, one should begin the construction of a village.
Now, I shall further explain [the layout of] a fortress (*koṭṭa*) equipped with watchtowers (*aṭṭālaka*).
In the hundred-square field, starting from the east and ending at the second square, one should omit three squares on that side;
that is the transverse length of the square.
Having established [the deity] in the northeast square, one should worship below that like a wing;
the wise know that the lengthwise and crosswise directions extend for one square to the left and right.
In the auspicious northeast, the two feet [of the deity] are divided by half and half again of a square;
having split the top of the *carakī* bulb, one should place them in the *yāmaka* vessel.
In the direction of the Pūtanā quarter, she enjoys a full step;
in the step to its north is Jambha, and in the transverse direction is the sinful Rākṣasī.

Even for that [planet], observe the *piccha* (tail) in the direction of Indra (the East), the *pila* and so forth in the South-East, the *carakī* in the South-West, and the *śakoṇa* in the North-West; while Parjanya is situated in the South.
After that, one should place the Māhendra mantra at the end of the Sūrya mantra for the two-footed [mantras]; then, one should firmly place Satya within Indra, and place Satyetiga within Satya.
Yama is situated in his own direction within the intermediate space;
Pūṣan is in the southeast, and Vitatha is in the southwest of the one called Yāvaka.
66b) From Vitatha to Bhṛṅga, the two-footed [deities] are situated in a row;
Hariṇāpada is alone, and likewise the Pitṛs are in that northern direction.
Two [units] belong to Vārika, while two others, ending with Śoṣa, are situated in the section of Dvipada;
O auspicious lady, one unit belongs to Roga-indra, and in the section to its east, Vāyu is likewise situated.
In that [direction] of Īśa (the northeast), the signs beginning with Nāga (Aquarius) and ending with Soma (Cancer) are situated as bipeds;
likewise, when it is in the southern direction, [the signs] beginning with Riṣi (Aries) are situated as single-peds.
Diti resides in the state of waking (jāgrat) in the four-footed [Veda] ending with Brahman;
however, the states of deep sleep (suṣupti) and the like belong to Marīci and others, while Vatsa and others reside outside in the two-footed [Veda].
The wall for the portion of the deities consists of the moving and non-moving world, beginning and ending with the calf;
the residence of Sarava is in the northeast, the southeast, the pitcher-corner, and in the center.
The *paṭṭālaka* (the upper story) of the building extends out by half the width of the enclosure wall;
I shall now describe the two bamboo poles and the ropes as they were before.
O beloved, when the state of the qualities resides in the wind and earth, two should be known as situated in the northeast and fire,
and likewise two as situated in the vowels and the sixth [taste].
Having identified the vital points (*marmas*) and so forth as before, one should begin the construction of the watchtowers;
the width of the wall of the enclosure should be made equal to its length.
The cooking of sacrificial oblations is likewise equal for the wise one everywhere;
so too is the arrangement of the other deities, like that of a city or a settlement.
One who knows the lineage, as well as those who are such [experts] in the vital points (marmans) and so forth—
by this procedure, he should be led until he becomes an Ābhālaka.
Again, from the forehead-mark (bhāla) to the wall (bhitti), and from the wall back to the forehead-mark;
thus, having circled in the four directions, it may be either with corners or circular.
The foundation of the wall is three parts, while the mobile and immobile [structure] is seven;
on the auspicious [side], it is two men in height, with walls measured by one man.
For the purpose of ascending, many steps should be constructed;
one should make the joints at the top and bottom, and they should be rounded at the upper part.
A hollow space should be made beneath the circular base, or else a gate-tower (gopura) or a lattice-work (jālaka),
for the purpose of the movement of the serpents, since that is the cause of their physical manifestation.
The door should face the four directions; above the door there should be a pediment (valabhī);
and below, both inside and outside, provide a support for the guardians of the door.

The northern gate should be opened by three [deities] belonging to Soma and Indra, while the southern gate should be opened only with great difficulty; for it is held that its door must always remain closed, as it is considered to be visible only to Yama.
And for what purpose is the city gate? Not otherwise is there victory in battle;
by means of counter-machines and enclosures, the site (vāstu) shall become of the nature of Rudra.
The external squares, numbering five, are occupied by the planets beginning with Mars;
one should place the nine planets there in the center of the nine squares.
The Ādityas, ending with Ketu, are situated in the middle within nine squares;
having placed Ravi in the center, one should place Soma and the others in order starting from the east (Indra).
The lord of the eastern circle is Soma; Ravi stands at the station of Soma.
One should further assign Bhauma and the others starting from the southeast, ending in the northeast.
O lady of virtuous vows, the husband likewise established Aṅgāraka and Agni;
then one should again place Soma, Āditya, Budha, and the others in their respective order.
Likewise, one should place Budhādhipa in the south; in the center of the wheel are Soma, Aṅgāraka, and Sūrya, as proclaimed by the gods.
"O Goddess of the gods, they should be deposited in due order and according to the rule.
Thus, the wise know that the Lord of the Cakras is indeed the God Maheśvara.
Soma is the lord of Aṅgāra, Budha, and Āditya; Śukra and the others follow in sequence.
Śukra is declared the lord of Āpya, while Soma and the others are the lords of Aravi.
Having again assigned [the deities] beginning with Śani, Śani becomes the lord of the Vāyu-cakra;
having again assigned those beginning with Soma, however, Bhāskara occupies the place of Śani.
O beloved, having placed Rāhu and Ketu in Aṭaṅga, Rāhu becomes the presiding deity of Soma;
having placed [the others] starting from Soma and Indra, Saumya, Śe, Ravi, and Ketuka [are assigned].
Īśa, Cakrādhipa, and Ketu, beginning with Soma and ending with Ābhāsvara—
having been thus installed according to the ritual, they are considered intent upon the dwelling of the planets.
One should cast [the thread] starting from the bamboo pole as before, but one should observe the vital points (marmas) and so forth;
where there is a place of stationing in the vicinity at the end of the enclosure wall.
One should also arrange eight or sixteen [deities] in the four directions;
O beloved, listen with a focused mind as I explain the ritual for the sacrificial altar (citi-vāstu).
For the planets, the Rākṣasas, and the deities of the cremation ground,
when the ground is level and divided, each square shall consist of fifty-two and a half units.
The wise know that one should place space (vyoma), the moon, wind, fire, the southern direction, water, the northern direction, and earth within the central wheel.
Having again assigned Vāyu in the east, one should place Agni in the south;
having again assigned Jala (Water) in the west, one should place Pṛthivī (Earth) in the north.
In the south, there is fire, and likewise for another; in the southeast, there is the space of wind.
In the northeast, there is water, and for another, in the east, there is earth.
Furthermore, having again assigned those two fires in the north, one should assign space (vyoman) as far as Indra;
at the end of space, earth (dharā) should be placed.
Having again assigned Dharā in the north, one should assign Gati and Pāvaka on Dharendra;
having again assigned Tadyāmyaka, one should assign Vāmaka in the west.
Having thus sequentially deposited [the deities] along with the planets beginning with Mars, he should,
as before, deposit those whose forms abide in the directions on the exterior.
O beloved, listen: there are two bamboo poles, as well as eight cords for the corners;
four are to be known as consisting of two units, and four others consist of four units.
Having correctly understood the vital points (*marmans*) and so forth here as before, one should act accordingly;
for, O auspicious lady, since it consists of the elements (*bhūta*), it is likewise called the "elemental site" (*bhūtavāstu*).
Thus, these are the truly proclaimed [deities] associated with the domestic site (gṛhavāstu).
This concludes the chapter titled "The Section on the Site" (vāstvadhikāra) within the Piṅgalāmata, consisting of twelve thousand verses, in the first section concerning Jayadratha.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord of the Gods, you have indicated the site-plan for the house;
O Bearer of the Plow, you have also explained the division of the channels and their constituent parts.
"O Moon-crested One, let all this be told in brief.
Bhairava said:
O Dear One, once the field has been made square, or in the form of a house,
one should first divide it into ten channels and then cause the laying of the thread.
I shall not give the names of the channels according to their number;
they are Sāntanī, Socanī, Kāntā, Viśālā, and Prāṇavāhinī.
Sācī, Vasumatī, Nandā, Subhadrā, and Manoramā—
these are remembered as the ten channels (nāḍīs) that have emerged facing eastward and westward.
Hiraṇyā, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā,
Śrī, Jayā, Jvālā, Viśokā, and Śubhā are the northern faces.
The auspicious [planets] are to be known by ten retrograde channels;
now listen correctly to the respective deities of the planets as they are.
Brahmā is in the navel within nine squares, and the Water [element] is situated as its lord;
he (Brahmā) is to be understood as being in two squares, and likewise the calf is from its lord.
In the fire of Brahmā, however, is Savitṛ; his Sāvitrī is in Pāvaka. One should know those two as the two-footed [mantras]; while Keticit is in the station of Indra.
In that same direction, on the side of Jayendra,
Brahmā stands upon an elephant, while Rudra and likewise the Rudrāsas stand upon tigers.
One should know that from the two-footed [state] arises Kapūrveṣan Marīcika;
the wise know that Vivasvān exists in the state of Padyadau, which is Bhavayāmya.
O auspicious one, the Lord of the Kalās, who resides in the seasons, moves according to the logic of the lotus;
O Supporter of the Earth, having placed the Self in the north, [he abides] in the six squares.
Having placed Vatsa in the east, Parjanya immediately after that;
then Jaya, Mahendra, Sūrya, Mṛtyu, and likewise Bhṛśa.
The intermediate space (antarikṣa), however, should be known as consisting of five one-footed [verses] arranged in a row;
likewise, Sāvitra, Āgnimāruta, Pūṣan, and Vitatha.
One should place Gṛhakṣata, Yama, and Gāndharva at Bhṛṅgaka;
Mṛga and Padika are to be known as situated in the southern direction.
In the Aṃśaka of Jayāditya, there are two Pitṛs, and after that, Vāri;
likewise, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Pracetas.
The Asura, Śoṣaroga, and Padikās are considered to be in the west;
one should place Rudradāsa and Vāyu in the northwest.
The chief of the Nāgas, Bhalvāṭa, as well as Somarīgi,
and those named Aditi and Diti, went northward on foot.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī;
beginning from the northeast corner and ending with the northwest wind.
Skanda, Yamāntaka, Jambha, and likewise Pilipiccha—
these, O fair-eyed one, should be placed starting from the east and ending in the north.
For the purpose of supporting the earth, however, the gods have established another arrangement:
two lineages as before, and likewise eight ropes.
O Dear One, the third [state] has three feet, while the fourth has four; the other [state], the sixth-footed, is likewise.
Just as there was previously a distinction between the vital points and the non-vital points, so it is here.
O Sulocanā, other vital points and the family [of channels] must also be known:
the forehead, the two eyebrows, the two eyes, the nose, and the chin.
The lips, the two cheeks, the palate, the tongue, as well as the jaw,
the throat, and the neck— know these [as the locations].
The shoulder and the upper arms are to be known [as the first pair], as are the two elbows;
likewise, the wrists, the forearms, the palms, the fingers, and the nails [are the subsequent pairs].
The chest, the heart, the breasts, the sides, the abdomen, the navel, the two flanks, the waist, the buttocks, as well as the penis, the testicles, and the anus.
The thighs, knees, as well as the calves, ankles, heels, and feet;
the toes, nails, back, anus, heart, chest, and the nape of the neck.
Combined with the three pungents (trikaṭu), there are more than one hundred Rudra-marmas;
its head is in the northeast corner, while the two eyebrows are in the middle of that.
Above that, however, the forehead should be known as being equal on all sides;
likewise, fire is in the south, and the mouth of Vāyu should be in the southeast.
In Khasaumya, however, there is water; in Jalandra, there is earth.
Furthermore, having again placed [the seed-syllables] in that northern direction, one should place the two *yāvakas*;
one should place the ether (*vyoman*) up to the end of the Indra-square, and at the end of the ether, there shall be the earth (*dharā*).
Having again assigned the gentle earth and the two fires at the direction of the Lord of Mountains,
and having again assigned one [element] to the south of that, one should assign the ether to the north.
Having thus sequentially assigned the excellent bow and so forth along with the planets,
he should place them on the exterior as before, their forms situated in the cardinal directions and intermediate corners.
O beloved, listen: the two lineages proceed thus; there are eight cords, and four are to be known as consisting of two parts, while the other four consist of three qualities.

Having correctly understood the vital points (*marmas*) and so forth here as before, one should act accordingly; for, O auspicious lady, because it consists of the elements (*bhūta*), it is thus called *bhūtavāstu*.

Thus ends the section titled "The Chapter on Vāstu," from the *Piṅgalamata* in twelve thousand [verses], within the first chapter concerning Jayadratha, which describes the true manifestation of houses and their foundations.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord of the Gods, you have indicated and described the site-plan for the house; O Bearer of the Trident, you have also explained the division of the channels and the constituent parts.
"O moon-crested one, let all this be told in brief.
Bhairava said:
O Dear One, once the field has been made square, or in the form of a house,
one should first divide it into ten channels and then cause the laying of the thread to be performed.
I shall not give [the names] according to the number of the channels;
for the sake of peace, the beloved Sōcaka is the one that carries the breath through the Viśālā.
Satī, Vasumatī, Nandā, Subhadrā, and Manoramā—
these are known as the ten channels (nāḍīs) that have arisen facing west and east.
Hiraṇyā, Suprabhā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Śrī, Jayā,
Jvālā, Viśokā, and Śubhā are the northern faces.
The auspicious son of the Earth (Mars) is to be known by ten western channels;
likewise, understand correctly the sequence for the other deities as well.
In the nine squares at the navel is Brahmā; Āpaḥ is situated as his lord.
He (Brahmā) should be understood as occupying two squares, and likewise Vatsa is the lord of that [Āpaḥ].
In the fire of Brahmā, however, Savitṛ and Sāvitrī reside; one should know those two to be in the Pāvaka fire. As for the words "keti" and "candra," they are in that [fire].
In its southeastern direction, O Jayendra, there stands a two-footed being;
the deer and the footless one are to be known as situated in the south, along with the birds.
Jayāditya, Śakaye...
[and] consumption (śoṣaroga), as well as foot-eruptions (pādikāḥ), are considered to be in the west.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise the Rudrāsas.
One should know that the two-footed [being] was formerly the six-rayed [Marīci].
O auspicious one, the wise know that whatever state Vivasvān assumes, he is beyond the lotus-born Brahmā; he exists in the state of the seasons and is the lord of the kalās.
Having placed Ātman in the subsequent six squares, Dharādhara resides there;
having placed Īśa, Parjanya follows immediately after that.
Jaya, Māhendrasūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa,
and likewise Antarikṣa are to be known as the *padikas* (single-footed verses) arranged in a row.
One should place Agni with the Sāvitrī mantra, Pūṣan, Vitatha,
Gṛhakṣata, Yama, and Gāndharva in the Bhṛṅgaka [direction].
The chief of the Nāgas was Bhalvāṭa, as well as Somoriṣi;
and Aditi, named Diti, and the Padikas went to the north.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī;
beginning from the northeast corner and ending at the northwest (the direction of the wind).
Skanda, Yamāntaka, Jambha, and likewise Pilipiccha—
these, O fair-eyed one, should be placed starting from the east and ending in the north.
For the purpose of supporting the earth, however, the arrangement of the gods was otherwise;
the two lineages were as before, and likewise there were eight ropes.
O Dear One, the third [state] has three feet, but the fourth has four; the other [state], the sixth-footed, is likewise.
The piercing of the vital points and non-vital points here is exactly as it was previously described.
Furthermore, O beautiful-eyed one, the vital points (marmas) and the family [of channels] must be known:
the head, the forehead, the two eyebrows, the two eyes, the nose, and the chin.

One should know that the two shoulders are in the camel, the two arms are in the cow, the two hands are in the twice-born (brahmin), and likewise the tongue; the chin is in Garuḍa, the throat-pit is in the well, and the throat is in the wise one.
The shoulder and the upper arm are to be known [as parts], as well as the elbows;
likewise, the wrist-joint, the base of the hand, the palm, the fingers, and the nails.
The chest, the heart, the two breasts, the two sides, the abdomen, the navel, the two flanks, the waist, the buttocks, as well as the penis, the testicles, the perineum, and the anus.
The thighs, knees, shanks, ankles, heels, and feet; likewise the toes, nails, back, the path, the heart, the tree, and the nape of the neck.
When the forehead is joined with the three-fold [line] and Rudra’s vital points exceed a hundred,
his head is in the northeast corner, while the two eyebrows are in its center.
Above that, however, should be the forehead, extending equally on all sides;
O fair-eyed one, the two ears should be known as Diti and Parjanya.
The bindu is said to be in the eyes, in the lower portion of the eyebrows, and in the middle of the eyebrows.
The nose joined with the *bindu*, the two joints below the nostrils,
the two cheeks, the two lips, the *gojī*, the two teeth, and the tongue— these seven parts are situated in the calf.
In the sequence from below and upwards, the tongue should be positioned in the middle;
likewise, the two lower lips should be separated by the distance of two cow-hairs.
The two [upper] teeth are said to occupy two parts; between them is the palate (kāra).
The wise know the joint at the root of the ear to extend from the jaw to the end of the foot.
This mandala of the mouth of Vāstu has been correctly revealed;
Garuḍa and the throat-pit (kaṇṭhakūpa) are each one and a half [parts], while those on the side are three parts.
One should conceive of that which was described as being below and above as the chest;
in Jaya, one should recognize the shoulder, and in Māhendra, it is called the arm.
The Āditya [nakṣatra] is to be known as the elbow; Salākā, Bhṛśa, and Satyaka are the hand; and Maṇibandha, Uttarā, and Ikṣu are the forearm, as is Agni.
Sāvitrī is to be known as the fingers, and Savitṛ is traditionally said to be the nails;
Vāstu is designated as the left [hand], while the right is called Aditi.
The wise know that the arm is located in the region of the liver (rigisthāna), the elbow in the region of the spleen (somasthāna),
and the forearm (śalākā) in the primary portion of the gallbladder (bhalvāṭa).
When [the breath] is situated in the Nāga [channel], it is the Maṇibandha; for Vāyu, the Kara is proclaimed.
Rudra’s servants are known to be five fingers, and likewise the nails are five in number.
Consumption (rājayakṣmā) resides in the feet; from the portion [of the body], it is distributed according to its divisions.
That which is the junction between Brahmā and Īśa, know that to be the heart.
One should imagine two breasts to the left and right of the junction of the heart;
in one part of the body, the left breast is thus described.
O beloved, the word *dharādharapada* refers to the right breast; that which remains of Marīci’s [portion] is indeed the *bhūtasaṃkhyāpada*.
There, the left side consists of water, while the right side consists of earth;
O fair-faced one, each side is joined by words numbering the elements.
By means of the *brahmāṇya* [vow], the abdomen is reached; at the end of the abdomen, the navel is designated.
Above and below the navel is the Lord (*īśa*), extending from the left to the right like a fourth step.
One should know the left side as the womb; the right side is likewise.
Between Indra and Indrajaya, it is divided into half-portions and quarter-portions.
For the wise one, the organs from the hips down to the anus should be visualized;
below Indra (the heart) are the two testicles, and half of half the hip is proclaimed [as their extent].
The hollow below the junction of the hips is the pair of testicles situated at the sides of that junction;
half a cubit below the junction is the penis, and below the penis is said to be the anus.
O Goddess, the wise know that the two testicles are located on the wings, while the buttocks are known as Vivasvat and the six-footed one; and the thighs are likewise understood by the learned.
Pūṣan, Arṇa, Dhaja, and Anu are declared to be above the knees; that which is below the knees is called Jaṅghā.
Starting from Vitatha and continuing as far as Gandharvagocara [is the sequence].
The length of the shank and the side [of the foot] should be equal; the ankle is above the shank, and the heel is below that;
they know the foot to be half of half of that [the heel].
The nails are half of half of a finger-breadth;
the left calf is thus described, while the right one is the lord of the embryo (kalala).
With six *pada*s, four *bodha*s, and a *guñjānuka* in the section known as "Diseases" (*rogasaṃjñaka*), and ending with *sraj* and *vijā*, this is proclaimed as the *jaṅghā*.
The ankle is indeed at the front half of the *sugrīva*, while the heels are from the rear half;
the foot is said to be above that, and the toes would be below the foot.
O lady of excellent complexion, the nails are said to be in the upper part of the feet as before;
when they reach the soul of Brahmā (the heart), the vital point of the back is declared to be in the back.
O beautiful goddess, one should not know the vital point (marman) as being downward-facing;
the wise know that the end of the heart is located at the region of the junction of the heart and the back.
The joints of the spine are the bamboo-rafters; the *kṛkāṭikā* is the vital tendon (*marmatantu*).
*Indra* and *indrajapa* are on the back, and the *trikaṭa* is there as well—of this there is no doubt.
If the footprint of the site (vāstu) is facing downward in houses such as palaces and the like,
then one should construct the dwelling so that one vital point does not afflict another vital point.
For the purpose of worship, it should be laid face-up; the extraction of the splinter must not be done otherwise.
As is the case with the site (vāstu), so it is with the vital point (marman); in its center lies the junction of the threads.
That would be a fatal blow; therefore, one must strive to avoid piercing the vital points (marmans).
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, if one should inflict pain upon the vital points (marmas), then how [is that permissible]?
Or rather, that which is declared as the conceptualization of what "should be" is the appropriation of the field (kṣetra).
In temples and similar structures, the arrangement of walls and other elements must be performed according to the sacred site;
for how else could it be appropriate for the builder, since that [site] is indeed his vital point?
As is the site, so is the vital point; therefore, the site itself is not worthy of worship.
If the commencement of construction is made outside [the site], that is the cause for its failure.
Therefore, with every effort, perform the worship of the vital points (*marmas*) themselves;
O Lord of Gods, the opening of the wound is performed by those very [acts] according to the ritual procedure.
Just as one should offer worship to the site (vāstu) at the time of performing a rite while presenting the sacrificial oblation (bali),
Bhairava said:
O Goddess of the Suras, at the time of constructing palaces,
whatever form of the site (vāstu) is prescribed— whether square, circular, or triangular— [should be followed].
O Goddess of the gods, O beautiful one, having led [the thread] slightly toward the southeast while reciting the Rakṣoghna mantra,
one should move the Vāstu [deity] in every direction according to this rite.
When entwined with the *vāstu*, the vital points (*marman*) and so forth become entwined;
thus, from the midst of the vital points such as the junctions (*saṃdhi*) and others, there is an avoidance of the center.
One should fashion the initial commencement of the square and so forth according to the prescribed rule;
O Goddess of the Gods, listen now to the procedure for the commencement of the walls, such as the enclosure wall.
Whatever wall [is built] that is deficient or excessive by even half a sesame seed in height, one should resolve to rebuild it; when there is doubt regarding the wall, one should not proceed with it.
Thus is performed that which brings about both seen and unseen fruits;
I shall now declare the extraction of the thorn (śalyoddhāra) exactly as it is—listen to that accordingly.
O Goddess of the Suras, a physician who is skilled in extracting arrows and one who knows the proper rules for laying out a site should first mentally plan the site itself.
O Goddess, in a place that is well-sheltered, well-concealed, devoid of people, and wrapped with a mat,
one should perform the extraction of the shaft using empowered and unempowered [substances].
The wise know that to be of three kinds: divine, non-divine, and mixed.
Vision of gods and the like is divine; that which consists of human beings is non-divine.
There is no doubt that it is mixed with dogs, owls, crows, and the like;
whereas for the Sāttvika person, the teacher is the best, and their vision is of gods and other superior beings.
The teacher of a rajasic agent is to be known as middling, characterized by a mixture [of qualities];
the teacher of a tamasic agent is inferior, consisting of the human nature.
Having thus understood the omen, one who knows how to extract the arrow should always remove it; I shall now fully explain the abnormality as it occurs within the body of the city.
One should bring the artisan to that place where the site (vāstu) has been prepared;
once the artisans have arrived there, the wise one should examine the guru.
When the practitioner, having positioned himself at the head, performs the rite for the head,
he should likewise extract the head-thorn from that [location] according to its measure.

Having placed [the tool] in the mouth and having made the wooden splinter enter the mouth, one should extract it from there with both hands; if it is located in the neck, [it is removed] by touching the neck.
71a) Therein,
the iron chain is three cubits in measure;
when the agent resides in the belly, he touches it within the belly itself.
There, the animal-peg (paśuśalya) should be two and a half cubits;
having made one cubit and two cubits, one should designate the feet of the bedstead (khaṭvā).
Having dug a pit twenty-two finger-breadths deep, one should place the wise person there;
when, standing in the arms, the arm undergoes a transformation within itself.
One should always extract that very root-thorn from there for the sake of pure consciousness alone;
thus it is prescribed on the left, while on the right it is at the level of the hip.
That arrow should be identified there as being composed of clay or a skull;
however, when the agent causes itching in the waist, it is located in the waist.
There, one should extract the iron nail from two cubits' depth;
and there, indeed, is the core-wood, which, when touched, causes the thighs to stand erect.
Having dug down one and a half cubits, one should clear away any underlying splinters;
when a deformity has arisen, those who know the science understand that the location of the splinter is at the level of the knee.
Or else, one should lift up the barber’s equipment from a distance of one cubit;
when it reaches the ankles, there is contact with the ankles, and one should indicate that both feet have been reached.
There, one should extract a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) measuring ten or eighteen finger-breadths;
or else, one should place therein a bone from the foot, such as that which touches the foot when standing.
The wise one should dig out the pits from below to the depth of a palm tree;
by the touch of the thumb at the place of the ancestors, the *kheṭī* [is revealed], adorned with peacock feathers.
That which is called a "spear-head" (śalya) must be extracted to a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths;
O Goddess, this applies when the father is present, or when the little finger is deformed.
Then, O beloved, a bronze dart was extracted by [the one] eight fingers [in height];
the one who had struck with the foot stood upon the foot, touching the area beneath the foot.
Then, one should extract a splinter of hide from that location using a probe eight finger-breadths long;
if it is lodged in the chest, one should indicate its presence there by the sensation of contact with the chest.
One should extract it from below the thigh at the distance of one finger-breadth; there is no doubt about this.
When a deformity occurs on the side, the foreign body consists of a *pāśulikā*.
In that position, the extraction from the "half-man" (narārdha) has been told to you. O auspicious lady, when the agent, staying upon the breast, touches the breast—
There, one should extract the "cat-cage" (mārjārapañjara) by contracting the self;
situated in Brahma, through the touch of the back, it becomes the "boar-forearm" (vārāhakūrpara).
71b) Therein, having pierced [the point] to be extracted at the level of the navel, there is doubt regarding the limit;
situated in the northeast (Īśa), by the contact of the eye, from that measure, it becomes a pearl.
Established in the Vedas through contact with the Vedas, whether it be coral or gold,
or silver— these indeed are auspicious, for they uplift one merely by being worn upon the ear.
O Sovereign of the Asuras, for the sake of the ritual purpose, that [substance] such as pearls and so forth should be removed;
then one should place back there another substance mixed with other ingredients.
Standing on the buttocks, one should touch that thread; there, one should designate it as lead (trapu).
O fair-faced one, having dug a pit at a depth of one hip-measure, one should extract [the thread].
And while it remains in the mouth, one should touch it with the teeth; there, within a pit measuring three cubits, one should properly extract the *abhraka-kapālaka* (mica-slate).
From the touching of the eyebrows, one should know Bhadrakā; from three cubits [of hair], Śalya;
from rubbing the armpits, one should know Kṛti; and from three cubits, Kṛṣṇaloha.
When a deformity occurs in the penis, it arises there from the three metals;
the determination of the scripture is that it must be excised at a distance of three finger-breadths below.
Alternatively, when the most excellent practitioner stands in the center of the site and shakes all his limbs, then the splinters are [removed] from every side.
Thus it has been said: "One who recognizes the previously mentioned foreign bodies in their respective locations—namely sand, charcoal, iron, bone, husks, shards, and pins—"
Because it is strewn everywhere with pearls, gold, coral, gems, and pearls, it is therefore called "Saṃkīrṇa" (the Mixed).
Having dug down to the level of a man's height, one should clear it with great effort;
once cleared of scattered debris and stakes, one should fill it back up according to the previously prescribed rule.
The site indeed becomes pure; thereafter, the planning of the lines and so forth is performed.
Having carried out the planning of the vital points (*marmans*) and other features, O Dear One, the installation of the deities takes place.
Having fully worshipped the Vāstu deity, one should then extract its lords;
O Goddess of the Suras, Brahmā and others are declared to be the lords, as are the planets and others.
Listen correctly to how their offering is prescribed:
during the Ghṛtadhāra rite, one should offer unbroken grains (akṣata) to that deity Parjanya.
O dear one, listen to me regarding the god Mahendra, the conqueror of the Kālakhañjas;
the Vaijayantī and the Pītā are synonyms for the banner (dhvaja).
Listen again: for Sūrya and Satya,
one who desires welfare should offer golden water and a smoky-colored canopy.
O beloved, [offer] a sacrificial oblation made of wheat, combined with ghee and milk.
If one desires success for oneself, one should not give [the offering] too abundantly;
rather, one should offer a fish or well-cooked meat to the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
I shall describe the oblation for Agni; listen with a one-pointed mind.
It consists of parched grain flour (śaktavaḥ) mixed with ghee, molasses, and milk, and is filled with clarified butter (sarpis).
O Goddess of the Gods, one who desires peace should offer [the oblation] with the *sruva* ladle joined with the *saṃyukta* [vessel],
and when the flame is glowing, the *bali* offering should also be given.
One should certainly bestow [the offering] upon Vitatha; O you who are honored by the foremost gods, one should give honey to Gṛhakṣata, who moves with the splendor of jewels.
O lady of virtuous vows, fish meat should be offered to the deity Yama;
and one should present sandalwood and other fragrances to the Gandharvas.
The tongue of a twice-born man should always be offered to Bhṛṅgadeva;
one should present the barley tree, together with its roots, to the deer.
One should cause kṛsara mixed with meat to be given to those designated as the ancestors;
two water-vessels, wood for fire, and a tooth-cleansing stick should also be provided.
One should offer pūpaka to Sugrīva, and one should offer kuśa to Śraḍvija;
a lotus (rājīva), which is called padma, is to be given to Pracetas.
To the Asura, however, liquor should be offered; up to clarified butter for the deity of swelling;
and to the Lord of Diseases, *maṇḍaka* should be presented, O lady of excellent complexion.
O beloved, one should offer a yellow banner to Vāyu; otherwise, there will be no success free from obstacles.
To the Lord of Serpents, a flower with five filaments (vaināyakesara) should be offered.
One should offer various kinds of fruits, such as grapes or mangoes, as well as cooked rice and soup; there is no doubt that these should be given with *bhalvāda* (or similar substances).
O Goddess of the Gods, one should cause food mixed with honey and ghee to be offered during the Soma sacrifice; it should be prepared for the ancestors and the gods in their respective places.
Milk gruel mixed with ghee and honey should always be given; for at the time of the offering, those who are bound by their vows are intent upon the ritual oblation.
One should cause the root of the kumuda, or even that of the saugandhika,
or of the utpala or the padma, to be offered to the mountain deity.
O Goddess of the Suras, the *mullōpikā* should be offered to Aditi;
one who desires welfare should offer the *pūrikā* to the god Aditi.
One should offer water mixed with sandalwood paste, and one should offer water mixed with milk to Priyā; a sweetmeat (modaka) should be given to Marīci, and water infused with kuśa grass to Sāvitrī.
O woman of excellent complexion, the flower should be offered with the *savitṛ* mantra.
O Goddess of the Suras, red sandalwood paste should be offered to Vivasvat,
and green turmeric should be given to Jayadeva.
That which is taken from a dyer's house, saturated with its dye,
and consists of green grain— this is truly said to be artificial thread.
O Indra, give food that is not stale to a deity; molasses-rice to the Lord of the Arts (Kālādhīśa); ghee-based offerings to Rudradāsa; and offerings with *phalguṣa* fruits to Rudra.
O woman of excellent complexion, Pṛthivī gave to Dhara a meal of boiled millet accompanied by fish and meat; some say it was spotted rice accompanied by sprouts.
Some, however, carry the husked flour, having been steamed, in an indrīka vessel;
or both [the husked and unhusked] should be given, having been steamed along with the sprouts.
Listen with a concentrated mind to that which is the oblation for Brahmā:
clarified butter, milk, sacrificial porridge (caru), as well as sesame seeds, unbroken rice, barley, and kuśa grass.
One who desires accomplishment should offer [the oblation] combined with the five products of the cow;
likewise, one should cause clarified butter, meat, and sacrificial porridge to be presented.
O Goddess of the gods, an offering consisting of a month's portion of food, along with the marrow, flesh, and joints,
should be presented to Skanda.
Combined with the heart-lotus and smeared with flesh, this bali-offering should be given to Vidārikā; of this there is no doubt.
And for another who is destitute,
one desiring his welfare should give a meal of rice and peas along with cakes, accompanied by *phalgu* (millet).
One should cause blood, bile, and flesh to be given to Pūtanā;
it should be given to Jambhaka together with fresh meat and blood.
When the sinful rākṣasī Pilipicchā bestows bone fragments, meat, blood,
bile, entrails, and red flowers, [one should know her presence].
Thus the bali offering for Vāstospati has been fully described; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now declare their mantra, as well as the worship and the ritual procedure for the bali.
O Dear One, one's own name, ending with the fourth case, adorned with the Praṇava at the beginning and joined with "namas" at the end,
is sufficient for worship.
One should offer incense, perfumes, and so forth with the word *svāhā* at the end; there is no doubt.
One should give the *argha* offering with *vauṣaṭ* at the end, and in the rite of *bali*, with *svadhā* at the end.
The wise know that the drinking [of the offering] should occur at the end of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
O lady of excellent vows, one should offer [the oblation] in all directions and times according to this procedure.
Likewise, one should offer to the hosts of spirits (bhūtagaṇa), and similarly to the guardians of the directions (diṅpāla);
one should indeed give every offering (bali) together with all food— an offering that fulfills all desires.
I shall proclaim their mantra; listen attentively, O beloved!
It consists of the Praṇava, followed by the syllable Śa, and likewise the word Diśā.
Having likewise written for Vāsina, it is proclaimed as Aghora;
O Goddess, having written for these, one should again write for Aghorāḥ in due order.
Having written "Ghoraśabda" again, and "Ghoratarā" again; then "Bhūyaḥ," and thereafter "Sarvataḥ," and then "Sarvam" again.
Having drawn all [the deities] and then "namas" (obeisance) after them,
he should likewise draw "sa ca" for himself, followed again by "abhyo" at the end.
*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, likewise *vauṣaṭ*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are used in their respective order;
they range from the beginning of the worship (*pūjā*) up to the end of the invocation (*āyāna*), and are conceptualized as ending with the [respective] seed-syllables (*jāti*).
At the end, one who is impelled by the ritual injunction for the elements should dismiss them with the syllable *hraṃ*;
however, one should not apply that [mantra] where there is the sound of the elements or the subtle constituents (*mātrā*).
That very procedure for crossing over has been stated, just as it was previously proclaimed.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, you have described the planetary deities and the spirits dwelling in the site;
now tell me clearly how the bali offering for them is successfully accomplished.
Bhairava said:
A golden lotus should be offered here to Sūrya, without a doubt;
to Soma, milk accompanied by white flowers should be given.
One should cause a svastika and a red flower to be offered to the son of the Earth (Mars);
one should cause a yellow garland filled with ghee to be offered to Mercury.
One should offer rice with curd and *kuśa* grass to the gods without hesitation;
one should present it to Śukra together with *pharṇa* and *sāli*.
One should properly and slowly offer [the oblation] joined with a sweetmeat (modaka) and a blue lotus (utpala);
one should present [the oblation] joined with a white water lily (kumuda) and honey to Rāhu.
O beloved, blue flowers are always dear to Ketu;
O beloved, their arrangement should be according to the prescribed method of placement.
One should offer the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and so forth to Ākāśa;
a soft cloth and a banner to Vāyu; and a lamp of ghee to Pāvaka.
Having fashioned a crocodile out of flour, one should cause it to be offered to Varuṇa;
a tortoise should be presented either as a live animal or one constructed from flour.
O lady of excellent hips, the ritual offering (valikarma) consists of the assignment (nyāsa) to the Earth;
their respective mantras by name have been declared as before.
In this manner, it should be offered everywhere; however, in that specific place, one should offer a row of offerings to the directions.
Having offered the bali-oblation, O auspicious lady, one attains favorable results that bring both visible and invisible fruits;
indeed, there will then be no obstacles in the commencement and completion of one's undertakings.
Otherwise, however, the Vināyakas will create great obstacles;
therefore, an offering (bali) that fulfills all desires must certainly be given.

In this way, even a deceitful person may attain prosperity through the performance of worship and offerings; thereafter, the construction of a temple and likewise the construction of a house [may follow].
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Piṅgalāmata.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord of the foremost gods, the characteristics of palaces have indeed been understood;
now tell us the characteristics of houses and the ancient methods for planning their dwellings.
In the sequence beginning with the twice-born (dvija), one should state "phaṃ" as the limb; for those beginning with the king, one should say "svaṣuram";
and for those beginning with the cumbaka, one should properly present the "bhaṃ-bhā" according to the commencement.
Bhairava said:
O King, O beautiful goddess, I shall describe the city of Cumbaka as it was constructed, according to the measurement and extent of the temple.
Having abandoned that measurement on the exterior, the space equal to it all around the enclosure wall is known by the wise as the interval between the city and the palace.
The conception of the city walls should be understood as being like the walls of a fortress;
furthermore, in that same manner, there is again a complete conceptualization all around.
Just as a courtesan should be diligently imagined for the sake of the cause, so too,
having understood the fame of the author, one should grasp [the meaning] from all sides upon the earth.

Or rather, let that same [boundary] be stated as starting from the city; however, there is again the conceptualization of fear. The previous [measurement] is doubled up to the end, where the protection of the city is located.
O Goddess, one should likewise imagine the city as being like Tārā,
[extending] to the east, the south, the west, and likewise to the north.
Then, from that, she clearly becomes four-armed;
one should visualize the deities beginning with Īśa and ending with Diti there in the four directions.
One should arrange the protection and other rites on the outside, and likewise at the beginning and end;
one should likewise arrange Vasudhārā and the house in the northeast direction.
One should construct a house under the Parjanya constellation,
equipped with furnishings such as conch shells, kāhala trumpets, kettledrums (bherīs), mṛdaṅgas, and paṭahas.
The *timila*, the *jayaghaṇṭhā*, the pair of cymbals (*tālāyugma*), and the *jharjharī*; the *muraja*, the *aṭakka*, the *nandi*, the *huḍukka*, and the *śāmunda*.
The *kāṃsī*, the *ḍamaruka*, the *karaḍī*, the *paṭṭamardala*,
the *suralī*, the flute (*vaṃśa*), the lute (*vīṇā*), the *madhurī*, and likewise the *kinnaraka*.
Khuṃkhunī, Dvisarī, Trisarī, and Nūtaṣaṭsarī—
these and other such [mantras] one should install in the house during the rainy season.
Having constructed a house at the site for recitation, listen now to what should be installed there:
vessels made of copper and other metals, as well as those made of gold and other precious materials, O fair-eyed one.
A water-pot, a small pitcher, as well as an arghya vessel,
an incense burner, a bell, a conch shell, and sandalwood paste.
Thus, these and other such items should be placed there as furnishings;
having taken one quarter from the *japa* [mantra], one should place the whole of the *māhendra* [mantra].
Having taken half of Āditya, one should place it in the city of Prabholīka;
[the goddess] is released from the foot of Māhendra and is endowed with half of Āditya.
And a main street (pratolī) should be constructed, O lady of excellent hips, in the middle of the city,
[measuring] twelve parts of the sun's rays and endowed with a portion of Mahendra.
In the best city, the cremation ground (pretolī) should be made one pada away;
likewise, the exit, the entrance, the gate, and the path [should be arranged].
The *toraṇa*, the *yatharasyā*, and the *pratolī* are thus proclaimed;
they are to be understood by these synonymous names, O beautiful woman of the asuras.
Between those two enclosures, there is a gateway known as the *pratolī*;
above it is a long, arched roof-structure (*valabhī*) supported by pillars.
Above the middle and front walls, there should be a similar support for the water-clock (ghaṭikā);
above the enclosure of the gods, the wise know that the dance hall (nṛtyaśālā) should be placed.
Alternatively, the wise know that the dancing hall should be at the edge of the pavilion;
or rather, the dance at the edge of the pavilion is desired in the city of Śiva.
Furthermore, O Sulocanā, in the supreme city of Māhendra, one who has found refuge [in the deity] should perform [the rite] endowed with the quarter-part of recitation (japa).
The foot of Mahendra, joined with the foot of Japa,
is declared to be the "refuge for those who have arrived" in the city conceived as the middle one.
In the southern half of the sun’s course, one who has come for refuge should build a dwelling for the younger [deities];
and in the northern half, a house for the purpose of an assembly hall should be constructed.
In Bhṛśāgnika, however, one should construct a vast kitchen;
in Pṛśni, one should provide a reservoir of water; and in Vitatha, a storehouse for vessels.
One should diligently install [the image] fashioned from gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or other materials, provided with its mechanical parts.
And Gṛhakṣata [is the deity] for the house and for the placement of weapons.
A sword, an arrow, and a bow, as well as an axe and a mallet;
a razor-edged blade, a spear, and an elephant-goad, and likewise a variegated staff.
The club, the spear, the noose, the mallet, the trident-bladed weapon,
the discus, the sword, the mace, the thunderbolt, the goad, the wheel, and the sharp-edged spear.
Weapons such as these, as well as various other missiles,
should be established in the house of Gṛhakṣata, the lord of the gods.
O Dear One, one should construct a monastery for the Yama-Gāndharvas on three levels,
or on two and a half, or even on a single level.
The superior, the middling, and the inferior [beds] are prescribed for the preceptor in due order; that very same [set] is declared to be his own, based on the reason of his own bed.
There, indeed, one should perform the daily rites of sacrifice, recitation, meditation, and the practice of yoga,
together with the heroes, using their food, drink, and other offerings fit for heroes.
A woman should build her house in the Bhṛṅga [year], but she should perform her ritual bathing in the Mṛga [year];
she who has previously resided in all places should likewise perform the rites for the ancestors in the Pitṛ-sthāna.
One who knows the mantras should always keep in his house clay for purification, wood, and two types of brooms for the cleansing of the twice-born.
The *bhojanāśraya* (dining hall) should be constructed for Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, as well as Praceta;
it should be very long, and Pradyota’s [hall] should be provided with lattices.
In the asterism Āśleṣā and the lunar mansion Śoṣa, there may be a refuge for ascetics;
in the asterism Pata, there are items such as a mortar and pestle; and in the asterism Roṅg, there is a house with a grinding stone.
One should construct a house in the place of Vāyu; there, sulphur (gandhaka) should be placed, as well as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and other substances for anointment.
In the Nāga, Mukhya, and Bhalvāṭa asterisms, a house that is long in extent should be constructed for the sake of prosperity; this is highly auspicious for ascetics.

O Goddess, *somirigau* (the syllables *so*, *mi*, *ri*, and *ga*) represent the treasury; *some* represents the collection of jewels and such; and *rigau* represents grain and so forth—either as a pair or even as a single unit.
If the left shoulder and the right side of Diti were to become the divine support,
then in this clockwise manner, this placement would not be situated in front.
Thus has this ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six-faced Śiva-Śiva been proclaimed;
now I shall likewise describe that of the god whose face is the lower one.
In the western half of the city,
at Śoṣa, there is a footpath; and in the middle of the street, it is devoid of Daityas and Asuras.
She was released from her portion as Varuṇa and endowed with a portion of the Daityas.
In the middle of the main gate of that very supreme city,
between Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, there shall be a dwelling place for ascetics.
When only three paths remain, there should be no dwelling or house there;
one should instead make that which remains of the western side a shelter for guests.
O Māhendrāditya, in that very place where the support for food exists, three movements are indeed specified; the remaining others remain as before.
Outside the main gate in front of Śiva’s city is the city of the courtesans;
it is always filled with rows of auspicious houses facing south and north.
In the northwestern direction, however, the *tūra* rests upon the *drāga*;
it occurs at four times, and that is declared to be the hour for incense (*dhūpavelā*).
At midday, at midnight, and at the times of sunrise and sunset,
[the temple] shall be equipped with banners and flags, and the day shall be accompanied by mirrors.
A staff, a raising, a lifting, accompanied by a white parasol,
joined with moonlight, and a lamp fashioned upon a pole.
A divine pedestal made of gold and other materials, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths, should be fashioned;
upon it, one should prepare a very beautiful liṅga made of cooked śāli rice.

O Goddess of the gods, having held that [liṅga] which is accompanied by perfumes, flowers, nectar, and the like, and resounds with the ringing of bells and hand-drums, one should worship it as either a male or a female attendant (gaṇi).
Endowed with beauty and youth, and adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
she should thus circumambulate and begin the incense offering.
One should rotate it three times, avoiding the drainage channel;
at the end of that, the offering (bali) should be carefully placed upon the pedestal.
Having arrived later, one should perform a dance in the dance hall,
or [recite] poetry, or a drama, or even a song composed by Āditya.
One should always perform the four-fold ritual before Śiva according to the rules;
however, when one quarter of the night has passed, one must not offer even a single drop before Śiva.
Furthermore, after three quarters have passed, O King, the fourth quarter is declared according to the tradition;
it is indeed preceded by all musical instruments.
Then, for one ghaṭikā, he should constantly play the śivadrāgaḍa;
moreover, there should be a flower garden and a lamp in the northern direction of the city.
75b) Whether it be a well or a pond, fashioned from pure stone,
or even made of brick or wood, it should be very beautiful.
The *viharī* pond should be provided with divine stairs;
alternatively, it may be one made by a potter, or one consisting of a well-stairway.
A water-wheel, a foot-path,
a small canal, a large channel, or even a trough should be constructed for the sake of providing fragrance to the flower garden.
Now listen to which trees are for flowers and which are for fruits:
the *vakula*, the *śrīphala*, the *punnāga*, and the *nāgakesara*.
The apsarā-campaka, the nāga-campaka, the pāṭala,
the sthala-campaka, the aśoka, the vṛkṣotpala, and the akiṃśuka.
Priyaṅgu, karṇikāra, mandāra, pārijātaka, ketakī, pāṭalī, vimuktā, bahusenā, and japantikā.
Kukhavai, śatapatrī, karavīra, and likewise tagara; surabhi, rājārka, jātī, kunda, pūṣika, and mallikā.
In this manner, one should cause noble and other fragrant flowers,
such as *damanaka*, *amaravaka*, and so forth, to be scattered.
Pomegranates, mangoes, nāraṅgas, and citrons are praised,
as are plantains, jujubes, kucī, kunduraka, and induka.
The palmyra, the date-palm, the *tāḍī*, the *śūpa* tree, the *jambīra*,
as well as the coconut, the *hintāla*, and the *śāla* tree.
Udāgas, tritittiḍi, khadira, aśvattha, kajambhana, plakṣa, udumbara, nimba, śrīpallī, vaṭa, and vallaka.
One should fill the Nandana grove with such beautiful trees;
O fair-eyed one, the dwelling for the artisans should be prepared in the northeast.
To the east, however, should be the residence of Brāhmaṇas and those who recite peace-mantras (śāntipāṭhaka) in front of Śiva;
to the southeast, the smiths and other artisans such as woodworkers.
To the south, the wise man should designate the groups of servants, as well as those engaged in agriculture and the like; and to the southwest, he should designate the outcaste classes.
The washermen and others [should be placed] in the western direction;
this is the placement outside the city, at the boundary of the city and the palace, and in the intermediate spaces, O beautiful one.
There, Rambhā was adorned all around with garlands of jasmine and the like;
Piṇḍasaṃjñā was likewise decorated with Tagara and Karavīra flowers.
76a) O lady of beautiful hips, this is declared to be the Śiva-pura, characterized by the Nandikāvarta; it belongs to the magnetizer who seeks both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śiva is auspiciousness and the state of beauty, the mental object, eternal, and pure;
he is firm, imperishable, and complete—the synonyms of whom have thus been declared.
Or else, there is no fault in [entering] the city of Śiva itself, provided it is preceded by the Guru;
or alternatively, [the entry] may be from the south, the east, or even the west.

A monastery (maṭha) should indeed be constructed, but one should have it built in a gentle manner; having abandoned the measurement for the width of the temple (prāsāda), one should leave an intermediate space.
Having understood that half, or even half of that, according to its proportion, [the field] is threefold:
inferior, middling, and superior.
Having understood that an image of the Earth-goddess (Bhūdevī) must be fashioned out of clay with the desire to obtain land,
one should make it a perfect square and divide it evenly into auspicious parts.
The ritual pavilion (sthānamaṇḍapa) should be located in the northeast or the east of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa);
it should contain water and be situated on a path for cooking, within the range of the water-cooking fire.
The preceptor himself should prepare his bed in the western direction of the monastery;
indeed, the excrement is located in the region of the ancestors, and that is what is called its sequence.
Viṭkuṭī, Brahmavardha, Candana, Pāprada,
and Utkarṣa-gūṣa— these, O beloved, are proclaimed as the nine designations.
A variegated pavilion for the liquor (vāruṇī) should be constructed in the west;
one should install the mechanical contrivances, the mortar and pestle, and so forth, in the northwest.
One should indeed cause the placement (nyāsa) in the site of the temple to be performed in a well-guarded manner;
it should have a beautiful courtyard in the center and be surrounded by an outer wall.
Prior to the consecration, the construction of the archway (toraṇa) or other arrangements suitable for the deity should be made;
everything may be composed of pure stone or even fashioned from wood.
It may be constructed entirely of wood, or perhaps made of clay;
it may be encircled by a fence, or even thatched with grass.
A wise person, according to their means and in accordance with the place and time,
should perform the second rite known as the *nandikāvarta* for the *cumbuka*.
O lady of excellent hips, the divine and most beautiful city of Narendrādika, which is adorned with sovereignty, has indeed been described.

O Dear One, I shall now fully explain the general rules concerning the selection of a site for a magnet and so forth, whether it be self-constructed or built by another; listen now also to the requirements for the hall.
The four-winged, the three-winged, the two-winged, and the single-winged—
these are the types according to the number of wings; now their proportions are being described.
The teacher's [mandala] has four halls, while that of the practitioner has three halls.
The Dviśāla belongs to the Putraka, while the Samayin indeed has the Ekaśālaka;
now I shall describe the directions and their respective individual names.
That which possesses eight *śāla* divisions is called the auspicious *vandikāvarta*;
first, one should divide the *āpacakra* for the purpose of determining the *śāla*.
To the east, however, the wise one should construct the Śrīgṛha (House of Fortune) with the Dhvaja (Banner) yoga;
to the south, the learned one should know that the Sayyāgṛha (Bedroom) is prescribed with the Siṃha (Lion) yoga.
The wise know that food and the house belong to Vṛṣāyaṇa in the west;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the north of the house for Asajāyaṇa, without a doubt.
Cooking should be performed by means of smoke when the Sun is in the domain of Agni;
however, when it is situated in the domain of Yama, cooking should be done by its own light, without a doubt.
O beautiful one, the grinding of grain and so forth should take place in the house in the northwest by means of a donkey,
while the sacrificial pavilion should be in the northeast by means of a crow.
Munītārā is with five hands, Rudra is indeed with three faces,
and [the deity] possesses ten, five, and seven hands, as well as the powers of the ten directions.
With twenty-one cubits, there should be a banner in the east;
the excellent Śrīgṛha (House of Glory) should be made square on all sides.
In that place, O ever-auspicious one, he dwells together with the glorious ones;
because he perceives Śrī herself there, it is therefore called the "House of Śrī."
It should be twenty-nine cubits from east to west,
and exactly seventeen cubits in width from south to north.
There should be five lion-thrones for them to lie upon to the south;
it should be very long from south to north, measuring exactly fifteen cubits.
With the number eleven (the number of Rudras), one should draw the eastern and western [lines];
by that, there should be five [units] for the bull, and thus in the west is the support for the meal.
Make it thirteen cubits long from east to west,
and eleven cubits wide from south to north.
By means of that superior treasury, this elephant is born;
it is eighteen cubits in length and thirteen in width.
From that, smoke arises; by means of that, the wise understand cooking in the fire.
It should be ten cubits in length and six cubits in width.
Therefore, it must necessarily be in the place of the ancestors;
its length should be ten cubits, and its width, O beloved, should be like that of the *svara*.
From Kharā, the Vaśyā and Kaṇḍalā are born;
their house is sixteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width, O Dear One.
This sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) should be situated in the northeast, either in a house or in an open space; it may be irregular or perfectly square.
Having understood that which follows the mind, it may be said to be either deficient or excessive;
the third is proclaimed as the Nandikāvarta of the magnetizer.
Furthermore, there is the Svastikāvarta, which is its four-winged form;
O auspicious lady, when it is devoid of a central core, I shall describe that to you.
He should first go to the place of sacrifice; then, at the end of the cooking and the lying down, he should eat his meal and lie down to rest in the northern direction.

Whatever is in close proximity to it, one should assign that to its respective direction; likewise, even for that which is devoid of a house, one should perform the assignment according to its direction.
Now I shall always describe the Triśāla house for the practitioner,
as well as the Hiraṇyāvartaka and the inferior Uttaramandira.
This should be performed by a preeminent practitioner who desires the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for even a wheel of great power, if preceded by [this practice], becomes a bestower of happiness.

O Goddess, a whirlpool at the hearth and one devoid of the southern side are not auspicious; likewise, a whirlpool that destroys the wings and one that is deficient by seven [units] are also inauspicious.
Two things are to be grasped and two things are to be avoided, since they indeed bestow pleasure and pain; O lady of excellent complexion, listen to the two-pillared [structure] belonging to the son.
That which is joined with Taurus and Leo is proclaimed as the "Accomplishment of the Abode" (dhāmasiddhārtha);
it constantly grants liberation from the mouth [of saṃsāra] to those seeking sons—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the wise know that a solar eclipse occurring on a Tuesday when the moon is in the Hasta nakṣatra brings death; therefore, it must be avoided with great effort.
Know that the one joined with the elephant-banner is called Daṇḍa;
he constantly inflicts royal punishment, yet he has not specifically attained that [state].
That house is called Vāta, being joined with the lion-banner;
there will be constant quarreling, it is not auspicious, and one should always avoid it.
One who is known by the name of a bird and is associated with the bull-bannered god (Śiva) will constantly suffer loss of wealth; such a person should be avoided with great effort.
That house is occupied by an elephant and a lion, and is named Kākākī;
one must undoubtedly abandon any conflict with the people there.
O fair-faced one, listen now to that which has a single hall for the initiates:
either the banner should face west, or the lion should face north.
O auspicious lady, one should indeed place a bull facing east or an elephant facing south;
the house should be eight cubits in length, while the pathway should be equal to its width.
In front of the Bull-house is the street known by the name Uṣṇīṣa;
however, in the case of the Lion, the street is on both sides, and that house is supported.
That [image] is undoubtedly well-situated all around in the flag-house;
behind the elephant, there should be a pathway, which one should avoid by resorting to the western side.
O auspicious lady, the arrangement of the streets is common to all, beginning with the magnet;
however, starting from the twice-born and so forth, I shall describe each dwelling individually.
If the width is measured by thirty-two units, then the length previously proclaimed is indeed one-tenth of that.
The southern house has a width of twenty-eight cubits and a length of one-eighth of that; the western house is twenty-four [cubits].
Its width is proclaimed to be six parts,
and its length is twenty parts plus a fourth part of the length.
And for a Kṣatriya, that which was previously the width of the enemy should become the length;
[the length] is increased by one-eighth, and the southern [side] is twenty-four [units].
One should determine its width as six *māṃsas* and its length as twenty *hastas*;
the western side should be twenty *hastas* long, and the thread [of the cloth] should be five *māṃsas*.
In the sixteenth [chapter], the northern [side] was indeed proclaimed in detail;
now hear about the length of the Vaiśyas, which is like the width of a wing.
First, [the width] is twenty-four cubits and six finger-breadths in length;
the southern [side] is twenty cubits in length and one finger-breadth in width.
In the western [section], the sixteenth, the length is not by a third part;
the northern house has a width of exactly fourteen cubits.
O beloved, listen now to the measurement for a Śūdra: it should not be longer than half of that;
its width is twenty cubits, and its length is one-fourth of that.
One should arrange the pair facing either east or north;
it may be a four-winged hall, or even a small hut in front of that very [shrine], for the sake of its maintenance.
Where water cannot be obtained, there it should be situated according to the previous rule;
for it has been stated that among the types of houses, there should be neither deficiency nor excess.
I shall describe the characteristics of the Nandikāvarta for the palace of a king;
according to my own system, it is divided ninefold and consists of eighty-one squares.
The assembly pavilion is at the navel, with the circumambulation of eight steps;
the worship pavilion is for the propitiation of the chosen deity and others.
To its south, O beloved, is the house that is the abode of garments.
For the sake of the path, one should place a single step toward the east; there is no doubt regarding the Āpya [direction].
Having placed [the deity] in the eastern path and the mouth, one should also provide ornaments such as gold and other precious materials.
When the [element] Ratna has been exhausted, there is then the abode of Gaṇikā in Āpya;
and when that too has reached its fullness, one's own vehicle and home are attained.
It may have three stories, five stories, or even seven stories;
it should be well-proportioned with a pavilion-like structure, resembling a mountain peak.
To its left, there should be the house of the chief queen and the turret;
in the eastern quarter (Indra) is the residence for the inner apartments, while in the northern quarter (Soma) is the great hall.
In the northern direction, one should construct the excellent house for women;
in the place of Rudra, however, camphor, karkola, and other such items should be placed within the dwelling.
To its east is the house of Punarājñī, which is exceedingly beautiful;
to the north of the assembly hall is the excellent repository for all materials, known as Nyāsa.
First, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should construct an auspicious house with wide eaves;
everything should be enclosed by a wall, and whatever line may arise there [is to be considered].
Furthermore, O Goddess, having abandoned the outer position, one should then proceed evenly for the sake of walking;
there, O Goddess, is the outer placement, and in that [direction] of Īśa is the house of pacification (śāntika).
In the center, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed, measuring two cubits and two finger-breadths;
it should be provided with a single girdle (mekhalā) consisting of eight finger-breadths.
In the center of the *yoni*, one should fashion a base twelve finger-breadths wide;
