its length is said to be sixteen finger-breadths, and the girdle (*mekhalā*) should be half a finger-breadth thick.
At the tip of the two fingers there should be a spout, and on the back it should be provided with two jars;
furthermore, the middle should be square, and the girdle (mekhalā) should be one finger-breadth wide.
[The apparatus] is suspended from above by an iron chain fastened to its inner shaft;
it consists of a copper vessel filled with clarified butter, beneath which is a hollow space.
Make a hollow in it, about the size of a blade of *darbha* grass, for the flow of the clarified butter;
arrange it so that the stream is broken day and night.

O Goddess, here the Brahmins are the reciters; the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas constitute the peace-offering, while the Atharva Veda is the Hotṛ priest; thus, there is constant protection at the three times of day.
The king must always protect them, for their command is abundant;
this is indeed a house of the stream of peace, for it is truly a house of the stream of wealth.
One's own limbs and so forth, banners and garlands, as well as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
a golden staff, a white parasol, and a chowrie made of peacock feathers and the like.
Having constructed a house for Parjanya, it should be installed there with great care.
Likewise, horse equipment and such, as well as armor and the like,
should always be kept by the wise after having constructed a house for them in the place of recitation.
The Sarvādhiṣṭhāna [conjunction] should always occur in Māhendra;
by means of Āditya, there is the Mārga [conjunction], and the Mārga consists of two ghaṭīs in the house.
The court of justice, where legal proceedings are determined according to truth,
should be established by constructing a very firm dwelling and installing the preeminent bull there.
One should establish the fire-altar in the intermediate space and construct the kitchen there;
the eating vessels should be placed in the Puṣṇa region, and the dwellings for the Trika and others should be situated accordingly.
The council hall and pavilion should be constructed in the Vitatha asterism;
the victor’s hall (jinaśālā) should undoubtedly be constructed in Gṛhakṣatra.
And this should always and constantly serve as a refuge for bodyguards;
it is the place for musicians and singers, and the collection of lutes, instruments, and the like.
An auspicious house for the commander-in-chief should be constructed in the Bhṛṅga location;
having built a house in the Mṛga location, one should establish the residence for musk and similar items.
In the location of the ancestors (the northeast), an auspicious house for essential activities should be constructed;
and in the two directions of Varuṇa (the west), an excellent bathhouse should be built.
The chamber for the doorkeeper and that for Sugrīva should always be located there;
the excellent dining hall should be constructed near Puṣpadanta.
O beautiful one, in the case of Pracetas, such a path must be followed;
and for the host of Asuras, their residence shall always be there.
In Śoṣa, there shall always be an armory with knives and other weapons, as well as a residence; or in Roga, there shall always be a cow-pen, a dog-house, and a place for physicians.
A very auspicious [consecration] must always be performed for Vāyu; of this there is no doubt.
In the place of the Nāgas, a pair of houses [should be made], along with the description of rubies and other gems.
And likewise, O auspicious one, there is one [pillar] at Puṣpāśraya, the second;
a half-face of Sumukha is to be fashioned, and two royal water-houses.
A peacock should be placed upon half of a cock; thus the auspicious house should be constructed.
Furthermore, the storehouse should be in the Bhalvāṭa division, which is the best location for all types of grain.
Ghee and other substances, as well as salt and other items, should be placed there with great care.
In the place of Soma, a large hall and a residence for the royal elephant should be established.
In the auspicious Aśvaśāla configuration, the king himself ascends [the throne] in whichever [year];
however, O beloved, when there are two houses in Aditi, buffaloes and thieves cause plunder.
Likewise, in the place of Diti is the house, and the pair [of horses] has as its support the knowledge of the cow.
The preceptor’s residence associated with princes and others is also described here as being surrounded by a wall,
just as previously stated.
Jaya is prescribed for the eastern gate, and Śayanottama for the southern;
one should always perform the Āsthāna rite facing east in the Bhadra hall.

That which is concealed is called the "entrance" (āyadvāra), while that which is not concealed is called the "exit" (apadvāra). Otherwise, that which is the root is the "vehicle," preceded by the entrance.
Likewise, one should then proceed to the assembly hall, the gate, and the bedchamber; then to the treasury in the south, according to the arrangement of all remaining [buildings].
Standing, sitting, and moving about are prescribed [as postures];
the city should be twice as large on the outside and separated by an inner wall.
Having gone to the main gate, he should face the pair of doors;
for those merchants and others, the protection of gold is indeed supreme here.
Regarding those courtesans who must be protected because they frequent the king's presence,
even in their case, there is the arrangement for facing [the fire] and the measurement of the length of the house.
In the west, there are the houses of prostitutes and servants by which one has no stable livelihood;
in the north, there is a long, single grove, auspicious and strewn with lotuses and water-lilies.
Likewise, O beloved, one should further imagine it externally, separated by a wall;
the residence of the Brāhmaṇas is in the east, and the residence of the Kṣatriyas is in the southwest.
Having settled the Vaiśyas in the eastern quarter, those of the Śūdra caste likewise in the north;
the smiths and others in the southeast, and the vintners and so forth in the southwest.
One should place the *prakṛti* of the elephant-riders and others in the northwest, and that of the *prakṛti* in the northeast;
furthermore, one should likewise arrange the outer fortification (*koṭṭa*) on the exterior.
As previously described, it is indeed joined with the *pravrājaka* and *bhālaka*,
provided with various dwellings, and adorned with diverse decorations.
The lord of the arts, like a wine-drinker, has fashioned this palace free from passion;
at the main gate, however, are the guardians with sixteen staffs in their hands.
In the second [enclosure], there are five hundred guardians with swords in their hands and likewise five hundred with bows in their hands;
these two groups of guardians number three hundred with swords in their hands.
In the third [enclosure], there are two hundred guardians resembling the sun, with swords in their hands;
in the fourth, there are one hundred and fifty guardians resembling the enemy, who provide protection.
In the fifth [period], there are one hundred guardians of the Vasus,
armed with weapons; in the sixth, eighty guardians of the Ṛtus are said to be equipped with arms.
Four guardians are assigned at the seventh gate;
there, fifty protectors stand with swords in hand, skilled in combat.
They were brave heroes, endowed with courage, and always devoted to their master;
[they beheld] the city with its wonderful layout, provided with seven ramparts.
O you of virtuous vows, that which was told to the Emperor of Great Kings has been stated;
now the second [type], pertaining to an ordinary lord of men, is called Nandika.
One should arrange for the residence of the deities, the kitchen, the bedchamber, the place for weapons, the dining hall, and the storehouse for leaves and vessels along the edge of the rampart.
Now the authority for the subsequent thread, beginning with Aiśa and the rest, is being stated:
by means of one hundred and eight [recitations], there is indeed a single state of being.
The length of the bed should be one hundred cubits,
while the dining hall is said to be ninety-two cubits long and one-fourth as wide.
The wise, experts in the treasury, [determine] the length by eighty-four cubits;
with fifty-four cubits for the width, the cooking area is very long.
Fifty [finger-breadths] by the hand alone is the measurement for the base of the weapon;
however, at the end of that, there is the measurement of the base of the weapon including the weapon itself.
O Dear One, one should construct a hall of forty cubits for the worship of the gods; the house used for the ritual of the deity should be provided with a loom and a shuttle.
The length of the feet there is likewise described as being no different from that;
furthermore, I shall now describe another matter: the royal treasury and storehouse.
The eastern house is proclaimed to be seventy-two cubits in length;
its southern side is sixty-five cubits, being a sixth part less than that.
The eastern side is fifty-eight cubits, and the other [the western] is fifty-one;
the southern side is thirty-six cubits, and the northern is thirty-two and a half.
The wind [mandala] is indeed twenty-seven [units], and it is further stated to be in the northeast;
all [the others] are twenty-five and a half cubits in length, with a sixth part as their width.
O General, I shall further describe the Nandikāvarta mark;
it was previously proclaimed that the house itself measures sixty-four cubits.
In the fifth month, the southern [wind] belongs to the long and short seasons;
the western [wind] is proclaimed to be by the hand [measure] of fifty-two.
The northern house should be provided with forty flavors;
it is proclaimed that the southeastern house has thirty-two cubits.
O beloved, the house in the southwest is proclaimed to be twenty-nine cubits, and that in the northwest is thirty-six cubits.
When the [planet] is situated in the house of Īśa (the northeast), the best of houses measures twenty-three cubits;
and the length of all [such houses] is proclaimed to be five-fifths (one-third) more.
Now hear concerning the great house at the end of the Samānta;
having turned the hand sixty times, the eastern house is thus proclaimed.
The length shall be one-fourth [of the circumference], fifty-four units for the south,
and forty-nine units for the north.
The fire-house is proclaimed to be at twenty-five and a half cubits [from the center],
and the south-western house is likewise said to be at twenty-seven cubits.
One should construct the excellent house in the northwest with twenty-four and a half cubits,
and in the northeast, one should fashion the house with exactly twenty-two cubits.
O Dear One, for the sake of all [the deities], one should calculate a fourth part as the length;
having understood this and having carefully made the expenditure, five [parts] should be given.
Having understood this, the house should be constructed; it must neither be deficient nor excessive.
A house is said to be "well-gated" when its doors are properly aligned from east to west as previously described.
Piṅgala said:
O Lord, how should the door of the house be constructed— tell me what is auspicious and what is inauspicious— and how, O All-pervading One, is the door of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) made?
Bhairava said:
The entrance to the sacrificial pavilion should be situated in the middle like a palace;
now hear about the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the door as it is described for a house.
The walls of the house should have a width equal to one-sixteenth of the total width;
the door should be one-eighth of the width and twice as high.
This rule applies to the smallest [size]; for the medium, it is one-twelfth;
for the largest, with a modification, the height is double the width.
Alternatively, having personally determined the dimensions by means of the fingers of one's own hand,
and having ascertained whether they are deficient, excessive, or equal, one should construct a door provided with a crow-ornament (vāyasa).
One should not obstruct the two branches at the door of one's own house while it is closed;
likewise, two equal branches made of udumbara wood should be fashioned in that same manner.
Now listen: one's own measurement should be divided into eight parts, and there should be eight doors;
the doors should be constructed in the cardinal directions, and never in the intermediate directions.
When the door is in the place of Īśa, it is fierce and extremely terrifying;
and when the door is in the place of Parjanya, one should predict the instability of women.
When the door is in the Jaya position, there is victory; of this there is no doubt.
And when the door is in the Māhendra position, one shall attain an increase in prosperity.
When the entrance is toward the sun, it increases one's prowess and fame;
when the entrance is toward the south, it increases one's armor and virtuous conduct.
When the door is situated in the Bhūyas-sthāna, it constantly increases quarrels;
when the door is situated in Antarikṣa, it is neither pleasant nor a giver of suffering.
The eight doors of a house facing east have thus been proclaimed;
now hear of the eight doors of one facing south.
When the door is situated in the place of Agni, there will be fear of water;
when the door is situated in the place of Pūṣan, there will be the happiness of acquisition and wealth.
When Vitatha is at the entrance, there is the destruction of enemies and the like;
when Gṛhakṣata is at the entrance, there will be the ruin of everything.
When the gateway is at the station of Yama, one should predict death;
and when the gateway is at Gandharva, it portends the destruction of friends.
At the Bhṛṅgi gate, however, there is craftsmanship, skill, and the increase of intelligence;
at the Mṛga gate, when it is the door, there is certainly manliness and valor.
Now listen to the eight doors of the one facing west:
when the door is in the place of the ancestors (pitṛ), then there is the Puṣpapravardhana.
When the door is at Dvāravatī, there is the characteristic of renunciation;
when the door is at Sugrīva, there is the prosperity of agriculture and trade.
When the door is in Puṣpadanta, it is taught for the sake of obtaining a son;
but when the door is in Vāruṇa, it bestows health, peace, and happiness.
When the door is in Asura, there is an increase in wealth, prosperity, longevity, and intelligence day by day; however, when it is in Artha, there is a decline day by day.
When there is a double door in the location of emaciation (śoṣa), there is constant increase of disease;
furthermore, eight doors for a house facing north are now described.
When the door is at the station of Vāyu, there will be immediate shouting;
when the door is at the station of Nāga, there will be fear of one intoxicated with pride.
If the door is at Sumukha, sovereignty and preeminence are attained;
if the door is at Bhalvāṭa, there is an increase of wealth day by day.
When there is an opening in the house of the Moon, there is an increase in lifespan and freedom from disease;
when there is an opening in the house of Mercury, there is poverty and diminished livelihoods.
One should always have a wrinkled mind that is constant, harsh, and a cause of aversion.
When the syllable *advāra* is situated in *Aditi*, it bestows poetic skill and increases the intellect;
but when the syllable *advāra* is situated in *Diti*, it then produces pride and arrogance.
Knowing this, one should always accept what is auspicious and avoid what is inauspicious;
other directions and so forth should be taught according to one's inclination, as they give rise to auspicious results.
Having correctly understood the cord for the site with diligent effort,
the wise man attains his desired enjoyment, or liberation, or the crushing of enemies.
Without knowing this, there is neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation, nor indeed any means [to attain them].
Therefore, having understood this with every effort, one should undertake the practice.
In this manner, one should perform the consecration of the city of Śiva and the other deities for the sake of attaining all desired objects,
according to one's wishes, with the desire for fruits in both this world and the next.
The section on houses in the Piṅgalāmata.
81b) Piṅgala said:
Tell me, how can there be an installation for one who is without a *liṅga*? What is the measurement of the pavilion for the installation, and of what kind is it?

In what place should it be performed, or from what materials? Tell me this; describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), as well as the sruva-ladle and other implements for the pits.
Please, out of your grace, tell me in brief all these and other things that occurred at that time.
Bhairava said:

Consecration is considered to take place in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and the installation in the temple (*prāsāda*). When [the image] has moved from the temple, it is not called "installation of the stationary" (*sthitasthāpana*).
The first is the consecration pavilion (pratiṣṭhā-maṇḍapa), the second is the bathing pavilion (snāna-maṇḍapa),
the third is the pavilion for the [deity’s] characteristics (lakṣaṇa) at the entrance, and the fourth is the workshop (karma-śālā).
On the uppermost part of the palace, however, there should be an auspicious consecration pavilion;
further in front of that, half its size, is the pavilion for the installation of the auspicious marks and the opening of the door.
To the north of that, half its size, a pavilion should be constructed for the purpose of bathing;
the ritual hall may be built according to one's desire, in whatever location is appropriate.

O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall now describe the measurements for pavilions (maṇḍapas) of one cubit and so forth, as well as the supporting beams (dhārikās) and arches (toraṇas) for the various lingas.
O beautiful one, having first made the hands of that [liṅga] starting from the Raudra-liṅga,
the consecration pavilion itself should be endowed with ten cubits.
The supporting pillars shall be five cubits long, and the architrave (toraṇa) shall likewise be five cubits;
the lower parts of both the pillars and the architraves shall be one cubit in measure.
O lady of virtuous vows, that excellent pavilion for the two-armed [image] of the Liṅga, starting from the feet,
should be constructed with a span of thirteen cubits.
The supporting pillars shall be seven cubits in height, and the archway (toraṇa) should be equal to that;
the lower supports and the archways should each be two cubits in height.
O virtuous lady, he should have that excellent pavilion constructed starting from the foot of Kaliṅga, measuring three cubits for him, with a width of fifteen cubits.
The *dhārikās* and the *toraṇas* should likewise be three cubits lower than the *anavahas*.
Both the *dhārikās* and the *toraṇas* must be at least three cubits in height.
O lady of virtuous vows, for that Linga whose feet and other parts are proportionate,
the auspicious installation pavilion should be ten and seven cubits [seventeen cubits] in size.
The pillars and arches are [measured] by the number of hands minus one, like those of Rudra;
the height of the base (adhaḥ) is three cubits, provided with an increment of eight finger-breadths.
O observer of good vows, one should have the best of pavilions constructed with a height of nineteen cubits, starting from one and a quarter cubits up to five cubits.
The supporting archway (toraṇa) should be made with thirteen hands;
it should be twelve finger-breadths thick and three cubits high from the base.
O lady of virtuous vows, that most excellent pavilion for the sixfold liṅga beginning with the foot should be constructed with twenty-one cubits by hand.
The [deities] beginning with Dhārikā are proclaimed to have fifteen fingers;
having grasped the modified finger-measure, the wise one should erect [the structure] at three cubits.
O lady of excellent vows, one should cause the best of pavilions to be constructed with twenty-three cubits for that [shrine] which measures seven and a quarter liṅgas.
Provided with nine finger-breadths and supporting five arches,
the *toraṇa* should be known as equal to that [in measure], with three projections and twelve [parts] combined.
O lady of virtuous vows, for a liṅga measuring one and a quarter [tala],
the wise man should cause a pavilion to be constructed with a side of twenty-five cubits.
Provided with seventeen fingers [in width] and measuring three cubits in height, the archway (toraṇa) should be known as equal to that; its lower installation should be four cubits.
O lady of virtuous vows, one should cause the best of pavilions to be constructed with twenty-seven cubits for the linga measuring one and a quarter cubits up to the end of the randhra.

The architrave (toraṇa) should be measured at twenty-five finger-breadths and supported by three hands; it should be described as being equal to that [measurement], with the hand-structure placed below the fourth part.
It is proclaimed that [the post] should be made of pure iron and provided with four finger-breadths [of a base];
or, when such a location does not exist, one should fix it for the sake of firmness.
Where there is the absence of trees, there you should plant what is beautiful;
yet even there, it must first be a positive state, for everything has its root in existence.
Non-existence is said to be duality, or existence is characterized by duality;
therefore, non-existence should be abandoned, and one should establish oneself by conceiving of existence.
However, one should indeed perform everything that is to be accomplished with effort;
for there is no fault in the disposition toward what has been attained through such effort.
The first pavilion (maṇḍapa) consists of twelve supporting pillars;
they know the second pavilion as being joined with twenty supporting pillars.
The third is joined with thirty; the fourth is two and two parts;
the fifth is fifty, and the sixth is seventy-two.
And in the seventh pavilion, there are likewise ninety Dhārikās.
They know that in the eighth pavilion there are one hundred and ten [pillars],
and in the ninth pavilion there are one hundred and thirty-two.
In accordance with that, one should fashion the *buddhārika* and other ornaments,
as well as four archways (*toraṇa*) in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions.
Without doubt, this is common to all pavilions;
it is devoid of the rites known as the ritual bath and so forth, and for those two [pavilions], there is only a single archway.
Leaving aside two cubits, one should fashion the arches; the measurement that has been prescribed for the branches should be planted above.
Therefore, two sacrificial posts made of Udumbara wood should be prepared from branches of that same species;
here, the path should be four *nadīs* wide and equal in measure.
One should fashion three roots situated upon an udumbara branch extending upwards—one in the middle and one on each of the two sides; the measurement for this is now stated.
The horn should be nine finger-breadths in length, with a width equal to one-fourth of that;
the central horn should indeed be straight, while those on the two sides are slightly curved.
For the first [type], the insertion at the base is declared to be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
for the second, it is eleven finger-breadths, and the penetration is three finger-breadths.
In the third [section], however, there are thirteen [fingers], with a planting of four aṅgulas;
in the fourth, there are fifteen, with a planting of five aṅgulas.
In the fifth [year], the entry into the earth is seventeen finger-breadths and six finger-breadths;
in the sixth, however, the planting is twenty-three [finger-breadths] and seven finger-breadths.
In the seventh [section], the twenty-first [verse] concerns the planting at eight finger-breadths below;
and in the eighth, the twenty-third [verse] concerns the planting at nine finger-breadths.
In the ninth [section], there are twenty-five [units]; the planting is ten finger-breadths, and the insertion and entry of the two branches and the spikes are likewise.
O Lord of good vows, everything should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and the syllable Om (praṇava).
Below the middle peak is the Śrī-devī, and below the side peaks is the Svastika.
One should have a lotus, a *nandikāvarta*, or a *pravartaka* made for the sake of auspicious purposes;
that which was fashioned from *nyagrodha* wood is known as "the bestower of peace" (*sāntida*) and is to be placed in the east.
A vessel made of udumbara wood bestows prosperity when situated in the southern direction;
likewise, one fashioned from pippala wood bestows nourishment in the northern quarter.
The Āyudha [Kalpa] is to be known as occurring in the Uttara [Kuru], but it is not at all established in Plakṣa.
Beneath each archway, two door-latches should be fashioned upon the two side-posts;
listen now to how exactly each should be bound.
Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka are the two guardians at the southern gate.
In the northwest is Vṛṣabha, and in the west is the door-keeper;
Gaurī and Caturaḍīśa are the door-keepers in the north.
One should not conceptualize Nandin and Mahākāla with [the letters] beginning with *ṇ*;
one should conceptualize the other two, Bhṛṅgin and Nāyaka, with the group of letters beginning with *caṭ*.
O Goddess of gods, even with the *varga* of *tapa*, one should conceive of *durmukha* as charcoal; however, the *śita* and *aśita* [syllables] should be placed by means of the *yasavarga*.
Now listen: near the outer archway, one should place the pitcher named Śānta, presided over by Indra in the east.
Furthermore, Śiśira is adorned by Pāvaka (Agni) on another [side],
and Parjanya, together with the water-pot, is adorned by Yama in the southern direction.
In the southwest is another named Viśonāmaya, accompanied by the Pitṛs;
in the west is the one named Ghaṭa, accompanied by Varuṇa, who provides nourishment.
One should place the vessel called Amṛta in the northwest, situated transversely;
one should place the vessel named Hrada in the north, accompanied by Soma.
Nidhīśakalama is situated in the northeast (aiśānī) direction;
another, named Valada, is in the southwest (paitra), accompanied by Viṣṇu.
One should fashion the thread below; the arrangement toward the northeast is auspicious.
One should place there the one named Śubhada, established by Brahmā.
Beginning with the Praṇava, [recite] ... to Agni, obeisance.
Śauṃ, salutation to Śauṃya, adorned with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) at the beginning;
and ṣauṃ, salutation to Nirṛti, likewise endowed with the syllable *tāra* at the beginning.
Vauṃ! Homage to you, O Varuṇa, the father who is the primordial source of all that flows; yauṃ!
And homage to Vāyu at the end, adorned by all the pure essences.
"Hauṃ! Obeisance to you, Īśa, accompanied by 'pravādi'; and 'kṣauṃ', obeisance to Viṣṇu, accompanied by 'natyaṃtādi'."
Oṃ Oṃ! Homage to you, Brahmā; all [deities] are adorned with weapons.
This is the mantra prescribed for the water-pots (kalaśas) as well.
O virtuous lady, those [deities] fashioned from the syllable Oṃ serve as the support;
the guardians to be supported therein are fashioned from the Avirṇābha.
Those [vessels] containing medicinal herbs and gems, filled with water and beautifully adorned,
should be smeared with perfumes and other substances, and a thread together with *kuśa* grass should be tied around their necks.
Those [pillars] should be well-bound with flower garlands and adorned with mango leaves;
likewise, one should cover all the archways (toraṇas) with cloth.
One should fasten garlands of mango sprouts above the archway;
these garlands, fashioned from cut kusha grass, should be hung with flowers and tender leaves.
The banana trees, adorned with marks and encircled by threads of cloth,
should be placed in the intermediate directions along with bamboo shoots.
Now listen with one-pointed mind to the characteristics of the banners:
that which belongs to Indra in the east shall indeed be yellow in color.
In the southeastern direction, she is red in color;
in the southern direction, she is designated as black, and she is black in color.
That which is designated as Dhūmra by Ādhaumya shall be of the color of smoke;
in this regard, it is proclaimed to be of that same color in the western quarter.
Kapilā is considered to be in the intermediate direction of the south-east, and she is of that same color;
Pītā is in the northern direction, and she would be yellow in color.
In the direction of the Veśanadī, she is described as being white in color;
in the south-western direction, she becomes blue in color.
Padmā shall be in the northeastern direction, and she shall be lotus-colored;
Citrā is prescribed for the center, according to the intention and the cause.
A banner of a single color should be fashioned from Khaṇḍala and the others;
[it should bear] La, Ra, Śa, Ṣa, Va, Ya, Sa, Ha, Kṣa, and also the syllable Oṃ.

The [syllables] beginning with Viśva, each having three morae (*mātrā*) and joined with the *bindu*, ending with the word "namas," should be joined with their own names placed in the middle and the dative case (*caturthī*).
Those born in the form of weapons should be known as being in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
they are auspicious when fashioned from a rod of power and raised with the syllable Om.
In the central part of the pavilion, however, there is a seat for the purpose of sacrifice;
it is square, level, brilliant, and resembles the surface of a mirror.
It should be made eight finger-breadths high and four cubits in width;
however, O fair-faced one, it must be made one cubit in depth for a liṅga.
For a linga measuring two cubits, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be smeared with the scent of the Bhūtakas;
its width and height are declared to be nine finger-breadths.
O Goddess of the gods, for a liṅga measuring three cubits, the pedestal (pīṭha) should have the same width as Śaṅkara; its height, however, is declared to be ten finger-breadths.
O lady of excellent complexion, the pedestal for the liṅga up to the fourth stage (turyānta) should be seven cubits in length,
and its height is proclaimed to be eleven aṅgulas.
The pedestal for a liṅga measuring five cubits should be one cubit in width;
its height should be twelve finger-breadths. Now hear concerning those ending in one cubit.
The pedestal should be nine cubits long and thirteen finger-breadths high;
for a liṅga up to seven cubits in height, the pedestal's width should be one-tenth of that measure.
The height is said to be from two finger-breadths up to eight cubits;
the pedestal should be eleven cubits [in length] and five finger-breadths in height.
For a liṅga measuring nine cubits in height, a pedestal of twelve cubits is briefly proclaimed to have a thickness of thirty-six finger-breadths.
The sacrificial pit for the first [rite] is proclaimed to be twenty-four finger-breadths;
for the second, it is twenty-six, and for the third, twenty-eight.
The fourth [fire-pit] is thirty finger-breadths; the fifth is two more than that;
and the sixth fire-pit is proclaimed to be thirty-four finger-breadths.
The pit for a seven-cubit [altar] is thirty-six finger-breadths; that of the eighth is thirty-eight;
and the pit for a nine-cubit [altar] is proclaimed to be forty finger-breadths.
O you of excellent vows, I shall describe in detail its extent, its depth, and the number of its forms according to each of the directions.
It should be square in the east; in the southeast, it has the shape of a vulva (bhaga);
in the south, it is a half-moon; and in the southwest, it is a desirable triangle.
It should be known as circular in the western direction, hexagonal in the region of the wind (northwest),
resembling a lotus in the northern quarter, and eight-cornered in the region of the Lord (northeast).
O beloved, listen with one-pointed mind as I describe the characteristics of the *bhaga* and other parts;
having made it a perfect square, [divide] again from the midpoint of the Brahma-thread.
Having cast two lines from corner to corner across both the left and right sides of the enclosure,
it is then divided into halves.
Having set aside one part of that, one should rotate it like a crescent moon;
having rotated it beyond count, fifty [parts] from the field are outside.
O beloved, after having first drawn the two lines for the *vṛtta-sūtra*, a junction (*saṃgama*) should be made;
thus, one should cause the remaining lines to rest so that it takes the form of a vulva (*bhaga*).
In a field divided according to the Ṛṣi system, excluding two and a half parts,
and having established two cubits at the eastern Āpya and the region of the Lord of Gods (Deveśa);
By means of the application of chalk and thread, one should rotate [the instrument] like a sword-moon;
in the center of the straight line, there should be a womb (yoni), which was previously described as being from the center of the circle.
In a field divided according to its qualities, one should carry forward one part;
in the east, on both the left and right sides, one should carry forward a part for each.
One should indeed cast that thread situated at Vatsa three times;
thus the triangle is accomplished in the west within the womb.
Taking half of the ear as the field and drawing it forward, make it possessed of its qualities; then, having taken one part of that, rotate it like a full moon.
For the square is thus established; now hear concerning the hexagon.
When the field is divided into six parts, there is one [unit] in the east and also one at the end.
Taking half of those two, O Vahni, fashion a fish;
likewise, [place it] first before the Pitṛs, and similarly before the Lord of the Tiryaks.
Having abandoned the [direction] from Īśāna to Mīna according to the mental instruction,
[one should draw] the thread going from the West to Īśa, and likewise to Pāvaka.
First, the thread goes forward and likewise across; it goes across and likewise returns.
It goes across and returns again, and so on until it reaches the hair.
Having laid down six threads, a hexagon is clearly accomplished;
at each corner there should be a womb (*yoni*), and outside it, a lotus-like form.
Having formed a circle in the center, one should indeed mark the outer petals;
O Goddess, O beautiful one, this is done on the sixteen-spoked [mandala] within the girdle.
One should fashion the twelve-spoked [cakra] with vacā, or likewise with eight spokes; it is described as having the luster of a lotus. Now listen to the description of the eight-sided [cakra].
Having divided the field into two halves like the sun, one should discard the eastern half;
having established the [remaining] field, one should then destroy the eastern field again.
85a) Having taken half of that [dimension] in sequence toward the east, south, west, and north,
by the laying down of cross-lines, the supreme desired hermitage is accomplished.
Now listen to the characteristics of those [altars] at the other corners as well:
having made them like the leaf of an aśvattha tree, they are marked in the center like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Measuring one finger-breadth at the lip and equal to one finger-breadth at the tip of the womb, it has the shape of two jars at the back; this is the general characteristic common to all.
The northern direction is to be known as facing north, while the eastern and southeastern directions, O fair-faced one,
as well as the southern and southwestern directions, are proclaimed to face east.
The wise declare that the western wind-pot (vāyu-kumbha) faces north;
likewise, one should indicate the northern pit (saumya-kuṇḍa) and the northeastern one as facing east.
Leaving a space of one finger-breadth from the edge of the pit, the placement of the girdles (mekhalā) should take place;
there should be one girdle, or three, or five, O beloved.
When there is one girdle six finger-breadths in height and width,
the first girdle is considered to be four finger-breadths in height and width.
The second girdle should be three finger-breadths in height and width;
the third girdle should be two finger-breadths in height and width.
O auspicious lady, when one should fashion it with three girdles according to this sequence,
then for the five girdles, there should be five initial windings.
O Lord of Devas, at a distance of one finger-breadth [from the previous], with the same width and height as before,
there is another ninth pit (kuṇḍa), either in the east or in the direction of Vāpīśa.
O Dear One, the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be made by leaving aside half the space of the pedestal; they may be either circular or square.
An auspicious and excellent throne should be fashioned from heartwood;
its width should be twice the Brahma-portion, measured crosswise.
Its thickness at the middle should be half of its height, and it should have a cavity like that of Brahmā;
it should be made very firm, with a width and depth equal to one and a half times [the thickness].
One should fashion a square base, beautiful and variegated with the fourth [layer] and so forth;
having established the Liṅga there, one should perform the bathing and other rites.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the *kaṅkatī* and *parṇī* leaves, and wood from the *khadira*, *āsana*, and *śiṃśapā* trees;
likewise, sandalwood, *ucandana*, or even red sandalwood.
It may also be made of Devadāru wood, or of Samī, Aśvattha, Kiṃśuka, Udumbara, Bilva, or Yajñodumbara.
O beloved, whether it be an *aśoka*, a *vākula*, a *nāgakeśara*, a *punnāga*, a *campaka*, or whatever other beautiful trees there may be.
One should first take a piece of wood thirty-six finger-breadths long and fashion it into a *sruk* ladle;
its mouth should be seven finger-breadths in length, and its handle one finger-breadth thick.
The altar (vedī) should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) square, even, and beautiful;
likewise, the neck (gaṇḍikā) should be two finger-breadths, and the staff (daṇḍa) fourteen.
O Dear One, the pitcher (kumbha) should be four finger-breadths [in height] and made of the essence of the dhātrī tree;
one should fashion the circumference of the middle of the pitcher as nine finger-breadths.
The body of the pitcher should be circular, provided with a mouth and joined by a neck;
the handle should be six finger-breadths in circumference and perfectly round.
The *gaṇḍikā*, the central flower, and the *vitata* are made of *nāgakeśara*;
from the middle of the pedestal (*vedikā*), there is a circular depression (*svabhra*) measuring four finger-breadths.
At a depth of three finger-breadths, there should be a hollow such that its capacity is four palas;
one should fashion a girdle two finger-breadths wide all around on the exterior.
The ornamentation should be one and a half finger-breadths, either uniform or variegated;
the neck should be in the middle of the altar, with a width equal to one-third of that [height].
The circumference of the neck should be nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and one should fashion the front of the face with a measurement two [finger-breadths] less.
O Aśvattha tree, one should always fashion a very beautiful mechanical device;
there, one should cause a pit to be made with a measurement of one finger-breadth.
One should cause the girl to enter [the fire] below the neck, the emergence of the clarified butter there,
and the piercing with a red-hot iron rod.
It should be beautiful, circular, and pleasing at the base;
the *sruva* ladle should be made with a cavity of one *mātrā*, and its handle should likewise be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in circumference.

Having made it circular all around, O Lord, one should indeed dig that [pit] according to the measure; then, two jars should be placed outside, each having half of half a *pala* according to the measurement.
One should fashion the end of the staff with a circumference of four fingers;
alternatively, one may fashion a well-rounded *dhātrī* fruit at the base of the staff.
That which is produced by the mind is well-accomplished; now hear regarding the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī):
it should be fashioned in the shape of a womb (yoni), with a neck-like form provided with a handle (graha).
That pit should be beautiful, and there, twelve palas of [substances] should be collected;
the offering vessel (arghapātra) should be prepared, measuring twelve finger-breadths in width.
The four-fold circular stalks should be beautifully adorned with a single stalk;
the *praṇītā* vessels should also be made well-rounded and twelve finger-breadths in length.
With thick lips, very dense, bright, firm, and possessing complete auspicious marks.
A vessel for cow products should be made with a fine rim and consisting of that same material;
likewise, a sesame vessel should be properly circular and twelve finger-breadths in size.
A vessel for foot-unguent and likewise a vessel for perfume,
as well as a vessel for garments and ornaments, or even a vessel for the waving of lights (nīrājana).
One should fashion eight well-rounded *kalaśas* (pots) for peace, as well as auspicious jars,
and all other vessels made of gold and other precious materials.
O beautiful lady, they should end in a dead leaf,
be as long as possible according to what is available, smooth at the tips, and characterized by being uncut.
The sacrificial seats (viṣṭara) should likewise be auspicious in their length and circumference;
they should have green tips, possess leaves, be neither thick nor thin, and consist of uniform kuśa grass.
O Beloved, for the sake of non-separation, one should take fuel-sticks produced from trees that have not been praised [for this purpose], measuring a span in length, moist, and of uniform size.
The *pratisaras* are prescribed to be four, eight, and sixteen in number;
they should be made separately in vessels that are fragrant and very beautiful.
A seat, a bed, a vessel provided with a stand,
sandals, and vehicles— these are the requisites for the sacrificial ground.

Having thus completed these, one should likewise fashion other seats as well, without which the ritual action would not take place; furthermore, one should construct a seat within the central seat using colored powders.
Whether it be square or elongated, consisting of three sections and endowed with nine squares, one should deposit the nine principles therein; listen accordingly to how that is done.
One should place the Śivatattva in the center and Sadāśiva in the east;
having placed Īśvara in the southeast, one should place the Vidyātattva in the south.

One should place the principle of Time (kālatattva) in the western direction, which is the station of the ancestors; the principle called Niyati in the northwestern direction; and the principle of Puruṣa in the northern direction.
Having placed Prakṛti in the northeast, O beloved, hear of their intoxication:
the name is joined with "Oṃ" at the beginning and "Namaḥ" at the end, with the name itself inserted in the middle.
The reality of all these principles has been explained; it is not otherwise. There, four water-pots (kalaśas) are well-established as before.
Having placed Suśānta in the south, one should place Tejāḍhya in the west;
having placed Amṛta in the north, one should place the one called Ratna in the direction of the entrance.
One should place curd in the eastern direction, and ghee in the southern direction;
one should also place cow dung in the western quarter and cow urine in the north.
Having established it in the midst of milk, within the range of the Lord of Kuśodaka.

In that direction, one should perform the rites of pacification and so forth with the mantras of the faces, starting from the lowest face; O Śivā, one should not perform the wrathful rite (*māraṇa*) in a single location.
One should place the purifying five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water from the kuśa grass in the northeastern direction; if there is a specific requirement, it is stated as follows.
One should place spittle in the east, blood in the southern region,
extremely pungent substances in the west, and auspicious water in the northern region.

Having properly placed the fragrant water in the center of the *mada* (the vessel), and having consecrated it once with the heart-mantra and other mantras, one should bring it together as one using the root-mantra.
Having performed the single *nṛ-saṃkhyā* (human-counting) rite once, one should place it in the direction of Śaṅkara;
then, having gone to the pavilion called Snāna, one should collect the materials for the bath.
And the clay from the bank of a river, free from grass, insects, and the like,
as well as pure cow dung situated in a clean place— apart from the cows' own infirmities such as disease or old age— is [fit for use].
One should avoid honey from iron ore and that which comes from bees,
even if it be fresh, most delightful, and derived from leaves, flowers, or fruits.
One should avoid from afar any vessel that is broken, stolen, or faded;
a golden vessel for eating is best, or else one made of copper that is free of tarnish.
There, O beloved, having prepared an auspicious seat consisting of three parts as before,
one should likewise provide a pair of garments, incense, a lamp, and ornaments.
O Goddess, one should place a leaf and a flower belonging to Śaṅkara in the southeast,
as well as saffron, sandalwood, and a richly fragrant unguent.
O beloved, O Goddess, one should place the astringent, the milk-paste, the chowrie, the collyrium, the sprinkling, the side-dish, and the Vāyavya [offering].
The wise man should place the cow-dung, the clay, and the weapon, as well as the honey and the *nairājaṇa*, in the southwest direction, according to the proper sequence from the beginning.
In the cardinal and intermediate directions, there should be water-pots purified with cloth,
nine, six, or five in number, made either of copper or even of clay.
O beloved, it should be fashioned with gold or with gems within;
having placed white water to the east, well-perfumed with milk-water and incense.
In the southeast (Agnigocara), one should place a vessel filled with pure water and stainless liquid;
in the south (Yāmyagocara), a vessel filled with sandalwood water and fragrant liquid.

One should place water with jewels and gold, as well as jeweled water, in the region of the ancestors (Pitṛloka); one should place water with fruit and gold, or water with fruit, in the western quarter (Vāruṇa).
One should place flowers, water, and gold in the direction of Vāyu;
and one should place a jar filled with grain and water, resembling a heap of grain, in the direction of Soma.
One should place [the vessel] filled with medicinal herbs and water in the direction of Śaṅkara (the North),
and one filled with all substances and water in the domain of Īśa (the Northeast), which is the self of all.
Having consecrated eight water-pots once with the *kūṭamantras*, the wise one should place them there;
he should then lead the restrained *liṅga* from the ritual chamber to the bathing pavilion.
Having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious seat, one should thereafter perform the ritual bath;
first with earth and water, and subsequently with water alone.
Then there is bathing with cow dung, and after that, bathing with water;
then again bathing with a decoction, and after that, bathing with water once more.
Then there should be a bath with milk-pastes, followed again by a bath with water;
at the end of that, he should be bathed with water from a weapon, and then once more.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and with auspicious songs and instrumental music,
and having applied the *tilaka* that wards off demons, [he should do so] in the pavilion for the marriage ceremony.
Having brought it with great effort to the accompaniment of songs and auspicious musical instruments,
[he placed] that [horse] born of golden hair upon a spread of soft pairs of garments.
O one of excellent vows, one should first place the *liṅga* together with its pedestal facing east;
then, having determined the cardinal directions, one should perform the opening of the characteristic marks.
Having divided [the area] with saffron threads, or with red threads, or likewise with yellow pigments (rocanā),
the wise one should divide it into nine parts and discard the upper third.
At a depth of one-sixth [of the total height], one should mark the excellent opening for the drainage;
even there, at half that depth, one should likewise observe the opening for the destruction of demons.
One should never, even through negligence, touch that which rises above;
there may be a fracture of the face, nose, forehead, neck, and so forth.
Therefore, one should not perceive a characteristic below that which is desired;
having made half of the worship like a substance, make that one [half] like a rite.
O Dear One, in the middle of those two, between the two hanging threads,
the width of the lower line of the excavation for the best eight-yava liṅga is as follows.
O lady of virtuous vows, this has been described to you for a linga measuring eight cubits, or one endowed with three intermediate sections, O beloved, provided it is joined with the three below.
It should be provided with a pin, seven spans long, and have a width and depth of one line;
or else, for the liṅga, it may be seven cubits long, or three and a half.
One should cause two *yūkas* together with sixty *yavas* to be marked by a line;
and likewise in the six *liṅgas*, joined with three internal [divisions].
One should fashion five barley grains joined with three [units];
and in the case of a linga measuring five cubits, there should be a space of three [units] between them.
One should fashion a line there at four barley-corns and four yūkas;
likewise, on a four-cubit liṅga, it should be joined with three internal [units].
It should measure three barley grains and five *pukas*, characterized by broad lines;
and on a linga measuring three cubits, it should be joined with three internal divisions.
O auspicious lady, one should fashion a mark six *yūkas* long on a two-faced [liṅga],
and likewise on a two-cubit liṅga that is joined with three internal sections.
The characteristic measurement, whether one, seven,
or twenty-one *yūkas*, or even up to a full cubit (*hasta*) in width, applies to the *raudra-liṅga* when it is endowed with the three [aspects].
The characteristics of the wood for the *pūka* and the lines on the broad excavation, as well as the arrangement of the lingas arising from the womb, are determined by this rule.
O Dear One, listen: for the Raudra weapons, such as the hand-weapon (hasta) and others, one should fashion a superior [image] consisting of hanging threads, devoid of the wing-thread (pakṣasūtra).
I shall explain correctly how their wing-line (pakṣasūtra) is formed:
the descent of the wing-line is measured by half the length of the plumb-line.
One should perform the suspension in such a way that the merit is equal to that of the Takshita;
and the rule for the two fortnights is that it should be divided by eight times half of the Lamba.
One should lead the thread from corner to corner until the seasons have met;
having discarded the two lower portions, one should join them behind the two [upper corners].
Having fashioned the head-piece in the shape of an umbrella, which bestows happiness and grants the enjoyment of sovereignty,
one may then, according to another method, apply the wing-threads.
One should divide that measurement, which is half of the long cord, into nine parts;
then, according to the division, one should bring down two wings and the squares for the Ṛṣis.
Without abandoning the two below, one should apply the yoga at the back;
and by using a cotton wick (*śirovarti*) made of *trapuṣa* [flax], for the sake of accomplishing the remainder of enjoyments.
Alternatively, the introduction of the wing-lines may be performed by another method:
having made them like the multiplier of half the height, they are likewise on both wings.
Having taken two and a half parts, one should discard half a part below;
having led it to the back, it should be applied at the "cock's head" (kukkuṭāṇḍa) as the head of the *vṛtta*.
Whatever other means for accomplishing auspiciousness exist for the sake of perfecting the yoga of knowledge,
or else, by another method, the introduction of the thread of the wings [of the mandala].
Having made the half-lamba (lambārddha) like a vowel, and likewise on both sides,
one should draw the lines from corner to corner across fourteen squares.
One should apply the yoga on the back, having abandoned the two [states] in both;
with the crescent moon placed upon the head, this is for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now they shall proclaim another characteristic common to all:
first, having divided it ninefold upwards, make the seventh one possessed of qualities.
Leaving one part above and making it two parts below, there should be a barley-corn [in width];
having grasped the middle thread and drawn it out like a half-moon.
Devoid of the long thread and likewise the side threads,
there should be only the Brahma-thread, which should extend as far as Viṣṇu.
One should split [the image] at the two hands, the two eyes, and also on the two sides;
for this characteristic of the barley-grain indeed accomplishes all desires and purposes.
O beloved, the first characteristic has been described as "the umbrella on the head";
that same [mark] should also be made in the Aindra-liṅga for the accomplishment of Indra-hood.
Thus, both the characteristic mark and the head-ornament, like the power itself,
are beneficial for the accomplishment of those qualities in the Linga and in the fire-pit.
That very same characteristic is said to apply to the head of the staff as well as to the Yāmya-liṅga;
it is the means for accomplishing the enjoyment of Yama.
The characteristics of the sword are indeed those very same [as the head], and the head is like the sword; in the southwest (nairṛta) and at the linga, that portion is thoroughly established.
The head of the banner is indeed characterized by that very same mark;
the head of the serpent on the Vāyu-liṅga is likewise like a head.
Indeed, on the Varuṇa line and the Liṅga line, that is the best means for determining the portion;
at that very point is the characteristic of the flag, which is like the head of a head.
Indeed, in the Liṅga and in Vāyu, there is the accomplishment of the enjoyment of wind;
O auspicious lady, that very characteristic belongs to Gada, whose head is like that of a mace-bearer.
In the Liṅga and Kauveryaka [traditions], the accomplishment of the Kauverya state is taught;
that very characteristic should be known, as well as the head being raised three finger-breadths high.
In the Īśāna face of the Liṅga, there is the accomplishment of the state of Śaṅkara;
its characteristic is exactly like that of the petal of a lotus, and the head [of the Liṅga] is likewise.
In the Liṅga known as Brāhmya, one accomplishes the state of Brahmā and its realization.
One should mark that very same characteristic upon the head of Rudra;
it is to be known as being on the Vaiṣṇava liṅga for the perfect accomplishment of Viṣṇu-hood.
Learn the characteristics of those who bear the marks for determining the directions:
between the elephant’s eye and the age [of the wood], fashion a sharp-pointed tip.
And that which is proclaimed regarding the Vajra-liṅga is for the accomplishment of those rites;
likewise, it applies to the Śakti-liṅga as it does to the Śakti, and to that known as the Daṇḍa-liṅga as it does to the Daṇḍa.
As with the sword, he is known as Khaḍga; as with the noose, he is known as Pāśa;
as with the banner, he is known as Dhvaja; and as with the mace, he is known as Gada.
And regarding that which is called the "spear" (śūla) as being like a spear, however, due to the drawing of the six parts;
and also in that called the "lotus" (padma) and the "wheel" (cakra)—listen, I shall explain that according to reality.
First, divide [the circumference] into nine parts; then, discard the upper third part.
Next, form two parts into a lotus-like shape, and the four parts into the base and bowl of a water-pot.
Two long threads are prescribed, free from feces and devoid of feathers;
this has been told to you regarding the lotus-named [liṅga] and the liṅga itself, and not otherwise.
Above the portion of Viṣṇu, one should draw two circles within two divisions;
this is to be known regarding the liṅga called Cakra, O beautiful goddess.
Now I shall explain another [method], the characteristics of the minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasādhana*):
whichever of these signs is preferred, its half is divided by nine.
The cord for the head-line should not consist of separate parts;
the cord for the wings should be half of that, and for the two back-lines as before.
O auspicious one, when the plumb-line consists of eight parts and is established at the desired point where the serpent-king Śeṣa is located, it constitutes the eighth part.
The side-line (pakṣasūtra) is half of that, and the back-line (pṛṣṭhayoga) is of the same measure;
by this, one should predict the loss of sight for enemies and their death.
When the plumb-line consists of seven parts, the wing-line shall be half of that; and on the back, the junction is as before.
Through that [state], there is silence due to lack of nourishment; by that enemy, death [is brought about].
It is said that the sixth [limb] is the neck, and the hanging cord (ālamba-sūtra) consists of that very essence.
One should likewise determine the side-line as half of that, and the junction on the back;
one should predict the destruction of the enemy's circle of kinsmen.

O Goddess of the Suras, the hanging thread (lambasūtra) and the wing-thread (pakṣasūtra) are likewise described in the fifth [chapter], as well as the characteristic of the arm-penetration (bhujavedha).
By means of that, one effects the bending of the arms of enemies, and through it, their destruction shall occur.
In the fourth [section], there is the hanging thread (*lambasūtra*), while the wing-thread (*pakṣasūtra*) is as before.
The characteristic of the breast-piercing [mantra] is indeed as described and not otherwise;
by the piercing of the enemies, there is the destruction of their wives, sons, and so forth.
The third is the hanging thread, and the wing-thread is half of that;
this indeed is described as the characteristic of the heart-penetration, and not otherwise.
By that [measurement], one should predict the death of the host of enemies and heart-piercing pain;
the plumb-line is at two parts, and the wing-line is at half of that.
O lady of virtuous vows, the piercing of the belly (kukṣivedha) has been described to you as a characteristic;
by that, the enemies suffer abdominal pain, and their death follows without a doubt.

O lady of virtuous vows, it has been explained to you that the vertical line (lambasūtra) is at one part, the wing-line (pakṣasūtra) is at half of that, as well as the mark (lakṣaṇa) and the piercing of the navel (nābhivedha).
And for enemies, there will be fear of death from that *nābhisūtra*;
even by half of that which is declared to be a *pīḍana-sūtra*, [the same result occurs].

Having understood correctly that each half-yava increment is declared auspicious, one should draw [the diagram] according to the distinctions of the states of being, their functions, and their characteristics; this is the means for accomplishing everything.
Through the conjunction of the operation of non-existence, one may establish a contradictory object;
if, through the conjunction of existence and non-existence, a result is obtained from a mark (liṅga) and so forth.
Nothing would be firm by means of a mere definition; therefore, I shall explain this:
both the linga and its characteristics must be endowed with these defining marks.
Even if this [body] is devoid of auspicious marks, it is called "devoid of marks";
therefore, with every effort, strive to bring forth those marks.
When the liṅga is endowed with the characteristics desired by oneself, it becomes identical with that [Self]; O beloved, I shall likewise explain how this applies to the Self through an illustration.
The great-souled Śaiva energy should be joined with your own self;
that is declared to be the supreme characteristic, which must be extracted by the wise man.
O Goddess, if there were a great contradiction, it would be like heat in a tail;
yet your auspicious nature, as it has been perceived, is clearly distinguished as peaceful.
O Śambhu, the proximity of specific qualities is distinguished by their characteristics, as is the case with lingas made of gems, such as those produced from coral, jewels, and pearls.
O beautiful lady, when crystal and other such materials are consecrated by the rays of impurities,
they do not attain the pervasive characteristic [of purity] that is attained by those fashioned from the eight metals.
Their own splendor is their characteristic, and likewise in the case of the *vāla-liṅga*;
their ritual acts, such as bathing and so forth, are marked by the characteristics of their own respective *liṅgas*.
The opening of the eye is characterized by the manifestation of the meanings of the unmanifest and other principles previously described.
The Guru should fashion that [image] from a rod of Jāmbūnada gold according to the instructions in its manual;
or, endowed with skill, he should carve it by the path taught by the Guru.
One should turn it with a very sharp blade and great skill,
so that it is neither lacking in drops or fragments nor possessed of cracks.
It is neither interrupted nor coarse, nor is it thin in any place;
it should be drawn as a complete line by those who seek the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the ritual practice (*sādhana*), lines such as the *viddha*, *āsphoṭita*, and others should be drawn;
an auspicious [line] brings obstacles in an inauspicious [rite], while an inauspicious one brings obstacles even in an auspicious [rite].
Therefore, having understood [the procedure], one should extract [the mantra] with every effort;
when it has been scattered, a marriage of honey and ghee should be performed by means of the Mṛtyujit mantra.
O Goddess of the Gods, the [mantra] Mṛtyujit is proclaimed by the Teacher himself as auspicious, beautiful, and the cause for the nourishment of the lines.
Furthermore, in that regard as well, one should perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth,
using decoctions, milk-pastes, and other auspicious substances for bathing with water.
One should perform a bath with perfumes, milk, and ghee, followed by baths with curd, honey, and water,
using eight jars in the auspicious sequence starting from the east.
One should anoint [the image] with sandalwood, saffron, musk, and other such substances;
likewise, it should be adorned with pairs of divine garments and ornaments made of gold and other precious materials.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth, and with unbroken grains, sesame seeds, and rice,
and having applied a protective mark (tilaka) that destroys demons, one should perform the rite of waving lights (nairājana).
Accompanied by women whose husbands and sons were living, by auspicious songs sung by maidens,
by proclamations of "Auspicious Day" and shouts of "Victory!", and by the sounding of conchs, panegyrists, and musical instruments.
Having established a well-defined limit according to one's mental capacity and enjoyment,
one should subsequently perform the immersion (avamana) and again offer worship with libations (vṛdā).
O lady of excellent vows, the preceptor should perform all this with the *praṇava*;
then, once the chariot has been well-prepared and brought forward, he should cause the disciple to mount it.
Then the bed-frame, the splinter, and likewise the vessel of honey,
the pair of garments, the water-jar and so forth— whatever had been brought for the purpose of the bath.
One should give all of that to the artisan and honor him at that time;
one should have him well-seated in a chariot and cause him to circumambulate the city procession.
One should offer the oblation, go toward the directions, and scatter a mixture of precious gems.
One should scatter garlands of cloth and garlands of pearls on all sides;
one should also scatter vessels of cloth, copper vessels, and silver.
One should place various bronze vessels, as well as tridents and other such items;
one may also place various garments, goods, or cowrie shells.
One should scatter parched grain along with flowers and surround it with all kinds of crops;
it should be provided with a canopy and filled with flags, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments.
Adorned with hanging strings of pearls and embellished with mirrors and the like,
it was provided with flowers, incense, and other offerings, and was densely filled with rows of lamps.
In this manner, one should indeed wander through the city, the hamlet, and the village;
and within that, every sanctuary beginning with Śiva was previously established.
One should worship with effort using lands, jewels, elephants, horses, and cattle;
and one should gratify the twice-born according to one's ability, as well as the blind and the wretched.
Or, wearing a Śivaliṅga, one should give a special gift as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thus, according to this division, the king and those from the city perform the circumambulation.
Or it may be performed by others as well, according to their own means,
so that the chariot reaches the station of Śiva while provided with food and drink.
And he shall become the performer of ten million sacrifices;
and after that time has been established, on that day every year, [he shall do so].
O King, as long as the linga remains established, one should not cause it to be broken like a vessel;
by doing so, one obtains that very fruit—there is no doubt.
Whosoever possesses a particular land at any given time, for him that land yields its fruit at that time;
if it is not protected out of delusion, he is cooked in the Raurava and other hells.
The power of Śiva is proclaimed as the imperishable nature of protection;
it is like a lord who, having set a well-constructed chariot in motion, remains seated within it.

Having performed the rite for auspiciousness there, one should cause him— who has arrived from the southern land and is seated upon a chariot on an auspicious throne— to cross over by means of the Praṇava.
And with the *hṛdinī* mantra, O Lord of Gods, one should then offer eight handfuls of water;
likewise, an offering (*argha*) of curd, clarified butter, honey, and well-husked rice.
One should present the eightfold offering (arghya), consisting of siddhārtha seeds, sesame seeds, white flowers, and likewise stalks of dūrvā grass.
Having bowed again with the head and all one’s limbs, O Lord,
one should then cause the liṅga, which is fixed upon an auspicious pedestal, to enter [the base].

In the center of the sacrificial pavilion, or at the eastern gate, or elsewhere; on the northern side of the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), he should place the one who is seated upon that seat with diligent effort.
Then one should prepare a bed with various items such as cotton mattresses; it should be provided with pillows on its sides and furnished with bolsters at the feet.
Having covered it with a white cloth, or especially with mats and other such materials,
one should spread out the bed with the head [of the cloth] facing forward and place the pillow with the tuft.
Having performed the covering with the Kavaca mantra as prescribed by the rules of one's own scripture,
one should cover the deity with the Hṛdaya mantra and sleep upon the bed with the Śiras mantra.
The golden pitcher at the head region is called the "sleep-pitcher";
sleeping with the head toward the east is declared the best, while other directions are said to be ordinary.
It is completely filled with the five jewels, well-adorned with garments and other offerings,
provided with perfumes, incense, and the like, and furnished with mango sprouts.
One should place an auspicious vessel well-covered with flower garlands upon jewels;
having offered various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) as well as fragrant drinks and the like.
One should worship with the heart-mantra all things, including meat-offerings, those beginning with Vāsava, garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Or else, whatever else is to be given, such as household utensils and the like,
one should then offer clarified butter and honey at its foot.

One should not apply foot oil for the sake of a causal purpose, nor should one ever do so in the heart; likewise, one should not perform ear-cleaning and such acts toward the Praṇava, the Lord of the Gods.

Having conceptualized entities such as Phalgusā and others as non-dual, and that which is like death, one should indeed establish them in the universal; thus, one should perform the ritual action within the universal.
For one's own sake, for the sake of a beneficial disciple, or for the sake of wealth, one should have [the rites] performed through non-duality.
One should offer flower-garlands and *sarā*; the *pratisarā* is offered to you.
One should arrange the four, eight, and sixteen [parts] starting from the Brahma-portion in sequence;
one should then designate the Bhūti, Darbha, Tilā, and others as the protective guardians.
Dakṣiṇā and Bhūti provide protection in the south, while Darbha grass is the protector in the east; sesame seeds guard the northern quarter, and the destroyer of demons protects from the west.
One should indeed perform protection with the Astra-mantra, or alternatively, in the place called *kaṣa*;
having stood upon the Guru-pāda, one should first install the eight *mṛtyus*.
91a) Kṣamāgni, Yajamāna, Turaviśvāyu, and Prabhañjana;
joined with Indra and Vyoman— the division is now being explained.
Having first placed Kṣamā in the east, one should place Pāvaka in the southeast;
the Sacrificer in the southern quarter, and Arka in the southwest.
Having properly placed Varuṇa in the western quarter, Vāyu in the northwestern quarter,
and Candra in the northern quarter, one should place Vyoman in the northeastern region.
Having thus installed the eight forms (mūrtis), one should again install the guardians of those forms (mūrtipās):
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, and likewise Bhava.
Īśāna, Deva, Eka, Aśva, Bhīma, and Mūrti are the presiding deities;
one should install them in sequence starting from the east and ending with Īśāna.
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Bhaumī,
Valotkaṭā, Dhātrī, and Viśvī— these are the Mūrti-śaktis to be assigned starting from the east.
Now hear from me the sequence of the other Vidyeśvaras:
Ananta is placed in the east, and the one known as Sūkṣma is in the southeast.
Having installed Śivottama in the south, which is the sole station of the ancestors,
one should install Ekarudra in the west and Trimūrti in the region of Vāyu (the northwest).
Having placed the auspicious Śrīkaṇṭha at the crest within the range of Īśa,
one should likewise place Vidyāśakti in the sequence beginning from the east.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī as the fourth;
then Kalavikaraṇī and Balavikaraṇī.
And likewise Valapramathanī, the crusher of all beings;
having thus assigned the eight Bhairavas, hear their sequence from me.
One should place Aśitāṅga in the east and Caru in the direction of Agni (southeast);
having placed Raṇḍa in the south, one should then place Pitṛkrodha.
Having placed Āpya in the northeast, Kapālī in the northwest,
Bhīṣaṇa in the northern direction, and Saṃhāra in the northeast;
In the general case, for the purpose of attaining liberation, one should install the powers of the forms;
however, when one desires supreme enjoyment, one should install the powers of the Vidyās.
For the purpose of accomplishing minor rites, Bhairava was desired through the power of his form;
likewise, there are [deities] beginning with Ananta—now hear their mantras.
O Dear One, a male is to be conceived by means of the final letter of each group of the Mātṛkā or by the first letter of each group;
however, a female is conceived by means of a short vowel, while a male is conceived by means of a long vowel.
Or else, they should be struck down by their own weapons, as discerned in their own scriptures.
Or, O fair-faced one, they should be installed with the mantras consisting of the letters of their own directions:
la, ra, śa, ṣa, va, ya, sa, and the letter ha; these are the three mātṛkās.
O lady of excellent hips, the [letters] beginning with *pra* and so forth are to be known according to their sequence;
for all of them, the single letter *va* is the common *vyaya*.
Having understood the pervasion of their own recitation, concentration, and meditative absorption, one should properly place [the syllables] as yellow,
red, black, blue, cloud-colored, and smoky.
One should meditate upon the deity who is lotus-like and white in color, preceded by the [presiding] deities;
likewise, there are the lords of the forms (mūrtis) and the powers (śaktis) of those forms.

O lady of excellent vows, the concentration (dhāraṇā) on the earth and the other elements, extending up to primordial nature (prakṛti), serves for the pervasion of these— the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), their Śaktis, and the Bhairavas.
The pervasion up to the end of the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva) has been described by you, and not otherwise;
indeed, Śiva, who is the pervader of all, is to be meditated upon in the center.
Having thus established [the deity], one should restrain it while equipped with armor and weapons;
likewise, one should station twice-born men initiated by mantra as lords in the various directions.
The Ṛgveda is in the east, the Yajurveda is in the region of the west,
the Sāmaveda is likewise in the south, and they know the Atharvaveda to be in the north.
Reciting their own respective hymns, all the Rudras as well as Akaṣi,
Yāvāmāna, and others who were reciters of the Cumbaka and other sections [did so].
In the intermediate directions, one should likewise arrange the ascetics and the virtuous ones,
who are endowed with the realization of the five Brahmans and possessed of perfect victory.
Having visualized her as possessing a physical form, the skillful preceptor should perform the rite sixty times with Kuṣṭha,
or sixteen, or four, or even once.
There, those who have mastered the Saṃhitās should perform that rite; it is called the Tithi-tumvuka.
For the sake of enjoyment and other goals, one should indeed prepare sixteen sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the installation.
In the middle [category], the arrangement of eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is endowed with excellence;
there are four common pits, and one is arranged for inferior purposes.
Having thus consecrated the image-makers, one should perform the *adhivāsana* rite;
[the asterisms] Rohiṇī, Anurādhā, and the three Uttaras [are auspicious].
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śravaṇā, Ārdrā, and likewise Śatabhiṣā—these are indeed auspicious for stable undertakings; they are characterized by stability and are favorable for consecration ceremonies.
I shall now describe the sequence of the castes, beginning with the twice-born, so that it may be auspicious:
Uttarā, Pāṭha, Āḍhaka, Hasta, Puṣya, and Rohiṇī.
For these indeed bring auspiciousness to the twice-born; now hear [the rules] for the Kṣatriyas.
Punarvasu, Citrā, Dhaniṣṭhā,
and Śravaṇa are declared to be auspicious and gentle for Vaiśyas.
Uttarābhādrapadā, Revatī, and Aśvinī are considered auspicious;
Pūrvāphālgunī and Svātī are joined with the mudrās of merit.
The Moon, the Sun, Mercury, and Jupiter are declared to be auspicious;
these four days of the week should be accepted, while Venus, Mars, and Saturn should be avoided.
Friends who provide prosperity, means of accomplishment, and security, and who are supreme friends—these five types of Tārās should be well-accepted; the other four one should avoid.
In the sky [of the zodiac], every birth is accompanied by its own death;
therefore, neither inauspicious nor auspicious planetary configurations exist here by name alone.
The Vava, Vaṇija, and Taitila karaṇas are considered auspicious for six [periods];
Viṣṭi should always be abandoned, and one should also avoid the first three of the fixed (sthirā) karaṇas.

The four-day periods (catuḥpada) should be grasped; those in the bright fortnight are considered auspicious, while in the dark fortnight they are auspicious provided they are not the "empty" (rikta) days, namely Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā.
The sixth and subsequent [houses] are never exhausted during the waning fortnight;
in the conjunction of planets, the pair ends at the mouth.
One who seeks merit should avoid this [action], whether for the sake of another or even for one's own;
however, it may be performed even when there is opposition, based on the intention of the agent.
One should act in such a manner that, out of a desire for the fruit,
the consecration of the axe is performed— either as the most excellent preliminary consecration or even as an immediate consecration.
Wearing a turban, with cool fragrant garlands, and adorned with white garments;
his two hands have golden bracelets, and his fingers have golden rings.
The ears have golden earrings, the feet have golden anklets,
the waist has a golden girdle, and the neck has a golden necklace.
Adorned with various ornaments and fashioned by craftsmen,
he who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation first bows down to the noble Hotṛ priest.
The image-worshippers (mūrtipas) shall not wear turbans, but be adorned with all ornaments;
they must be made by the artisan exactly according to the prescribed sequence.
And for what purpose are they bound by their names without the *uṣṇīṣa*,
when those who have reached the reality (*tattva*) assume their respective forms as lords of the *mūrtis*?
When one embraces the supreme consort, then those who possess Īśvara should adorn her;
they are great, endowed with strength, full-bodied, and possessing the marks of complete limbs.
Those who have renounced the Rudra-mantras, being of steady character and firm in their vows,
should place the funeral pinda in the northern direction of the linga at a reservoir of water.

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the forms and mantras should be performed in that manner by means of the ritual marks; she too, clad in a pair of white garments, remains established at the conclusion of the rites.
The ritual concludes with the *śatkṛnta* [mantra], and those [deities] are called Kuṇḍalinī;
here, the procedure beginning with the bath is like that for the Liṅga in the auspicious sphere.
And here, one should fashion the extraction of the characteristic marks in the form of a vulva;
at the inner edge of the excavation, however, there is the characteristic mark of the *liṅga* below.

Just as it is not seen by worldly people because it consists ultimately of secret power (*guhya-śakti*), it is therefore the excellent essence and the primary; such is the characteristic of that secret.
Having carved its secret organ like a linga with a golden probe,
one should install a stone representing Brahma at the base of the linga.
The ritual procedure beginning with bathing has been obtained, yet it is devoid of the defining characteristics;
indeed, that which is endowed with the characteristics of its own essence was previously set forth.
She is declared to possess infinite power and is renowned as Dhariṇī;
she is called Sthirakārīśā, the one who brings about the cessation of the universe.
