Having first worshipped the triad according to the desired ritual procedure, the preceptor should cause this single form, which is the self of all, to enter [the disciple] by means of yoga.
Then, in his own sacrificial pit, the illustrious Guru should worship the one who is the soul of all;
he should then generate an auspicious fire according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Having thus produced the Śivāgni with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), O lady of excellent vows,
one should then divide it into nine parts and take refuge in the directions starting from the center.
Having conceived Śivāgni in the center, one should arrange the eight fires of the Mūrtis;
the Guru should then lead the fire that is in the eastern portion to the eastern pit.
In the southeast, the fire is in the southeast fire-pit; in the south, the fire is in the southern fire-pit;
in the southwest, the fire is in the southwestern fire-pit; and in the west, the fire is in the western fire-pit.

One should offer oblations oneself to Vāyu in the northwestern direction, to Soma in the northern region when he is in his northern course, and to Īśāna in the northeastern direction during the middle period.
93a) O Dear One, just as the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipa*) gather around their own forms in the fire,
so too should the *homam* be performed by the guardians of the forms according to their own yoga.
Likewise, having fashioned a jar for peace (śānti), all the image-mantras (mūrti-mantra) combined,
struck by the residual drops (sampāta), [should be offered] one hundred and eight times.
The Guru, joined with the Śiva-mantra and the Astra-mantra, should fashion his own vessel;
knowing the mantra of his own form, he should assign the faces and limbs [to the parts of the vessel].
Having each performed his own sacrifice and offered oblations according to the prescribed rule,
he should perform the purificatory oblation (śodhyahoma) with the mantras of his own form, face, and limbs.
Having unified all time-periods, one should perform ritual action as if it were a single entity;
having conceptualized the three principles (tritatva) according to their characteristics of the pervaded and the pervader.

O beautiful goddess, beginning from the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) and so forth, with the lords of the forms associated with the magnet (cumbaka), one should offer the oblation after ascertaining the strength of the sacrificial materials.
One should conceive of the reality of the Brahman-portion as the reality of Vidyā in the Vaiṣṇava [mandala],
and the reality of Śiva in the one called Rudra, in due order.
The principle of Ātman extends up to Pradhāna, while the principle of Vidyā extends up to Vidyā;
the principle of Śiva extends up to Śiva—this is proclaimed as their pervasion.
O Āsureśvarī, having performed the rite of raising up that which is called the Self, and having purified it through pervasion,
one should rise and touch with *kuśa* grass the other *arghya*, the portion belonging to Brahman.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should again perform the rite of raising up (utthāpana) known as the Vidyā;
then, for the purpose of purifying its pervasion, one should return and perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having risen again, one should touch the vessel containing the arghya water with kuśa grass;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one performs the rite of raising the deity named Śiva once more.
Having returned to complete the meaning of the pervasion of that cause, one should perform the oblation again;
then, having offered water for the guest-offering (arghya) once more, one should touch the one named Rudra with kusha grass.

O fair-faced one, the lords of the forms (mūrtipas) should likewise perform [the rite] part by part using the mantra taught by the guru, following the sequence beginning with the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
Having purified that respective *tattva* with *vyāsa*, one should touch it with *kuśa* grass held in the hand together with *argha*.
Then the *cumbaka*, the *antaḥkṣamādhyakṣa*, the *agnyādhyakṣa*, and his follower [should do likewise].
The presiding deity of fire (Yama) follows that [deity of earth], and the presiding deity of the sun follows him;
the presiding deity of water (Varuṇa) follows the deity of space, and the presiding deity of wind follows him.
Indra is the presiding deity at the end of the wind [quarter], and the Sky is his follower;
in the portions known as the Moon, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, the ritual procedure for all [deities] is prescribed.
Whether it be a thousand, or even a hundred, or half of that, or even half of that again;
this should be performed by the image-keepers (mūrtipās), while the preceptor (ācārya) should carry out the principal rite.
Then the Piṇḍikā, pervaded by the ritual action and endowed with the form to be purified,
should be touched with Kuśa grass and water in the hand by the Cumbaka together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
That action is the ritual procedure (vidhi) even in its mere measure; however, the conceptualization of it as an object of enjoyment pertains to the state of being an enjoyer.
And in that state of being an enjoyer, the Lord is the all-pervasive one whose nature consists of the power of knowledge.
And as the enjoyer, he is the supreme lord, all-pervasive, whose nature consists of the power of knowledge;
the stone which is of the nature of Brahman is known as the support (dhāraṇī) in the path of Sīdhvara.
And one should purify that [deity] which is common to all beings and corresponds to that [state],
O fair-faced one, by having the image-bearers offer one hundred oblations for each of the principles (tattvas).
Once again, one should properly apply the power (śakti) to be purified;
and when this triad of purifications has been performed, [one should establish] the linga and the altar consisting of stone.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite, one should subsequently install the triad of powers:
one should install the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in the liṅga and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in the pedestal.
One should place the *dhāraṇī* and the *śakti*, whose nature is Brahman, upon the stone;
then, having meditated upon the union through the application of the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, one should join them together.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should observe the appropriate time;
by the word "attained" (prāpta), both external and internal time are understood.
But if that [knowledge] which is external, as taught in the sciences of astrology and so forth, is the knower of the Guru,
it becomes subtle and internal through the application of the Guru.
One should observe the period of the menses for the purpose of ensuring conception for both;
when that time is near, then one should perform the act with conciseness.
If the time should be distant, then the fire-oblation (homa), recitation (japa), and so forth—
whether with an abundance of materials or deficient, or whether concise or extensive— may be performed.

O Goddess of the gods, when rites such as the fire-oblation have been performed, but those such as meditation and recitation are deficient, they must be performed correctly and in their proper sequence.
Having risen, this [mantra] should be recited for the noble god Śravaṇa on the right side:
*Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, to Rudra; O Rudra, the fierce one, obeisance to you!*
Whether complete or incomplete, may it be accepted, having been fulfilled according to one's capacity; Svāhā!
One should offer whatever ritual procedure has been performed by means of the power of gnosis:
*oṃ namaḥ śāṅkari pūraya 2 svāhā*.
Whatever arrangement of the altar (vedikā) one who is capable of action may offer,
he should offer it upon that which is called Ananta, using this very mantra.
Having offered [the oblation], one should thereafter restrain the armor and the weapon-mantras;
having thus restrained them, one should afterwards proceed to the temple with humility toward Śiva.
Having uttered the great and most fierce weapon known by the name Pāśupata—
the great Mahāpāśupata, proclaimed as the king of weapons: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ haḥ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having destroyed the obstacles, O Goddess of the gods, [reside] within the temple.
One should perform the installation of the Guru upon the stone which is of the nature of Brahman;
by means of the ear-thread, one should avoid the center of the womb [of the altar].
The center of the Brahma-stone should be slightly less than the center of the door;
having divided the door according to the sages, make the middle one endowed with the three qualities.

Among those, one should again divide one into two; then, in the northern half, one should again place a quality. Then, in the interior, one should again place two, and likewise abandon one in the southern [half].
That which is the higher sūtra between those two is the middling wealth;
by this method, there is the avoidance of the middle self-delusion.
And the abandonment of the center is not prescribed by any other rule, O lady of virtuous vows;
having thus first established the center, one should place a pure stone there.
First, the measurement of the site and the ritual cord (sūtra) are as before;
having envisioned the deities as before, the offering of oblations and worship is also as before.
Having carefully observed the center of the stone, one should establish it by means of its own quality with this mantra:
Oṃ, homage to the pervasive, stable, immovable, and eternal one! Hrīṃ Laṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā!
This has been declared as one's own quality by the Supreme Lord previously;
having become the basis for meditation on pervasiveness, it is the supreme, all-pervading state of equanimity.
One should place the desired object upon a firm path with steadfastness;
because of the connection between the support and the supported, that state is called "unfailing."
The substrate is indeed infinite power, while the superstratum is Supreme Śiva;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should certainly not obstruct their union.
One should place jewels in the respective pits that were previously prepared;
one should place a vajra in the eastern pit and a sun-crystal in the southeast.
One should place an indranīla gem in the southern [direction], a mahānīla in the southwest,
and one should place a pearl, O Goddess, in the western circle of one's own [mandala].
One should place a puṣparāga gem in the northwest, a padmarāga in the north,
a vaiḍūrya in the northeast, and all [the remaining gems] in the center.
In this manner, the wise teacher should place the jewels in due sequence;
having performed the placement of the jewels, he should then again perform the placement of the metals.
One should place gold in the east and copper in the south-east; iron in the southern direction and tin in the south-west.
One should place Tāra in the north-eastern direction according to the tradition of Pracetas;
and one should place Saumya and Ghāṣa in the eastern direction of Rītikāmbo.
One should place Tīśa in the northeast, and then place Pāśāṇaka;
one should place Haritāla in the east, and [place] the stone in the southeast.
One should place green vitriol (kāsīsa) in the western direction, and colocynth (akṣika) in the southwest;
having placed mercury (rasa) in the west, it is taught that [one should place] [the next substance] in the northwest.
O Goddess, gold and red ochre should be placed here; of this there is no doubt.
Scented stone (gandhapāṣāṇa) is in the north, and Bhr̥ṅgarāja is in the northeast.
O Goddess, one should likewise place the measures of iron and stone;
furthermore, other roots must be deposited—listen as to how.
Having placed uśīra in the east, viṣṇukrāntā in the southeast,
red sandalwood in the south, and likewise black aguru in the southwest;
Having placed the white sandalwood in the west, the *sārika* and blue lotus in the northwest, the sacrificial pit in the north, and the conch-flower in the northeast;
Having correctly placed the root [syllables], one should again place the shoots;
having placed grain in the east, and wheat in the southeast.
Having placed sesame seeds in the southern direction, beans in the region of the Nairṛta;
one should place sugarcane in the quarter of Varuṇa, and barley in the northwestern direction.
O gentle one, having placed *nīvāraka* rice in the south and the northeast, one should place all types of grain and likewise all roots in the center.
O lady of excellent vows, one should place all the stones and metals in the center;
again, one should place the backbone in the center, and one should place the bull upon the tortoise.
Alternatively, one may fashion all of them, or even just one, out of gold;
however, in the absence of all of these, one should install at least a single foot-ornament.

95a) One should not apply [the ointment] too thickly on the seed-vessel, nor likewise on the root-vessel; for there is a great fault in excessive thickness, therefore one should administer it in the proper measure.
O lady of excellent vows, the fourfold [powers] consisting of radiance, satisfaction, memory, and the destruction of disease— endowed with these, O Vidyā, is infinite power.
Having performed meditation upon the end of the earth, one should install [the deity] with all the syllables;
having smeared the upper surface with milk-rice (pāyasa), one should cover it with a cloth for the eyes.
One should begin according to the specific characteristics [of the site] and perform the binding of the pedestal (pīṭhabandha) in a pit;
O auspicious lady, when there is a separate pedestal, one should then carry out this procedure.
Otherwise, one should not begin the pedestal in a solid mass for each individual image;
rather, O observer of good vows, having covered it with a pair of cloths, one should proceed with the Śikhā-mantra.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, with a purified inner self, one should perform the protective enclosure by means of the *varman* mantra; however, one should not perform the enclosure with the sword mantra.
Having completed the ritual, one should then offer the directional oblation (digbali) in that same external location;
having offered the oblation to the lords of the directions and having sipped water (ācamana) properly and with care.
Having returned once more, one should subsequently commence the fire-oblation (homa) in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
For what purpose is this purification of the stone-line (śilāsūtra-viśodhana) to be explained?
For the sake of purification through the ritual cord of the site and for the purpose of expiation, one should offer oblations;
having offered a hundred, a hundred, and a hundred oblations, one should then propitiate the Liṅga.
The knower of mantras should raise the *liṅga* from the heart and should not offer it water for honor (*argha*). Then, having performed praise, he should move it again with his head.
Having made the family resound with the sound of recitation, filled with the noise of the Vedas,
accompanied by the shouts of bards, and endowed with the songs of women;
It was accompanied by the auspicious rites of maidenhood, joined with the ascetic practices of those striving for liberation,
endowed with the benedictory words of the twice-born, and filled with the sounds of "hili-hili."
Accompanied by conchs and trumpets, with various musical instruments being played,
crowded with flowers and incense, with lamps, and fanned by the waving of chowries.
The preceptor should not extract the deity who is accompanied by the image-keepers (mūrtipas),
joined with the artisan (kartṛ), and provided with companions as previously arranged.
Having thus lifted [the image], one should proceed near the temple;
having performed three circumambulations, one should bring it to the doorway.
The auspicious eightfold offering (aṣṭāṅgārgha) should be presented to the one seated upon the auspicious throne;
the image-keepers (mūrtipās) should offer the argha, and all the women should offer rocanā.

Having placed unbroken grains, water with *kuśa* grass, and the *saṃha* [mixture] before the Brahmins while he remains upon the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) between the door and the inner sanctum; 95b) |||
And when [the deity] has previously entered the palace, then there is the entry through the door.
Upon entering, one should never touch the lower, upper, or side doorways;
for by such touching, a great fault arises here for the patron and others.
O lady of excellent vows, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in that direction with that very mantra;
and in that same direction, O lady of excellent vows, it should be done in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) under the supervision of that presiding deity.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and likewise performed the recitation,
a gift should be bestowed upon him, as well as a vehicle appropriate to his rank.
An elephant, a goat, a buffalo, a slave, a crocodile, a deer,
a celestial chariot, a bull, and the king of birds (the peacock).
One should give a swan as a visible gift, or half of one's wealth if such a gift is unavailable;
when this is done, peace will arise for the performer and others in the future.
The preceptor should unveil that which was previously covered by a white cloth;
he should then discharge the armor and weapon mantras that were previously restrained.
By means of the Great Pāśupata weapon as previously described,
one should hold the liṅga situated within the yantra and refine it from the center to the center.

One should contemplate the deity as residing within the yantra, surrounded by the image-protectors (mūrtipās) and marked with clear signs and long threads, maintaining this visualization until the attainment of the previously mentioned qualities.
Having meditated upon the power of the powerless one, which is established as manifold through thought,
and having brought it to the end that transcends meditation, one should therefore cause it to enter into emanation.
Having stabilized the Brahma-stone at its opening, he becomes firm;
then, having meditated upon the supreme abode, the cause of all causes, with his own mantra.
Having joined that with the meditation on the Dharma, one should place it upon the conscious and unconscious;
at the equinox, through yoga alone, the well-composed practitioner becomes a magnet.
Having placed the pedestal, one should thereafter worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
O lady of excellent vows, one should protect the pedestal and the *liṅga* with the leather-weapon (*carmāstra*).
Having returned, one should offer oblations a hundred times for the pacification of faults;
for the purpose of averting portents and other calamities, the recitation should be performed in the same manner as the fire-offering.
One should again press the pedestal with the hands, having worshipped and praised it as before,
together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipas), the emblems (cumbakas), the assistants, and the craftsmen.
Having performed songs, instrumental music, and so forth, accompanied by a multitude of bards and twice-born brahmins,
he should bring [the image] from above and below according to the ritual procedure as previously described.
Having performed three circumambulations, she arrived at the gateway.

Having offered yellow pigment, water for honor, and unbroken rice along with the image-keepers and the kissers, one should not touch the door; thus, having entered with great care, one should proceed.

Standing in the posture of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should correctly determine the entry point and the portion of the direction to be accomplished by means of two suspended threads, characterized by the marks of the altar.
Having established the conduit in the north, one should begin the ritual installation;
having understood that which consists of subtle time, one should observe it during the season of the *ṛtu*.
Just as the embodied soul is appropriately situated within the body, so should one apply action to knowledge;
just as an enjoyer is appropriately engaged in enjoyment, so should one apply action to knowledge.
But when the act of awakening is engaged, the object of knowledge is understood as being supported by knowledge,
just as the orbs of the sun and moon appear as a single digit when they have become one.
Likewise, here too, having recollected [the deity], one should establish the powers of vision and action;
the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is to be known as the body, and the liṅga is proclaimed to be the embodied soul.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be known as possessing enjoyment (bhoga), and the linga likewise possesses enjoyment; it is not otherwise.
O auspicious lady, the pedestal is said to possess knowledge (jñāna), and the linga is said to possess that which is to be known (jñeya).
The pedestal is said to be like Indra, and the linga like the sun;
having conceived the ritual action as residing in the body, the embodied soul is likewise conceived as knowledge.
When there is an object of enjoyment, knowledge appears in the form of action, and the enjoyer is perceived;
in both action and knowledge, the seer is to be seen, and knowledge and the object of knowledge are perceived.
Action is to be understood as being like the moon, while knowledge is said to be like the sun;
O fair-faced one, the power of action is to be understood as being like the maiden of the seasons.
One should know that [the soul] endowed with passion is like a male; there is no doubt that it possesses the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
The arrangement of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*) should be known as being like the union of a male and a maiden.
Now, what is the use of much speaking or these illustrated arguments?
You and I were previously joined together by the cause of our prior existence.
Vision and action are likewise the yoga of the possessor of attributes (dharmī), which is caused by action;
and you, who abide as both the form of direct action and the form of the embodied aggregate (piṇḍī).
O Great Auspicious One, O Sovereign of the Gods, he who abides in the form of the Liṅga as the very essence of knowledge—
thus is the installation described, both in the temple and within [the self].
But if that [fire] is not upright, O beloved, the directions have been declared;
having gone there, the preceptor must offer oblations into his own fire-pit for the pacification of defects.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and performed the recitation while being absorbed in meditation,
and having made offerings to the deities of the directions, one should move [the image] and lead it forward properly.
But when the [new] cord has been properly prepared, one should perform an expiatory oblation;
having performed a hundred recitations for each [defect], the preceptor then attains freedom from fault.
At that very time, O Teacher, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at that moment:
either the vehicle itself, its value, or a replica made of gold.

By means of this very gift, one is liberated from the defects caused by falling meteors, atmospheric portents, and the like, as well as by those resulting from crooked movements and the confusion of the cardinal directions.
Then,
O Dear One, that gap should be filled with fine, sifted sand until the opening is completely filled so that it becomes level.
Having carefully collected conch-shell powder along with very fine powders of alkaline metals and impurities,
as well as tin powder, one should cook them with linen oil.
Then, having performed the baking properly, one should cause it to be joined without gaps,
so that it does not shift even when struck by water or other elements.
One should construct the foundation in that manner; otherwise, one incurs fault.
If water should happen to seep into the joint below due to negligence, [it causes harm].
There may be loss of accomplishment, mental distress, disease, or even death;
therefore, with every effort, one should [use] auspicious water that has passed through the nose.
Having made the lower conduit and the upper conduit either of stone or of wood,
one should provide an exit for the water by means of a very firm vessel.
At the edge of the temple, there is a large excavation like a well, constructed with slabs;
from that point, all the deities bearing the forms [of the guardians], beginning with the East, are to be placed in successive order.
One should not bathe [the deity] with even half of one's own peace-pitcher;
rather, the *cumbaka* should perform the bath using half of his own peace-pitcher.
Furthermore, afterwards, the preceptor should bathe Śiva according to the divisions;
first performing the honey-bath (madhusnāna), and after that, the water-bath (jalasnāna).
Then a bath with milk is performed, followed by one with water;
having again performed a bath with curd, a bath with water is prescribed.
Furthermore, after performing a bath with ghee, one should next perform a bath with water;
having first performed a bath with honey, a bath with water follows immediately thereafter.
One should bathe [the image] again with pieces [of fragrant substances], and then bathe it once more with warm water;
having rubbed it again with dry [powder], one should provide many jars [of water].
The general rule alone has been stated regarding bathing with the five products of the cow and so forth.
O blessed lady, first there is this special bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
then a bath with blood, and after that, a bath with scented water.
O lady of virtuous vows, one should bathe within the depths of the water with the heart-mantra;
having performed the bath, one should install the desired mantras within oneself.
One should place [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śakti upon the general seat;
or else, one should place them according to the specific [tradition] taught in one's own scripture, ending with Preta.
O Dear One, one should place the root mantra conjoined with the form, faces, and limbs;
the wise practitioner should then place the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) upon the circular portion like the form itself.
O Goddess of the Gods, being intent upon that, one should place the root mantra and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) upon the seat; this is said to be the form of the preta.
Having assigned the collection of mantras to the village, one should offer the eightfold flowers;
thereafter, for the sake of securing prosperity, one should perform various types of ablutions.
Then one should anoint [it] with sandalwood paste, saffron, and other fragrances;
having performed a most beautiful worship, one should adorn it with a variegated cloth.
One should adorn [the deity] with golden ornaments and fumigate it with incense such as guggulu;
then, having created splendor with lamps, one should offer various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).
Whether it be solid food, various kinds of edibles, or that which is to be licked,
sucked, or drunk— O beautiful one, whatever is to be given, whether it be common or exquisite.
Or else, O beloved, various special offerings (naivedya) should be given,
consisting of eighteen kinds of fish and sixteen kinds of meat.
O Goddess, one should offer intoxicants produced from fruits, flowers, or molasses, accompanied by songs, dances, and festivals, and resounded with the ringing of bells and *ḍamaru* drums.
May the fourfold assembly be repeatedly honored with divine festivals by day and night through the offering of flowers,
incense, food offerings, betel leaves, and other such gifts.

One should always perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in general, as well as the washing of the hands, feet, and so forth; however, the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) should especially sip water with the appropriate mantra and wash the feet and other limbs.
Since the wise who know both duality and non-duality understand that the universal (sāmānya) has two meanings,
this term "particular" (viśeṣa), which denotes a single object, is the definition of absolute non-duality (kevalādvaita).
One should cause the days to pass with keeping vigils at night, singing, dancing, and instrumental music,
or with great festivals, whether on ordinary days or otherwise.
During the day, one should cause gifts to be given to the poor and the helpless at an uninterrupted sacrificial session;
if it is a special occasion, O Hero, then together with the yoginīs and their attendants.
One should partake of food, drink, and other offerings fit for heroes during the day or at night;
thus, for many days, one should hold a great festival accompanied by dance, song, and musical instruments.
The Cumbaka, together with the image-worshippers, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) three times during the day;
or, according to the availability of materials and one's disposition, the rule for the oblation is three and a half times daily.
When the fourth day has arrived, the wise one, being well-composed,
should offer the Cukra oblation on the fourth day, having understood the relative strength of the substances.
Accompanied by a hundred or even a thousand image-keepers (mūrtipas), he should present food offerings consisting of whatever is edible, chewable, lickable, or suckable.
Having performed the bringing together of all [the materials], as well as the bringing together for worship,
she is praised by the maiden, her brothers, her sons, and her female relatives who are without a protector.
An offering of food (naivedya) should be presented for consumption without doubt;
likewise, divine flowers should be offered for wearing by the wise man.
Since no "offering remains" (nirmālya) has been prescribed except for Caṇḍeśvara,
it is therefore declared to be entirely without fault whether one consumes it or wears it.
O you of excellent vows, whether in giving or in receiving,
because there is a presence of distinction even within the common, they are therefore more highly joined.
Just as it is considered appropriate for the *caruka* [sacrificial food] to bestow both accomplishment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*) upon the atoms [of the devotees],
then, having performed the ritual sweeping and having bathed the deity in the prescribed manner, [one should proceed].
O beloved, with great concentration, one should worship using the various substances previously specified, such as scented water and others, according to what is appropriate for oneself.

Taking fragrant flowers and other offerings, one should present the oblation to the quarters; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and returned, one should again take up a position facing Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
When the general characteristic is present, one should set aside the specific distinction;
one should perform one's own sacrifice established in the source (yoni) and cause it to abide within that very self.
One should install Caṇḍa, renowned as Caṇḍakrodha, in the *liṅga* and the image;
having meditated upon him as arising from that [source], one should proceed to the self through the embodiment of knowledge (*jñānamūrti*).
98a) With matted locks of flame, difficult to behold, possessing fangs and a distorted face,
he who is fierce with rage emerged, white as an autumnal kunda flower or the moon.
Maheśa himself, though formless, assumed a form;
having meditated upon Caṇḍarudra, he emerged from the god as wrath.
And one should place that [liṅga] upon my crest,
O Lord of Gods, within the Īśa-liṅga, using a flower together with the mudrā of withdrawal.
Having thus established [the deities] once again, one should likewise imagine [them] upon the lord of the seats (pīṭha) and so forth;
for that power called Ananta possesses both mobile and immobile forms.
She should be visualized in the form of a vessel, and Caṇḍa in the form of a seat;
having first prepared that seat, one should then install the form of Caṇḍa.
That which is called the discourse with the *visarga*, beginning with *oṃ namaḥ* at the end, is designated as having form; it would be merely the latent impression (*vāsana*).
One should fashion the six limbs with those same [syllables] using long vowels;
however, when employed with short vowels, one should fashion the five faces.
The root mantra is "kṣauṃ"; he himself is the supreme Caṇḍeśvara, appearing in that place in a black form, resplendent with four arms.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the gods, who was indeed fashioned by Śiva in the beginning;
having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then restrain [the elements] with that Dharma-weapon.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should thereafter perform the visualization of Caṇḍeśvara;
then, one should look again toward that direction in the vicinity of the inner enclosure wall.
One should construct a dwelling there— whether made of bricks,
stone, wood, or clay— and ensure it is well-protected.
One should conceive of stability in that power which is the primordial support;
having first prepared that seat, one should install Caṇḍa well-established there.
Having established Caṇḍa and performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the expiatory fire-oblation (prāyaścitta-homa);
then, having bathed the deity again, one should worship him according to the general procedure for the Liṅga.
One should arrange the common faces and the six limbs;
one should likewise arrange the three common deities in three parts.
In the Brahma-portion, one should visualize Brahmā at the end of the Pārthiva;
and in the Viṣṇu-portion, one should likewise visualize [the deity] at the end of the Vidya-mantra.
Within the portion belonging to Rudra, the wise one should himself directly fashion [the deity] by means of the power of knowledge;
having thus conceptualized it, he should offer seven oblations.
Oṃ, for Śiva, be firm, svāhā! Oṃ, for Śivā, be immeasurable, svāhā! Oṃ, for Śiva, be awakening, svāhā! Oṃ, for Śiva, be eternal, svāhā! Oṃ, for Śiva, be all-pervading, svāhā!

Svāhā! Oṃ, O Śiva, be one whose sound is auspicious; svāhā! Oṃ, O Śiva, be fully satisfied; svāhā! Whether for one's own sake or for a specific purpose, at that time one should certainly not [worship] Caṇḍeśvara.
One should not entertain any conceptualization regarding its origin or its separation.
The *liṅga* itself is said to be Bhairava, established because of its nature as Bhairava;
however, one should designate a place for the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) according to the requirements of that location.
But Caṇḍeśvara says that in his own Yoga system there is an avoidance of that;
one should not avoid the specific [rite], nor indeed the *cāturthaka* oblation.

Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, no fault arises there from the remains of offerings (nirmālya); this applies to the food offerings—both those to be chewed and those to be swallowed—as well as the perfumes and flowers.
Whether taken entirely or even partially, those [offerings] originating from the deity are never *nirmālya*;
they belong to Caṇḍeśvara, and there is no fault in taking them as gifts.
Whether in eating or in wearing it, that which has been consecrated (bhṛta) leads one to purity,
because it is specially present as that which is conceived at the beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, there is no doubt that the sacrificial pap (caru) should be offered to the mantras that grant accomplishment;
one should not give it to those who eat cows or fire, but should give it to the sons of the samaya.
There too, one should offer seven oblations with the words "to Bhairava," joined with those [seven] qualities, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending in *svāhā*.
Having entered again at the end, the practitioner, well-composed,
stands in the northeastern direction of the deity and indeed conquers a hundred.
The great Pāśupata weapon wards off defects in the ritual procedure;
it always makes the rite complete, whether there be an omission or an excess in its performance.
Having thus recited the Pāśupata mantra, one should recite the Śrāvaṇaka verse:
"O Lord, at the time of the ritual, has the sacrificial act been performed or not?"
The Supreme Lord shall make [the vessel] full through the union with his own power;
thereafter, Cumbaka, together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipas), shall perform the rite of peace with half-vessels.
These groups of practitioners bathe the agent and liberate him;
this occurs clearly through the sprinkling performed during the initiation leading to liberation (nirvāṇikī-dīkṣā).
99a) Having bathed [the image] once more, a beautiful golden bracelet should then be placed on the right hand; or, if gold is unavailable, one made of darbha grass may be used.
By that, the fruit called "establishment" is perfectly bestowed upon him;
this is the certainty of the scripture regarding the agent alone.
One's own vessel of peace (śāntighaṭa) should likewise be placed first;
having prepared that as the Śiva-tīrtha, one should sprinkle a hundred cloths upon the ground.
The conception of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is for the sake of the liberation of those groups [of beings] and for the sake of their attainment of nirvāṇa;
however, the Śiva-tīrtha should extend all around to a measurement of one hundred cubits.
And those virtuous ones who die by means of renunciation in that place shall become three-eyed, equal to Śiva, and attain the world of Śiva.
Therefore, having worshipped Satyaśiva and prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation like a staff,
the preceptor should go to the ground on his knees and bow down preceded by a hymn of praise.
Having performed three circumambulations, once again accompanied by the performer,
and having bowed down once more, he should indeed proceed to the sacrificial pavilion.
The consecrator should prepare a seat in the center of the pedestal;
it may be a lion-throne or a couch, fashioned by a twice-born artisan or made of gold.
It may be made of silver, or copper, or iron, or even of wood;
or it may be made of clay, or leather, or cloth, or covered with a canvas.
Having grasped the feet of the guru and having diligently sought his favor,
one should rest while seated before him, beginning from the head and ending at the feet.
Then, having gone to the ground on his knees and bowed to the guru,
he should smear him with sandalwood paste and other unguents and worship him with divine flowers.
One should fumigate the perfected pair of divine garments with divine incenses;
[one should honor them] with golden ornaments, jewels, fine cloths, excellent horses, and cows.
By means of the lands of the various districts, servants, daughters, and so forth, as well as vehicles,
heaps of grain and other crops, queens, thieves, and the like;
Having diligently satisfied the guru with abundant and divine sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
one should offer gold for the removal of the guru’s bodily marks and for the smearing of one’s own forehead.

During the procession of the chariot while moving, one should cause the "jewel of the earth" (bhūratna) to be given; at its conclusion, those who bear the forms of the deities should be saluted and worshipped with sacrificial fees.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is proclaimed to be equal to half of half [the total] for the Sthāpaka;
for the other Mūrtipas, an equal distribution of the gift is prescribed.
O fair-faced one, one should give a portion of that to the practitioners, though it be diminished.
Half of that [is for] the sons, half of that again for the initiates (samayins),
one-quarter less than that for the twice-born (dvijas), and half of that for the assistants.
Half of that should be given to the groups of bards, and half of that to the jesters;
it should be bestowed according to one's capacity even upon those who are blind from birth or the destitute.
One should honor the women of one's own kin and young maidens, as well as servants and kinsmen; those held in bondage should be released, and one should not harm living beings, my dear.
O beloved, having first fed [the deity] with various kinds of food as an offering,
one should then feed the kissers (cumbakas) and others with special, auspicious meals.
One should offer the *bali* for all desires at the end;
therefore, having first worshipped Śiva and then bowed to the Guru.
O beloved, she makes this request for the sake of rejoicing in the fruit;
and through his grace, O Lord, all of this has been revealed.
One should rejoice in that [merit] even more, and one should cause the Guru to rejoice as well;
for by my grace, the entire fruit, which consists of the perfect Liṅga, shall indeed be attained.
One should also rejoice in whatever brings about what is desired;
for those motes of dust that are seen when the sun is within a speck of impurity, [so many kalpas does one remain in hell].

As long as one who seeks a wife regards the marks, the Vedas, the banner, and so forth of their own kind as authoritative, for that long he shall proceed from place to place in this world, transcending what is proper and improper.
At the conclusion of the *piṇḍa*, the causal agent first goes to the world of Brahmā;
having enjoyed temporary pleasures there, he subsequently attains the partless state (*niṣkala*).
Accompanied by his wife and sons, he should bestow abundant wealth, sufficient to uplift both his paternal and maternal lineages and to support both sides of the family.
One should offer oneself, as well as one's own merit, to the Guru;
then the illustrious Guru, being satisfied, shall call to mind the reality of Śiva.
Having made it complete and equal, the mantra-practitioner should worship it with the left hand using perfumes, flowers, and so forth; he should honor its head with that arghya offering.
Then, with his soul purified, having bowed down again and again,
and acting in accordance with her will, he should remain so for as long as he lives.
The auspicious installation of stable [deities] in the form of liṅgas has been described;
now I shall likewise describe to you here the installation of those that are mobile.
100a) The chapter on the consecration according to the Piṅgalāmata.
Bhairava said:
Furthermore, I shall now fully explain the consecration of a mobile [image];
that is declared to be of two kinds: the pedestal (pīṭha) and the pedestal-composite (pīṭhapiṇḍita).
The pedestal may be separate from the image, or it may be integrated with it;
O auspicious one, that integrated pedestal is likewise of two kinds: filled and engraved.
Copper that has been smelted and solidified is considered to be filled with wax;
crystal, gem, pearl, and coral constitute the five jewels.
That which is engraved upon its own source is indeed the best, as is that which is formed from the massed [particles] born of that same source;
however, in the absence of their own source, it may be made of crystal and the like.
Having prepared the pedestal separately from materials such as gold or metals, one should consecrate it.
Their pavilion is of two kinds: the one called the sacrificial pavilion and the bathing pavilion.
Furthermore, those for whom the previously mentioned characteristics of the door are auspicious,
it should be constructed together with those characteristics, measuring one internal cubit of iron.
Therefore, O beloved, they did not reach the third pavilion,
for the proximity of the fire is not desired by gems, pearls, and corals.
The deities present were Sūrya, Candra, Candro-dhanādhipa (Kubera),
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, as well as the Nāgas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Yama.
The Pitṛs, Pāvaka, and Rudra are the presiding deities;
the Sun resides in the sun-gem, and the Moon in the moon-gem.
The king of the gods resides in diamond (vajra), while the lord of wealth resides in lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya); Viṣṇu is situated in sapphire (indranīla), and the rākṣasas in topaz (puṣparāga).
Brahmā resides in ruby, and the sacrificial fire in coral;
Varuṇa is in pearl, and likewise Śaṅkara is in crystal.
Vāyu resides in emerald, as well as in the species of gems known as nāga and māṇikya;
furthermore, he is always established there in the great sapphire (mahānīla).
Therefore, the wise one should sprinkle the characteristic [substances] of those who have transcended [the world];
likewise, the rite of bathing is performed in the solar temple as before.
O Dear One, having performed the bath with the five products of the cow and other substances at dawn during the day,
one should worship the assembly of those worthy of honor along with various brahmins and bards.
Accompanied by various kinds of food and likewise by the husbands of the maidens,
he should lead the one being praised to the sacrificial pavilion provided with a fire-pit.
The Yoga-pīṭha, however, is in the center and measures four cubits;
its height is eight finger-breadths, O auspicious one, neither more nor less should it be made.
For all movable liṅgas, the pavilion shall be eleven cubits;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall be one cubit in measure, but the number [of other features] remains as before.
And likewise, O auspicious lady, the characteristics established in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
as well as the supporting pillar and the archway, have been declared just as they were described at the beginning.
Likewise, having installed the pitchers and banners of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and others,
as well as the door-keepers, the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), and the image-guardians (mūrtipās).

Having likewise adorned oneself with fine garments and so forth as before, as well as the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ), on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion and weekday, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
O lady of excellent vows, for one who is of the nature of the *padya*, there is the *liṅga* known as *cala*;
and the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) takes place in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), according to the ritual procedure of the Tantras.
In the case of the general and the moving liṅga, as well as the general action and that which is preceded by it,
there is the pervasion of the three-fold path through the oblations, the formless, and those whose nature is mobile.
Having understood the strength and weakness of the materials according to the ancient injunctions,
and having first completed the preliminary rites, one should then perform the consecration.
One should place separate seats upon the [central] seat, having meditated upon knowledge and action in that way;
however, when the seat has arisen, it is established as non-dual.
Having performed the rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) separately, one should then perform them;
for the pervasive power of sustenance (dhāra-śakti) resides therein, somewhere upon the seat.
One should install the pedestal at the base of the *liṅga*;
the three powers (*śaktitraya*) should be perceived through the awakening of the infinite action of the mind.
Since this is both moving and stable, it is therefore called the "moving liṅga.
Likewise, one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon another, as well as upon oneself, through the mouth and the venerable self.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in that manner, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
whenever one so desires, having performed the placement, one should indeed perform the dismissal (visarjana).
Then there is the night vigil and the Hero’s Feast at that time,
with divine sacrificial porridges (caru) produced from those [substances], combined with all kinds of edible offerings and the like.
Accompanied by all kinds of divine foods, combined with all types of meat and the like, joined with all varieties of fermented liquors and spirits, and provided with all heroic attendants.
O lady of excellent vows, at the conclusion of the consecration, one should indeed pass the entire night with assemblies of all yoginīs and with dances, songs, music, and festivities.
Or, O Dear One, when the general sign is mobile, it is beneficial to perform the stabilizing rite during the day;
then, having dismissed the limbs of one's own vidyā, one should deposit that maṇḍala.
But Caṇḍeśvara is never present in a mobile liṅga;
here there is no Caturthikā oblation, nor should one conceive of duality, O Dear One.
For this very mantra, there is never a need for invocation or dismissal;
nor is there any defect arising from impurity or lack of cleanliness when it comes to giving or even crossing over.
Whether for eating, for wearing, or indeed always for the sacrificial porridge (caru),
whatever has been given by one’s own chosen deity— that is the caru, without a doubt.
One should bestow that [knowledge] oneself through one's own wisdom and not entrust it to another;
one should not give it to an unworthy person, nor should one give it for water or fire; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
O lady of excellent vows, if the food offering (naivedya) has been consumed at the time of sacrifice,
then one should indeed cause it to be given to one's brothers, sons, and sisters.
At the time of worship, one should cause that water-pot (gaḍḍuka) to be offered;
having first established the seat, it should be arranged appropriately with leaves and flowers.
One should perform the sacrifice upon a pedestal, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or on a baked brick, or even within a mandala; but never upon the bare ground.
Or else, in the absence of a garment, one may remain with half a cloth or even with a small cloth-bag;
however, one must never display to the world the signs of personal possession.

The wise one should display the Lord of Sacrifice, who is common to all, and who is worshipped within the sacrifice itself, for the purpose of showing favor to sentient beings and for the benefit of the worlds.
And at the time of initiation, during the rite of purifying the disciple before the Lord of Gods,
one should place [the sacred substances] in a secret, well-concealed box made of mudga beans.
Or, having placed it in a wicker basket or a bamboo box,
one should cause the gift and other rites to be bestowed as before, starting with the *cumbuka* and so forth.
Salutation and worship, as well as the act of performing them and rejoicing in them, the fruit of the offering of bali, and the dedication upon completion; these [are the stages].
One should perform this entire rite in the same manner as before;
thus, in brief, is the procedure for a movable liṅga.
O lady of excellent limbs, I have thus explained the certainty according to the scriptures;
now I shall fully describe the ritual concerning the mouth-linga.
The practice for the consecration of the *mukhaliṅga* is now described to you.
As before, one should prepare three pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) for them.
101b) Having performed the ritual procedures such as bathing as before in the bathing pavilion,
one should then bring [the image] once again to the entrance pavilion for the purpose of inspection.
Having conquered [the obstacles] and honored the assembly, those by whom the opening of the eyes is to be performed—
first, the preceptor should open the eyes with a golden probe.
Thereafter, the artisan should gradually carve it with a tool using the Mṛtyujit mantra; then, the mantra-adept should fill it with honey and clarified butter.
Having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious throne, with festivals of instrumental music, song, and so forth,
and having mounted him upon a chariot and secured him, one should perform a circumambulation around the edge of the city.
Having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion according to the previous procedure,
one should present the eightfold offering (arghya) and then cause [the deity] to take up residence as before.
Having divided the pedestal into three sections, the assignment of the principles (tattvanyāsa) is now described:
having assigned Sadāśiva in the center, one should assign Īśvara in the east.
One should place the Vidyā in the southeast, and one should place Māyā in the south;
one should place the principle of Time (Kālatattva) in the southwest, and place Niyati in the west.
The principle of passion (rāgatattva) is in the northwest, the principle of being (bhūtatattva) is in the domain of the north;
the primary principle (pradhāna) is in the direction of Ishana, and the presiding deities of the forms are as before.
O lady of excellent hips, they should be installed together with the Mūrti-śaktis;
furthermore, one should install them in the five Brahmans, even now, O gentle one.
One should place Ghorarāja in the south and that Puruṣa in the east;
having placed Īśāna in the center, one should then arrange the bed and so forth.
But that [offering] placed upon the couch for lamentation and that on the auspicious seat—
both of these, O blessed lady, one should likewise offer in the fire in due order.

According to the procedure for the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), together with the image-protectors (mūrtipa) and the Cumbakas, the three-fold purification (tritatvakapanā) is performed in the same manner; however, it may also be done in a circular arrangement.
One should place Sadāśiva there, who has five faces and a great body;
for those with one, three, or four faces, one should perform the general procedure.
One should likewise consecrate the double-crust cake;
having thus performed the rites of ritual fire-offerings, recitations, and so forth.
Having led [the deity] into the center of the palace, one should perform the installation as before;
having installed the Lord, one should then perform the rite of the two-fold [seed-syllable].

Having joined it together with pegs, he entered it, which had been inhabited by his ancestors through their wealth; in the midst of the womb was a jointed petal, formidable and fashioned by those who came before.
102a) Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow and so forth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
and having performed the *caṇḍakalpana* fire-oblation for the fourth day, O Dear One.
Having dismissed the limbs of one's own vidyā, one should install the Brahmans in due order;
first, one should arrange the seat of Ananta, and likewise Dharma and Jñāna.
Having placed [the principle of] dispassion and sovereignty, one should place unrighteousness and ignorance; likewise, having placed non-dispassion, one should similarly place lack of sovereignty.
Having placed the lower covering and likewise the upper covering,
and having properly arranged [the seat] upon the lotus, one should install the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā.
Likewise, Vilvī, Cā, and the others should be installed; the conceptualization of the circle is like that of the [deity’s] form.
Action (kriyā) is said to be the pedestal (pīṭha), and the pedestal is called the seat (āsana).
From the seat comes the accomplishment of action, for action indeed bestows fruit;
therefore, O Dear One, one should prepare the entire seat with the *praṇava*.
Seated here, the Lord of the Gods, the Master himself, having become manifest in form,
should place Sadyojāta, endowed with eight kalās, upon the western face.
One should place the left [moon], possessing thirteen digits, upon the gentle face;
and one should place the terrible [sun], endowed with eight digits, upon the right face.
O Goddess, one should place the four-part [mantra] Naranda on the eastern face;
one should place the five-part Iṣa on the circle, in the middle, and at the top.
Aghora is his heart; that which is called Puruṣa is his head;
Īśāna is his crest-lock; and Vāma is declared to be his armor.
Having indeed immediately installed the weapon, the deity, the power of knowledge, and the three-eyed one in their general form, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Understand the distinctions in the scripture through the clearly defined designations:
the seat and so forth for the Lord of Gods, as well as the faces, limbs, and eyes.
One should likewise place that four-faced [liṅga] facing both east and west;
the three-faced [liṅga] faces east, and the Sadyojāta face is indeed the udāna.
One should not fashion a human face on a [liṅga] facing west or having three faces;
rather, it should face east and have a single face—such is the conception of the human form.

In the western direction (Āpya), one face should be fashioned immediately; of this there is no doubt. Having established the remaining [faces] according to that same direction, the arrangement of the faces is completed.
O noble lady, having offered seven oblations beginning with the *sthirā* mantra,
and then having given the directional offerings (*digvali*) as before, one should likewise provide gifts and food.
Salutation, worship, rejoicing, and likewise the dedication of the fruit.
Thus has all this been told, concerning the state of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Bhairava said:
Now the consecration of images with manifest forms is described.
The pavilions should be constructed as before, and there should be three of them, not painted.
And when it is painted, two types of [images] should be made, endowed with the characteristics and the opening [of the eyes]:
those made of wood and those made of cloth; that is the painting, of this there is no doubt.
An image made of stone or metal shall always be devoid of painting;
for them, the rite of bathing is always performed, whereas for a painted image, it is never done.
O observer of good vows, the pavilions (maṇḍapas), beginning with eleven cubits and ending at seven,
should be constructed as before, according to the measurement of the door-cubit.
The supporting pillars and the archway are described as before;
O beloved, the smallest pavilion measures thirty-one cubits.
O beloved, it is stated in the mantra of the Mahāpratima-kalpa that there are seventeen pillars together with the archways.
A pavilion measuring forty cubits on each side is known as the medium-sized;
it should have nineteen supporting pillars and be provided with archways.
O Dear One, the praise of the Mahāpratisarā Samādhi has been told otherwise;
the excellent pavilion is fifty-one cubits in size.
The supporting pillars and the arches should be twenty-one cubits long;
their planting should be done in sequence, measuring five, six, or seven cubits respectively.
In the center of the pedestal, one should fashion [the space] measuring fifteen cubits;
its height should be sixteen finger-breadths all around, like a mirror on the outside.
The medium [pedestal] is twenty cubits with a height of twenty finger-breadths;
the excellent pedestal should likewise be twenty-five cubits.
O auspicious lady, one should place two sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) each one cubit in height for the middling rite,
three cubits for the middling, and four cubits for the best.
One should likewise imagine their forms and numbers as before,
[for the purpose of] images made of stone and other materials in the pavilion known as the bathing hall.
Having performed the preliminary ritual bath,
one should perform the closing of the eyes while reciting the mantras characterized by the *netra* [mantra], after having rinsed and worshipped them with the *saṃgerya* [mantra].
According to the procedure prescribed by the predecessors, the opening of the eyes of the Citrabhānu [image] should likewise be performed here by the Cumbaka together with the artisans.
Having rubbed it with ink and then wiped it with a stylus,
what could not be filled there now with honey and clarified butter, O lady?
One should visualize her in the intermediate space by means of the King of Mantras that conquers death,
having placed her upon an auspicious throne and well-established within a chariot.

Having brought [the image] to the sacrificial pavilion within the city, performing a circumambulation according to the previous procedure and having performed auspicious rites such as the *svasti-vācana*, etc., [he should proceed].
Having offered the eightfold water for the feet (arghya), one should cause [the deity] to descend with the Praṇava;
whatever has been mentioned or left unmentioned, all that is accomplished by means of the Praṇava.
Then, one should prepare a bed and so forth facing east where the visualization is to take place;
indeed, that [seat] on the western side of the pedestal should be made of solid wood.
And two pegs should be fixed, along with one horizontal beam;
or else, in a palace facing west, [the orientation] faces west.
One should place the great [image] there, situated upon an auspicious throne and facing north;
O lady of excellent hips, one may also install a statue facing east.
One should place a bright seat two cubits below the manifest [deity], having divided it into three sections; the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon that is now described.
O lady of virtuous vows, [this is the power] of the god Sadāśiva, the Lord of Destruction,
and of the form of Śrīkaṇṭha Mahādeva.
That which is considered [the mantra] of Bhairava, Vighnarāja, Ṣaṇmukha, Bhṛṅgin, Cāmuṇḍā, Durgā, Gaurī, and the others;
Having first established the Lord in the center, one should deposit the principles (tattvas) there in sequence;
according to the rule for the face-linga, one should deposit them ending with the form and power (mūrti-śakti).
The deposition (nyāsa) of the form of Keśava is now declared according to its true nature:
[it consists of] Vidyā, Māyā, Kalā, Kāla, Niyati, and Śuddhavidyā.
One should place Passion (Rāga), the Person (Puruṣa), and Primordial Matter (Pradhāna) in sequence;
O fair-faced one, Viṣṇu becomes the single embodiment of Brahmā and the others.

One should also cause the visualization of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) and so forth to be performed; the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) for the Lord of Gods, who is of the nature of Brahman, is now described.
Having placed the Pradhāna in the middle, one should place the three qualities (traiguṇya) in the east;
having placed the syllable "Haṃ" in the fire (southeast), one should place that which is called the intellect (buddhi) in the south.
One should place the mind in the southwest and the sense organs of cognition in the west;
O lady of excellent hips, one should place the organs of action in the intermediate directions.
Having placed the subtle elements (tanmātras) in the subsequent [parts], one should place the gross elements (bhūtas) within the sphere of the abode.
By this very procedure, one becomes the King of the Gods and so forth;
by the procedure for the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one becomes a Cumbaka together with the presiding priests (mūrtipas).
The fire offering (homa) should indeed be performed for the universal deity;
however, it is proclaimed that for those ending with Brahmā, the reality is solely the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).
One should contemplate the two principles of Ātman and Vidyā as belonging to Viṣṇu;
one should install the three principles in Rudra, and those beginning with Nātha as originating from Śiva.
And as for their very seat, which is characterized by two powers:
having conceived the support of one's own delusion, the power consisting of action resides above the seat.
And that which is the seat (pīṭha) of the goddesses is the singular conception of infinite power;
it becomes manifest as the form of action, endowed with the knowledge of the image.
Having performed the ritual consecration (adhivāsana) for the image together with its pedestal,
O beautiful goddess, one should then bring the pedestal before the temple.
One should place those for whom bathing and other rites have been performed within the interior;
however, in the center of the womb, one should install the Lord of Gods, adorned with a variegated wall-painting.
Having brought back the image to its end, one should place it upon the pedestal as before;
then, having performed a proper arrangement, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
For those [images] whose form has been destroyed, there should be a rite of degradation (adhaḥkriyā);
likewise, there is the fourth-day oblation (cāturthika-homa) and the ritual procedure for Caṇḍeśvara.
And for all images, no specific distinction has been reached;
therefore, O beloved, listen to the placement of mantras (nyāsa) for the sake of the particular worship of the limbs of one's own vidyā.
Having prepared the seat as before, or having invited it from the source of Śiva,
one should install the five Brahmans upon the Lord according to the yoga of the eastern face and so forth, as previously described.
I shall tell you the mantra of Anantīśa: Oṃ aṃ anantīśāya svāhā.
The mantra for the invocation of Anaṃtīśa is as follows:

having fashioned the letter *A* in its sixfold form, adorned with the *Tāraka* (Om) at the beginning and endowed with the six *Jāti* syllables at the end, one should perform the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Oṃ śrauṃ, svāhā to Śrīkaṇṭha. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Śrīkaṇṭha. Having performed the sixfold emanation of the syllable Śrī and the six limbs as before:
Oṃ māṃ, svāhā to Mahādeva.
The mantra for the vehicle of Mahādeva:
having formed the syllable *na* in six ways, one should perform the six-limbed ritual as before.

Oṃ bhaumamahābhairavāya svāhā. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Bhairava. Having formed the syllable *bha* in six ways, one should perform the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Oṃ gauṃ gaṇapataye svāhā.
Having divided the syllable *ga* into six parts, one should fashion the six limbs.
Oṃ kauṃ, svāhā to Kārttikeya Kumāra. This is the mounting mantra (vāhana-mantra) for the Six-faced One. Having formed the syllable *ka* in six ways, one should assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Oṃ āṃ khatholkāya svāhā. This is the invocation mantra of Āditya. Having fashioned the syllable Ā in six ways, one should assign its limbs accordingly.
Oṃ nauṃ, svāhā to Nandikeśvara. This is the vehicle-mantra (vāhana-mantra) of Nandikeśvara.
Having made the syllable *na* sixfold, they indeed become its limbs.
Oṃ mo mahākālāya svāhā. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Mahākāla. Having divided the syllable *ma* into six parts, one should assign them as its limbs.
Oṃ bhoṃ bhṛṅgiriṭaye svāhā. This is the invocation mantra for Bhṛṅgin. Having formed the syllable Bha in six ways, these indeed become its limbs.
O lady of excellent hips, for Indra and the others, it has been declared as before:
the letters *la*, *ra*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *va*, *ya*, *sa*, and *ha* are the three mother-letters (*trimātṛkā*).
Oṃ cauṃ, svāhā to Cāmuṇḍā. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Cāmuṇḍā. Having divided the syllable *va* into six parts, one should assign them as her limbs.
Oṃ iṃ indrāṇyai svāhā. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Indrāṇī.
Having divided the syllable *i* into six parts, these indeed become its limbs.
Oṃ vauṃ vāṃ, svāhā to Rāhu. This is the mounting-mantra (vāhana-mantra) for Vārāhī. Having formed the syllable *va* in its sixfold aspect, one should assign its limbs accordingly.
Oṃ vauṃ vaiṣṇavyai svāhā. This is the mantra for the mounting of Vaiṣṇavī. Having formed the syllable *va* in its sixfold manner, one should assign its limbs accordingly.
Oṃ kauṃ kaumāryai svāhā. This is the mantra for the vehicle of Kaumāryā. Having performed the sixfold [meditation] on the syllable *ka*, one should assign its limbs [to the body].
Oṃ mauṃ, svāhā to Maheśvarī! This is the vehicle-mantra (vāhana-mantra) of Māheśvarī.
Having divided the syllable *ma* into six parts, one should assign them as her limbs.
Oṃ śryoṃ, svāhā to Śrī. This is the invocation mantra of Śrī. Having fashioned the sixfold form of the syllable Śrī, one should assign its limbs.
104b) Oṃ nauṃ iṃ, svāhā to Arddhanārīśvara. This is the invocation mantra for Arddhanārīśvara. Having performed the sixfold [nyāsa] with *naṃ* and *iṃ*, one should assign its limbs.
Oṃ hauṃ śauṃ, svāhā to Hariśaṅkara. This is the mantra for the invocation of Hariśaṅkara. Having divided the syllables *haṃ* and *śaṃ* into six parts, one should assign them as his limbs.
Oṃ oṃ moṃ, svāhā to Umāmaheśvara. This is the mantra for the invocation of Umāmaheśvara.
Having divided the *umā* into six parts, one should fashion its limbs;
or else, having separated them individually, one should install them so that she rests upon his lap.
Oṃ vauṃ vaṃ, svāhā to Vaiṣṇava! This is the mantra for the invocation of Viṣṇu.
Having divided the syllable *va* into six parts, one should assign its limbs:
*oṃ vauṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*. This is the mantra for the invocation of Brahmā.
Having fashioned the syllable *vraṃ* in six ways, one should arrange its faces; then, having again fashioned *vraṃ* as the fourth [face], those indeed become its mouths.

Oṃ rauṃ revatāya svāhā. This is the invocation mantra for Revanta. Having divided the syllable *ra* into six parts, one should assign them as its limbs. Oṃ nauṃ nāgarājāya svāhā. This is the invocation mantra for the Nāga King.
Having divided the syllable *na* into six parts, one should fashion its limbs.
Oṃ pauṃ, svāhā to the ancestral deity. This is the mantra for invoking the ancestral deity in the cremation ground.
Having divided the syllable *ya* into six parts, one should assign its limbs;
one should likewise provide a seat for all of them using the *tāraka*.
Whatever is the reality and the path for those [deities], that very same [reality] is to be established from the head downwards;
and the arrangement of the forms, faces, and limbs must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Whichever deity is pervaded by that [mantra], those [deities] are brought into proximity within that pervasion;
one should employ the dative case for the general [deity] and likewise for the oblation.
First with ointment and then with perfume— the worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth—
and likewise the feeding of the *cumbaka*s and others, as well as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the beginning and the end.
O Goddess, the application of sandalwood paste, the worship, the fruit offering, and the hymn of praise— all that should be performed by the wise man as previously described.
Now, the installation of the Tūras is described according to that specific region;
the form and the ritual procedure as established in their own scripture have been analyzed therein.

O Maheśānī, the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) should be performed by oneself either during a sacrifice or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), using the mantras specifically explained in one's own scripture.
Or, having informed one's own guru, one should have him perform the consecration;
one should then install the mantras of the form there, with the seat separately conceived.
Having performed the conjunction of the mantras, one should fashion the faces and limbs;
having thus fashioned that which has been impelled, remain present and firm in reality.
One should never perform the invocation (āvāhana) or the dismissal (visarjana) there;
at all times during the period of worship, the practitioner of mantras should arrange the seat and other requisites.
Either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in a mandala, or upon a seat fashioned with divine materials,
one should place [the deity] above that and perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Whether on a cloth or during the consecration, it should be accompanied by the rites of worship and so forth;
however, when held in mid-air, the offerings of fragrance, flowers, and the like are performed below.
For those whose physical form has perished, the mere display of incense is sufficient;
yet, having again covered it with cloth, one should always contemplate the six marks.
And during the time of meditation, O fair-faced one, one should always clearly contemplate the cloth painting and so forth for the purpose of consecrating yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
For their pervasion, O lady of excellent hips, is achieved by reciting their own names as mantras ending with "namaḥ"; however, the conceptualization of these ends with the word "pārthiva."
Bhairava said:
I shall now describe to you the consecration of the *vāṇaliṅga*. Having performed the ritual bathing as before in the pavilion known as the *maṇḍapasnāna*, [proceed as follows].

Having performed a circumambulation around the edge of the city with festivities such as the sounding of musical instruments, he brought [the deity] to the pavilion known as the *yāga*, which is equipped with a sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, one may act according to one's own desire for the sake of worldly prosperity; however, that which is to be purified is not for the sake of non-liberation.
Having led [the deity] into the center of the palace, one should establish it by means of one's own higher knowledge;
and having placed the pedestal in front, if the *kṛṣa* or the *vāṇaka* is below, [one should adjust it].
When the upper part of the phallus is slender, one should subsequently perform the ritual action,
having completed the drawing of the lines for the characteristics of the form and the like, such as the circumambulation.
Since he is thus described by the ritual injunction as being eternally present here,
Piṅgalā said:
How is the word *vāṇa* explained, and what is proclaimed as *vāṇa*?
In what place, however, is it to be grasped? Tell me all of this.
Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, since I have been urged by you;
I shall speak without doubt according to the certainty of the scripture.
O auspicious lady, in former times the Asura Vāṇa was exceedingly dear to Śiva;
he had conquered anger, was devoted [to him], and was intent on the rites of Śiva’s worship.
Being skilled in intellect and knowledge, and endowed with the characteristics of one who knows the arts,
he should personally fashion [the image] day by day, install it as a *liṅga*, and worship it.
In this manner, one should worship for as long as a hundred divine years;
then, having cast aside that devotion and being free from all doubt, one should depart.
Śaṅkara said:
"I am pleased with you, O Bāṇa; choose a boon—what do you desire?
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, Bāṇa spoke these words.
If you are pleased, O Lord, for the sake of me, the unfortunate one; O Lord of the gods, I have been distressed day after day by the task of the linga.
And that perfection of characteristics is a characteristic fashioned by the scriptures;
O Lord, the meaning of the scriptures is difficult to attain, and the goals of accomplishment are even more difficult to attain.
Therefore, if you are pleased with me, O Lord, bestower of compassion upon all and sympathizer with all sentient beings, grant me that mark of the *liṅga*.
"And for the sake of the welfare of all, O Śaṅkara, show favor.
Upon hearing these words of his, Śiva, the supreme cause, [responded].
O beautiful one, having gone to the summit of Kailāsa,
Bāṇa constructed fourteen crores of liṅgas.
All those self-manifested lingas of eternal radiance were brought by him to a state of perfect completion and offered to Bāṇa.
Having established the arrow that is inexhaustible and undecaying, and having constantly maintained his pride,
he then, with effort, gathered the arrows and made them into a load.
Having brought that burden back to his own city, the pure one reflected further upon it as it was being established day by day, inexhaustible and fully perfected.
For the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings, one should accumulate [merit] at a place of merit;
O lady of excellent hips, ten million shrines have been accumulated in the linga and other such sites.
There are thirty million [deities] on Śrīśaila, and one crore at Kanyakāśrama;
there are three crores at the site of the funeral pyre for the Naga Gandha, who was the object of Kālikā’s desire.
There is one crore at Amareśvara, one crore at Kanyātīrtha,
one crore at Mahendra, and one crore situated at Nepāla.
The *liṅga* known as *vāṇa* is said to be made of bamboo; thus it is called a *vāṇaliṅga*.
Alternatively, "vāṇa" is said to mean Śiva, and that which is fashioned by him is called *vāṇa*.
Or else, because it is uncreated, it is eternal by its own nature in accordance with its characteristic;
therefore, in those regions, there are holy places, or otherwise as well.
That which abides as the true being of Śiva, possessing a body formed by the specific [energies],
is known as the perpetual emergence of both the pure and the impure.
Whether situated on a seat or released from a seat, whether abiding in power or devoid of power; whether the arrow is stationed here or there, whether born of mantra or devoid of mantra.
O Lord, whatever has been consecrated by one who kisses the Saṃskṛta [linga], it shall eternally bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; or whatever else [is performed] shall become fruitful.
Having always established both the mobile and immobile manifestations in the proximity of Consciousness for the sake of prosperity,
one should not employ Caṇḍa at all once that which was attained through the fourth oblation has been reached.
Furthermore, that which was not mentioned regarding the path of distinction, as well as the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*),
is established by practitioners within the applications of mantra-sādhana.
Mantras will certainly succeed in that [place], there is no doubt;
the ritual procedure should be exactly as it was previously, or it may be otherwise here.
O lady of excellent vows, having first performed the ritual with other consecrated arrows, one should again perform one's own rite and the placement (nyāsa) with one's own mantras.
One does not incur any fault therein, because it is common to all;
[one may use] substances such as wine, nectar, and so forth, or others prescribed in the *tantra*.
Having performed the rite, one shall attain success; one shall not incur any fault therein. When joined with the mantra of the Siddhānta, Śaṅkara is installed by means of one's own portion.
Because the consciousness becomes eternally stable when deposited in that liṅga,
likewise, when it has grown in the form of a liṅga, it becomes a river arising from a spring.
Furthermore, regarding the production of other stones, the procedure for arrows and arrowheads is described;
since they possess specific forms, they must be fashioned there by the teachers.
In that regard, when the ritual of nyāsa is performed with mantras, a special presence comes to be;
this is likewise true for a thousand-angled liṅga and for a hundred-liṅga.
As before, the installation and the three principles (*tritattva*) are performed as previously described;
one should install Śiva there as many times as there are numbers of *liṅgas*.
Having thus performed the breaking of the head and the stabilization within the consciousness,
one should again place the ever-risen power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) into each and every liṅga.
Through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), there is a single support for all; thus, the conception is one.
And as for the fourth, the fierce fabrication (*caṇḍa-kalpanā*), it may or may not arise from what preceded it.
One should establish [the deity] in either the universal or the particular for the rite of accomplishment;
as for the installation of the fierce ones, it is in the cave and thicket of the mine of qualities.
Because that [measurement] exceeds the pedestal, it therefore yields a contrary result;
because it yields a contrary result, O Goddess, one should not install it elsewhere.
One should never employ this fierce power (bala) which is always unstable;
for even regarding their power, it is as stated in the ritual of placement (nyāsa) that it leads to success in one's undertaking.
The fourth [rite], the fierce ritual (caṇḍakṛpti), involving invocation and dismissal,
