does not apply there to the Lord of Gods, since it is traditionally held that [the rite] bestows success (siddhi) [only when performed otherwise].
O Goddess of the Suras, having firmly established Manahshiva upon the arisen seat,
one should conceive of that very seat as consisting of mere dhāraṇā.
One should install the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in the liṅga; it bestows liberation alone.
It is to be worshipped by the *putraka*s and likewise by the *saṃkha* and *īśvara* initiates with devotion.
For both the practitioner and the preceptor, there is neither inaction nor mere consciousness;
one should perform the ritual according to the rule for the earthly category, like a mountain.
But for one who is unripe, O auspicious lady, one should instead perform the stabilization of the state (sthitisthāpana),
just as strength is described as being like that of a person seated upon a stool.
One should cause those [mantras] situated at the crown of the head to be performed day after day;
one should place the mantras according to their own specific characteristics, but they must be devoid of the *vāma* (left-hand) path.
Having again established [the deity] within oneself, one should dismiss it along with the flowers;
in the case of one or more [deities], they should be dismissed in sequence according to the number of Vasu-liṅgas present.
Having established [the deity] in the center of the root [mandala], one should perform the fierce conceptualization at the root;
the installation of the remaining [deities] should likewise proceed from the middle enclosure onwards.
Indeed, no separate sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) was prepared at their base;
for those honored by the world-protectors (lokapālas), the rite was performed according to the ancient rule.
Established through both the general and the specific,
this system is proclaimed as common to all for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And hear, O beloved, the installation of the signs for determining the directions.
In a square pavilion and within a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should perform all services with yellow materials, such as garments, flowers, and ointments.
On a Saturday, during the Viṣkambha yoga and the three Uttarā asterisms,
one should install the one known as Vakra.
I shall proclaim his mantras, by which he becomes present:
Oṃ lauṃ vajreśvarāya laḥ svāhā.
Having fashioned the sixfold ornament, one should arrange its constituent parts in the pavilion,
in the form of the womb, and in the womb-shaped fire-pit in that direction.
With every protective rite, including garments, flowers, and ointments,
on the day of the son of the Earth (Mars), O virtuous one, during the Yoga-caṇḍa [yoga].
One should install the deity named Śakti under the constellation Bharaṇī;
I shall now proclaim his mantras, by which he becomes present.
Oṃ rauṃ, svāhā to Śaktīśvara, raḥ.
Having fashioned the syllable *raṃ* in six ways,
one should arrange its parts within the pavilion shaped like a half-moon and in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In that direction, O lady of excellent hips, one who performs all the rites for Kṛṣṇa should install the one known as Daṇḍa with garments, flowers, and unguents.
O lady of excellent vows, one should arrange the three constellations beginning with Pūrva by means of the bright [Venus] planet, through the application of mantras, and by means of the Vipanta star.
I shall proclaim his mantras, by which mantras he becomes present:
Oṃ srauṃ, to Daṇḍeśvara, saḥ svāhā.
Having divided the *saṃkāra* into six parts, one should assign its limbs [to them],
O virtuous lady, by means of the day of the week, the planet Venus, and the *gaṇḍa* conjunction.
One should arrange the three starting from the east according to the asterism and Sunday;
likewise for the triangular pavilion and the triangular sacrificial pit.
O wise one of virtuous vows, on a Saturday, one should offer oblations in that direction during the Viṣṭi,
Śūla, Mūla, Ārdrā, or Bharaṇī yogas.
With every kind of blue offering— cloths, flowers, and ointments—
the Guru himself, appearing in the form of Kāla, should install the Khaḍgaliṅga.
I shall proclaim his mantras, by which he becomes present:
Oṃ prauṃ khaḍgeśvarāya ṣaḥ phaṭ svāhā.
Having divided the letter *ṣa* into six parts, one should fashion its limbs from them.
In a circular pavilion and in an elliptical sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
and having offered oblations in that pit which is twice as wide [as the former], the preceptor himself [should perform the rite].
With entirely white offerings— clothes, flowers, and ointments—
and under the auspicious conjunctions of Jupiter, the Moon, and Mercury, as well as under favorable stars.
In the constellations Hasta, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, and likewise the three Uttaras,
one should install a Pāśa-liṅga for the purpose of pacification and nourishment.
I shall declare the mantras by which he becomes present:
*oṃ vlauṃ pāśeśvarāya vaḥ svāhā*. Having performed the sixfold [emanation] of the syllable *vaṃ*, one should assign its limbs.
Oṃ mlauṃ, svāhā to Dhvajeśvara!
Having divided the letter *ga* into six parts, one should assign them as its limbs.
Oṃ slauṃ, svāhā to Gadeśvara!
Having made the letter *sa* sixfold, one should assign its limbs [to the various parts].
Oṃ hlauṃ, svāhā to Śūleśvara! Haḥ svāhā!
Having divided the syllable *haṃ* into six parts, one should assign their respective locations.
Oṃ kṣlauṃ, svāhā to Cakreśvara, kṣaḥ. Having divided the syllable *kṣaṃ* into six parts, one should assign them as its limbs.
Oṃ oṃ plauṃ va padmeśvarāya oṃ svāhā.
Having performed the sixfold Oṃkāra, one should assign its limbs [to the respective parts].

The practitioner of mind-mantras, endowed with the appropriate ritual materials and actions, should employ self-dependent mantras fashioned according to the [deity's] class, face, and limbs, in accordance with the [specific] linga.
It accomplishes the successful completion of one's task, as well as the stabilization [of the body], the destruction of burning sensations,
death, peace, health, movement, and the increase of nourishment.
Enmity, severance, illusion, the accomplishment of knowledge-yoga,
and the auspicious consecration— these have been briefly described as the types of worship for the liṅgas.
At the conclusion of the consecration, the ritual bath, the giving of gifts, the wake, and so forth are prescribed;
as well as land, gems, radiant horses, servants, maidens, and vehicles.
Then, O Śivā, one should offer as a bali at the conclusion of all rites all grains, ornaments, and garments,
which fulfills all desires.
At the conclusion of that, having fed those who bear the forms of the deities with devotion,
there should be the donor’s approval of the fruits [of the rite], the giving of gifts, and the formal dedication.
All this should be performed by the wise one as previously described;
having enjoyed temporary pleasures, he then attains the partless state at the end.

108a) Beginning with one, if one constantly remains in this state, the fruit will be ten times greater than the previous, and by practicing even once, one shall attain an infinite result ten times greater than the former measure.
Likewise, in the restoration of a ruined [temple], the fruit for the agent will certainly be the same as the root;
this concludes the chapter on the consecration of weapons in the Piṅgalāmata.
Piṅgalā said:
How could the term "worn out" be applied when [the debt] is being extracted?
Furthermore, tell me: how can there be an attainment of these two, given their all-pervasiveness?
Bhairava said:
The term "jīrṇa" (worn out) refers to that which has decayed; it does not apply to one's own sapinda.
Just as there is no extraction of what is grossly decayed, so too some indeed die [in this state].
Just as in the world one who is devoid of ritual action remains like a corpse,
so too here, the scriptural rite for the linga is empty if it lacks vision.
A wheel that is burnt, shattered, devoid of ritual preparation, containing defective parts, thin,
deficient or excessive in measurement, or too thick, is considered ruined.
Whether it be a liṅga or a pedestal that is cracked, broken, jagged, or exceedingly terrifying, one should remove whatever has been thus observed.
Likewise, among these images, there are those that are manifest and those that are unmanifest;
some are deficient in ears, nose, or fingers, while others have missing limbs or have had parts previously removed.

O lady of excellent limbs, those [images] which cause the destruction of the face and body of the glorious one must be abandoned by all the inhabitants of that region, as well as by the founders, the artisans, and the craftsmen.
There would be a great transformation of defects; therefore, one should extract these [impurities].
Just as the all-pervading [space] resides in another [vessel], so too does Śiva reside therein.
Whether one is devoid of ritual action or engaged in it, one should extract the *piṇḍikā* together [with it];
whether it is well-established or poorly established, how could one not be free from fault?
Even for one who has deviated from the prescribed rule, that defect is remedied by speech preceded by the ritual;
it is not considered a fault because of the pervasive presence of Śiva at the time of dismissal.
To the south of that, at the edge of the palace, O future one,
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) together with a fire-pit (kuṇḍa), one should invoke Śiva and worship him.

Oṃ, salutation to Vyāpakeśvara; come, come, svāhā! This is the invocation mantra (āvāhana-mantra) of Vyāpaka Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to the heart of Vyāpaka. Oṃ, svāhā to the head of Vyāpaka. Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā) of Vyāpaka.
Hūṃ to the armor (kavaca) of Vyāpaka. Phaṭ to the weapon (astra) of Vyāpaka. [The seat is established] within the Praṇava.
Having prepared [the site], one should worship the Supreme Lord;
having worshipped the deities of those directions, one should then commence the fire offering (homa).
Having offered the directional oblation (digbali) outside at the conclusion, one should perform the rite of the door (dvāra).
Then one should offer oblations of the Mahāpāśupata weapon portion by portion;
one thousand in the portion of Brahmā and one thousand in the portion of Viṣṇu.
Having performed one thousand oblations in the portion of Rudra, he should extract [the essence];
having sprinkled it with that [liquid], he should bind it with the Śikhā-mantra and the Vajra-Arjuna.
The preceptor, accompanied by the people, should then lead the bull-shouldered [deity] away;
being impelled by the ritual procedure for extraction, he should utter the words, "May there be well-being for Śiva."
Having led it to the southern side— whether in a city, a village, a hamlet, a town, or even into water— one should deposit the mountain there.

One should melt metal and cast it into a mold; however, that which is made of wood should be burnt. For the sake of nourishment, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the direction of the presiding deity.
Having performed the fire-oblation for the purification of the palace and likewise for the purification of the site (vāstu),
one hundred and one oblations should be offered in succession with the Mahāpāśupatāstra mantra.
One should protect that temple and its pedestal even more thoroughly;
it must be guarded for as long as such a configuration remains.
In accordance with the previously described procedure, such an image— whether small or medium— is installed there, as characterized by its prior measurements.
One should cause the practitioner to enter through the middle of the door without touching it;
having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's ability, following the previously mentioned procedure.
Having fashioned a stone slab adorned with jewels and having applied plaster, one should install it;
and the bathing ceremony for both the maker and Śiva should be performed as previously described.
And when a temple has become dilapidated and is being renovated,
then the mantra residing therein and the entire collection of its essential principles [must also be restored].
Having properly transferred [the essence] into the sword, one should indeed worship it constantly;
having placed it to the south of the *liṅga* and performed a thousandfold *homa*, one should proceed.
A wise man should construct an auspicious wooden frame above the linga between two wooden planks;
having raised it by means of touch-points, he should then remove the bricks.
Furthermore, by that same measurement and in that very form,
a mountain must be made from a mountain, and likewise, a brick from a brick.

Whether made of wood or even of clay, one should fashion it from baked brick or stone; it should be made excellent by being free of flaws, for a defective image was never intended for the highest [deity] in the past.
O Dear One, that which is made of stone is to be known as the best; that made of baked brick is middling;
the work involving wooden spokes is for intermediate purposes; and that made of clay is the lowest.
Wood is a hundred times more meritorious than clay; from that, brickwork is a hundred thousand times more so;
and that made of baked bricks or stone is a crore of crores times more meritorious.
When the union with the body has been completed, one should cause [the deity] to be extracted from the sword according to the procedure of the ancestors;
this constitutes the collective consecration.
O lady of excellent limbs, one should indeed carry out the repair of a dilapidated temple;
when the restoration of a ruined structure is performed, one clearly attains the same fundamental fruit as that of building a new one.
The pedestal of that [liṅga] which rests on the ground is four finger-breadths [in width],
and the height of Umbarā is proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths.
Of that [pedestal] measuring two cubits, the portion embedded in the ground shall be eight finger-breadths;
and of that measuring three cubits, the portion embedded in the ground shall be twelve finger-breadths.
One should fashion the remaining pedestal (pīṭha) and its complete cutting;
for a four-cubit [image], the pedestal should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) high.
The pedestal of a five-cubit [image] should be eight and three (eleven) finger-breadths below the ground;
that of a six-cubit [image] should be thirty (three and ten) finger-breadths below the ground.
One should fashion the pedestal-base (pīṭhabandha) from whatever remains above the plinth (ḍamvara).
As for the pedestal of a seven-cubit [liṅga], it should extend thirty-eight finger-breadths below the ground.
The pedestal for an eight-cubit [image] reaches forty-six [units];
the remaining height of the pedestal is specified in finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The pedestal for a nine-cubit [liṅga] should have four feet extending sixteen finger-breadths into the ground,
and the height of the pedestal should be three cubits plus eighteen finger-breadths.
By this very arrangement, however, there shall be no *vikarālaka*, nor a common *padāliṅga*; in front [of it], there should be a bull.
In the Piṅgalāmata, this is the restoration of what has decayed.
Piṅgalā said:
The bull has been indicated by you through the characteristics of the *devanāgata*;
what is the measure for a maiden, and what is the measure for the middle and the highest [categories], and of what kind is it?
"Tell me, how indeed is its installation performed?
Bhairava said:
For a *liṅga* that is one cubit (*hastamātra*) in height, the bull (*vṛṣa*) should be of equal size;
for a *liṅga* of one and a quarter cubits, the bull should be twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height.
For a *liṅga* measuring one and a half cubits, the bull should be two *mātra*s;
for one slightly less than two cubits, the bull should be thirteen finger-breadths.
For a liṅga measuring two cubits, the bull should be thirty-four finger-breadths;
for one measuring two and a quarter cubits, the bull should be thirty-six finger-breadths.
For a liṅga measuring two and a half cubits, the bull should be thirty-eight aṅgulas;
for one measuring exactly three cubits less a quarter, the bull should be forty aṅgulas.
For a bull with three cubits [in height], the height of the horns should be two cubits;
for a bull with three and a quarter cubits, the height of the horns should be two cubits and two eyes (two digits).
The Liṅga of three and a half cubits should have two eyes and two hands;
the Bull (Vṛṣa) of three and three-quarter cubits should have three eyes and two hands.
For a four-cubit liṅga, the two-cubit [image] should consist of eight kalās;
for a four-cubit [liṅga] plus one-quarter, the two-cubit [image] should have nine eyes.
For four and a half cubits, there are two hands and ten eyes;
for less than five cubits, there are two hands and eleven Rudras.
The *liṅga* is five cubits, while the bull (*vṛṣa*) is three cubits;
for a *liṅga* of five and a quarter cubits, the bull should be provided with eyes.
The bull of the [deity] with five and a half cubits has two eyes and three horns;
the bull of the [deity] with five cubits less a quarter has three eyes and three horns.
For a six-cubit linga, the base should be three cubits and one finger-breadth;
for a six-cubit and a quarter linga, it should be three cubits and five fingers.
The Taurus [sign] has six eyes and three cubits when it measures exactly six and a half cubits;
the Aries [sign] has three cubits and two eyes when it measures slightly less than seven cubits.
For a liṅga measuring seven cubits, the bull should have three cubits and nine eyes;
for a seven-cubit liṅga, the bull should be three cubits and one-quarter high with ten eyes.
The quality (guṇa) of one measuring seven and a half cubits is endowed with the eyes of Rudra;
likewise, for one measuring eight minus a quarter cubits, there is the four-armed Vṛṣabha.
For a liṅga of eight cubits, the pedestal should be two kalās; for one of four cubits, it should be four cubits plus a quarter.
For a liṅga of eight and a quarter cubits, the pedestal should be four cubits and four eyes (four faces).
For a body measuring eight and a half cubits, the height is four cubits plus six eyes (twelve finger-breadths).
For a body measuring nine cubits less a quarter, the height is four cubits plus eight eyes (sixteen finger-breadths).
For a liṅga measuring nine cubits, the bull (vṛṣa) should be five cubits;
its height should be five cubits, and one must not make it less than one cubit.
Among the fierce [deities], there is no bull, nor indeed among those of a specific poison-nature;
in the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, there is no bull at all, and one should have it made by a self-manifested [image].
In Loṭṭana there are a hundred liṅgas, and in Mukhaliṅga there are a thousand.
O one honored by the world-protectors, one should never perform the *vṛṣotsarga* rite for a consecrated image (*astraliṅga*),
nor for a self-manifested image (*siddhaliṅga*), nor for any other such [image].
In front of a single-linga image, a bull should never be placed;
nor should the bull-weapon or the installation of a flagstaff ever be made there.
O lady of excellent hips, I shall now describe, in due order and as it truly is, the measurement of the bull, its installation, and its auspicious characteristics.
On stone, one made of stone should be fashioned; on wood, a bull made of wood;
among metals, one made of metal; and on clay, one consisting of clay.
One should have the desired bull made of gold and other materials, beautiful in every respect,
under an auspicious conjunction, a favorable lunar mansion, and an excellent day and hour.
On a very auspicious day and at a favorable time,
the measurement for the bull that has been proclaimed should be made according to the preference of these [donors].
The length divided into seven parts—of those, one part is twelve *aṅgulas*; that which is declared as a single such part shall here be known as a *maṅgula*.
Likewise, we shall describe the *netraka*—namely the *tāla*, *tārā*, and so forth—as before; and according to those measures, I shall explain each of the *mānaka* and other dimensions individually.
It should be eight *netras* in length and its face should be slightly elevated;
the width of its back should indeed be equal to two *netras*.
One should determine its length to be half of that [the central eye], and its width to be twice that;
the two pupils are like stars, and the two lights are like the light of the eyes.
The two eyebrows are each half a *kavi* (one-sixteenth) in width and not even half of that in redness; they are half a *kalā* (one-eighth) in thickness, and their length, O beloved, is two *kalās*.
One should decrease it by half a barley-corn at a time until it becomes a single barley-corn at the tip;
the two nostril-pits should be made well-rounded, like the eyes.
The distance between those two should be known as twice the width [of the face];
the width of the mouth is six eyes, and above that, it is five eyes.
And above that, one should indeed fashion the width as four eyes;
and further above that, there should again be an increase such that it becomes five or six eyes.
The distance between the eyes is seven, eight, or nine units;
the width established for the face is said to be the measurement from the jaws.
The face should extend from the root of the ear, with five eyes above it;
the space between the two ears is the pedestal, which has seven eyes.

One should fashion the two ears with a length equal to the diameter at the root of the ear; that circle [of the head] should have five eyes (five units), and above the circle, one should arrange the two ears with a length of four eyes (four units).
At the front of the plow-shaped [structure], one should fashion a space measuring half a finger-breadth;
at its end, two holes should be made, each half the size of an eye and perfectly circular.
One should draw a straight line equal to half of a quarter of the eye-measure;
from the intersection of the thread at the base of the ear and the upper part of the nose, one should lead it evenly.
The portion for the belly should be slightly protruding so that it appears beautiful from both sides;
at the base of the horns, one should fashion two eyes and make them circular.
One should lead the rows [of lines] by half-and-half of the eye-measure up to the tip of the eye-measure;
at the slightly curved front, there is the elevation of the three eyes, which is sharp.
The distance between the two horns should be two eyes (two units) in width;
below that, O beautiful lady, it is said to be six eyes (six units).
The neck is said to have eight eyes, extending from there up to the hump;
O auspicious one, one should fashion the hump with three eyes according to its full extent.

The height of that [image] should indeed have two eyes; the upper part of the face should be slightly rounded, and below the hump there should be two eyes—this is the description of the goat-legged [pillar].
The length of the shank is declared to be five eyes (pañcanetra), and it is also celebrated as being equal to that. The joint is said to be half an eye, and the lower part of the shank is four eyes.
Below that, one should fashion two ankles measuring one and a half eyes;
the two eyes and the two hooves should be made, with their length and width being one cubit.
Below the ankle, the *khurikā* (ankle-bone) is to be known; it is described as being one-quarter of a *netra*.
One should fashion the circumference of the *khurikā* to be equal to that of the *netra*.
The circumference at the base of the shank is seventeen [units],
while the circumference at the interval between the eyes is joined with fifteen kalās.
Again, having passed two intervals [of fingers], there is the [center] consisting of thirteen digits;
again, having passed two intervals, the Anāhata [cakra] is located by means of the Rudras and digits.
One should not calculate a joint of fourteen digits for the circumference;
the interval between the eyes is twelve digits, as is the circumference of the upajaṅghikā.
Again, having set aside another two eyes, there is the encircling of the directions and digits;
again, having set aside another two eyes, the calves consist of eight eyes at their tips.
There should be two eyes and a blanket hanging from below the neck;
they know the blanket to extend eighteen eyes in length down to the end of the shanks.
From the hump to the measurement of the back, there should be eighteen eye-units;
the end of the three-angled part (trikaṭa) should be known, and the three-angled part again consists of three eyes.
Likewise, six *netras* should be known from the three *kaṭās*, resulting in the continuity of the tail;
the base of the tail should have two *netras*, which is proclaimed as its width.
In the middle, it should be known as equal to the eye; the tip of the tail should be half the length of the eye.
Its length is declared to be three tālas for the tail-staff.
Furthermore, O Punarbhadra, the hair-line on the handle of the staff is at half the height of a palm tree;
the circumference of the staff at its base measures four finger-breadths.
The *daṇḍanetra* is proclaimed to be at the joint with a broad back;
it is also broad in the middle, and its width is declared to be eight *kalās*.
At the tip of the back, however, it is proclaimed as *pṛthu* and *saptanetra*;
in the region of the belly, that which is *nāha* consists of thirty and a half *netra*s.
The circumference at the three joints is proclaimed by the thirty-eyed one [Śiva] to be twenty-one kalās;
likewise, the circumference at the base of the back is also twenty-one kalās.
One should fashion two eyes there at the navel, and likewise fashion the penis;
one should fashion the two testicles with two eyes, making them broad in that same manner.
O lady of excellent hips, the shanks are said to be five cubits long, and the ankle-joint is one cubit;
the lower leg (upajaṅghikā) is six cubits in length.
The two eyes and the two ankles are considered to be two finger-breadths [in length], while the two hooves are considered to be five finger-breadths;
at the tip of each hoof, there should be a measurement of one finger-breadth, and the hoof should be shaped like a sphere.
The circumference at the knee is said to be five kalās, and it is not otherwise;
however, the circumference at the base of the shank is twenty-one kalās.
Furthermore, I do not know an interval of two eyes as consisting of eighteen digits;
rather, having set aside two eyes, it is by means of five times three eyes [fifteen].
Furthermore, having abandoned the interval between the eyes, the *nāha* consists of the sun and its digits;
however, the *nāha* of eighteen digits is proclaimed to be the junction (*saṃdhi*).
The circumference at the back of the calf is three and five kalās;
having subtracted two netras from the interval, the circumference consists of twelve kalās.
Again, having abandoned the two eyes, the navel has nine eyes;
and the cavity at the back should be known to be two finger-breadths in length.
111b) On the auspicious [pedestal], the width is half a finger-breadth; its depth is one-quarter of that.
Having thus perfectly fashioned this most beautiful characteristic, like a bull, [one should proceed].
The teacher, who is an expert in the characteristics [of the bull], has declared the definition by way of a brief indication;
he should likewise have a bull fashioned that is endowed with all the defining characteristics.
Both are remembered as being on the flagstaff, or well-situated upon its pedestal;
facing east, or in the front of the pavilion, or in the western direction, like Varuṇa himself.
The four-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), however, is characterized by the same measurements as before;
one should divide the pedestal (pīṭha) into three parts as before and place it therein.
One should perform the reality (tattva) according to the sequence of the nine [deities], beginning with Śakti and ending in the middle;
and likewise, starting from the eastern direction, one should place the primordial nature (prakṛti) at the beginning of the chariot and so forth, as before.
One who has offered you, the embodied one, as well as the power of the embodiment (mūrti-śakti), with the respective meditations on the forms,
using the same mantras and all the previously prepared materials for the concluding rites;
O Dear One, having performed the bathing as before with the five products of the cow and other substances,
and having performed the opening of the eyes, one should perform the consecration while the image is placed upon the bed.
O Dear One, having performed the installation of the principles (tattvas) and empowered the power of action (kriyā-śakti),
one should then purify the three principles (tritatva) by means of a thousand oblations in due order.
Having offered oblations, performed sacrifices, and wandered about accompanied by songs and instrumental music played beforehand,
one should lead [the deity] to the throne on the four-sided platform, which is established as a noble seat.

Then, having performed the *argha* offering and other rites, accompanied by the auspicious recitations beginning with "Bhūtaḥ Svasti," and having prepared the central quadrangular area (*catuṣkī*), one should begin the installation of the stone slab (*śilāsthāpana*).
Leaving aside half of the Rakṣoghna [line], situated from the Garbhasūtra,
it is firmly established as a square slab resting upon a stone platform.
Having first constructed the ninefold foundation (navābhra) according to the dimensions of the bull— whether in length or in thickness— and having performed the placement of jewels and other rites;
One should deposit the power of retention (dhāraṇī-śakti) either in mercury alone or in another [substance].
The conceptualization of the power of retention consists of the movements, fixations, and the preservation of the vital breaths.
One should contemplate the bull as the form of action and establish it by means of its own quality,
contemplating its inseparable connection and its reliance upon both knowledge and action.
Just as the burden of the kingdom primarily bestows royal enjoyments upon the king,
so too does the bull of Śiva, due to its inseparable oneness with Śiva, [bestow the fruits of liberation].
The bull should be known as having the form of Śiva; it is three-eyed, all-pervading, and supreme.
It has four feet, two wings, and likewise a chest and a back.
One should then install the principles of formlessness, beginning with forbearance, in their proper sequence.
But the one whose function is the power of the steady path is established in the state of oneness with Śiva:
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Vṛṣabha.
One should fashion the sixfold syllable *Ha* as the limbs of the body; O Dear One, having fashioned Vāmana with Viśveṇu according to the previously stated rule.
The specific rites of bathing and worship, the offering of grace (prasāda), the teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā),
the offerings to the directions, and the feeding and giving of gifts are declared to be as before.
Having understood that the refuge of the gods is the refuge of the Bull (Vṛṣabha),
one should construct a four-sided structure provided with a pinnacle and adorned with four doors.
The Vimāna should be made very beautiful with binding;
having thus established the bull, one should set up that which is called the Banner (dhvaja).
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on the Bull," in the Piṅgalāmata, within the first section concerning Jayadratha.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, it has been indicated that it is called a "dhvaja" (banner); what is meant by the name "dhvaja"?
For what purpose is it to be established, and if it were not raised, what would happen?
"What is its measure, what is its form, and how is it to be established? Tell me this.
Bhairava said:
The banner is renowned as the insignia; it is the characteristic of our divine power.
May he be unimpeded, embodied, and in close proximity to the lineage of Śiva.
Because the path of the particular (viśeṣādhvan) leads to Śiva when it is present in the particular,
its obstruction is declared otherwise [as a defect], O sinless one, due to the absence of the banner and the power.
Therefore, with every effort, one should ensure the preeminence of the banner;
it should be made firm and auspicious with white, red, yellow, and black segments.
With pieces twelve finger-breadths long, the width should be eight finger-breadths;
one should join the two wings together with auspicious *ḍamaruka* pieces.
White, red, white, yellow, and white-black again and again;
by this very sequence one should proceed as far as the measurement of the temple.
At the tail of the fish, however, one should make it yellow and indeed red;
for that power which is said to consist of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) has Śiva as its refuge.
Therefore, that great banner (mahādhvaja) should be carried by maidens of that same measurement;
eight banners should be fashioned for the protectors according to one's desire.
Likewise, yellow-red, black, blue, and smoke-colored clouds.
One should visualize the lotus-like [deity] of white complexion in the eastern direction and so forth,
within the fourth level-maṇḍala at the end of the temple sections.
One should place the stream formed by the bamboo tube there as the substratum;
she is the pervasive power (Vyāpinī), the support of all supports, the auspicious and imperishable one.
O lady of excellent hips, one should imagine the binding of the knot of impurity and the rope of karma at the root of consciousness by means of the single-syllable mantra of Viśva.
The various worlds are his diverse forms; the great banner is the form of the sacrifice (adhvara);
the supporting thread and fibers are the foundation; and the two feathers are the great weapon.
It is variegated with various paintings, the locus of diverse enjoyments and qualities;
therein reside all the primordial deities, the lords of the worlds, together with their weapons.
Those who abide in the power of the Teacher, in the egg of Śakti, and in both the conscious and the unconscious—
those blazing ones, whose nature is the withdrawal of the principles (tattvas), should be established as the specific [deities] of the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā].
Therefore, the primordial reality of that which is other must be purified through the yoga of withdrawal;
one should then establish it by means of the yoga beginning with Ananta, according to the principle of emanation.
Then, by means of reality after reality, the lords and the non-lords [attain] proximity;
from that arises conceptualization, radiance, stability, and thereafter wandering.
The command of *niyoga* is the will of Śiva; having thus purified it, one should establish it.
The eternal presence of Śiva, which was previously described as being grounded in ritual action, is thereby established.
One should perform the oblation according to the eightfold procedure for the sacrificial pits together with the guardians of the forms;
the oblation is considered universal in its measurement of substances.
The installation should be performed auspiciously; it is the fulfillment of fullness through the completion of knowledge.
[This is achieved] by circumambulating the temple, the *liṅga*, and the altar, and by wearing a neck-garland.
The fruit of a banner [erected] at Vāptīraṇa is proclaimed to be ten million times greater;
it is like a well-sown field that is ruined without protection.
O sinless one, it was likewise declared that the presiding deities of the installation,
including the planets, spirits, and vetālas, were chosen by Śiva in ancient times, even without a banner.
Those who perform worship, fire offerings, and so forth, yet do not protect their recitation (japa),
shall also become pure by this procedure on the grounds of the temple.
For indeed, the directions, illuminated by the Śiva-weapons, have vanished;
therefore, the wise magnetizer should, as before, restrain the banner above.
113a) When the hoisting of the banner is out of sight, it should be performed by oneself directly;
and when the installation of the feet and so forth has previously been performed without a presiding officiant.
At the time of hoisting the banner, the performers are traditionally required to be present;
for the purpose of raising it, one should have them perform [the rites] at that very moment.
Having performed that rite everywhere, including the purification of the lineage and the fore-offerings,
one should place the great Pāśupata weapon there, with the presiding deity.
One should install the banners in the east and other directions, and likewise the weapons;
from that, the full fruit of the rite is obtained by the performer through the consecration.
Having rescued all families from their remaining dependents and kinsmen who have passed away, one should lead them through the intermediate states to the reality that is free from affliction.

The deity who was designated at the end of the banner and established according to the ritual rules should be properly consecrated in one's own homes by those same [initiates], in accordance with the prescribed method.
Or, in that [temple], he should install the offering-platform (balipīṭha) in front of the pillar at the edge of the chariot-pavilion for the Lord of Gods,
using the *bali-mantra* for those who subsist on offerings.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the bali offering with the Astra-mantra in front of the pedestal;
or, one should consecrate the flagstaff together with the bull, joined with the Astra-mantra.
Thus, one should cause the installation to be performed exactly as prescribed in the scriptures and complete in every respect;
thereby there shall be peace in that kingdom, and the king shall be victorious while the subjects are happy.
All women shall have good offspring and be free from disease for a long life;
there shall be abundant rain, plenty of food, and the successful growth of crops.
The preceptor should perform the rite, and having been delighted by the temple,
he should give abundant wealth and, having obtained permission, rejoice.
O Lord, through your grace, I have attained that which brings about the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
which effects separation from saṃsāra, and which is known as action (kriyā), the means for accomplishing one's purpose.
Indeed, you alone have gone for refuge to the self, which is not a substantial entity;
[you have abandoned] wife, son, wealth, grain, country, and the accumulation of jewels.
He should offer this, along with his servants, wife, and kinsmen, as well as his merit;
then the illustrious Guru, being satisfied, shall meditate upon the principle of Śiva.
Having made his own head equal in fruit to that [of the disciple], he should place his hand upon the head of that disciple; then, to one who is disciplined and fit, he should speak that reality.

Whatever fruit is obtained from the Guru, which is full of Śiva and is the means for achieving liberation— that very same fruit, infinite and ever-arising, is attained through the teaching of Śiva at the end of the cycle.
Having become serene and established constantly in the fulfillment of his desires,
he shall attain the entirety of nirvāṇa without deliberation.
Having constructed a most beautiful monastery to the south of Śiva’s image, or else a well-constructed city surrounded on all sides and rich with mountains.
One should offer everything to the Guru: grain, ornaments, clothing, all kinds of articles, household utensils, and so forth, filling [the vessel] completely.
Having first assigned the wealth of knowledge and the support for ascetics,
one should provide an abundance of villages and clothing for those who have arrived and those yet to come.

If it is approved by his preceptor, he may further assign the property of the deity for the purpose of repairing broken or cracked parts, as well as for the maintenance of temple courtesans and others.
The dancers, actors, Gandharvas, and others who are messengers sent by Śiva—
one should provide them with abundant livelihoods and means of subsistence, and protect them.
One should diligently protect its stability; by failing to protect it, one goes to hell.
Thus has the characteristic of the installed liṅga been briefly explained.
O auspicious lady, regarding the substances, temples, and sacred sites, that which you have asked concerning the fivefold consecration— what else do you wish to inquire about?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Hoisting of the Banner," in the *Piṅgalāmata*, within the first section concerning Jayadratha.
Piṅgalā said:
And since the signs of accomplishment (siddhi) have already been explained by you as being dependent on the *liṅga*,
what *liṅga* should the wise man rely upon at that time, and how should he rely upon it?
O Pradyumna, please explain briefly all of this: the dependence [of the effect], its occurrence at a later time, the restriction, the injunction, and the action.
Bhairava said:
O beloved, the self-manifested (svayambhū) and the bāṇaliṅga are the primary supports;
likewise, a wise man should resort to those known as the hundred-fold, the thousand-fold, and the raudra.
One may accept a rolling stone, a moving banner, a horse, and even a wife;
however, one must not accept a lifelong vow nor an equal marriage.
Or one who desires accomplishment should take refuge in that which is honored by the world-protectors;
for the purpose of accomplishing the directions, he should then take refuge in a weapon or a symbolic emblem.
This indeed always grants success to the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
It is not [afflicted] by the previously mentioned defects, such as those pertaining to the womb and so forth, nor by the navel... [and so on].
114a) Or, having established [the image] yourself when it is unmanifest, hear now what is suitable and what is unsuitable:
that which has been established by gods, daityas, sages, and likewise by men.
By those who have transcended the latent impressions of conceptual construction, who possess the vows of the Vedic tradition,
and who are intent on relying upon the signs and the signified as established therein— one should rely upon all that.
One should not rely on unestablished dualistic mantras;
likewise, one should not rely on Vedic [mantras] established by those who have formally renounced worldly life.
One who desires spiritual perfection should not take refuge in a Linga established by those seeking liberation who subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits, or who consume milk and vegetables.

One should not resort to that which is deformed, pregnant, deficient, shattered, decayed, afflicted by disease, or joined with a crack; for such a limb of the Śrīmukha [structure] brings about destruction.
All the Asuras are non-dual; one should not differentiate among them. Among those who possess the characteristics of both duality and non-duality, I shall speak of the Suras.
Indra, Śukra, as well as Pakṣa, Sādhyas, Agni, Yama,
the King of the Rākṣasas, Vāyu, Ravi, Tārkṣya, and the excellent Guhyakas.
The Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa and others, as well as the Siddhas,
Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Apsarases, and Gandharvas, were non-dual and devoted to the mantra.
O future one, the practitioner, being well-composed, should rely with non-conceptual mind upon those among them who are well-known by name alone.
Vyoma, Vālmīki, Śākalya, Parāśara, Bhṛgu,
as well as Kāśyapa, Nāsiketu, and Śālaṅkāyanaka.
O lady of noble nature, as for the other kings who were royal sages and ministers—
namely Māndhātṛ, Anagha, Bhūpāla, Bharata, and Śaka.
All the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas were devoted to the contemplation of mantras;
a wise person should likewise take refuge in that Liṅga through the Atharvaveda and the other Vedas.
Brahmā, Soma, Budha, Kārtikeya, and Bṛhaspati are always associated with duality; one should therefore avoid their lingas.
In this world, the wise should always avoid [the company of] Nāgas;
likewise, all such as the Vālakhilyas, Mātaṅga, Pulaha, and Kratu [should be avoided].
Śuka, Nārada, Mālyavat, Bharadvāja, the sage Aṅgiras, Tumburu, Varuṇa, Śatrughna, Śāntanu, and Dhūma as well.
Those who are always devoted to duality there, who delight in bulbs and roots,
and others such as Kaca and the rest established by those seeking liberation— that [effort] is indeed fruitless.
Having thus examined with effort what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected, the wise person should act accordingly.
The wise person should rely on that which is graspable and avoid that which is ungraspable;
for the sake of establishing what is [otherwise] unestablished, one relies upon it for human beings.
Furthermore, that linga which is perceived as possessed of duality, or which is seen as lacking luster,
is unworthy of worship for six months and brings misfortune unless it is honored by people.
Furthermore, that which is suitable for the activity of refinement becomes so once again;
even that linga which possesses defects is indeed enveloped by the womb and other such coverings.
The practitioner of mantras should not resort to undesirable means for them;
rather, he should drive away the lords of obstacles situated all around that place.
Having discharged the great Pāśupata weapon through the yoga of high recitation—
[a weapon] possessing a terrifyingly fierce form with fangs, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
With a glance from her squinting left eye, she snaps her fingers;
scorched by the fire of the great weapon, the beings are destroyed and filled with distress.
The supreme practitioner should contemplate those [deities] who are to be approached from the ten directions;
others, in the form of temples, are to be purified within the refuge of Śiva.
The personified railings, those others situated in the form of gateways,
the planets, cruel spirits, piśācas, bhūtas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth.
The mothers of serpents, the Yātudhānas, the Rākṣasas,
the Sākinīs and others, the Vetālas, and whatever other harmful beings there may be.
Except for those who take refuge in Vighna, all blessings reside in Śiva;
for all the Vināyakas have previously been granted boons by Śambhu.
All their ritual acts are devoid of prescribed rules, and they are even dedicated to those [demons];
therefore, O gods, you who desire to obtain the fruit of worship must indeed purify yourselves.
One should bathe the liṅga with clay from the sacred site using the Mahāstra mantra, and then with water;
next, a bath with cow dung, followed by a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water.
Thus, one should perform the three ablutions with the Mahāpāśupata mantra;
afterwards, the final bath is performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Furthermore, having bathed [the deity] with water, one should bathe [him] again with milk and ghee;
thus, having performed the fourfold bath according to its general characteristics.
Furthermore, specifically, one should perform the bath according to the injunctions of one's own scripture,
using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), honey, blood, and another liquid.
The steadfast practitioner, being composed, should bathe [the deity] with his own mantra.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite within oneself with various auspicious substances, or even with human flesh, goats, and so forth, according to one's own capacity;
Then again, there should be a row [of deities] fashioned from the spokes;
having invoked one's own form along with its seat and so forth, one should worship that which consists of the self.
Having always consecrated the palace with banners according to the previously prescribed method,
and having performed the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's capacity, one should carry out this ritual procedure.

Then, having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), one should protect [the disciple] with the armor and weapon mantras; likewise, one should protect one's own secret cave as well as that of another with the Great Weapon mantra (mahāśastra).
One should avoid giving gifts that are dependent on a specific field, those obstructed by a group of people,
as well as movable lingas, musical instruments, and domestic possessions within one's own home.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] along with the mantra, and having established protection, the wise one should take refuge [in the deity],
sitting upon a single linga that is devoid of the bull and the weapon.
In the process of accomplishment, seekers should not seek another object to be refined, whether it be at the beginning, middle, or end;
for even if it were common, there would be no fault, since [the deity] is always present.
The supreme practitioner should resort to a pleasant place for the sake of worship;
however, one should not apply the mantra to whatever is seen in the world at that time.
If one should install [the image] otherwise, then defects arise and the loss of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs;
therefore, one should not install it by means of a mantra, unless it be self-manifested (*svayambhū*).
The first [section], consisting of the Vāṇa and others, was taught through direct perception or by tradition;
however, the Nyāsa [section] along with the Tīrthayātrā has not been obtained there.
There will always be great misfortune, and one will be overcome by obstacles;
however, the scent should not be discarded, for it must be honored by the practitioner of the Tantra.
One should wander during the time of the journey in accordance with worldly conduct,
so that there may be an encounter and the sight of yoginīs and others therein.
And when one beholds the heroes who speak of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi),
and when one addresses the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), then the offering of the bali-oblation should be performed.
If [the worship] is not performed even when one watch of the day has passed, that fruit shall not come to pass;
furthermore, for the Tauras, this rule is not desired by others, since he is worshipped by them.
One who desires spiritual accomplishment should personally perform the consecration and worship of [the deity],
and likewise here, one should avoid images that have been consecrated by others. 115b)
And one should employ the manifest [mantras] composed by oneself; otherwise, it is considered to cause defects.
One should diligently perform the rite according to the previously mentioned procedure, taking refuge in a face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga) that has been either self-made or made by another.
Whether it be a movable liṅga or a fixed pillar, whether installed on the left or the right side,
once it has been consecrated according to one's own intention, it does not require re-consecration.

Once the consecration has been performed, however, one should not personally perform the fire-oblation and other rites for self-manifested (svayambhū), arrow-made, or stone liṅgas, as these have already been offered by Śaṅkara upon his own shoulder.
However, having performed the ritual bathing and other rites, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa),
by which [the deity] is always attained and remains eternally present.
The Raudra-liṅga, as well as the Vajra, those known by the names Śakti and Daṇḍa,
the one called Khaḍga, the one named Pāśa, the one called Dhvaja, and the one named Gada.
O beautiful one, desiring spiritual perfection, one should construct the bases for the *bhūti-liṅgas*, known as the Śūla, the Cakra, and the Padma.
Those who desire liberation should not rely on the finality of a single means;

however, one who desires sons and the like may rely on them. But he who relies [on such things] is considered a hater. The authoritative measure of movement and dimension that has been declared is characterized by the *liṅga*.
Having correctly understood that knowledge, the wise one who bears the *liṅga* should perform it;
indeed, all *ratnaliṅgas*, as well as those consecrated by other verses, [should be worshipped].
That should be applied according to the nature of the mantra; therefore, if uprooting is possible, one should perform the ritual procedure once again and then install one's own mantra.
Likewise, the method known as the "iron net" (lohajāla) applies specifically to jewels;
however, the support must not be made of clay, nor should it be prepared from any other material.
Just as one makes molasses from grain-based food, or a fragrant, well-ground cake from sesame seeds, creating ever-new forms and performing the refinement day by day.
The practitioner desiring success should always perform, sacrifice to, and then relinquish [the offerings];
however, for them, there is merely the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra without the fire-oblation (homa).
The practice known as the *liṅga* should be joined with the *sārdhata* [mantra], and never otherwise;
for those who previously [practiced] the *liṅga* through duality, let that which is not desired in duality remain as it is.
The moving liṅga is non-duality from the city; one should take refuge in the non-duality that is to be consecrated,
because the supreme and lower state is characterized by both non-duality and duality.
"O beloved, they say that non-duality is supreme, while duality is inferior."
And with certainty, one should contemplate non-duality free from doubt—
pure, endowed with all virtues, perceptible, and established through direct experience.
And non-duality, O blessed lady, has been proclaimed as supreme by the Creator;
O beloved, success is seen to be threefold according to scripture, conduct, and freedom from negligence.
For one who is negligent, liberation is easily obstructed;
therefore, one should practice non-duality, which is free from conceptual construction and superior to all objects.
The two paths of Dvaita are established as being with ritual conduct and devoid of ritual conduct;
it is observed that one who possesses ritual conduct attains liberation, whereas the other is seen through its very nature of striking down.
For one who is devoid of the conduct prescribed by the scriptures, there is neither spiritual accomplishment nor attainment of liberation;
such a person goes to hell, being unapproachable, though claiming to speak the truth, and remaining fixed in dualism.
Therefore, there is no higher or lower station for Him, whether He is joined in yoga or not; for since He is omnipresent, He does not abandon His presence even when not worshipped.
Touched by dogs, crows, and the like, it does not become impure;
for those mantras which reside therein do not truly abandon it.
Beyond this, one should resort to the supreme duality of those who possess the marks of duality;
the King of Mantras abandons that duality which is unworthy of worship, such as that involving the touch of a crow and the like.
Therefore, according to the well-known Bhairava-āgama, the ritual procedure should be performed by those who maintain duality;
one should arrange the bath using the mantras composed by those established in Śiva.
Furthermore, O sinless one, Vāṇa and Svayambhū have been declared by me to be equal.
Since these two are not present in his absence, just as they are common to all,
the presence of the gods in Citī never occurs after a hundred years have passed.
And as long as it remains in wood, its presence lasts until that wood becomes decayed;
once decayed, the wood is abandoned, for there is no [further] manifestation of the limbs.
As long as there is no limit to the loss of luster in pearls, corals, and other such things,
one should abandon those whose brilliance has faded through proximity to them.
But that which is burned through negligence, lacking flames and fuel and devoid of constant effort— that, O lady, is not a true conflagration.
However, no loss of mantra occurs if it is engraved upon gems;
nor does it occur for lingas made of gold, silver, or copper due to the breaking of the sacrificial oblation.
Furthermore, the consecration for those whose lifespan has not yet expired has been taught;
O auspicious lady, when [the lifespan] has indeed expired, then its state remains as before.
It should be performed by the foremost of practitioners; one should certainly not cause it to be done by another.
If I should be born again, then the expiation would be great;
for those whose bodies have been ruined or lost through negligence or due to the failure of yoga.
The expiation is prescribed as one hundred thousand [repetitions], followed by the ascent of the mantra;
this applies to those made of conch-shell and the like, O man, provided they are without a lattice-work.
Otherwise, there would be stagnation; even what has been seen [as established] must be abandoned again. One should perform ever-new creative acts and let go of that which is prior.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a vessel completely filled with ghee;
having offered that sacrificial grain, one should recite one million times one's own mantra.
"Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should worship the object to be consecrated (*navasaṃskārya*).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Support of the Liṅga," in the *Piṅgalāmata*, within the section on Jayadratha.
Bhairava said:
And here, O Sovereign of the Lord, listen as I describe how, by means of the lunar month, one attains success (*siddhi*) when established in the support of the *liṅga*.
Possessing the conduct of independent practice and free from conceptualization regarding one's own performance,
one should engage with enthusiasm, identifying oneself with the nature of one's own mantra.

One should perform the meditation on ritual action (kriyādhyāna) as established, including the recitation of mantras and so forth according to the rules; likewise, one should carry out the fire sacrifice (homa) for daily and occasional rites as prescribed.
Having first performed the ritual demarcation of the ground, one should undertake the sacrifice;
O lady of noble hips, this general rule has been declared to you.
I shall proclaim the specific distinction; listen with a one-pointed mind:
on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
On the full moon day, at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign, and during lunar and solar eclipses, one should perform worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings twice as much.
One should perform more recitations for the sacrifice than for the *iṣṭi*, using collections of special substances;
[this applies] to Śiva when accompanied by fragrant water, provided that which is not superior...?
Moreover, O Dear One, on other festival days as well, worship and so forth are especially dear;
for the sake of the Guru and for the attainment of success by the heroes, whether in his presence or in his absence.
They declare that eating, with various kinds of food such as rice and drinks, is for the purpose of performing rites such as worship and fire-offerings (pūjā-homa). 117a)
And during a thunderclap, a conjunction of planets, an earthquake, or a celestial vision;
Through the offering of water-pots and the like, and especially through recitation (*japa*) and other rites,
when auspicious or inauspicious dreams are seen, there shall be further recitation, worship, and so forth.
When a heroic brother has arrived at the home,
having come as a guest, one should offer hospitality according to one's ability with wealth produced through one's own efforts.
During the direct descent of the Goddess and the subduing of the Kṣetrapāla,
the offering of the bali should be more abundant, accompanied by the *phalgu* and the *sālī*.
When a hero has died during the fall of a meteor, there should be recitation of mantras, worship, and other rites;
likewise, when a substance of accomplishment (siddhadravya) has arrived, one should worship Śiva with great festivals.
Having partaken of special food and become heedless, one should take hold [of it];
if a meeting with the Yoginīs occurs, O lord of perfected Yogins.
Worship of them and of Śiva should be performed according to the specific attainment,
by means of food, drink, and other offerings fit for heroes, in accordance with the established rules for those who have attained [the state].
A yoga consisting of a full year should be performed for the sake of increasing the equinox;
and another yoga should likewise be performed during the Viṣṇupadas.

One should perform the yoga at the commencement and conclusion of the sixfold eighty [observances], at the commencement and conclusion of the taking up of vows, at the commencement and conclusion of the recitation of mantras, and at the commencement and conclusion of the fire oblation.
Furthermore, yoga must be practiced,
and the filling of the *liṅga* itself should be performed with flowers that are pleasing to the mind, such as lotuses, blue water-lilies, and so forth.
One should fill [the vessels] with various divine fruits, or with radiant rice mixed with curd,
or with rice mixed with ghee, or with side dishes and soups, or with milk-rice.
One should fill [the vessel] with sesame seeds soaked in ghee, with *maṇḍaka* cakes and other such edibles,
with jaggery, with *laḍḍuka* sweets, and with candied sugar.
One should fill [the vessel] with divine fish-flesh, having stirred it with wine;
after performing the filling of the liṅga, there is subsequently a meal with the heroes.
In front of Śiva, while dancing, these five should be performed, either collectively or optionally;
those who desire spiritual accomplishment should perform them all, relying upon devotion.
Even one seeking liberation must act free from mental deceit;
otherwise, there will be no liberation, and even spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) will be very far away.
O beloved, those seeking ritual efficacy— namely teachers, practitioners, sons, and lords who have taken refuge in the *liṅga*— should perform [the rites] according to the meaning of the scriptures.
For even the female organ has been enjoined in the ritual manual for the purpose of restraint.

In this very Sūtra, it is stated that men who have resorted to the specific characteristics [of the path] would not be fit for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation if they were to harbor darkness [ignorance].

O wise one, if the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) is omitted due to absence, or if it is performed under circumstances such as misfortune by those seeking the merit of the rite, the recitation (japa) must be performed twice as many times.
O auspicious lady, if [the rite] is performed out of negligence or desire, it must be fourfold;
likewise, if the daily observance (āhnika) is interrupted through negligence, it must be performed fourfold.
And while reciting, it should be performed according to desire by the foremost of practitioners;
if the left-hand [recitation] is interrupted through negligence, one should offer oblations and recite two hundred [times].
Having offered four times the number of oblations due to desire, one should likewise perform four times the recitation;
and if the recitation is interrupted through negligence, one should recite that same amount to complete it.
If the recitation is interrupted by desire, one should complete it and then recite four times;
if the meditation is severed through negligence, one should resort to double the meditation.
If the meditative absorption is interrupted by desire, one's own mantra should be recited at that very moment four times; this is declared to be the special rule.
I shall declare the common mantra as it should be for the rite of atonement:
first one should write "Oṃ namaḥ," and then one should write "bhali" again.
Having drawn a *drāyaśūla* (a trident with a long shaft), one should then draw it on the palm;
having drawn two *hana*s (strikes), two *daha*s (burnings), and likewise five *paca*s (cooks).
Having drawn two nostrils, one should again draw all the sins;
having drawn two mouths, one should then inscribe: Oṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ.
Then, having written the syllable *svāhā*, this knowledge which destroys all sins is declared for the purpose of the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Physical, verbal, and mental sin— whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—
is [purified] by reciting this mantra, just as copper permeated by mercury becomes gold.

Whether the *liṅga* has been moved through negligence or remains steady despite being known as "unsteady," or whether it is the pedestal (*pīṭha*) or the base (*piṇḍikā*), the wise man should chant the mantra while focusing on the *vidyā*.
Having recited the mantra for the purpose of expiation and performed a *homa* ten thousand times,
one should perform the re-installation (*sthitasthāpana*) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the wielder of the trident! Kill, kill! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Destroy, destroy all evil! Devour, devour! Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ ṭha ṭha!
O Dear One, when the linga has moved, or has been burnt by fire, or has been stolen by a thief,
the prescribed expiation is said to be the recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras]; in that case, one should master the Vidyā.
If a cloth-offering falls from the hand onto the *liṅga*, whether it has been installed or not,
one must repeat the recitation one hundred thousand times and undergo the consecration ritual once again.
If the rosary falls while reciting, one should perform ten thousand recitations;
furthermore, if the practitioner, overcome by sleep, causes it to fall upon the ground, [the same penance applies].

Then half of that [number] should be recited as a *japa*, or one should recite ten thousand (*ayuta*). If one touches a deity, a guru, or likewise a scripture with one's foot, [one must perform this].
If one recites the mantra ten thousand times due to negligence, or one hundred thousand times out of desire,
and likewise uses the bed, seat, or sandals belonging to the Guru;

If one touches the water-pot or other vessels belonging to the deity with one's foot, one should recite the mantra two thousand times as an act of propitiation; if done intentionally, one should recite it ten thousand times.
Whether the book has fallen from the hand or remained in some place,
or even if that thread has gone to the ground, one should read the book upon the ground.
Having placed [the image] upon a seat, a bed, or within a cloth painting or a house, one should recite the five hundred vidyās; according to one's desire, it may be performed in two ways.
One should offer into the fire-pit the decayed Āgamas and the worn-out Siddhāntas soaked in ghee; having offered them, one should recite the Vidyā a hundred times.
At the time of consecration during the Puṣya asterism, when cutting grass, wood, or similar materials,
one should perform whatever action is required while reciting the vidyā only once.
Having uttered the word "Rudrāya," all ritual actions beginning with the syllable Om (Tāra) are performed;
likewise, hiccup, sneezing, and yawning should always be [neutralized] by uttering that same word.
For the destruction of bad dreams, one should recite it seven times with purity;
for the unprovoked killing of living beings, one should chant it a hundred times.
O noble lady, for the killing of birds, one should not perform the *ninimaha* rite;
instead, being pure, one should recite three hundred times the mantra known as *vidyāpāpāriṇī*.
By killing four Brahmins who were innocent and without fault, the minister, acting according to his own will, incurred a hundredfold slaughter.
Having slain the twice-born without any diversion of mind, he committed this through his own desire.
O auspicious lady, one should recite the Vidyā that destroys sins ten thousand times;
and having slain an animal for the sake of sacrifice, [one should slay] one who defiles the tantric conduct.
118b) There is no fault in killing two types of animals constantly; there is no fault in killing two [types] that cause adversity.
But for others, having killed humans, whether for their sake or out of sport, [there is fault].

There should be no causeless distinction between those who bear the upward-pointing sectarian mark (ūrdhvaliṅgin) and those who bear the Vaiṣṇava mark; however, if a distinction has arisen, one should recite the mantra joined with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
By killing those who revile Śiva, the fire, or their guru, one incurs no fault;
however, by stepping over the shadow of one who observes the vow of Śiva, one shall be split into a hundred pieces.
Having killed them against their will, one should recite the mantra fifty thousand times;
if intentionally, one hundred thousand times; and for causing a quarrel, ten thousand times.
If one does so unintentionally, one should recite the mantra fifty thousand times with the breaking of the ritual marks;
however, if done intentionally, the recitation should be ten million times, with the permission of the gurus.
In the censuring of heroes, in the reviling of yogins,
in the beating of women, and in the disparagement of the knowledge of Śiva;
One should recite the mantra thirty thousand times; one should not recite it otherwise, for then one becomes subject to obstacles.
This also applies when there is defilement of ritual substances or when the Vīracakra has been established.
At that time, when the *kahala* has arisen, one becomes pure by means of a thousand [repetitions];
or else, food should be taken according to the consensus of the heroes (*vīras*).
If, after committing an offense against the guru out of ignorance or the latent impression of delusion,
one undergoes further penance and prostrates before that guru;
O Dear One, having performed the recitation until that sign appears, one should satisfy the Guru;
however, out of delusion, one should never even once touch the Guru’s wife, and should abandon her thereafter.
Having abandoned remorse and performed expiation,
one should also unhesitatingly grant him the recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras].
One should not abandon [the practice] out of desire or delusion; otherwise, one will undoubtedly become a denizen of hell.
No expiation has been prescribed for such a person, who acts in contradiction to the fruit of initiation.
One who commits suicide, one who kills his guru, or likewise one who kills another,
having caused torment through negligence, seeks expiation.
While he is reciting the hundred thousand-fold mantra of knowledge (vidyā), the Cumbaka should bestow [the initiation];
having diligently satisfied the Guru, he then deserves the consecration (saṃskāra).
If one sees blood through negligence, that act is more serious than [offending] a guru;
for that offense, if the teacher so permits, one must perform ten lakhs of recitations.
He destroys the status of the Guru, his conduct is transgressive, he opposes the sequence of what is to be recited, and though unstable himself, he acts as if he were established.
119a) Not fearing the next world, he approaches his teacher;
having abandoned conduct contrary to the rules, he seeks expiation.
Those who know the scriptures should grant it to one who has recited [the mantra] one million times;
he too, having cultivated devotion, being pure and with his mind fixed upon that [mantra].
It should be recited in a solitary and pure place until it is completed;
once the recitation is finished, one should dedicate that recitation to them.
To them, food should be offered consisting of substances known as *vīra*;
even if they are unfit for consumption, it should be given once the mantras have been recited.
Alternatively, there is purification by consuming flowers, betel, sandalwood paste, and so forth;
or by wearing them or applying them as an ointment, provided they have been authorized by the Guru.
Those who know the mantras should perform the restriction according to their capacity;
once the penance has been completed, they should conduct themselves without contradiction [to the rules].
Furthermore, even if he has completed his penance, if contact with faults occurs again,
no atonement is prescribed for him that must be pursued.
Thus, according to the meaning of the scriptures, the mantra-practitioner, avoiding contradiction with worldly norms and following the traditional lineage, should proceed without hesitation.
If the left foot moves to the left and the right foot moves to the right,
it is declared to be a common expiation for both the left and the right.
Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra should never engage in contact with those who follow contrary practices, even if they belong to dualistic systems, nor with others who are defiled.
The contemplation of the Siddhāntika is not always attained by the ministers; and the ministers themselves are neither established nor ninefold in their contemplation.
O beloved, there was no contact whatsoever with others, nor even with Vālin;
moreover, everything else was perfectly auspicious, including the sacred ascent.
Furthermore, that which is the best among observances is for men who have taken refuge in the *liṅga*;
having performed that, one would not be unfit for the attainment of perfection, liberation, and their realization.
The section on expiation according to the Piṅgalāmata.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, at what time and for what purpose is the *pavitrārohaṇa* performed?
The word *pavitra* denotes age; please explain to me that which is above it.
"By what is that performed, O Śambhu, and how should it be done? Please tell me.
Bhairava said:

When one's own time has arrived during the Bhairava period, the Pavitrārohaṇa should take place; however, if the day has passed, it should be performed for the gods at night, during the Bhairava period.
O auspicious lady, the wise know that for these six months, beginning with Capricorn, it is said to be day for the gods, while for the other six months, beginning with Cancer, it is night.
And when that mouth of yours, O blessed lady, rains with the roar of clouds,
it is not satisfied by the waters alone, desiring rather the crops, sprouts, and new shoots.
When the forest trees, grasses, and herbs have covered the characteristics [of the site],
and when the sixfold [state] has arrived— whether at its beginning or at its end— then indeed there is no [further need for action].
The rite for the Goddess Bhairavī should be performed according to one's ability before the deity;
the procedure for ordinary lingas is the same as that for those fashioned on a sacrificial mound or in a pit.
And this must be performed upon one's own body by those who abide within their own circle of disciples:
by kissers, practitioners, sons, initiates, lords, and masters.
If performed then, O beloved, it would not succeed in yielding either visible or invisible fruits;
therefore, he [the practitioner] should perform it on an auspicious day of his own choice during either the bright or the dark fortnight.
They know that the *pavitrārohaṇa* on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is for Śaṅkara;
on the second it is for Brahmā, and on the third for Gaurī.
On the fourth day [is the worship] of Vighnarāja; on the fifth days, of the Nāgas;
on the sixth, of the god Kumāra; and on the seventh, of Bhāskara.
On the eighth day, [the worship] of the manifest Rudras; on the ninth, of Caṇḍikā and others;
on the tenth, of the god Yama; and on the eleventh, of Indra.
On the twelfth day, one should worship the god Viṣṇu; on the thirteenth, one's chosen deity;
on the fourteenth, Śiva alone; and on the full moon, the ancestral deities.
On the very day before the sacrifice, one should prepare the elevated seat,
as well as collect the earth, ashes, tooth-stick, and the wealth intended for the fire-oblation.
In this case, however, one’s own youth is not at all required for the performance [of the rite];
rather, all those necessary materials, such as the collection of medicinal herbs and so forth, must be gathered.

The *śruva* and other implements have been specified; they must not be absent, nor should there be two *śruca*s. The water-pitcher, the *argha* vessel, the *gaḍuka*, and so forth, have also been described.
Having abandoned others, one should fashion nine [images] from gold or other minerals, but never from base metals;
the thread should be made of cotton, which is best, or from silk.
One who desires the fruits of enjoyment and liberation should also perform this rite;
furthermore, for the sake of the underlying intention, one should wear linen, silk, or woolen garments.
To the one who possesses knowledge, the thief of men, whose form is the scripture, and who is the embodiment of the directions—
one should multiply the three qualities by three and perform one hundred and eight recitations for the supreme one.
For the [first] eight [planets], it is one hundred; for the seventh, ninety.
For those following that, it is decreased by one for each according to their respective positions.
The thread for the middle and supreme liṅgas should be eighty finger-breadths long.
For a hand of seventy-five [aṅgulas], there are sixty-four [parts] in four cubits; for the smallest and largest liṅgas, it is joined with threads according to the [prescribed] color.
For a two-cubit [liṅga], the number of kala-s and the number of tattva-s are prescribed for the smallest size;
likewise, one seeking worldly enjoyment should fashion it with equal lines and knots.
For those seeking liberation and for the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), the cord of knots is uneven;
as is the number of those cords, so many are the knots in the dhātu.
If it is thin, it should be stuffed with cotton;
it should not be smeared with saffron, nor with cow-dung ash, O Beloved.
O auspicious lady, at night one should paint the binding of the knot with auspicious substances such as yellow palāśa, red ochre, or stone-paste; it is not auspicious [to do so] during the day.
O beloved, having placed it in a golden vessel, or one of copper or silver,
or else in a vessel made of clay or fashioned from lotus leaves.
Having established [the deity] in the sacrificial ground consisting of six pits, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa);
O Dear One, having performed one's daily rites there oneself, one should carry out the recitation of mantras (japa), fire-oblations (homa), and so forth.
Having offered half of what was poured as a *sāmpāta* oblation, one should give it to the *kaṭitrika*;
then, that vessel should be sought out so that it is not submerged in clarified butter.
Having meditated upon it as being the soul of the year, one should encircle it with three threads,
beginning first with the temple, the water-vessel, the altar, and the bull.
Having performed the worship and adoration of Kṣetrapāla, Caṇḍīśa, and likewise the guardians of the world (Lokapālas), one should encircle it with three threads.

Having done this, and then having meditated upon that which pervades all times, O Dear One, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered; thereafter, at the end, one should present the sacrificial offering (bali).
After sprinkling [the site] and touching the mountain, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having honored the teacher who knows the meaning of the scriptures, one should likewise worship the heroes.
Having bathed the liṅga in that manner and having obtained [the water] through ritual baths performed according to the rules,
one should worship it with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, and then perform the binding of the worship.
One should cause tooth-sticks, roots, and so forth to be given in the east;
ashes in the south; earth in the west; and pure water in the north.
And in the northeast, one should offer perfume or even the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
