using the mantras of the faces in their respective directions and the mantras of their own names for the mouth.
Having joined [the mantra] with the root-mantra of the Lord, one should offer the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka).
One should offer fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, auspicious food offerings (naivedya),
and all such items as water for honor (argha) and water for the feet (pādya) with the heart-mantra.
Having given [the gift], he should cause the deity to hear it while standing in a pure place and remaining silent:
"The Blessed One has not been invited; nevertheless, worship has been offered by me."
Accept her, O Mahādeva, the cause of all ritual procedures:
*Oṃ namo vrataniyameśvarāya pūraya 2 svāhā*.
Having been thus addressed, one should remain in the presence of Śambhu’s minister;
thereafter, one should cause the *argha* offering to be presented with the substances prescribed by the ritual rule.

Then, having emerged [from the inner sanctum], O Dear One, one should worship the guardians of the field and other protectors with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and invite those guardians and others.
All ritual procedures should be performed joined with that very *vali* mantra and the word of invocation; and in the sacred field (*kṣetra*), the ritual remains stable.
Or one may perform it in a house according to the prescribed rite;
or in a cave, provided there is no [other] possibility, using roots, fruits, and the like.
Having performed the fire-sacrifice for the attainment of cessation (nirvāṇa), he, accompanied by his disciples, should consume the food produced from the radiant [fire];
or else, with excellent companions, in the practice of the supreme adept.
Then, having eaten a small amount, he should sleep alone while remembering the Lord with devotion;
and at dawn, he should perform a great rite of prosperity according to his means.
Likewise, one should offer incense, flowers, perfumes, lamps, food offerings, and the like,
as well as abundant cooked rice, wine, and other varieties in great detail.
Having performed the preparatory rites, having offered oblations, and having bathed the deity with ghee and other substances,
as well as with curd, honey, and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) consisting of milk and so forth;
Having anointed [the deity] with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, saffron, and so forth,
and having performed the worship as prescribed, one should commence the binding of the worship (pūjābandha).
And by means of the specific [mantras] spoken by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, those fashioned by Nandin,
those belonging to Kumāra, those created by the Gaṇas, Kāla, Śakra, and the Ṛṣis;
With variegated leaf-cuttings, well-fashioned floral paths,
or various beautiful cloths adorned with auspicious eyes and other designs;
One should perform the rite of worship and salutation over the flower pavilion;
having offered incense and water for the guest, one should cause the offering of betel and food oblations to be presented.
One should offer the lamp and other items that have been prepared, and likewise again to the deities of the sacrificial grass.
Having offered worship consisting of perfumes, flowers, and other requisites, as well as food offerings and the like,
one should satisfy them with a particular kind of ritual gesture.
Having entered the interior, the disciple, being disciplined, should present the *pavitraka* together with the Lord and other seekers of that [merit].
Having meditated upon the performance of all times, together with the mantras whose essence is all substances,
and having performed all mudrās, vows, recitations, fire offerings, and the thread for the purpose of sacrifice;
The preliminary ritual for seizing the ground, meditation on what has been performed and what remains to be done,
the invocation of the Siddhas and so forth, the Gurus, and the Heroes, as well as the performance of the melaka.
Having withdrawn that which was entirely performed, or both performed and unperformed,
one should announce it to the Lord Vrateśvara and take up the household *pavitraka*.
Having recited one's own chosen mantra, one should cast it into each respective reality (tattva).
Having meditated thus for a year, the mantra becomes like a triple-thread bound at the end.

One who desires liberation should place the consecrated [liṅga] together with its attendants upon the top of the [main] liṅga, according to the sequence of emanation beginning from the Śiva-tattva, and perform the three-fold division.
One who desires worldly enjoyment should likewise offer the triad in reverse order from the reality of the Self;
one should present the three purifiers consisting of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva.
And that has been stated: "One should give the second Brahmā-mantra, and Viṣṇu should give the third; it is declared for Śiva, perfectly fulfilled in each respective reality (tattva)."
One should extend [the visualization] upward by one unit at a time until it reaches the end of the Vedas;
for he contemplates all the deities of every path as the locus of all reality.
It should be fashioned as it appears beautiful, without regard for fixed numbers.
Outside, one should worship Vṛṣa, Caṇḍīśa, the deities of the directions, Ātmā, and the others.

One should indeed offer to them according to one's ability, for there is no fixed characteristic for Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas; and at the cremation ground, one should worship the ancestral deities.
Śākinīs, kṣetrapālas, and others should be given a small portion for the sake of removing obstacles;
one should offer these to them in sequence with special offerings of incense and worship.
Whether on a moving ground, on a fixed altar, or even within the body of the self,
one should perform it according to what is beautiful, having understood it in its proper correspondence.
For images of manifest forms, as well as for pedestals and temples,
the sacred thread (pavitraka) should consist of three strands, reaching to the end of the body and suspended from the head.
121b) Likewise, for those of the Raudra type, the binding of the knots is considered to be the same;
the length of the books should be very long, according to their measurement and as is aesthetically pleasing.
For the eldest [image], there should be one hundred and eight great pratimas;
for the middle one, the number is like that of the feet, namely eighty-one.
The measurement of the Mahāpratimā-Kanyā should extend down to the knees;
having sipped water for purification and entered, one should stand at the end and offer it to the Lord.
Whatever has been performed deficiently due to ignorance or misfortune, or whatever was done intentionally or unintentionally, or even partially performed; [may all that be made complete].
Therefore, I have been afflicted by those who do not keep their promises and the like;
O Lord of living beings, protect me, protect me as I sink in this worldly existence!
Because it protects from suffering and from destruction in the hells and other realms,
and because it accomplishes the goals of the three worlds, it is designated as "pure" (*pavitra*).
Thus proclaimed, this rite brings the Lord of Vows to fullness;
when worshipped by yogis, it accomplishes everything in its entirety through his powers.
Once performed here, that purificatory rite (*pavitraka*) protects one from falling;
it is declared to be the fulfillment of all requirements and the revealer of the signs of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Success may be achieved even through a rite devoid of formal rules; therefore, one should perform this [practice] alone. This is because it is for the sake of liberation, and it is accessible even after one has received initiation.
Initiation, when conjoined with the prescribed rite, yields results such as the observance of the *samaya* and other ritual actions;
therefore, the *pavitraka* must be performed by those seeking liberation, as it is an integral part of initiation.
For the sake of the fruit, all practitioners must certainly perform this;
whether they are seekers of enjoyment and liberation, or others who possess the requisite qualification.
Whether by men, women, or eunuchs, whoever performs this act brings about auspiciousness;
for the Pavitrārohaṇa is the most excellent of all vows.
Or, at the conclusion of his own ritual practice, he may partake of food without restriction;
furthermore, he should feed the ascetics who acknowledge a Lord, as well as the poor and the helpless.
One should feed the Śiva-yogins with various kinds of foods and drinks, such as sweets filled with ghee, *laḍḍukas*, *vaṭakas*, and candied confections.
Having fed them, one should honor them with pairs of garments, sacred threads, loincloths, medicines, and so forth; and having given these to them, one should then give [the remainder] back to them.
O Blessed One, you have become exceedingly gracious since the commencement of the Cāturmāsya; therefore,
for the sake of this special occasion, food should thereafter be offered to those situated within the maṇḍala.
Whether in his absence or in his presence, one should worship with pairs of garments, purifying threads,
abundant food, wine, and various kinds of edibles.
With various well-prepared substances— those produced from water, those cooked in diverse ways,
those derived from fruits, those from flowers, others, as well as those made from flour and molasses.
The heroic feast (vīrabhojana) should be performed according to the appropriate time and place,
as well as the sacrificial porridge (caru) arising from the ritual by the sisters and the circle of brothers.
One should project [the consciousness] with non-conceptualization, especially at that time,
by means of the stages, the seats, and those established in samādhi, free from the conceptualizations urged by the learned.
At the time of sacrifice, as well as for amusement or in the presence of the Guru,
this rite— which is of a secret nature— should be performed at the onset of night.
There too, at the conclusion, sacrificial fees and other offerings should be given to the ascetics,
having ascertained [the recipient's] mental disposition by means of the power of consciousness, just as was previously described.
O Pārvatī, having made a request for the sake of the distressed, even if one acts in opposition [to the usual rule],
there is no fault in such a performance of the prescribed duty.
On an ordinary day as well, the preceptor, having bathed and being thus pure,
should bathe the deity and likewise worship him with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Standing before the gods, the wise Cumbaka was accompanied by his own disciples,
along with his companions, heroes, residents, lords, and monkeys.
Having first proclaimed the rule to them as they please,
[one should address] the sin consisting of eight months or even that consisting of a year.
Whatever physical or mental purification was previously performed, that must not be done again; it would be a transgression of the conduct of the samaya.

The Tantric practice is contrary [to worldly norms], it is a transgression of the conduct prescribed by one's own scriptures; it involves the contemplation of worldly existence and is a violation of the words of Śiva.
Act in accordance with the words of your guru and according to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures;
observe a vow for one day, or even for that very day.
Having ascertained the three, five, or nine-fold aspects according to one's own capacity,
[one should consider] those who have set out for foreign lands and those who have transgressed the words of their guru.
And for them, O beloved, the rule is stated as a vow lasting one day or more,
for those who are established in their place, steady, self-dependent, and independent.
For one month, or two months, or for three or four months of restraint;
or [the practice of] not asking for food, eating only at night, or even taking only eight mouthfuls.
Whether subsisting on alms, or eating at five [houses], or even at one or several seats.
Having performed this vow, one who eats little meat and subsists on excrement becomes pure;
one may do so for ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even fifty thousand [repetitions], according to one's own capacity.
Just as with recitation, so too with fire-offerings, meditation, and likewise worship;
those who seek self-discipline must ensure that not a single day is made void of their observance.
By that, his performance of the vows, sacrifices, and so forth becomes complete.
Having performed the removal of the *pavitra*, the withdrawal of the worship should take place.
Again, O lady of beautiful limbs, one should worship that very same [object] just as before;
it should be well-perfumed with incense, such as camphor, agallochum, or other fragrant substances.
O noble lady, this must be performed day by day at the conclusion of the observance;
and when the observance is complete, one should perform the sacrifice as before.

Having performed the bathing, worship, recitation, and other rites with all the requisite substances and materials, and having offered the desired oblations, one should indeed ask the deity for forgiveness.
Whatever recitation, fire-oblation, vow, or other rite has been performed according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer all of that, dedicating its fruit to the God of gods.
Having aimed for no low fruit, he stands firm in the treasury of his perfected vows;
in what [place] is there a vessel [for him], established by his power in the common ritual procedure?
As before, one should give gifts such as clothing for the cold and so forth; and to the wives, one should give garments such as loincloths, as well as footwear and the like.
Furthermore, one should provide special food and other necessities with special care;
according to one's ability, one should also give them protection from cold and so forth.
Having honored the ascetics and fed them as before,
and having performed the ritual offering to the God, he should stand in a pure place and give [the remainder] again.
Whatever [the Supreme Lord] performs, whether it be full of ritual injunctions or arising from existence and non-existence,
let the Supreme Lord perform it according to His own power, yet always complete with the prescribed rites.
Then, having offered the *argha* with the ritual implements, one should perform the rite;
or, if seeking liberation, one should perform it correctly according to the prescribed rule.
In the Piṅgalāmata, [the ritual of] Pavitrārohaṇa.
Piṅgalā said:
The status of inferior, middling, or superior does not apply to the Śivaliṅga;
if it were so applied, then a fault would arise, just as it does in the case of human effort.
The relationship of pervasion and the pervader was previously declared by you to be one; yet,
through the union of the means of proof and the goal to be proven, it is threefold or even hundredfold.
Even there, there is a very great fault: it is always of a single form and ever-changing.
It is not logical that he should be both gentle and fierce; how can Śiva, who is one, be twofold?
Please explain all of this to me briefly out of your grace.
Bhairava said:
And that pervasion which I have declared through the equality of reality—that applies to all and non-all genders; therefore, O lady, let there be no doubt in this matter.
But in the case of the lowest and middle [classes], the state of being a *mātra* (measure/letter) may or may not exist according to the speaker's intention;
it does not follow from the mere utterance of the word, but follows from the speaker's intention to act.
For a Brāhmaṇa, three gurus are prescribed according to his mental disposition;
for a Kṣatriya, two in the middle, according to the sequence of his material wealth and disposition.
The highest, the lowest, and the middle [grades] are indeed proclaimed for the Vaiśya alone;
O lady of excellent complexion, whatever remains is for the Śūdra castes, consisting of two types of maidens.
Even when the fruit is the same, the arrangement [of the teachings] is made for those who are discerning of the worldly path;
whether through the commonality of the Dharma or otherwise, it is according to what is appropriate for each.
O Lord, [the measurements] of the temple are determined by the patron's wealth;
however, the lowest and other [sizes] may be measured by the cubit, for no distinction between these has been proclaimed.
And as it has been said: "The threefold accomplishment depends upon the will of the practitioner and of Śiva;
having understood their disposition, he may speak from wherever he may be situated."
One should bestow [the portions] in three ways: whether in the smallest, the middle, or the largest;
likewise, that which has been declared regarding gems and so forth applies also to the characteristics of the mudga-bean and the finger-measure.
For it is not the case that because an inferior result is accomplished, the gift would be inferior; rather, what is it that is being valued?
Because the giver is superior, the gift is never valued as inferior.
A virtuous person is not afflicted by the faults of wicked laborers,
just as a king bestows the fruits of their work upon those who serve him.
Because of their superior share, they never suffer any loss;
likewise, the protectorless do not suffer loss on account of [the distribution] of the lowest and other classes according to the authoritative means of knowledge.

Just as the single state of being (puṃbhāva) appears as two within the multitude of principles through the distinction of separate states and so forth, so too does Śiva appear as distinct due to the differentiation of his forms.
The distinction residing in the locus is said to be like the sun accompanied by its rays;
likewise, Raudra resides in the Saumya, just as Bhairava and the others are manifested in their forms.
The intention to speak is the universal means of accomplishment; it arises from that very desire.
Thus, for some even in fierce activity there is fierceness, while for others there may be gentleness even in gentle activity.
And when their afflictions have ripened, that [desire for liberation] arises in them as a longing for emancipation.
They are to be understood through the descent of power (śaktipāta), whether it be intense, more intense, and so forth;
for as there is a distinction in grace, so too is there a distinction in the form of Śiva.
And just as the attainment of the fruits occurs, so too is his understanding;
having realized omniscience in its manifestation, the Lord became one whose very nature is that [omniscience].
In the world of the stars, he brings about the manifestation of karma for those who possess forms;
since that is the means for the accomplishment of his purpose, he creates it accordingly.
In this way, the Supreme Lord assumes the forms of Rakṣasas and Piśācas, as well as Bhūtas, Vetālas, Pālakas, Gaṇas, Vidyādharas, and so forth.
Having become identical in nature with the Yakṣa deity, one will obtain the desired fruit,
because that [deity] is both the supreme essence and all-pervading at all times.
He is omniscience, self-sovereignty, characterized by being the creator of all;
the Lord who is compassionate toward all, merciful, eternal, and everlasting.

Therefore, because it arises from the existence of the Śiva-atomic particles (śivāṇu) and the future fruit, this sign (liṅga) is characterized by such [auspicious] marks; the practitioner, however, must likewise possess the proper characteristics.

One should practice with patience upon a target possessing characteristics, or otherwise, upon that which is without characteristics; at that time, his sign is perceived as being characterized by the marvelous.
Transcending the mind and being the support of the mind, it is realized upon being attained;
for this ultimate method brings about all accomplishments.
O auspicious lady, this has been told by me without doubt for the sake of practitioners, according to the Piṅgalāmata.
Piṅgalā said:
"O Lord, I have heard all the characteristics and signs from the beginning;
now tell me the characteristics of the mantras, for everything was previously taught by you."
Bhairava said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of mantras,
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall become a partaker of accomplishment.
In a secluded and auspicious place adorned with heaps of flowers,
the preceptor, girded with mantras and joined by the practitioners, [should perform the rite].
The wise one should arrange the Mātṛkā beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ha', excluding the six peak syllables (kūṭas), and then write the desired mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the sequence of their respective colors,
one should likewise [place] the syllable of union, as well as the letter *ra* together with the *anusvāra*.
One should cause those mantras that consist of short vowels and visargas to be separated individually; having then performed this disjunction, one should write the name below them.

Or it may be a name well-known in the world, or one assigned by the mother and father through their word; for ascetics, it is that which has been given by the Guru through the rite of the falling of flowers.
One should cause the letters of that name to be divided just as they were stated for the mantra; the division of the letters of the name is exactly like that.
O Goddess, the characteristics of the *sādhya* and the *sādhaka*, as well as their respective *vāṃśakas*,
are [determined] by a straight line rising from beneath each letter of the *sādhya*-alphabet series.
One should likewise perform the insertion of the practitioner’s name according to the number of syllables in the mantra;
it should be repeated again and again until the king of mantras is completed.
Alternatively, if the letters of the name begin with the same letters as the syllables of the mantra,
one should always avoid that mantra, provided it does not actually contain those mantra-syllables.
Having understood this, one should write the syllables; once written, they are to be calculated.
The first is *siddha*, and the second is *sādhya*.
The *susiddha* belongs to the third [class], while the *ari* (enemy) is the fourth;
furthermore, the *sādhya* follows that, and likewise the *susiddha-ari*.
O Goddess, with these syllables as names, the wise practitioner should perform the counting of the fourfold collection of mantras until the mantra is completed.
Starting from the first letter of the name up until the letters of the mantra are counted;
when the mantra is completed, the instruction is then prescribed.
O beloved, through this, all accomplishments are attained, yielding both visible and invisible fruits;
one who accomplishes everything remains equanimous, experiencing neither loss nor gain.
The mantra is perfectly accomplished in every respect; success is established in three ways.
It is declared that it cuts through all enemies for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
When a mantra is [consecrated] according to the primordial Siddhānta,
one shall partake of the fruit of its accomplishment in a very short time.
When a mantra has the word *sādhya* at the beginning or end, it is accomplished only with great difficulty;
however, when it is well-established at both the beginning and the end, it bestows the fruits of the three worlds.
If there is an enemy at the beginning and likewise an arrow at the end,
it quickly kills the wise practitioner along with all his followers.
When a mantra is established as having been accomplished from the very beginning according to the fundamental tenets,
it becomes successful even after performing twice the ritual actions prescribed in the *kalpa*.
If the final goal is to be accomplished, it is achieved through what is declared in the Kalpa;
and when the goal and so forth of the mantra are well-established within the Siddhānta, [success follows].
Even in that case, success does not occur through doubling [the practice], nor otherwise;
provided that the mantra is already established at the beginning and remains perfectly effective until the end.
When the rite is performed fourfold, the King of Mantras becomes perfected;
however, when the mantra is well-perfected against an enemy, it becomes [destructive].
By performing twice the rite prescribed in the Kalpa, one indeed attains success;
by reciting it eight times that number, one succeeds—of this there is no doubt.
If a mantra is produced with an enemy syllable at the beginning and a well-accomplished concluding syllable,
then that rite performed sixfold shall attain success.
Established at the beginning, well-established at the end, and likewise balanced in the middle—
thus, together with the mantra, that which is desired by the practitioner is swiftly accomplished.
In the Siddhānta, the Susiddha and other [mantras], situated between the Sādhya as before, constantly grant all accomplishments to the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
When there is a Siddha at the beginning, a Susiddha at the end, and an enemy at the conclusion, one does not achieve power in the mantra; rather, it requires an excess of victory.
O Dear One, when the *susiddha* and other categories are at the beginning and the *siddha* category is at the end, as previously stated,
and the ritual action is performed fourfold, then success is attained.
When the goal is at the beginning and the accomplishment occurs in the middle, there is neither attainment nor loss; rather, one succeeds only with great difficulty.
Both the *sādhya* and the *susiddha* require an excess of recitation (*japa*).
Likewise, the *siddha* and the *susiddha* are [distinguished] by being enclosed within the *ara* [syllables].
One should predict the loss of wealth, grain, sons, and wife;
likewise, a Sādhya planet separated by a Siddha, as well as a Susiddha separated by a Siddha.
Whether the accomplishment be inferior, middling, or superior, no obstacle arises therein;
likewise, even when the accomplishment is excellent, an enemy may intervene.
A woman does not prevail there; rather, it is in a wound consisting of hardship that [the results] occur—whether as *sādhya*, *antarasiddha*, *siddha*, or likewise *susiddha*.
O lady, even that may be accomplished with effort, though with great hardship;
likewise, [the mantras] *siddha* and *susiddha* are accomplished when separated by enemies.
Having seen such a characteristic from afar, one should avoid it.
A mantra corrupted by enemies must never be accepted;
rather, O fair-faced one, one should subsequently cause the performance of the *yātana* rites for the mantras and other such elements.
Having combined both the *siddha* and the *susiddha* positions,
one who knows the ritual procedure should then multiply the *sādhya* and *ripu* positions by ten.
When that [number] has been multiplied by two, one should subsequently divide it;
from that established quotient, one should take the remainder and divide it by eight.
One should add those enemies to the solar [digits];
for those remaining after the enemies are subtracted are indeed called the "residues."
And those months are declared at the end of the Sāman, O Supreme Goddess;
as for the remaining ones, the wise know them to be the praharas and the āsūs.
One should perform the reception of the mantra during its specific watches and within its specific month;
however, at that time, it is beneficial to partake of the sacrificial porridge (caru) and other offerings, distinguished by their respective times.
Within that month, the practitioner attains accomplishment; there is no doubt about this. Thus has been declared the characteristic of mantra, as you requested.
He who performs [the rite] with full knowledge shall dispel many obstacles;
thus, having understood the nature of the mantra and having correctly understood the characteristic of the Self.
The *argha* offering for the mantra should be presented according to whatever is desired by the practitioner.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Characteristics of the Parts of Mantras" from the *Piṅgalāmata*.
Piṅgalā said:
O Lord, the two practitioners are said to be the "magnet" (cumbaka) characterized by general characteristics;
now tell me their specific characteristics as they pertain to the individual self.
Bhairava said:
Those who are born in remote regions, excluded from the noble lands, should be known as not attaining accomplishment here; nor do they grant accomplishment to anyone else.
Those who are subject to the power of another do not attain liberation by themselves;
[liberation comes] from the purification of the six paths through the union with the fire of exhalation.
O lady of excellent hips, for those who possess devotion according to Śiva’s will or who have cultivated the remembrance of Śiva, liberation is theirs; it is never otherwise.
Those born of a remarriage, those born from the womb of a courtesan, storytellers, those born of the same lineage, as well as red-beggars and pale-skinned ones;
And this cloth was the Nirgrantha Gautama, likewise a bearer of the great vows.
Having undertaken the Pāśupata vow known as Bhagavakāla,
those who violate the vow and those who have merely assumed the *liṅga* [are also included].
There is a confusion of seeds and a confusion of wombs when a Śūdra [begets children] in the wombs of Brāhmaṇas; this does not occur with Vaiśyas nor with Kṣatriyas.
Those born there who are deficient do not attain success;
they are those produced by the mutual mixing of castes, resulting from the confusion of wombs.
They do not attain accomplishment here, nor do they attain liberation through initiation;
for those born of the four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—are all equally possible [to attain these].
In a pure and great lineage, endowed with all the auspicious marks of the limbs,
[one should fashion] a form resembling an elephant's trunk or else shaped like a parasol at the top.
He was adorned with very glossy, curly hair resembling bees,
and possessed a broad forehead made beautiful by a long, ornamental mark.
His eyebrows were like long bows, with the eyes as their targets;
his white ears reached to the ends of his long [hair], and his pupils were like those of a deer.
His eyes were reddened at the corners and reached as far as the petals of the blue lotus;
his nose was prominent, straight, and possessed a broad base.
Slightly bent at the base, joined at the junction of the eyebrows,
and likewise with a pair of cheeks that are slightly reddish-white.
Her cheeks were symmetrical and well-proportioned, her eyebrows were clearly defined, and her lower lip was of the color of the bimba fruit, joined with a pair of beautiful eyes.
The jawbone of the cold-toothed fanged one is slightly elevated at the front,
divided by the chin, prominent, and accompanied by a mustache.
His ears were prominent, his temples were adorned with excellent ornaments hanging down,
and his neck was shell-like while his shoulders were broad and well-developed.
With his rounded arms, which rested upon the base of his jar-like belly, shone with many peaks [of muscles], and were long with hidden joints; and with his hanging [limbs].
From the base of the wrist to the tip of the fingers, his two hands were as red as copper, with beautiful fingers that were long in length, like the tail of a cow or the trunk of an elephant.
With joints that are perfectly aligned and nails as sharp as the tips of arrows,
he possesses a broad expanse of chest and a slender, unprotuberant belly.
The navel, which spirals clockwise and is characterized by alternating depressions and elevations, is auspicious.
The sides are indeed rounded, ending at the waist and the chest,
and are distinguished by the region of the hips and neck as well as the back portion.
Nor should he be endowed with a backbone that is depressed in the middle,
but rather one that is perfectly square and bound by the excellence of its girdle-like curvature.
The buttocks and the two thighs were well-proportioned, yet there was no stiffness in the hips; the thighs were shaped like the trunks of elephants, well-rounded, and not overly rough.
The shanks are like those of a crocodile; the knees are devoid of bone;
the feet are elevated like the back of a tortoise, fleshy, and with very level arches.
The ankle-joints are well-concealed and free from a network of visible veins;
the big toes are rounded and have tips that are elevated.

He whose feet are marked with lines resembling red lotus roots, which are white-hued and elevated at the tips, and who possesses the grace of a fully blossomed lotus— [he is one who has attained the goal].
He may be dark-complexioned or fair, with a complexion like green mung beans or like the priyaṅgu plant;
neither too dark nor too fair, his voice is like the sound of clouds or a kettledrum.
Neither excessively delighted nor enraged, and turning away from contentious debate—
this indeed is the specific characteristic of both the practitioner and the teacher.
He is the source of all perfections, the one who demonstrates right conduct,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and characterized by the complete set of defining features.
Having thoroughly understood that, he who is impelled by power,
firmly devoted and attached, and permeated by the mantra;
The meaning of that tantra should be explained according to the number of its teachings;
having purified it through the purifications of oneself, one should reveal that mantra-tantra.
And he, dwelling in a solitary cave and strengthened by the mantras and tantras,
when desiring his own enjoyment, then applies himself to those [practices].
Then, accompanied by very firm and heroic companions who are equal to himself,
and provided with all necessary materials, the man should begin that undertaking.
In this regard, the practitioner is of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling;
according to those types, there are three kinds of accomplishment, which I shall explain one by one.
Atomicity, levity, and indeed magnanimity, as well as reach, mastery over the elements, and the power of irresistible will— wherein one has command over all desires.
Through the eight great siddhis, it becomes endowed with the ten causal conditions.
O Dear One, the supreme practitioner should likewise accomplish the supreme [deity],
who holds a rosary, a conch, a trident, a lotus, a discus, an axe, and a bow.
A vetāla, a sandal, a staff, a lotus, a sword, a water-pot,
an ash-receptacle, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), chalk, and even a game of dice.
The spear, the noose, and the goad, along with their respective implements;
likewise the mace, the razor, the chisel, and the mallet.
And for the skull, there is the means of protection both after death and again while alive;
likewise, there are eight others, and the middle [practice] belongs to the middle.

Pacification (śāntika) and enrichment (pauṣṭika), as well as subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa); likewise, causing dissension (vidveṣa), expulsion (uccāṭana), bewildering (mohana), and killing (māraṇa).
Paralysis, healing, hatred, punishment, beating, and killing—
these and other such acts constitute the minor [rite], as well as the minor-minor and the minor-minor-minor.
The characteristics of the linga and the temple, endowed with the fivefold consecration (pratiṣṭhāpañcaka),
as well as the characteristics of the image and the characteristics of the face-linga (mukhaliṅga).
The characteristics of the cloth-strip, the arrow, the pedestal-base, and the architectural treatise on site-planning, as well as the rules for construction in cities and other settlements.
The characteristics of substances, the characteristics of monasteries and watchtowers,
the characteristics of artisans, magnet-makers, and practitioners.
The restoration of dilapidated temples and the manner in which the observances (niyama) should be performed,
as well as the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and the specific characteristics of the mantra portions.
The inferior, the middling, and the superior— thus the threefold world as it exists, the entire domain of the Omniscient One, is all auspicious and possesses every excellence.
I have now related everything that was requested by you—
the characteristics of the teacher for the accomplishment of siddhi according to the Piṅgalāmata.
Piṅgalā said:
"O Lord, one understands the characteristics of all things from scripture;
O Master, tell us whether that scripture itself is endowed with characteristics or not."
O Lord of Gods, how is the connection of this scripture described?
Speak the explanation for the sake of the practitioner, the individual, and the purpose, so that it may be understood.
Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, who is skilled in formulating inquiries and conceptual analysis!
I shall explain the characteristics of the scripture; of this there is no doubt.
But its manifestation is understood as being from all sides; thus, it is considered to be "coming from everywhere."
Because it instructs and protects, it is called a "śāstra";
that by which one knows and is led is designated as "jñāna."
The wise do not understand it in this way—that it merely expands and constantly protects;
rather, they know it as consciousness, composed of both word and meaning, as conceived by the tradition of the scriptures.
The attainment of perfection in the characteristics of prosody, received through the lineage of transmission from the lotus-like mouth of Śiva, is here called *chandolakṣaṇasaṃsiddhi*.
That [teacher] should be understood by the wise according to the logic applicable to the listener;
however, the teacher who speaks may primarily be a practitioner, or in some cases, he may be a perfected adept (sādhaka).

The initiate and the spiritual son should certainly not [teach] those who have not mastered the meaning of the Śiva-scriptures; even if those two understand the meaning, it must not be heard by those seeking [worldly] fruits.

The listeners of the Āgama are indeed the initiates (samayin), the sons (putraka), the practitioners (sādhaka), the teachers (deśika), and the masters (meśvara); they are all devotees of Śiva, firm in their vows.
The minister, consecrated by the mantras and devoted to the rules of conduct therein,

[issued this on] the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Caitra in the year 297, on the tenth day of the month, under the Uttaraphalgunī nakṣatra, during the reign of the illustrious Rameśvara, the supreme lord, the great king of kings, the glorious Rudradeva.
In the reign of Vijaya, this book was caused to be written by Śrī Śivācārya Vijādharavarman, a resident of the illustrious Mahāvijakarathyā and the Śrī Candanamaṇḍapīrathyā;
it was transcribed by the scribe Paśupati.
